name: Advanced Sensitivity Analysis for Strategic Decision Making
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course the student is expected to know, be able to select and apply a variety of methods and techniques of global sensitivity analysis at each stage of the analysis (modeling input variability, sampling, analyzing, visualizing); be aware of the specific nuances and needs of different types of models; implement a comprehensive model analysis from scratch; draw well-justified conclusions and analytically discuss the implications of the analysis results.
content: 1. Intro to global sensitivity analysis , its relation to one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis and uncertainty analysis 2. Modeling uncertainty & sampling techniques (Uncertain vs. decision input variables, different types of probability distributions, correlated inputs; simple random sampling, full factorial design, Latin hypercube sampling, quasi-Monte Carlo (Sobol' sequences). 3. Global sensitivity analysis methods (Variance-based methods (Sobol' indices), regional sensitivity analysis (Monte Carlo filtering), screening methods (Morris method), derivative-based methods, polynomial chaos expansions, methods for correlated inputs and given data) 4. Simulation decomposition (SimDec) hybrid uncertainty-sensitivity analysis method. 5. Applications (Investment valuation, system dynamics, multi-criteria decision-making)
prerequisites: A220A0053 Investment and Business Analysis with Excel
learningMaterial: - Lecture handouts; - Saltelli, A., Tarantola, S., Campolongo, F., & Ratto, M. (2004). Sensitivity analysis in practice: a guide to assessing scientific models (Vol. 1). New York: Wiley. PDF - SALib - Sensitivity Analysis Library in Python - SimDec open-source packages
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0 – 5 based on course performance. Evaluation 0-100 points, in-class exercises 30%, Moodle quizzes 30%, and project work 40%.
workload: Preparation for lectures & quizzes 22h; In-class lectures & exercises [Excel & Python] 28h; Project work (individual) 30h; Total 80h

name: Business Analytics in Action
learningOutcomes: At the end of this course a student is expected to have a concise overall understanding of, and experience with the practical use of business analytics in real-life problems, including all the phases of the process starting from business analytics problem definition, data collection, curation and preparation, analytical methods application, validation of the results, critical discussion of the results and their applicability, validity and limitations. The content of the course is designed so that after its completion the student will (either alone or in a small team): - be able to formulate a problem definition allowing for the analytical deconstruction of the problem, to frame it in a proper theoretical framework and to design a viable mathematical model of the problem and the system within which the problem is being solved - be able to communicate with the stakeholders concerning the problem, its components, the needs of the stakeholders, potential limitations etc. - be able to design and carry out a business analytics project from start to the end, assess the appropriate methods and choose the ones that fit the given purpose best (including appropriate justification of the choice and a risk-analysis thereof) - be able to justify the choice of methods and modeling frameworks, to identify and discuss the consequences of these choices - be able to present the solution to the problem in a clear, concise and complete way that includes all that is needed for a well informed use of the results - be able to defend the choices made and the results obtained in the process of solving the problem publicly
content: This course presents the students with a practical business analytics related problem and requires them to solve the problem applying the knowledge and skills obtained during their previous studies. The students are required to solve the problem starting from a problem definition specified in collaboration with the problem stakeholders (decision-makers, managers, etc.) and ending with the presentation of the proposed solution and defending it in front of the stakeholders. The practical solution of the problem requires the students to design the whole analytics project, select appropriate methods to approach and ideally also to solve the problem, obtain relevant data and prepare it for processing, carry out the actual analysis, perform validation, sensitivity analysis and other steps to assess the quality, reliability and robustness of the model(s) used and of the solution(s) and output(s) obtained. The final solution is presented in the form of written reports including the problem description, suggested solution, justification of the use (or dismissal) of specific tools, the performance assessment, validity, reliability and robustness assessment of the proposed model and its outputs. Performance of the model, its assumptions and limitations as well as the limitations of the use of its outputs need to be discussed. The solution is also defended publicly in front of relevant stakeholders and other teams of students. The course consists of: - introductory seminar where the parameters of the problems, their initial formulation by the stakeholders and other issues concerning the course are discussed and clarified - a workshop on problem definition, where initial brainstorming concerning the potential solutions of the presented problems takes place - a workshop on business analytics model results presentation and validation, including the ethics in business analytics modelling and problem solving and responsibilities of the analyst - a progress report seminar where the work in progress is presented and discussed with the teachers, present stakeholders and other groups, feedback is provided - independent (instructor-guided) work on the problem - creation of the final report - a public final result presentation, defense and open discussion The seminars and workshops will be held on-campus in Lappeenranta.
prerequisites: Compulsory prerequisites: Only for 2nd year MBAN students. Recommended prerequisites: ideally all first year + 1-2 period second year courses of MBAN done (participated in).
learningMaterial: In-course instructions, materials available in Moodle and Uni portals.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail based on the quality of the submitted reports and final result presentation and defence.
workload: Active participation in course workshops and seminars (30 h) Group project work: solution of a chosen business analytics problem, preparation of reports and presentation (114 h), active participation on the progress report seminar and project defence seminar including feedback to other projects (8+8 h). Total course workload 160 h.

name: Critical issues in International Business and Entrepreneurship - Anticipating global challenges managerially and entrepreneurially
learningOutcomes: -To be able to critically reflect and rethink theoretical assumptions and ways of doing business in different contexts -To develop an understanding on complex, multi-stakeholder and transboundary challenges -To develop skills and competences needed for sustainable and legitimate managerial and entrepreneurial action -to enhance entrepreneurial innovativeness and -thinking, global mindsets and collaboration skills for problem solving across contexts
content: The purpose of this course is to allow the students develop an overview to recent theory but also to relevant challenges and global concerns. The course combines economic, social and environmental sustainability aspects and the UN SDGs with managerial and entrepreneurial issues on international business triggering the students to rethink and critically address ways forwards. Students develop skills and competences to tackle complex real-life problems in collaboration with others while facilitating their entrepreneurial mindsets and sense of purpose. The variety of theory application settings develops global mindsets and fosters students’ sensitivity on diverse aspects international business.
prerequisites: No formal prerequisites. Previous courses in entrepreneurship, international business and management are beneficial but not mandatory.
learningMaterial: Selected journal articles and book chapters are provided as pre-readings and in-class readings throughout the course. Additional in-depth material is provided by request. The course builds on inclusive learning and uses videos, seminars and other types of materials to support the written sources.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points, consisting of: - In-class assignments and participation 50 points: Pre-readings combined with active doing, re-reading, collaboration and production of a case in the classes (including theory hackathon, case solutions, seminar participation, group work, presentation and critical discussions) - Written assignment 50 points: A short essay on a selected theme (academic writing, APA refs), highly individual reflection and critical thinking application

name: Fundamentals of Accounting and Finance
learningOutcomes: Upon completing this course, students will achieve the following learning outcomes: Establish a solid foundation in accounting and finance to support informed decision-making. Learn fundamental principles of financial and managerial accounting. Understand the financial statements and apply ratio analysis. Develop an understanding of cost accounting and its role in business operations. Gain a skillset in the valuation of major asset classes and their risk-return characteristics. Learn the principles of Modern Portfolio Theory and its applications in investment decisions.
content: The course covers key areas of accounting and finance, including financial and managerial accounting principles, financial statement preparation and analysis, cost accounting and budgeting, corporate finance fundamentals, valuation of cash flows and financial assets, capital structure and payout policy, risk and return concepts, short-term finance and working capital management, and long-term financial decision-making.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes and the following recommended textbooks: Financial Accounting (11th Edition or newer) by Libby, Libby, and Hodge Managerial Accounting (17th Edition or newer) by Garrison, Noreen, and Brewer Principles of Corporate Finance (13th Edition or newer) by Brealey, Myers, and Allen

name: Investment and Business Analysis with Excel
learningOutcomes: After the course the students: - are able to collect and handle data in a spreadsheet environment performing tasks such as data consolidation, data cleaning, and basic data analysis - are able to plan and perform various business and finance related analyses - know how to create simple models for optimization and investment analyses - are able to handle, record and write own simple macros to automate operations in Excel.
content: I. Basics of data visualization. Basic rules of data visualization, conditional formatting, waterfall chart, combo chart, treemap, 3Dmaps, flowcharts. II. Data collection and analysis. Creating a watchlist, making investment program consolidation, performing data analysis with pivot tables and charts, creating an interactive dashboard, performing simple statistical analyses. Instruments: power query, pivot tables and charts, data analysis toolpack. III. Portfolio optimization. Practicing with optimization problem setting, creating a stock portfolio optimization model, recording macros. Instruments: matrix multiplication functions, solver, VBA. IV. Liquidity budgeting. Creating a liquidity budgeting model, recording macros, learning basics of VBA. Instruments: data tables, scenario manager, goal seek, VBA. V. Investment analysis. Creating a profitability analysis model, performing break-even analysis, sensitivity analysis with a given macro, writing a Monte Carlo simulation macro. Instruments: data validation, goal seek, VBA.
prerequisites: Basic proficiency in Excel, either from previous experience or some basic Excel course. This is an advanced course and catching up with basics is a student's own responsibility Assigned reading Beginning Excel What-If Data AnalysisTools: Getting Started with Goal Seek, Data Tables, Scenarios, and Solver, PaulCornell, 2006, Apress - available as an eBook in the library database. For B.Sc students recommended A130A0620 Basics of MS Excel for Business Students. Non-Windows Excel versions (e.g. Mac, Linux) are limited and would not be enough for working on this course.
learningMaterial: Video lectures
evaluationCriteria: Grade pass-fail, evaluation 0-100 points, 65 is minimum to pass. 50% exercises, peer to peer evaluation (negative points if not done), 50% Moodle quizzes.

name: Multivariate and Econometric Analysis Methods
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to give extensive general knowledge about the main econometric and multivariate analysis methods. After completion of the course students: - understand the role of multivariate analysis in scientific research - can evaluate and compare the applicability of various multivariate methods - are able to collect numerical data about the market environment in different countries - can apply multivariate analysis methods for cross-sectional, panel and time series data - can conduct the analyses with Stata software - can interpret and evaluate the results of the analyses - can report the results according to good scientific practice General aim of the course is to improve following personal skills of the students: - written and oral communication - group work skills in a multicultural team context - problem solving and project management skills
content: Measure development and factor analysis, linear regression, linear models, logistic regression, panel data regression. Use of Stata software, use of international databases of statistical data. Special features of countries.

Hill, R.C. - Griffiths, W.E. - Judge, G.G.: Undergraduate Econometrics, 2nd edition, 2001 or newer edition: Hill, R.C. - Griffiths, W.E. - Lim, G.C.: Principles of Econometrics, 3rd or 4th edition, 2008 or 2012.

name: Operational Research Made Easy: Critical Approaches and Cultural Perspectives
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: Recognize key concepts of operational research and its applications. Discuss the historical, philosophical, and sociological context of OR. Critically evaluate modeling practices and their implications. Appreciate the limitations of models and the importance of assumptions. Identify ethical dimensions and issues of uncertainty in model-based decision making.
content: This course introduces students to the foundational ideas of operational research (OR) with minimal mathematical formalism. Designed for accessibility, the course focuses on concepts rather than calculations. It includes: An introduction to statistics and model building. A historical and philosophical overview of OR’s development. Case studies of OR applications and misuses. Reflections on the culture of quantification in science and policy. Discussions on ethics, uncertainty, and the limits of modeling.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with high school-level mathematics. A short statistics refresher is provided at the beginning of the course.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides by Andrea Saltelli.
evaluationCriteria: Pass-fail. Engagement and participation: 30%; Quizzes: 35%; Learning diary: 35%.

learningOutcomes: During the course, the students will deepen their knowledge on management accounting. Upon completion of the course the students are able to: - Evaluate the disruption in the accounting industry; - Combine the fundamental issues pertaining to strategy and the design and the use of management accounting and control systems; - Understand, interpret, and apply the management accounting research tradition and the most used theoretical frameworks; - Apply management accounting techniques in cost and revenue management widely when producing and analyzing information for managerial decision making; - Describe the role of corporate responsibility (CR) and CR reporting from the perspective of accounting.
content: The course covers contemporary themes and issues affecting the field of management accounting, such as accounting industry's disruption and development trends especially related to digitalization and artificial intelligence, research on management accounting and corporate responsibility (CR) and CR reporting from the perspective of a controller.

name: Advanced Decision-making
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: The students learn the principles of selected modern methods for multiple criteria decision-making, decision analysis, and about systems for supporting decision-making. Students learn about the history of decision-support and operational research and understand that there is a constant evolution in decision support methods. Students are able to understand the benefits of modern decision-support methods in real world business situations as well as their limitations. Students can put the presented models and analysis methods into use with MATLAB or Excel, where applicable, and solve real-life decision-making problems using the methods. Students are able to design models for managerial decision support and to evaluate their fit for the problem being solved.
content: Core content: This course covers the main topics of multiple criteria decision making under certainty, uncertainty and risk. The topics discussed during the course therefore include: principles of decision making under certainty, uncertainty, risk and ignorance, multiple criteria decision-making (MCDM) and evaluation methods (TOPSIS, AHP), the use evaluations of absolute and relative type, efficiency assessment models (DEA), game theory (non-cooperative games of two players, cooperative games of two players with/without transferable gains, games against nature), validation of decision support systems and models and sensitivity analysis. MATLAB and Excel are used to build the models and solve assignments, to showcase the practical application of the presented methods. Additional content: fuzzy logic in decision-making is also covered, along with topics such as decision-support systems (DSS), expert systems and optimization. Special content: The course also introduces students to the basics of multiple expert decision-making and reaching consensus.
prerequisites: Suggested: BM20A4301 Johdatus tekniseen laskentaan or BM20A5001 Principles of Technical Computing or BM20A9001 Numerical Simulation, A210A0601 Information Systems in Corporate Management and Decision-Making
learningMaterial: Lecture materials, Assigned reading and assigned course books MATLAB / Octave materials available on the mathworks www-site Mengov, G.: Decision Science: A Human-Oriented Perspective, Springer, 2015. Srinivasan, R.: Strategic Business Decisions - A Quantitative Approach, Springer, 2014. San Cristóbal, J. R.: Multi Criteria Analysis in the Renewable Energy Industry, Springer, 2012.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, based on a written exam. Grade improvement is possible based on bonus points awarded for voluntary homework assignments.
workload: Lectures and exercises approximately 24 h, reading materials, watching videos and preparation for the lectures (60 h), preparation for the exam (76 h). Total workload for the student 160 h.

name: Advanced Topics in Business Ethics
learningOutcomes: The management of business ethics is professionalizing, as companies increasingly adopt and implement ethics management policies, practices and programs. As examples, business ethics management can include components such as codes of conduct, education and training, auditing and reporting, risk analysis, and diversity plans. This course introduces business ethics management, its role in organizations and its connections to other areas of managing business. This course aims for the following learning outcomes: 1. Recognize the role and components of business ethics management in organizations 2. Develop policies, practices and programs for business ethics management 3. Enhance professional skills (e.g. team work and interaction skills)
content: Professionalization of business ethics, components of business ethics management, assessment of ethical behavior.
prerequisites: Students enrolling must have completed course A350A2000 Business Ethics or other basic (bachelor’s or master’s-level) course on business ethics, corporate social responsibility or sustainability.
learningMaterial: Materials provided during the course, incl. readings, videos and cases.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points. The assessment is based on an individual (60%) and group work (40%). Some of the assessment is done through peer-review.
workload: Lectures and workshops 10 h, course readings and preparation for lectures 20 h, independent and group work on assignments 50 h. Total hours 80 h.

name: Analytics for Business
learningOutcomes: This course enables to learn a significant understanding of data science: the fundamental concepts and principles that underlie techniques for extracting useful knowledge from data. These concepts underlie the analysis of data-centered business problems, the creation and evaluation of data science solutions, and the evaluation of general data science strategies, and proposals. Through several practical examples, at the end of the course the student will acquire a broad range of techniques and practical skills to independently plan and create analysis tools able to finding anomalies, patterns and correlations within large data sets to predict outcomes. Students will be also able to put some models and analysis methods into use with MATLAB
content: Data understanding and data preparation; principal component analysis, supervised regression methods: linear regressions, decision-trees , principal component regression) classification methods: logistic regression, classification trees; support vector machines); Performance measure and overfitting: (Mse(mean squared error); Roc curve & area under Roc (Auc), confusion matrix, cross-validation) unsupervised learning (clustering methods, including K-means and hierarchical clustering)
prerequisites: User knowledge of Matlab is required.
learningMaterial: Lecture materials, assigned reading, course book (Data Science for Business: What you need to know about data mining and data-analytic thinking, by Foster Provost, Tom Fawcett, 2013- available as an eBook in the library database)
evaluationCriteria: Numerical assessment (0-5) will be used. During the course there will be quizzes (counting 20%), one home assignment (together counting 40%) and a group project (40%)

name: Applied Consumer Behaviour
learningOutcomes: After taking the course, the students are able to: · Search and synthesize academic literature and theoretical frameworks pertaining to consumer behavior. · Develop research questions and hypotheses based on academic literature on consumer behavior. · Identify the most suitable research methods to address specific research questions related to consumer behavior. · Collect and analyze qualitative consumer data. · Collect and analyze quantitative consumer data · Interpret the results of a consumer research project and reflect on their academic and practical implications. · Work effectively and systematically on a consumer research project. · Understand and apply the principles of academic writing to their own research reports. · Present the results of a research project effectively to a professional audience.
content: This course provides an overview of consumer behavior as a field of research and practical skills related to consumer data collection and analysis. During the course, students will learn different methods of collecting consumer data along with practical methods of analyzing this data and interpreting results. The key contents are: The process of conducting a literature review in the field of consumer behavior. Basics of critical reading and synthesis of academic literature. Key theoretical frameworks and their applications in the field of consumer behavior. The process of developing research questions and hypotheses pertaining to consumer behavior. Basics of qualitative and quantitative research methods in the field of consumer behavior. The process of collecting and analyzing qualitative consumer data (interviews). The process of collecting and analyzing quantitative consumer data (experiments). Statistical analysis of consumer data. Basics of academic writing and reporting of research results. The process of working on a consumer research project as a team. The process of preparing and conducting a presentation of a consumer research project to a professional audience.
prerequisites: Basics of marketing (Markkinoinnin perusteet). Recommended prerequisite course for students of SIB-programme: A130A0420 Research Methods in Business Studies.
learningMaterial: The reading and study materials will be distributed via Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation (0-100 points) consists of the following components: 3 group assignments: 60p. (each 20p.); individual quizzes: 25p.; and final presentation: 15p. In order to be graded, students must pass all the course tasks. Grades for the group assignments may be adjusted individually based on students' involvement in the group work. Penalty points might be applied in case of delayed submission of the assignments. Turnitin anti-plagiarism service will be used to ensure the originality of returned assignments. Using AI technologies for course assignments must be transparently disclosed, and the acceptable use of AI technologies will be discussed during the lectures.
workload: The lectures and seminars require physical presence in Lappeenranta. First period: Lectures 8 h, seminars 6 h, individual work and quizzes 10 h, group work on a project 56 h. Second period: Lectures 2 h, seminars (including final presentation) 6 h, individual work and quizzes 5 h, group work on a project 67 h. Total workload for a student: 160h.

name: Applied International Business
learningOutcomes: After taking the course the student should be able to: · understand and apply relevant theories in the context of international business practice · discuss how the practice of international business can influence the grand challenges our world is facing; · understand how business scholars can influence the practice of international business; · evaluate international business challenges that companies face and offer practical recommendations; · retrieve and analyze international business data to facilitate managerial decision-making
content: This course covers practical challenges faced by international business enterprises including sustainability, cross-cultural and social issues, internationalization, innovation and entrepreneurship.
learningMaterial: Study materials including journal articles from magazines such as Harvard Business Review and MIT Sloan Management Review as well as practical business cases are made available on the course Moodle page.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Learning diaries 20%, electronic exam 50%, Case study reports and presentations 30%. Each of the components has to be passed acceptably.

name: Authentic Leadership
learningOutcomes: Upon completing the course, the PhD students should be able: · To develop an advanced knowledge and critical understanding of the concept Authentic Leadership (AL) · To demonstrate conceptual and theoretical understanding of AL · To critically reflect upon self-awareness in AL · To reflect upon and evaluate practicing AL in different contexts · To illustrate how development of authentic leadership would benefit the PhD learning process.
content: The purpose of the PhD course in ‘Authentic Leadership’ is to contribute to PhD training through discovering as well as nurturing and developing leadership authenticity skills among PhD students. The course is a 5 ECTS course which will provide the PhD students with theoretical and conceptual understanding of the concept of Authentic Leadership as well as train the students in critical reflection and application of AL in different contexts. The course will be based on the principle of complex problem solving, bringing in real life problems, to which the students find solutions.
prerequisites: Students should be admitted to the doctoral education at their university. Teaching language is English demanding proficient level of oral and written English communication skills.
learningMaterial: Turcan et al. (forthcoming) The Emerald Handbook of Authentic Leadership (selected chapters, ca 200 pages). Will be provided as pre-reading for the course Selection of articles (Reading list ca 200 pages) plus own choices in collaboration with supervisor (ca 100 pages) Audio and video material.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Group and individual written reports, group and individual presentations, peer evaluations.
workload: The course contains lectures, simulations, PBL-oriented workshops, problem-solving and reflection exercises. Blended learning and online tools will be utilized. Pre-course work: material for the course will be available 1 month before the on-site session. There will be online communication as well as written assignments before and after the on-site session. a) teacherled studies: lectures, PBL-oriented workshops, simulations (25 hrs), b) independent work: written reports, essays, presentations (individual preassignments 45 hrs, individual and group reflection essays and presentations 5 hrs, individual post-assignments (50 hrs), C) field training: structured company explorations, lectures on site at companies, student reflections (10 hrs). Total workload 135 hours. Lectures and workshops will be held online

name: Consumer Behaviour in the Age of Digitalization
learningOutcomes: After taking the course, the students will be able to: 1. Analyze consumer behavior, decision-making, and experiences in digital contexts from theoretical and practical perspectives. 2. Critically evaluate and develop digital marketing activities from the perspective of consumer behavior. 3. Deeply understand issues of responsibility, sustainability, and ethics pertaining to consumer behavior in digital environments, and critically evaluate business decisions from these perspectives. 4. Effectively communicate their ideas to professional audiences in video format. 5. Collaborate constructively and in a goal-oriented way in multicultural teams. 6. Search, process, and apply academic research on consumer behavior and develop well-argued perspectives and ideas based on the literature.
content: · Introduction to recent developments in consumer behavior in digital environments, including their ethical and marketing implications. · Consumer perceptions, emotions, motivations, attitudes, and attitude change in digital environments. · The processes and ethics of persuasion and social influence in digital environments. · Consumer experiences and decision-making in digital environments. · The implications of consumers' self-concept, identity, personality, and individual differences on consumer behavior in digital environments. · Consumer behavior in groups and communities in digital environments. · An introduction to state-of-the-art consumer research methods and their applications for studying consumer behavior in digital environments. · The implications of digital consumer marketing to consumer well-being and sustainable consumption.
prerequisites: Basics in marketing and in consumer behavior.
learningMaterial: Articles and other reading and study materials will be announced on the Moodle platform.

name: Databases for Business Analysts
learningOutcomes: Knowledge and understanding: • Basic knowledge of relational Database and Database Management Systems, their components and the role of them in Business Analysis • Basic knowledge of database interaction through queries, summary queries, forms and reports • Basic Knowledge of data management using SQL • Knowledge about how to model and how to read a database • Deep knowledge of querying a database using SQL Applying knowledge and understanding: • Advanced ability to analyse and organize information into a database • Ability in data organization through a relational database • Ability in data extraction from a database management system • Ability to perform complex data extraction using SQL language Making judgments • Evaluating the role of Database Management systems inside a modern organization • Distinguish different Database Management Systems available on the market • Decide which techniques to use when organizing and managing data Communication skills • Building efficient and appropriate reports • Building data summaries Learning skills • extracting, cleaning and transforming data • Understanding advanced database structures • Writing SQL queries to extract data from any relational datasource
content: The course will provide a deep understanding and a “hands-on” knowledge about the world of databases, where most of data of business applications are stored today. For a business analyst, ignoring how to access, extract and manipulate information from data storage means to rely (if not depend) on ICT support, so not to be autonomous in data management. The course objective is therefore to create a solid, theoretical but also practical knowledge about a) how to understand a data model using the most common design methodology in relational database, and b) how to extract and manipulate data using the SQL language. Practical examples of data extraction and manipulation from real-world, business and financial databases will be provided. Topics covered in the course: · Relational model for databases · Tables, records and fields · Relations, Keys and constraints · Objects of a Relational database · From conceptual models to physical models · DB and DBMS · SQL language – structure and syntax · Select, Select Top and Select Distinct · Where clause and logical operators · Like, between and in operators · Order by clause · Managing NULL values · SQL Union clause · Aggregation queries: sum, count, avg, min, max · Tables aliases · Join operations: Inner, Left, Right, Natural, Full, Self · Group by and Having clauses · Exists clause · Insert, Delete, Update in SQL · SQL peculiarities
prerequisites: Basic computer usage, in particular Microsoft Windows and file handling.
learningMaterial: For the theoretical and practical parts, specific materials will be provided in form of slides by the teacher
evaluationCriteria: Electronic/on-line exam covering 1. the knowledge on basic information systems from the theoretical material and 2. the ability to understand a basic data organizational problem and extract data from a relational database. Grade is the weighted average of part 1 (30%) and part 2 (70%). Particular emphasis is given to solutions which are optimal, efficient and extensible.
workload: Frontal lectures in standard classroom with examples and class exercises (24h). Interactive exercises in standard classroom or in computer room will be carried out using students’ own notebooks. Self study and preparation for the exam (56 h). Total 80 h.

name: Digital Marketing in Action
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, students will be able to: Perform a digital marketing audit and critically evaluate digital marketing strategies. Plan and execute strategic and tactical digital marketing campaigns based on business needs. Create high-quality digital content across various platforms (social media, SEO, paid advertising, etc.). Collaborate in teams to solve real-world marketing challenges . Deliver compelling client presentations based on data-driven insights.
content: This hands-on boot camp immerses students in the world of digital marketing through real-life casework in collaboration with a marketing company. Students will conduct digital marketing audits, develop strategic and tactical marketing campaigns, and create engaging content for real businesses. The course emphasizes practical, team-based problem-solving and direct industry engagement. Preliminary structure: This intensive course consists of three offline days on campus in Lappeenranta and self-directed teamwork: Day 1 (Kickoff & Briefing): A marketing company presents real business challenges at the university. Students form teams and receive their project tasks. Day 2 (Strategy & Planning): Teams collaborate on campus to plan their marketing campaigns, conduct audits, and develop initial content strategies. Self-Study Phase: Teams execute digital marketing strategies, conduct analytics, and create content. Day 3 (Final Presentations & Feedback): Teams present their results to the agency and receive industry feedback.
prerequisites: A330A0352 Strategic Issues in Digital Marketing must be completed before taking this course.
learningMaterial: Readings and online material assigned and provided by the lecturer.
evaluationCriteria: 0–5. Continuous assessment during the course based on: • Team Report: A digital marketing audit and campaign plan (25%) • Content Development: Submission of digital assets (social media posts, blog articles, ads, etc.) (25%) • Final Presentation: Pitching campaign outcomes to the client (30%) • Individual Learning Diary (20%) • Attendance of the campus days in person (Pass/Fail) • Peer-evaluation may influence the points.
workload: Lectures 22h; Assignments 48h; Readings, 10h; Total 80h

name: Free Analytics Environment
learningOutcomes: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of Python programming, with a primary focus on applying it to typical business analytics problems. By the end of the course, students will be able to, - understand and apply basic Python syntax (using Jupyter notebook) and programming concepts - understand and apply loops, built-in and custom functions, and Python packages, especially for data visualizations - understand and apply data pre-processing for data analysis and evaluate exploratory data analysis in Python - identify different types of machine learning problems (Regression, Classification, and Clustering) - construct their own linear regression, classification, and clustering models in Python for real data - evaluate model performance based on certain metrics (such as R2, the classification accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, etc.)
content: The course will incorporate knowledge for 6 distinct areas using Python: (1) Introduction to Python and its packages, (2) Data visualization, (3) Data pre-processing, (4) Linear regression, (5) Classification with a focus on selected machine learning models (6) Clustering with hierarchical and heuristic methods, including methods to determine the optimal number of clusters. Exercise classes accompany the lecture, in which the students will be introduced to selected examples for which they will perform programming tasks together with the lecturer in class that are related to the content of each week's lecture.
prerequisites: None. Basic knowledge in analytics and statistics is helpful but not required.
learningMaterial: Attending the lectures and exercise sessions, studying the material provided in Moodle, and participating in weekly quizzes, assignments, and exams are sufficient for completing the course. There is a wide variety of (free) resources available - here are some examples. - Allen B. Downey (2024), “Think Python: How to Think Like a Computer Scientist” (3rd Edition). Read online version of the book: https://allendowney.github.io/ThinkPython/index.html - AL Sweigart (2020), “Automate the Boring Stuff with Python.” (2nd Edition) Read online version of the book: https://automatetheboringstuff.com - Python official documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/contents.html
evaluationCriteria: Weekly Online Quizzes: 20%, Assignment: 30%, Exam: 50%. Overall: Grading 0-5 [each course component (Quizzes, Assignment, Exam in the exam system) needs to be passed to pass the course overall]
workload: Lectures 14 h, exercises 14 h, weekly online quizzes and preparation for the quizzes 14 h, independent study 60 h, the assignment and preparation for the assignment and the exam 58 h. Total workload 160 h.

name: Fuzzy Data Analysis
learningOutcomes: In the end of the course the student is expected to be able to - understand theoretical aspects of data analysis - understand basic mathematics from fuzzy set theory related to data analysis - apply fuzzy set theory based models in data analysis - analyze and interpret results from the models - apply fuzzy principal component analysis, fuzzy clustering and classification methods to data analysis problems
content: Fuzzy sets and relations. Uncertainty measures. Qualitative and quantitative analysis of fuzzy data. Principles of individual multi-person, multi-criteria decision making, feature selection, fuzzy principal component analysis, fuzzy clustering, fuzzy classification, fuzzy regression analysis.
prerequisites: A240AA0060 Fuzzy Sets and Fuzzy Logic course
learningMaterial: Lecture materials, Course book Bandemer, H., Näther, W.: Fuzzy Data Analysis, Kluwer Academic Publ., 1992.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 100 %. Quizzes.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises 26 h. Practical assignment. Independent study 106 h. Total work load 160 h.

name: Introduction to Programmatic Business Analytics
learningOutcomes: The course introduces business students to the core concepts of algorithmization and programming, to give the students the needed background to start using procedural and object-oriented programming languages for business analytics purposes. Specifically, after completing the course, the student will: Understand the big picture of how programmatic business analytics works from the start to the end, and understand the value of data analytics in facilitating evidence-based business decision-making. Be able to structure problems and break them up into subparts, that can potentially be solved or approached through already available techniques and tools. Modularization and procedural thinking will be developed during the course. Be able to apply basic algorithmic structures (loops, logical conditions, recursive algorithms, sorting algorithms, …) in general in problem solving tasks and in a chosen programming language. As such the course aims to develop student competences and skills to be able to implement a simple, but complete data analysis process in a chosen programming language or in pseudocode for solution planning purposes. Specific examples from the business analytics context concerning, for example, data scraping, data cleaning and pre-processing, data analytics using statistical methods, data visualization and machine learning will be provided.
content: Basics of programming and algorithmic thinking and its implementation in programming languages used in practical business analytics - both procedural and object-oriented (e.g. Pseudocode, Matlab, Python, R, etc.) - and their application in business analytics problems. This involves a recap on basic statistics (e.g., linear regression) and an introduction to machine learning algorithms. The focus is heavily on hands-on learning (i.e., actual problem structuring, modularization and basics of programming) and on examining business-related problems with real world data.
prerequisites: A130A0350 Kvantitatiiviset tutkimusmenetelmät (Quantitative Research Methods).
learningMaterial: Lecture slides and other presented material.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Self-learning exercises 25%, in-course group assignment(s) 75 %.
workload: Period 1: Seven 2h learning sessions (lectures - 14h), self-learning (20h) and independent study in Datacamp (30h). Period 2: Three 2h learning sessions (lectures - 6h), self-learning (20h) and independent study in Datacamp (30h), work on course assignment (40h). Total workload 160 h.

name: Marketing Analytics
learningOutcomes: This course is designed to prepare students for data-driven marketing roles by enhancing their capability to derive well-informed marketing insights from Big Data. It aims to develop a strong analytical mindset while addressing the ethical considerations involved in using data for the benefit of consumers, businesses, and society. Key topics covered in the course include customer segmentation, marketing mix modeling, attribution modeling, user-generated data analysis, customer mindset metrics, and sentiment analysis. Adopting a practice-informed approach, the course features real-world examples, datasets, and case studies to connect theory with practical application. Students will gain hands-on experience with R/RStudio, including its various packages for statistical computing and visualization. Additionally, they will explore tools such as Google Trends, sentiment analysis libraries, and machine learning techniques where applicable. By the end of this course, students will be able to: ILO1: Critically evaluate the impact of marketing decisions (e.g., advertising) on key performance metrics (e.g., return on marketing investment and customer mindset metrics) ILO2: Develop targeted and meaningful marketing strategies by analyzing customer segments and various touchpoints in the customer journey. ILO3: Employ user-generated data responsibly to improve brand positioning while adhering to ethical standards.
content: Key topics: Introduction to Marketing Analytics, Customer Segmentation, Marketing Mix Modeling, Attribution Modeling, User-Generated Data Analysis, Customer Mindset Metrics, and Sentiment Analysis. Lectures include interactive activities and require active student participation. The online tutorials provide practical, hands-on experience with R/RStudio, using case studies as a foundation for learning.
prerequisites: A240A0030 Introduction to Analytics with R OR A220A0010 Free Analytics Environment R OR A240A0031 Introduction to Analytics OR A220A0011 Free Analytics Environment OR A240A0032 Marketing Research with R. Basic knowledge in statistics.
learningMaterial: Recommended textbook: Yildirim, G. & Kübler, R. (2023). Applied Marketing Analytics using R . United Kingdom: SAGE Publications. Students can borrow the recommended textbook from the library for reference. In addition, lectures incorporate several journal articles and book chapters as ‘required reading’. All required readings are accessible through the library. Supplementary readings are outlined in the lecture materials.
evaluationCriteria: Grading Scale: General scale, 0-5; Types of Assessments: Conceptual assessment (Quiz) 20 points; Group activities 60 points; Final exam (Quiz) – 20 points; In-class activities (Pass/Fail). To pass the course, students must "Pass" in-class activities, "Pass" individual assessment components (conceptual quiz, group activities, and final exam) and accumulate at least 50 points across individual assessment components.
workload: The course has a total student workload of 160 hours, distributed as follows: In-class lectures 21 hours; Online tutorials 14 hours; Course assignments, including data analysis with software 55 hours; Independent study, including lecture and tutorial preparation, and course assignments 70 hours

name: Marketing of High Technology Innovations: Applications
learningOutcomes: After the course, student should be able to: 1. solve real life high technology marketing problems 2. create and develop skills in theory application, information acquisition, analyses, and communications. 3. develop social and intercultural competence by working in intercultural groups. Course aims to provide a deep understanding of the functions of marketing regarding challenges and opportunities in high technology products and markets, assist the participants to understand the virtue and limitations of traditional marketing thinking and tools in emergent high technology markets.
content: Contingency model of high technology marketing. Special characteristics of high technology markets. Strategy and Corporate Culture in High-Tech firms. Partnerships and Alliances. Marketing Research in High-Tech Markets. Understanding High-Tech Customers. Product development and Management issues in High-Tech markets. Pricing Considerations in High-Tech Markets. Advertising and Promotion in High-Tech Markets. New product launch strategies.
prerequisites: A130A0010 Basics of Marketing (Markkinoinnin perusteet or equivalent), A330A0300 Strategic Global Marketing Management
learningMaterial: Mohr, Jakki, Sanjit Sengupta, and Stanley Slater (2010) Marketing of High-Technology Products and Innovations. Third Edition. Pearson Prentice Hall. Web site http://marketinghightech.net/
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Written Case assignments (60 points). NOTE: Peer evaluation of the group work may effect on the grade. Video Case Presentation (40 points).
workload: This is an online course. 6 h online case assignments, 2 h online lecture on new technologies (artificial intelligence, machine learning, blockchain) to marketing, intensive week 20 (13.5-17.5). Total 8 hours. Other assignments: 48 h for doing case assignments, 24 h for preparing video presentation. Total workload for student 80 h.
equivalentCoursesInfo: Can't be included into a same degree with A330A0201 Marketing of High Technology Innovations 6 cr.

name: Master's Thesis, Business Analytics
learningOutcomes: The overall goal of the thesis is for the student to display the knowledge and capability required for independent work as a Master of Science in Economics and Business Administration, and especially in the area of business analytics. After completing the thesis, students will be able to carry out independently a scientific research project and will thus be able to: - delimit and define the purpose and the topic of the research - have a deep understanding on the theory, current research and research methods relevant to their main subject - design and apply theoretical frameworks in own research and in solving empirical research problems - independently identify and formulate research problems and to plan and, by using appropriate methods, carry out advanced tasks within specified time limits - integrate knowledge and to analyze, assess and deal with complex phenomena, issues and situations - report scientific research in written academic format; clearly present and discuss conclusions and the knowledge and arguments behind them.
content: The student applies the knowledge and skills of previous studies and attends the Master's Thesis seminars covering the specific features of a scientific research process and related requirements.
prerequisites: Thesis project idea that has been preliminary approved by the thesis supervisor. Approximately 30 ECTS cr. Business analytics studies.
learningMaterial: Master's Thesis - instructions, seminar materials available in Moodle and Uni portals.
evaluationCriteria: Thesis: 0-5. Master's thesis seminar: pass/fail. All theses submitted for evaluation will undergo similarity check for plagiarism.
workload: Seminar work on 1.-4. periods. Seminars start in the beginning of the 1st and 3rd periods. Active participation in research seminars, successful completion of the required seminar assignments on topic selection, literature review, research aim, research questions and theoretical framework, presentation of the research plan, acting as discussants for other's work, writing of the thesis and completing the final version of the Thesis under supervision of assigned Master's Thesis supervisors. Total workload consisting of research seminars, seminar assignments, research execution and written reporting 810 h.

name: Supply Chain Analytics Projects
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to design end-to-end data analytics project plan based on business goals, be able to evaluate requirements of data-analytics projects in the supply chain management and be capable to implement simple data-analytics projects independently. Students will be able to breakdown data analytics solutions in supply chain management, will be able to apply data mining techniques for business process data, will be able to communicate goals and results of data analytics projects, and will be able to acquire information from developer communities independently. After completing the course, students will be able to 1. Evaluate strategies and solutions to analyze the supply base 2. Design plan and communicate goals of data analytics projects 3. Search and assess available data sources 4. Use visual programming for analysis of business data
content: Frameworks for data-analytics project planning and management (CRISP-DM, SEMMA, KDD). Principles of data manipulation and modeling techniques. KNIME Analytics Platform for implementing automated datamining using no-code/low-code approach. Data sources for supply chain analytics.
prerequisites: Bachelor's studies. A310A0101 Strategic Supply Management. For exchange students: B.Sc. studies related to operations management, supply chain management, supply management or similar are required.
learningMaterial: 1. Course book: Berthold, M.R., Borgelt, C., Höppner, F., Klawonn, F., Silipo, R. (2020) Guide to Intelligent Data Science 2 nd edition, Springer, 2. lecture materials and other assigned readings.
evaluationCriteria: Grading scale General scale, 0-5. Essay 40 %, Group Assignment: 40%, Discussions, Weekly Assignments and Exercises 20%. Each course component needs to be passed to pass the course overall.
workload: Workshops 14 h, exercises 14 h, essay 30 h, independent study 38 h, practical assignment 60 h. Total work load 160 h.

name: System Dynamics with Applications
learningOutcomes: The course provides an introduction to system modeling and simulation in a diverse range of applications across industrial and business contexts. After completing the course, the student recognizes the potential use cases of computational models and is able to implement and critically analyze them in practice.
content: Computational modeling in graphical modeling environments, Matlab, Excel, and Python. Deterministic, system dynamic, multi-agent, digital twin, and surrogate models. Uncertainty analysis, probability distributions, stochastic processes, and sampling techniques. Global sensitivity analysis. Visual tools for computational model analysis. Urban dynamics, investment analysis, carbon footprint, policy impact assessment.
learningMaterial: Course material on the course’s Moodle homepage. Sterman, J. D. (2000) Business Dynamics: Systems thinking and modeling for a complex world. McGraw Hill. Kozlova, M., & Yeomans, J. S. (2024). Sensitivity Analysis for Business, Technology, and Policymaking: Made Easy with Simulation Decomposition (SimDec) . Taylor & Francis. Open Access .
evaluationCriteria: Grading scale 0-5. Active lecture participation 10%, quizzes 30%, homework assignments 60%.
workload: Self-preparation to lectures 12 h, synchronous lectures & exercises 28 h, quizzes 10 h, homework assignments 30 h, 3rd period. Total 80 h.

name: Globalizing Business: How to Become a Global Company?
learningOutcomes: The course aims to provide the students with the knowledge of the processes related to the corporate strategic decision making. Small, mid-size and large companies are constantly looking for opportunities to enlarge and develop operations and conquer new market shares. This requires dynamic capabilities and competences and strategic decision-making processes. The main objectives of the course are: 1) to inspire students to investigate how companies build competences and how they transfer from local to national and finally to global markets. 2) to increase the understanding of internal and external factors that shape the strategic decision-making process. 3) to equip students with the frameworks that explain why some companies are more capable for succeeding in making transformation and entering to the global markets. 4) to give students practical knowledge on how to study and investigate strategic decision-making processes
content: The course builds on the theoretical foundations of the corporate strategy research. The focus is on three case studies of major Finnish corporations (KONE corporation, Vaisala corporation, METSO corporation). The case studies open the complexity of the strategic decision making within a company that explores opportunities to transfer from national into global markets. The core topics are as follows: 1. How companies move from national into international and global markets? 2. How the strategic decision-making process evolves over time and what are the roles and tasks of corporate institutions (CEO, Board of Directors and Executive team)? 3. How companies recognize opportunities and how they build strategic capabilities and competences? 4. What role technology, innovation and specialization play in the strategic decision-making process? 5. What role tradition and history play in the strategic decision making?
prerequisites: Previous studies in international business (e.g. Introduction to International Business or International Business Strategy)
learningMaterial: - Journal articles on the theory of the strategic decision-making process - Video clips and expert analyzes -Case study articles -Magazine, newspaper, and popular journal articles. All materials will be distributed prior to the lectures, group assignments and workshops. Students are strongly encouraged to prepare before meetings and engage in discussion and learning.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: - Engagement and activity in lectures 20% - Workshop activity 40% - Group-work 40%.
workload: - Interactive lectures and in-class assignments 30 hours - Group-work assignments 30 hours - Workshops 20 hours. Total workload 80 hours.

name: Advanced Engineering Mathematics
learningOutcomes: Student is able to - recognise different functions - solve exponential and logarithm equations - solve inequalities - solve simultaneous equations with the software - basics of differential calculations
prerequisites: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching

name: Immaterial Rights and their use in Entrepreneurship
learningOutcomes: Student knows immaterial rights and their legal regulation and phenomena more extensively, and knows the immaterial rights especially from the point of view of business usage.
content: The legal framework of immaterial rights and their use in contracting practices and legal questions of information-technology contracts, publishing contracts and electronic commerce including customer's rights. Issues connected with evaluation of patents and trademarks as well as taxation of immaterial rights. Basics of standardization and legal questions of scientific and commercial cooperation of commercial corporations.
prerequisites: Recommended: A130A0700 Basic course in Business Law
learningMaterial: Material announced by the lecturer, updates available in Moodle 1. Haarman, Pirkko-Liisa: Tekijänoikeus ja lähioikeudet, Talentum 2005 2. Työ- ja elinkeinoministeriön muistio tavaramerkkilain uudistamisesta, 38/2012, luvut 1 ja 2 (availble in the Internet http://www.tem.fi/files/34683/TEMjul_38_2012_web.pdf)3. evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points.
workload: Lectures 20 h and preparation for lectures 10 h. Written exam and preparation for exam 130 h, 4th period. Total workload 160 h.

name: Regulation of Securities Market
learningOutcomes: After completing the course the student will be able to understand how securities markets operate, to apply and understand the need for regulation of securities market and investment activities.
content: The essential actors in securities markets, investments markets and securities markets operational principle and need for regulation. Public limited company's obligation to notification. Securitization, provisions which constrains the misuse of inside information.
prerequisites: Basics of corporate law
learningMaterial: 1. Lecture slides and assigned reading 2. Parkkonen, J. ; Knuts, M.: Arvopaperimarkkinalaki, 2014 (5., uudistettu painos)
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points
workload: Lectures 14 h and preparation for lectures 12 h. Written exam and preparation for exam 134 h. 2nd period. Total workload for a student 160 h.

name: Banking and Insurance Finance
learningOutcomes: After successful completion of the course, the students will be able to understand and analyse: - The role of banks in the economy - Risk management in banking - Interest rate risk - Liquidity risk - Operational risk - Financial crises and regulatory response - Emerging markets' financial systems and banking issues - Introduction to the business of insurance - Types of insurers - Insurance underwriting, insurance pricing, using analytics in the insurance business
content: The content of the course consists of selected theories and applications related to banking and insurance underwriting. The topics include the role of banks in the economy, especially as providers of liquidity and payment services, transforming assets, managing risks, processing information, monitoring borrowers – with an international perspective, and asset and liability management of banks. The course provides an overview of selected management and monitoring tools used by banks and insurance companies, peer-2-peer financing and crowd funding. Additional content: Introduction to central banking and and role of banks in financial crisis as well as basic concepts of macroprudential risks and insurance. Introduction of International financial institutes (IMF, World Bank, BIS, and others), and sustainability and ethical issues in banking and insurance.
learningMaterial: Selected chapters of three Course books, Lectures slides, video lectures, and additional readings will be available on the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, on-line quizzes 20%, final exam 80%.
workload: Lectures 24 h, preparation for the quizzes: 27 h and preperation for exam 109 h. Total workload 160 hours.

name: Behavioral Economics and Management
learningOutcomes: The students are expected to orient themselves towards theoretical as well practical elaborations in this field of research, they should acquire enough knowledge to be able to understand in which real-life situations this approach can be preferred to “standard” methodologies.
content: Behavioral economics is a relatively new branch of economics that aims to improve the descriptive and the predictive power of the economic analysis by integrating agents’ limited cognitive abilities and limited willpower that, together with informational incompleteness, cause agents to behave sub-optimally. This course offers an overview of the theories and the empirical results in Behavioral Economics, allowing students to orient themselves towards further elaborations in this field of research. More specifically, the course is aimed to provide students with the opportunity to: 1) acquire a general overview of several important topics and empirical evidence in Behavioral Economics; 2) learn the essential tools for designing and carrying out a Behavioral Economics experiment; 3) acquire the essential skills for applying the Behavioral Economics insights to real-world applications, 4) acquire the basic statistic knowledge to interpret behavioral data. Main Teaching Modules: Psychology and Economics – the Role of Cognitive Biases and Heuristics; Experimental Methodology and Data Collection – How to Run an Experiment in Economics and Management Science; Risk and Uncertainty in Economics and in Management Science; The social dimensions of B.E. – Elements of Game Theory.
learningMaterial: Lectures materials and a list of required and optional materials (journal articles, books chapters, etc.) will be provided.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points. The evaluation will be based on assignments and a Moodle test.
workload: Lectures, independent readings and preparation for the test 80 h. Preparation for the assignments 80 h. Total workload for the student 160 h.

name: Big Data in Business and Industry
learningOutcomes: The course discusses the most important new tools for understanding the potential impact of big data analytics on decision making and business performance. Through analyzing typical business decision problems from the perspective of data requirements, the course discusses the role of big data analytics in modern organizations. After the completion of the course, the students: know the most important technological requirements of performing big data analytics, understand the role of big data in transforming modern organizations through data driven decision making, understand the impact of data volume, variety, and velocity, understand how to create value with big data, become familiar with the techniques and tools for capturing, processing, and interpreting big data, know the most important methods to reduce big data sets by extracting the most important information, are familiar with several real-world scenarios of big data use from different business sectors, understand the role of big data in creating business value, know how to apply the discussed concepts and tools to business projects.
content: Core content: big data technology, data and dimension reduction, role of data driven decision making in modern organizations. Additional content: machine learning methods for big data analytics, network analysis Special content: text analytics
prerequisites: A220A0010 Free Analytics Environment R and A130A0650 Tilastollisen tutkimuksen perusteet (basics of statistics) or equivalent knowledge.
learningMaterial: Materials will be distributed during the course.
evaluationCriteria: Course assignments (70% of the grade), written examination (30% of the grade), grading 0-5.
workload: Lectures 20 h, computer room tutorials 10 h, course assignments involving big data analysis (using relevant software) 75 h. Written exam and preparation for the exam 55 h. Total workload for the student 160 h.

name: Contemporary Issues in International Business and Entrepreneurship
learningOutcomes: After the course participants should be able to: To assess the contemporary concepts and issues ('hot topics') in international business and entrepreneurship.. To synthesize and evaluate contemporary international business and entrepreneurship phenomena. To debate on special topic of international business. To manage and facilitate cross-cultural collaboration.
content: Course covers timely issues contemporary concepts and issues affecting international business and entrepreneurship today.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of theories in international business and entrepreneurship
learningMaterial: Material to be assigned in the class.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Exam (50 points), In-class assignments and participation (50 points)
workload: 30 hours of intensive integrated lectures and exercises (assignments and cases). 20 hours of preparation for lectures and exercises. 30 hours of preparation for the Exam. Course total 80 h.

name: Contemporary Issues in Strategic Management and Innovation
learningOutcomes: This course focuses on the topical phenomena and concepts related to strategic management and innovation, which will be investigated from different viewpoints of academic research and business practice. Students will learn to assess, debate and synthesize the recent literature and examine the links of contemporary topics to previous research. The learning outcomes of the course are the following: 1. To assess and synthesize contemporary phenomena in strategic management and innovation 2. To constructively discuss and debate contemporary strategy and innovation phenomena
content: The content of the course is based on current topics of strategic management and innovation, including phenomena linked to broad mega trends such as digitalization and sustainable development. The course syllabus with detailed contents will be distributed in the beginning of the course. The course will utilize online methods and tools (blog posts and discussion threads) for student-driven content creation, discussion and reflection.
learningMaterial: Independent content creation based on academic and practical sources and familiarization of other students’ input.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points. Content creation 50 % Online activity points 50 % There is no written final exam.
workload: 3. period, full-online course. Independent familiarization with literature 36 h, independent content production 60 h. Online work: blog-thread moderation, discussion, and reflection 60 h. Wrap-up session 4 h. Total hours: 160 h.

name: Creativity and Entrepreneurship in New Product Development from Silicon Valley's Perspectives
learningOutcomes: Learning outcomes: - To understand important elements of marketing strategy that is related to product management. - To develop an in-depth understanding of new product/service development and management. - To understand and utilise a process-oriented framework for making new product/service development decisions. - To enhance business communication skills through preparation and presentation of new concepts for products and services via prototyping as well as its marketing plan.
content: This course is designed to explore two critical business topics related to product management strategy in marketing: - the design and development of new ideas for product/service innovations - the management of new and existing products and services for sustainable business. First, topics in new product development include idea generation and screening, design, planning, and prototyping, and new product roll-out, as well as the development of marketing strategies and implementation plans for new products and services. Second, management of new and existing products involves in integration of new products into the product line, management of the marketing mix, quality of service, and customer development strategies. Throughout this project-based course, the importance of creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship will be emphasised as the sources of initiating and managing new products and innovation.
prerequisites: Previous courses in basic marketing (ex: Principles of Marketing, Marketing Management, Essentials of Marketing) *Submit an application with transcripts if prerequisites are not met.
learningMaterial: - Main Textbook: C. Merle Crawford and C. Anthony Di Benedetto, New Products Management, 11 th ed. or 10 th ed. Irwin McGraw-Hill. - The additional reading materials from academic and business press articles (i.e., case, magazine, newspaper, and journal articles) will be distributed through the class time prior to the class discussion.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points:- Final exam 30 points- Group project 20 points- In-class projects 5 points- Group case studies 10 points- Individual projects 20 points- Class-participation 15 points
workload: Lectures and in-class learning activities and assignments 28 hours. Preparation for lectures and assignment 30 hours. Preparation for the exam, and exam 22 hours. Total workload 80 hours.

name: Derivatives and Financial Risk Management
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to deepen the students' knowledge about the use of derivatives for hedging purposes. At the end of the course a student is expected: - to understand the interrelationships of spot markets and derivative markets and their arbitrage relations - to understand the internal arbitrage relations within the derivative markets - to be able to form and implement the optimal hedging strategy for different hedging needs (including the choice of the most appropriate derivative for the particular purpose) - to be familiar with the standard methods of derivative pricing and to be able to apply these methods in the pricing of exotic derivatives - to know the principles of risk management practices of derivative market makers - to know the basic methods of Value at Risk calculations - to understand the principles of credit risk management and the causality between default risk and the risk premium of fixed-income securities - to know the most commonly used credit derivatives
content: Pricing of standard derivatives (i.e. forwards, futures, swaps and options), hedging strategies and practices. Value at Risk, credit risk management, credit derivatives. The principles followed in market making and in pricing of exotic derivatives.
prerequisites: Only for the second-year MSF students or other M.Sc. students that have comparable financial skills
learningMaterial: 1. Hull, John C.: Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 2006 or newer edition. 2. Lecture handouts and solutions to weekly assignment questions (available on Moodle course pages)..
evaluationCriteria: Graded 0 – 5 on the basis of the exam and exercise activity. Evaluation 0-100 points, written exam 85–100% and exercises 0–15% depending on the student’s activity in exercises.
workload: Video lectures 18 h, class exercises 18 h (six weekly 3-hour class exercise sessions, in which at least two a student is expected to participate at Skinnarila campus), preparation for class exercises 54 h. Written exam and preparation for the exam 70 h. Total workload for the student 160 h.

name: Essential Sales and Negotiation Skills
learningOutcomes: After completing the course the students should be able to: - analytically evaluate how sales and other types of business negotiations work - distinguish, compare and organize various types of sales and negotiation situations - critically evaluate the main sales techniques: transactional, relationship selling, solution selling - evaluate and develop sales and negotiation-related core competencies - convince and negotiate effectively - appraise the importance of ‘people' skills: empathy, trust, active listening.
content: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to sales and negotiation. It will cover a range of topics: - Structure of sales negotiation - Individual negotiation styles - Different types of sales and negotiation situation - The mutual gains approach in negotiation - The main sales techniques: transactional, relationship selling, solution selling, challenger sales - Move from an approach based on ‘convincing' to one based on ‘persuasion' - The scope of our approach to include: ‘other' (interests, culture…), situation… - Communication, both verbal and non-verbal - The use of enquiry & questioning - The use of framing techniques and other ‘nudge' approaches - Conflict management - Interact with others
prerequisites: Bachelor’s degree, A330A0300 Strategic Global Marketing Management or equivalent basic marketing course.
learningMaterial: Readings and assignments to be announced before / in the class
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Individual research report (100 points) Active class participation, including in-class assignments (accepted – fail) All assignments must be passed.
workload: The course will balance theory and practical application, with considerable use of case studies and student project work. 30 h of interactive lectures and cases, 4rd period (intensive format). 50 h of preparation for lectures and assignments and individual research report. Total workload 80 h.

name: French Restaurants and Cuisine
