name: Shape Memory Alloys and Their Applications
learningOutcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: Explain the fundamental principles behind the shape memory effect, superelasticity, magnetic shape memory effect, and caloric effects in shape memory alloys (SMAs) and magnetic shape memory alloys (MSMAs), including materials like Ni-Ti and Ni-Mn-Ga. Understand the microstructural features and phase transformation characteristics that enable these unique properties. Analyse and interpret the functional behaviour of SMAs and MSMAs, and evaluate their suitability for specific applications. Design simple components or systems that utilise these materials.
content: This course explores the functional properties and applications of shape memory alloys (SMAs) and magnetic shape memory alloys (MSMAs), such as Ni-Ti and Ni-Mn-Ga alloy systems. Students will examine the microstructural features and phase transformations that enable key phenomena such as the shape memory effect, superelasticity, the magnetic shape memory effect, and caloric effects. The course covers SMA and MSMA behaviour, alloy design, material processing techniques, and the challenges of manufacturing and integrating these materials into functional devices, including the design of simple components. Examples of practical applications in fields such as biomedicine, aerospace, and robotics are also discussed. Instruction includes weekly lectures and quizzes, laboratory demonstrations, and an individual assignment (literature review and presentation to fellow students).
prerequisites: A foundational course in materials science or engineering is recommended. Knowledge of solid-state physics or physical metallurgy would be beneficial but is not mandatory. Students without this background may need to undertake additional self-study to grasp the course material fully.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes, laboratory demonstration materials, and supplementary materials will be provided weekly through Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, lecture attendance and quizzes 50%, assignment 50%.
workload: Physical lectures 14h, quizzes 7h, assignments 38h, self-studying 22h. Total amount 81h.

name: Welding Digitalisation, Automation and Adaptivity
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to widen the knowledge about the various aspects of industrial welding digitalisation, automation and adaptivity. After having completed and passed this course, the student: · has a knowledge about the welding automation processes and their variations that are used in industry, · can compare and evaluate different welding processes and automation levels from productivity, usability and profitability point of view, · can choose the most suitable welding process and automation level for manufacturing different type of products, · understands the relationship between the welding process, automation, adaptivity and quality, · has a general overview of utilizing welding automation methods relative to welding production and quality management, · knows the different sensor techniques and data analyses used in welding.
content: The teaching method of the course is full digi. The course includes also practical exercises in the welding lab. However, if you can't attend, an extra assignment related to topics is done to compensate the lab exercise. The course comprises lectures, exercises and obligatory laboratory tutorials to make the student familiar with industrial welding automation processes and practices. Course themes are listed below: · The concept of weldability in terms of automation and adaptivity. · Automation levels of welding (manual / mechanized / robotized). · Essential parameters, productivity, usability, and efficiency of mechanized and robotized welding processes. · Welding preparations (e.g. groove cutting and beveling methods) and post-weld treatments as an automated welding production point of view. · Sensor technologies and jig systems used in welding. · Adaptive welding. Each lecture has an exercise, which consists of multiple-choice / open questions, and some practical assignments based on the industrial tasks of a welding engineer. Additionally, the course has an obligatory seminar, which is a report of 10-20 pages written by the student for the whole duration of the course. The course promotes UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) by increasing health and safety for welders working conditions by increasing knowledge of hazards, utilizing devices and automation of welding process to reduce the risk of any health issues. The knowledge also pursues good training for the welders in order to improve the safety and sustainability of the production (for example reducing waste and requirement for rework). Utilizing virtual technologies and automation as well as knowledge of health, safety and ergonomics increases equality in the means of creating a cleaner and more sustainable environment of the welding production. This also creates whole welding production more attractive to all people and further pursue equality. The sustainability aspect of the production is consisted of each lecture and training to support innovational thinking, responsible production as well as responsible choices in welding production. Thus, in a wider perspective reduces the impact on the climate and environment. This course supports P2X development from the manufacturing point of view. With correctly planned manufacturing and sustainable choices in production, the devices of P2X can be created better in terms of longer life cycles as well as operating with higher efficiency.
prerequisites: Prerequisite knowledge: Basic knowledge is required from the welding processes. BK10A3601 Valmistus- ja tuotantotekniikka (or similar knowledge) is recommended to be passed before attending the course.

Helzer, Pearson. · Modeling, Sensing and Control of Gas Metal Arc Welding, D. S. Naidu, S. Ozcelik, K. L. Moore, Elsevier. · Videos of automated and adaptive welding operations and processes in Moodle.

The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Brand Management
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to familiarize the students with the management of 'brand equity', which is clearly an issue of major strategic importance. Few would deny the importance of brands as valuable assets and potential source of sustainable competitive advantage. Brands provide a shortcut for customers when making a purchasing decision, seeking to avoid risk and obtain value for money. Brands provide a relevant, exciting experience. Brands connote a certain life style, values or attitude. Brands can become objects of affection: 'Lovemarks', even. Buying a brand is an integral part of an individual's quest for identity and meaning. After completing the course the students should be able to: - have a deep understanding on how companies manage 'brand equity' - critically evaluate and compare different brand management strategies - analyze and explain reason, affect and decision-making related to brands - assess the social meaning and cultural rooting of brands - identify and explain current trends and issues in branding - work in a multi-cultural team - compile academic reports about branding - apply knowledge gained from the course, to the events, activities and/or strategies of an actual firm or organization
content: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to strategic brand management, covering such areas as the building of brand equity, brand identity, brand extension, brand portfolios etc. in national, regional and global markets. Indicative and subject to change topics include: 1. Introductory session - branding exercise. Brand basics. 2. Brand overview - Dyson: the man, the brand, the product, the market. Understanding codes, discourses and the potential for renewal and disruption. Sponges and hedgehogs. Mums, kids and washing liquid. The importance of consumer insight: Got milk? Fathers and whiskies 3. More about brands and how we relate to them: reason, affect and decision-making. Brand personality, brand archetypes. Brand endorsement and meaning transfer. 4. Branding people and experience. Service and experiential branding: Starbucks case study + the Apple Store 5. Brands in context. The social meaning of brands. What consumer studies and anthropology teach us. 6. A diamond is forever, beer is for men: the cultural rooting of brands. How brands become icons. Case study: Reviving an iconic brand – Levi's in the 80s 7. Brands & communities: Harley Davidson and Jones Soda. Tribal marketing & social networks. 8. Brand placement, brand content, brand events 9. Conclusion: current issues in branding
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree, A330A0300 Strategic Global Marketing Management, or equivalent basic marketing course
learningMaterial: Readings and assignments to be announced before / in the class

name: Business Ethics
learningOutcomes: This course aims for the following learning outcomes: 1. Evaluate business situations from the perspectives of different ethical theories 2. Recognize ethical challenges related to business and assess them analytically
content: Business professionals regularly face situations where they have to weigh the consequences of their decisions upon a variety of groups and individuals. These situations may include conflicting interests and values that cannot be met simultaneously. This course introduces how these situations can be approached from the perspective of central ethical theories and explores these theories with the help of contemporary cases.

name: Business Strategy
learningOutcomes: On completion of the course the students will be able to: Understand the strategic management process and its importance in achieving organisational goals. Conduct external and internal analyses to identify opportunities and threats, strengths, and weaknesses. Evaluate organisational performance using various measures and frameworks. Formulate and select business-level, corporate-level, and international strategies. Understand the importance of ethical and sustainability considerations in strategic decision-making.
content: This course provides an introduction to the key topics and themes in strategic management. It is designed to help students understand how businesses achieve success by leveraging their competitive advantages. The course covers how to conduct case analysis, measure organisational performance, conduct external and internal analyses and implement strategy across various levels of an organisation. Students will explore various strategies used by firms at the business/competitive, corporate and international levels. Sustainability considerations are integrated throughout the course.

name: Case-Course of Business

The students engage in a self-oriented independent teamwork by making a business analysis of a real case . The teams contact a company and negotiate a case with them autonomously for the exercise. After the completion of the course, the students should be able to: - Negotiate real life business cases. - Define and dis-aggregate problems. - Evaluate and describe firm's business practices, markets, and explain their development using the frameworks she or he has learned at previous courses. - Provide concluding suggestions/ solutions for the development targets/ problems of the firm based on the analysis of the empirical materials collected during the exercise. - Synthesize results and construct a well-written report of a case and its business environment. - Develop work plans and team processes for successful project management.

name: Contemporary Issues in Strategic Finance
learningOutcomes: After successful completion of the course, participants should be able to: assess the contemporary concepts and issues (“recent hot topics”) in strategic behavioral finance. critically examine financial phenomena and market anomalies from a behavioral perspective. synthesize and evaluate contemporary behavioral biases and finance. analyze the practical relevance of specific topic of strategic finance and decision-making.
content: The specific topic of the course is: Behavioral Finance: Decision-making and market anomalies. The main goal of the course is to introduce students to behavioral finance. This approach to financial issues relies on weaker rationality assumptions than traditional finance and seeks to improve the understanding of financial phenomena. Main concepts in behavioral economics are discussed, in an interactive and participated way. Then, behavioral insights are applied to financial issues regarding both market and corporate dimensions. Topics covered are Economic rationality Biases Risk and time Market anomalies Investor decisions

Perform and interpret results of sensitivity analysis. - analyze the relationship between WACC and D/E ratio in the context of associated risks and have advanced understanding of capital structure decisions and their effect on firm business and financial position. - understand the connections of decisions concerning capital investments, payout policy and capital structure to corporate strategy - identify the agency problems between the stakeholders of companies - know the central elements of risk management related to corporate finance and the corresponding risk management practices. A student is also expected to be able to apply the practices in real-world hedging situations. - recognize the role of working capital management and its implications on key aspects of the business.

name: Corporate Social Responsibility
learningOutcomes: This course aims to familiarize the students with the basics of corporate social responsibility (CSR), including the meaning of the concept as well as its potential to achieve positive change. During the course, students will learn about various CSR issues and topics affecting businesses operating in a global environment and possible ways for companies to address these issues through CSR strategies, practices and interactions with stakeholders. A group assignment provides the students an opportunity to apply their knowledge to business practice. Finally, students can improve their professional skills during the course through a group presentation. Upon completion of the course, students should be able to: 1) Understand and examine key concepts and frameworks related to CSR. 2) Recognize and assess various environmental, social, economic and ethical issues caused by, and affecting, companies operating in a global context. 3) Distinguish and analyze various types of CSR strategies and practices. 4) Apply theoretical frameworks related to CSR and sustainability to business practice. 5) Produce CSR-related materials.
content: CSR frameworks; environmental, social, economic, and ethical issues; CSR strategy; CSR practice; CSR communications and reporting; CSR in supply chains; and interactions between firms, nongovernmental organizations, and government agencies.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5. Evaluation (0-100 points) is based on the small group assignment and presentation (40 % in total) and a final Moodle exam (60 %). The assignment and exam must be passed to complete the course.
workload: An introductory lecture (2h), group presentations (4h), a small group assignment (28h), and independent study for the final Moodle exam (46h). Total workload: 80h. The course requires successful completion of the group assignment, presentation, and Moodle exam. --- Implementation code in TimeEdit A350A3333

name: Creating value with Sustainability – Case Fashion Business
learningOutcomes: The fashion industry is currently contributing to several sustainability problems. For example, the fashion industry emits considerable greenhouse gas emissions, generates microplastics in the world’s oceans, and is notorious for the exploitation of workers. Despite welcoming a more sustainable mindset and developing initial solutions, many fashion companies continue to struggle with the sustainable renewal of their business. To address this challenge, it is essential to holistically understand and renew the fashion value chain from sustainable supply chains to sustainable business models and ultimately sustainable consumer behaviors. Thus, the broad objective of this course is to build holistic understanding of sustainable supply chains, business models, and consumer behavior, and to critically assess and develop solutions for the sustainable renewal of the fashion industry. In this course, the students’ theoretical and practical understanding of sustainable business will be deepened through their applications in the context of fashion. After taking the course, the students will be able to: Understand the role of sustainability as a cross-cutting theme throughout companies’ supply chains, business models, and marketing. Understand and apply relevant theories, concepts, and frameworks pertaining to sustainable business in the context of fashion. Analyze and evaluate the sustainability of companies’ supply chains, business models, and marketing in the context of fashion. Create well-argued ideas on sustainable fashion business based on academic literature and other relevant sources. Communicate effectively about sustainability in a business context Collaborate constructively and in a goal-oriented manner in diverse project teams.
content: Basic concepts related to transparent sustainable business. Sustainable supply chain management. Sustainable business models. Sustainable marketing, consumer behavior, and sustainability communication. Interconnections between sustainable supply chain management, business models, and marketing. Fashion as a business context.
prerequisites: Introduction to International Marketing and Purchasing
learningMaterial: The teaching materials will be announced in the course Moodle page.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Individual EXAM examination 30%, group work 70%. All tasks and assignments need to be passed in order to get the final grade. Grades for the group assignments may be adjusted individually based on students' involvement in the group work. Penalty points might be applied in case of delayed submission of the assignments. Using AI technologies for course assignments must be transparently disclosed, and the acceptable use of AI technologies will be discussed during the lectures.
workload: The course consists of lectures (18h), preparation of a video assignment in groups (80h), and a final seminar (8h), in which the video assignments are streamed and evaluated. Furthermore, the students prepare for and take an individual exam (preparation and taking the exam in total: 54h). The total workload is 160h.

name: Creativity, Innovation, Entrepreneurship in New Product Development
learningOutcomes: At the completion of this course, students will be able to: Grasp the concept of creativity and creative process to address creative challenges in new product development. Learn techniques for generating creative ideas using different methods. Create an organizational and team context for recognizing and unleashing creativity, and for developing innovation by collaboration .
content: This course is designed to explore three critical business topics related to product management strategy in marketing: (1) understanding the concept of product strategy within the framework of marketing strategy, (2) new product development based on the design and development of new ideas for product/service innovations, and (3) the management of new and existing products and services for sustainable business. First, we will review the concept of product strategy related to marketing strategy. Second, topics in new product development include idea generation and screening, design, planning, and prototyping, and new product roll-out, as well as the development of marketing strategies and implementation plans for new products and services. Third, management of new and existing products involves in integration of new products into the product line, management of the marketing mix, quality of service, and customer development strategies. Throughout this project-based course , the importance of creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship will be emphasized as the sources of initiating and managing new products and innovation. The objectives for this course are as follows: To understand important elements of marketing strategy that is related to product management. To develop an in-depth understanding of new product/service development and management. To understand and utilize a process-oriented framework for making new product/service development decisions. To enhance business communication skills through preparation and presentation of new concepts for products and services via prototyping as well as its marketing plan
prerequisites: For summer school students: previous studies in business recommended. For MIMM degree students at LUT: Internationalisation of the Firm and Global Marketing, Strategic Global Marketing Management.
learningMaterial: Main Textbook (Recommended) : C. Merle Crawford and C. Anthony Di Benedetto, New Products Management, 12 th ed. Irwin McGraw-Hill. (11 th or 10 th ed is ok ) Assigned reading.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Final Exam (Comprehensive) - 35%, Group project and case study - 30%, In-Class Projects - 5%, Individual projects - 20%, Class Participation/Attendance - 10% Total.
workload: Lectures and in-class projects and assignments 30 hours. Preparing for lectures 25 hours. Preparing for exam 25 hours. Total 80 hours.

name: Cross-Cultural Encounters
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will know why it is important to understand and appreciate cultural differences both in business and especially private life. Students will be able to explain the basic concepts of intercultural communication by the main course themes: cultures and communication, verbal and nonverbal communication, national stereotypes, intercultural sensitivity, cross-cultural interaction, culture shock, adaptation, expatriate assignments. Students will be able to describe themselves as an intercultural communicator, recognize symptoms of culture shock in their own life and especially know how to make intercultural adaptation process easier.
content: The purpose of the course is to develop students' abilities to understand and appreciate cultural differences both in business and especially private life. - cultures and communication - verbal and nonverbal communication - national stereotypes - intercultural sensitivity - cross-cultural interaction - culture shock - adaptation - intercultural effectiveness - expatriate assignments
learningMaterial: Reading material for the course provided by the lecturers.

name: Cross-Cultural Issues in International Business
learningOutcomes: The goal of the course is to give an understanding of how culture affects international business and advance students' global mindset by giving conceptual tools to increase their intercultural competence. After completing the course the students will be able to: 1. understand, define and discuss culture in general and in the context international business 2. explain cultural orientations towards time, space and context. 3. analyze and compare national cultures according to dimensions defined by studies of Hofstede, Trompenaars, and the GLOBE project. 4. reflect upon the relationship between culture, organizations and management. 5. evaluate the effects of the culture on various elements of international business, including marketing, negotiations and international teams.
content: The Concept of culture; dimensions of culture in business (Hall, Hofstede, Trompenaars, and the GLOBE project). The limits of globalization from a cultural perspective. The role of culture in communication, negotiations, and management. Cross-cultural issues in international teams. Standardization and adaptation in international marketing. Country cases of cultural differences .

name: Dimensions of Entrepreneurship Theory
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will be able to: · Identify and evaluate the characteristics of entrepreneurship and the entrepreneurial process; · Recognize the factors that shape entrepreneurship and the entrepreneurial process; · Compare and contrast the essential theories and frameworks in entrepreneurship; · Apply key theories in the analysis of entrepreneurial activity; · Compare and contrast various types of entrepreneurship.
content: The aim of the course is to provide an overview of the theoretical foundations of entrepreneurship studies. It seeks to help students explore diverse perspectives on and dimensions of entrepreneurship. The course introduces key theoretical perspectives and concepts connected to entrepreneurship as well as presents contemporary issues in today's entrepreneurship research and practice. Key themes discussed in the course include the entrepreneurial process, collaboration, psychology, sustainability, gender and ethnicity.

name: Doctoral Seminar in Business Research
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to support LUT Business School’s (LBS) doctoral students in their doctoral dissertation process and in establishing a role in the LBS research community. More broadly, the course aims to build and support a collegial culture where postgraduate students' research is presented, commented, and improved on a continuous basis and in an interaction with the LBS faculty and peer students. In doing so, the course will acquaint students with the research traditions and trends in their own field as well as helps to establish aspirations in making an impact on the field and the business practice.

Each student will make total of four presentations/deliverables during the doctoral studies with a progressively developing contents related to the doctoral dissertation. They include: (1) Research plan, (2) Research paper draft, (3) Practical relevance pitch, (4) Pre-defense version of the doctoral thesis.

name: Econometric Methods
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to explain what kind of assumptions and practices form the basis of regression analysis. Students can interpret and evaluate the results based on regression analysis. Students will be able to specify econometric models and estimate the parameters of the models with cross-section, time series, and panel data. Moreover, students will be able to evaluate critically the estimated model and methodology, as well as the reliability of the conclusions based on the model. Students will recognise that there are various estimation methods, and are able to explain what kind of method is suitable in a certain situation (and, when necessary, are able to use a statistical test to find the appropriate method).
content: Linear regression analysis and hypothesis testing. The use of Stata software and interpreting Stata output. Discrete dependent variables, simultaneous equations and instrumental variables. The use of time series and panel data. Prediction and basic assumptions.

name: Empirical Research in Finance
learningOutcomes: After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: demonstrate knowledge in the areas of empirical asset pricing and corporate finance interpret the results of recent and relevant research in financial economics examine the nature and extent of relationship among variables in line with stated hypotheses select appropriate models and testing methods to answer questions related to finance and business analytics determine and describe the statistical and economic significance of estimated findings develop a detailed research plan about an empirical topic for master thesis in strategic finance and analytics
content: This course provides skills and tools for conducting quantitative research projects in finance and business analytics. A key component of this course is reviewing literature on relevant topics and identifying research gaps. Students are trained to apply quantitative models and obtain relevant secondary data from various sources. The main topics covered include asset pricing models, volatility modeling, investment evaluation, mergers and acquisitions, capital structure theories, payout policy, corporate governance, and trading algorithms using technical and/or fundamental analysis or major multi-criteria decision-making techniques. Various analytical techniques are employed, including linear and non-linear regression models, event studies, panel data analysis, other time-series and cross-sectional variants, and machine learning models.
prerequisites: 1) Working knowledge of one of the following statistical tools is required: STATA, SPSS, Eviews, MATLAB, Python, R, Excel-VBA Good programming skills are an advantage. 2) At least three of the courses listed below must be completed before taking this course.
learningMaterial: There is no textbook of this course. The lectures will be primarily based on research papers and teacher’s own data analysis projects. The recommended readings include:
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0–5 on the basis of 100 points obtained in three assignments. 1. Summary of the selected research paper and presentation (20p), 2. Empirical project and presentation (30p), 3. Detailed research proposal (50p). Student must obtain at least 50% of points in each assignment to pass the course. The attendance in all three presentation seminars is compulsory.
workload: Lectures: 20 h, Presentation seminars: 12 h, Literature review and presentation: 26 h, Empirical project and presentation: 38 h, Research proposal: 64 h. Total workload 160 h.

name: Empirical Strategy Research
learningOutcomes: After taking the course the student - knows the basic empirical application types and theories of strategy research - is familiar with the evolution, state-of-the art and future directions of research within central themes of empirical strategy research - can independently select a specific theme related to strategy, technology or innovation research and conduct a critical and systematic literature review on this theme - collect and analyze empirical data around this theme, and subsequently report, interpret and evaluate the results and their practical and theoretical implications
content: Core content: Central themes of strategy research: empirical testing of main theories, research strategies and designs and main results. The themes may include e.g. resource-based view, organizational cognition, sustainable strategies and competitiveness of the firm. The themes are related to current research, and may vary each year. Additional content: measurement of firm performance, specific methods of empirical research, e.g. event study, qualitative comparative analysis. Special content: important authors and publication forums of empirical strategy research.

Students will understand the role of supply management in value creation. Students will recognize and be able to utilize the main theoretical perspectives of supply management. Students will be able to apply knowledge obtained from previous studies to practice in the company assignment. After completing the course, students will be able to: 1. develop and apply strategies for managing purchasing and supplier relationships 2. understand the role of supplier relationships and networks in value creation 3. apply and justify theoretical perspectives of supply management 4. able to analyze and solve real-life discipline related problems.

name: Financial Econometrics
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: At the end of this course a student is expected to have a concise overall understanding of the mechanisms behind the econometrics models covered in the course so that he/she: - Is able to describe the main ideas of the models and methods and assess the appropriateness of their use in specific application cases, incl. the testing of assumptions of the models - Is capable of formulating the main questions of his/her empirical research in terms of the econometrics models and their parameters - Is able to select appropriate methods for the given practical application in financial data analysis and construct appropriate econometrics models and assess their quality - Is able to design econometrics models for financial data prediction (in case of time series) - Is able to validate the models and assess their performance and the fulfillment of their assumptions. - Is able to interpret the outputs of the econometrics models in the context of financial data analysis - Is able to use the methods and their outputs to explain phenomena in financial data and to assess hypothesis concerning financial data - Is able to utilize the models in financial theory building and assessment as well as in time series analysis and prediction and financial data analysis in general. - Is able to implement the designed econometrics models in MATLAB using its econometrics package (or other relevant software, such as R or Python). The models covered in this course include for example: Classical linear regression models, univariate time series models, ARMA processes, multivariate time series models, models for simultaneous equations systems, vector autoregressive (VAR) model, ARCH and GARCH-type models.
content: This course deepens students' knowledge on empirical research methods in financial econometrics. The focus is on the empirical techniques used most often in the analysis of financial markets and how they are applied to actual market data. The course is designed to give advanced-level (Master) knowledge of financial econometrics – that is to provide sufficient insight in the financial econometrics models and hypothesis testing and practical experience with building models for financial econometrics in MATLAB (or Python or other relevant software). The course covers four different areas in econometrics: 1) univariate and multivariate statistical analyses, 2) time series models, 3) modeling volatility and correlation, 4) modeling long-run relationships in financial markets. The students will use MATLAB econometrics package to run analyses, alternatively they can apply Python or R. Instruction and modeling examples in the lectures will be done mainly in Matlab.
prerequisites: Suggested: BM20A4301 Johdatus tekniseen laskentaan or BM20A5001 Principles of technical computing or BM20A9001 Numerical simulation, Compulsory bachelor’s level courses in finance and economics.
learningMaterial: 1. Brooks, Chris: Introductory econometrics for finance. Cambridge, 2002 or newer (Text book) 2. Handouts in class and all additional material required by the lecturer 3. MATLAB materials available on the mathworks www-site
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, exam constitutes 50% of the final grade and homework assignments (including the term-paper) constitute the other 50%. Students are required to achieve at least 50 percent of the maximum points in both areas to pass the course.
workload: Lectures and exercises in period 1: 36 h, homework assignments (mainly in period 2): 80h; preparation for lectures and exam: 44 h. Total course workload: 160 h.

name: Financial Supply Management
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to familiarize students with the financial issues of supply management. The intended outcomes of this course are to: - identify the impact that supply chain management decisions have on the financial statements of the organization; - explain the relationship between supply chain management decisions on measures of firm performance; - introduce a set of financial frameworks that are used in business to illustrate the impact that supply decisions have on the financial performance of a business. During the course the students apply methods and tools of working capital and inventory management in hands-on assignments. After completing the course students are able to - describe the impact that supply chain decisions have on the financial performance of the organization; - identify how supply chain decisions impact on creating earnings, cash and value for a business; - identify the financial impact of a supply chain decision on the profitability, liquidity and asset utilization of a business - determine optimal lot size inventory and safety stock levels - use relevant supplier financing tools in practice - recognize financial ratios used to manage liquidity and working capital; - describe the components of a working capital cycle; - identify the initiatives organizations use to manage working capital components;
content: The financial impact of a supply chain decision on the profitability and liquidity of organizations. Components of working capital. Methods and tools for working capital and inventory management. Decision making in supply chain. The impact of cash flow on working capital management and the financial performance of a business. Means of Supplier Financing.
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Econ. ; Bus. Adm.) studies. For exchange students B.Sc. studies related to operations management, supply chain management, supply management or similar.

name: Global Business Environment
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course Global Business Environment, students will be able to: Identify the key features of the global business environment and understand the interrelations between globalization and international business. Compare and analyze business environments of different economies in terms of risk and opportunity. Apply relevant theories related to global competitiveness, international trade, and economic blocs. Evaluate the potential of emerging markets in international business and assess associated opportunities and challenges. Analyze the role of sustainable development in international business and anticipate its evolving impact.

name: Green Logistics
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course students will know the key principles and practices of green logistics management. Emphasis will be given to the changing role of logistics service providers in the supply chain and the importance of the environmental sustainability in their business models and strategies. By the end of the module, the students will be able to show a critical understanding of the basic principles and major evolving trends in logistics and supply chain management (SCM); to recognize different type of logistics service providers and to assess their development stage; to explore benefits and challenges in implementing the principles of green logistics; to analyze the role of environmental sustainability in the strategy of logistics service providers and related green actions; to design a decarbonization strategy for supply chain and logistics.
content: Basic concepts and evolving trends in logistics and supply chain management Logistics outsourcing: importance, activities, reasons and benefits Definition, categorisation and evolving role of third-party logistics providers (3PL) in the supply chain The environmental impact of transport and logistics Principles of green logistics management Environmental sustainability and green initiatives of 3PLs Decarbonisation footprint audit for supply chain and logistics
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Econ. & Bus.Adm.) studies. For exchange students, B.Sc. studies related to operations management, supply chain management, supply management or similar.

Alan McKinnon, Michael Browne, Maja Piecyk, Anthony Whiteing (2015) Green Logistics: Improving the Environmental Sustainability of Logistics, 3rd edition, Kogan Page. (Chapters 1 and 2) 3. Alan McKinnon (2018) Decarbonizing Logistics. Distributing Goods in a Low Carbon World, 1st edition. Kogan Page, UK. (Chapter 2) 4. Lecture slides, journal articles and other material defined by the teacher.

name: The Principles of Purchasing and Supply Management
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students are familiarized with the concepts of supply management environment and are able to analyze the economic impact of purchasing and supply management function in an organization. Students are able to evaluate the stages of the purchasing process and recognize the total costs involved in purchasing. Students are able to classify suppliers and evaluate supplier performance. Students understand the role of sustainability in purchasing and supply management.

The introduction of goals, total costs and the role of purchasing, purchase process, e-procurement and basic tools (e.g. TCO- and Purchase Portfolio -models), purchasing strategy and outsourcing, buyer-supplier relationships and networks, and sustainable purchasing and supply management.

name: Purchasing tools and cost management
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to give extensive general knowledge about the useful tools, systems and methods related to evaluation and management of supply networks and cost management and in improvement of transparency in supply chain. After completion of the course students: - recognize different inventory management methods - calculate the key figures related to material management - recognize the cost management methods in supply management - understand the role of working capital and cash management in firm's profitability - recognize the means of supply chain finance - know the supplier assessment methods and understand the principles of category management -understand the role of purchasing in supply chain management RealGame simulation is used to show how methods of purchasing can be used in planning and cost management as a part of supply chain. In the simulation the students justify and analyze their decision making and impact on cost management and customer satisfaction.
content: Key concepts of supply management, figures of inventory management, price and cost analyses, total cost management, business process improvement methods, transparency of supply chain, management of working capital, cost management and supply chain finance.

name: Innovation in Supply Networks
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: Identify the most important trends in supply chain innovation; Describe the role of innovation in supply network management; Explain the impact of innovation on sustainable supply network performance in a clear and substantiated way; Reflect on supply chain innovation in different application areas, for instance, pulp and paper and other industries; Create podcasts on the topic related to innovation in supply networks.
content: The importance of supply chain innovation to operational management practices is difficult to underestimate, especially as it concerns developing novel products and services or the use of digital technologies. Supply chain innovation is essential for enhancing supply chain performance and gaining sustainable competitive advantages. The goal of the course is to gain a holistic view of the development and management of advanced innovations through collaboration with supply network partners. The course covers a variety of contemporary topics related to innovation in the supply chain. Course Objectives: Develop a comprehensive understanding of advanced innovation development and management through collaborative supply network partnerships. Explore key internal processes crucial for successful innovation within firms. Analyze diverse perspectives on innovation in firm networks and their overarching impacts. The course is a fully online course that utilizes a novel teaching approach through a series of podcasts with experts from industry and academia. Learning tasks include (i) weekly podcast listening, (ii) weekly online forum discussions, and (iii) final group podcast recording.
learningMaterial: The core content of this course is uniquely delivered through a series of six " Link to Link " podcast episodes , featuring industry and academic experts discussing key topics. Each episode, about an hour long, is structured more as a friendly discussion than a formal interview. While the podcast doesn’t include video, transcripts are available for those who need them. Complementary Materials: Additional Readings . Final Project Support .
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points.Point Distribution (1) Independent Forum Discussion & Comments: max 39* points (2) Final Group Project Work: max 59 points (3) Course Feedback: 2** points

name: Innovation Management
learningOutcomes: This course explores the concept of innovation and how innovation process is managed. Students are expected to understand: - what is an innovation? - how innovations are created? - who innovates? - how innovations are promoted and supported. In addition, students are expected to know: - what it takes to maintain an innovative environment in a company? - what kinds of methods and tools can be used to enhance innovation process? - what makes an organization or a company innovative?
content: How to innovate within a corporation and how to maintain innovative spirit within a corporation. How the innovation influences corporate strategy and how to strategy is designed to attract creative individuals. How to different types of innovations shape corporate environment and affect competition. How a company could gain competitive edge with radical, incremental or disruptive innovation.
learningMaterial: Tidd, J. ; Bessant, J. (2010) Managing Innovation: Integrating Technological, Market and Organizational Change. 4th Edition. John Wiley ; Sons Ltd. Selected journal articles, secondary readings, video clips
evaluationCriteria: The grading scale is 1-5. Group work will give you 0-30 points. Research paper will give you 0-40 points. Moodle-test will give you 0-30 points. Total 100 points. What is valued: Group assignments: Team work, analytical skills and innovative questions and solutions. Term paper: Scientific writing, well organized paper, good argumentation. Moodle test: Three parts, each gives max. 10 points.
workload: Lectures 6 h. Workshops 8 h. On-line mentoring and tutoring 50 h, individual and group work 93 h. Moodle-exam 3 h.Total workload for student 160 h.

name: International Business Strategies
learningOutcomes: The aims of the course are: to familiarize students with strategic planning for international business in general and the management and execution of international business strategies within the context of multinational corporations in particular; to help the students understand various international, regional, or global strategies and their advantages and disadvantages. The business simulation game aims to expose the students to actual management challenges in an international context. After completing the course, the students should be able to: analyse technology-intensive international marketing environment, and generate and carry out properly justified international business strategies; decompose the corporate strategy into functional strategies (e.g. marketing strategy, production strategy, etc.), and coordinate and critically evaluate the implemented strategies, by interpreting key financial indicators of performance; interpret new information critically and systematically and be able to develop ideas and projects based on this information; apply knowledge gained from the course, to the events, activities, and/or strategies of an actual firm or organisation; Additionally, the students will develop the following soft transferable skills: work effectively in a multicultural team; show initiative and leadership abilities; manage and prioritize one's workload and time effectively; develop a mindset that fosters sustainability, and global, market, and technology orientation in a global business environment. participate in discussions on topics of international business interest, and stimulate and answer questions from a knowledgeable audience
content: Must Know: Strategic tools for analyzing the internal and external environment, for example, resource and product positions. The international business planning process and its content. International and global business strategies. Organization of resources, capabilities, and knowledge within a multinational corporation. Implementation methods of an international business strategy. Should Know: Corporate social responsibility and sustainability International finance, international production, and sourcing strategies. Nice to Know: The skills and application of critical inquiry into reading, discussions, issues, and experiences related to international business strategies. Real-life firm strategy examples (provided by guest lecturers).
prerequisites: A330A0252 Internationalization of the Firm and Global Marketing A320A2000 Global Business Environment
learningMaterial: Lasserre, P: (2012). Global Strategic Management (3rd edition or newer). Peng, M.W. (2014). Global Strategic Management (3rd edition or newer) Assigned reading (announced on lectures). Guide manual for the simulation (online). Slides from the lectures.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Assignments: project work in groups (written strategy plan, final report, and seminar presentation): 70 points (+ possibility to earn bonus points for best-performing teams); individual assignment (short essays based on case studies and lecture materials), 30 points. Active class participation (possibility to earn bonus points from participation in specific activities). All assignments must be passed.
workload: Lectures: 18h. Final seminar: 4h. Group assignment (simulation exercise and related assignments: strategic plan and final report): 120 h. Mid-term tutorial (each group independently with instructor): 0,5 h. Individual assignments: 17,5 h. Total course: 160 h. Participation requirements: • Lectures: no mandatory participation (but there is an opportunity to earn bonus points by participation in some lectures). Lectures are conducted in class, recorded but not streamed (recording will be available shortly after the lecture). • Final seminar: participation is mandatory (those who missed must complete the substitution assignment). The seminar is conducted in a hybrid format (remote participation is allowed, but not recommended, especially for presenters). • Mid-term tutorial: at least two members from each group must be present. The meeting can be organized on campus, online, or in a hybrid format (agreed individually with each group).

name: International Entrepreneurial Journey
learningOutcomes: Upon successful completion of the "International Entrepreneurial Journey" course, students will be able to: 1. Recognize entrepreneurial opportunities and transform them into viable business ideas. 2. Evaluate the potential of international entrepreneurial opportunities, considering market dynamics and global trends. 3. Cultivate creativity and employ effective methods for idea generation in the entrepreneurial context. 4. Develop comprehensive plans for international start-ups. 5. Effectively communicate project-related issues and collaborate with team members.
content: The International Entrepreneurial Journey course offers an immersive and dynamic learning experience that empowers students to embark on a transformative entrepreneurial voyage. Divided into two distinct phases, this course equips students with the essential skills and knowledge an entrepreneur needs to navigate the challenging landscape of international business by focusing on theoretical understanding and practical skills necessary for entrepreneurship. Phase 1: Ideation and Opportunity Development phase - Students will embark on a journey of discovery, unleashing their creativity and honing their ability to identify entrepreneurial opportunities. Through hands-on exercises and interactive workshops, students will cultivate their ideas, transforming them into robust and actionable business propositions with a global outlook. Emphasis will be placed on identifying international business potential and formulating strategies to maximize it. Moreover, teams will craft a persuasive pitching deck to communicate their business ideas effectively. Phase 2: Launching International Ventures - Building upon the foundation laid in the idea development phase, students will progress to the second stage, focused on launching international ventures in small, "start-up teams" made up of three to five members. This course phase emphasizes the practical aspects of turning ideas into reality. Students will acquire managerial and organizational knowledge skills necessary for launching a business successfully. Effective communication and collaboration within the entrepreneurial team are also emphasized, enabling students to engage and navigate complex interactions with project stakeholders. Culminating Event - The course culminates in a pitching event and feedback session, where each team will present their business ideas to a distinguished panel of experienced experts. This real-world experience provides students with valuable insights, constructive feedback, and the opportunity to showcase their entrepreneurial acumen.
prerequisites: Bachelor’s degree in business (Econ. & Bus. Adm.) or equivalent.
learningMaterial: Lecture materials and any additional material provided by the teachers.

name: International Entrepreneurship Challenge
learningOutcomes: The learning outcomes of the course are the following: 1. to be able to analyze and describe the processes of international entrepreneurship both from theoretical and practical standpoints 2. to be able to evaluate and discuss the main characteristics of successful international entrepreneurs 3. to be able to estimate the nature, benefits and drawbacks of an international expansion strategy in entrepreneurial firms 4. to be able to assess the actual opportunities and challenges that entrepreneurs have to deal with when internationalizing their businesses 5. to be able to evaluate and compare the variety of international marketing strategies available to organizations in a range of environmental contexts 6. to be able to develop internationalization plan and international marketing plan for early stages of internationalization 7. to be able to apply the knowledge on entrepreneurial firm internationalization in knowledge and technology-intensive environments 8. to be able to collaborate in cross-cultural teams 9. to be able to design and deliver various kinds of presentations focusing on international entrepreneurship and marketing for a corporate audience
content: Evolution of international entrepreneurship as a field of study, development of internationalization plan, competitive strategies and international business operations for small and medium-sized firms: e.g. marketing, human resources, R&D and financing, managing entrepreneurial ventures in the global marketplace, tools and frameworks in analysis of a particular international entrepreneurial opportunity and creation of a business plan and marketing strategy. Characteristics of successful international entrepreneurs, specific features of knowledge-intensive, high tech and software industries, project management.
prerequisites: A330A0252 Internationalization of the Firm and Global Marketing (or equivalent course)

name: International Financial Reporting
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, the student will be able to understand and apply IFRS standards in the preparation of financial statements. The student will comprehend key IFRS topics such as business combinations, leases, financial instruments, and asset impairments. The course also aims to develop the student’s critical thinking and analytical skills in the context of international financial reporting.
content: The course focuses on the knowledge and application of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) in financial statement preparation. It also provides insights into international differences in financial reporting and their practical implications for accounting practices. Key topics include IAS/IFRS standards, their application in business combinations, leases, financial instruments, and impairment of assets.

name: Introduction to International Entrepreneurship
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, students will be able to: 1. describe the phenomenon of international entrepreneurship from theoretical and practical viewpoint 2. characterise entrepreneurial/startup culture 3. describe, evaluate and reproduce the process of international entrepreneurship (startup internationalisation process including opportunity recognition, innovation and value creation, value delivery and value capture/opportunity exploitation) in a variety of contexts 4. understand and assess challenges of international entrepreneurship in a variety of international contexts 5. evaluate, compare and select in a justified manner different internationalisation strategies for new ventures in a variety of contexts 6. demonstrate competences in using tools, primary and/or secondary data sources for strategic analysis and management of a new venture 7. able to create a business development plan and its presentation for a corporate audience with a focus on growth and internationalisation 8. discuss and self-reflect on the role of different personal skills and organisational capabilities in new venture creation and new venture management 9. collaborate in a cross-cultural team.
content: Are you considering an entrepreneurial career, work in a small, agile and rapidly growing firm or do you want to develop entrepreneurial and intrapreneurial skills? In all these cases, this course is for you! Despite the rising popularity of entrepreneurship, several challenges await every start-up already at the stages of product/service development, proof of concept and prototyping. Furthermore, multiple managerial issues constantly emerge - dealing with limited resources and fierce competition, a need to build external relations being a small firm, a need in a constant change and agility along with a mission to grow rapidly and internationally. Large firms, as employers, in turn, seek for curious candidates with intrapreneurial mindset - self-motivated, proactive, and action-oriented people who take the initiative to pursue an innovative and international product, service or project. The course is designed in a way that every student gets a chance to understand the fundamentals of international entrepreneurship, gets a deep dive into the challenges of a start-up using a case study and to develop and test own skills in solving the case specific challenge. The students form teams to solve a complex new venture challenge of their choice. The course encourages a combination of theoretical and practical approaches to building a comprehensive understanding of international entrepreneurship. In addition to a group work on challenge solution, the course also has two individual assignments: a self-reflection assignment and an individual essay-based electronic exam.

learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will: Be able to model strategic sales, understand how value is sold, recognize what constitutes value, and comprehend how value may differ for various decision-makers. Be capable of articulating value creation through theoretical frameworks. Be able to assess the suitability of different sales models for various product and service offerings. Be able to identify digital sales technologies for different use cases and understand their potential in relation to various sales models. Additionally, the student will understand how to sell to different types of buyers, recognize the decision-making criteria behind purchasing, and comprehend how sustainability requirements relate to strategic sales.
content: Strategic, sustainable sales Value-based selling and value definition Different sales models Sales technologies and AI Customer purchase decision criteria Different buyer roles
prerequisites: For Master's Program in Strategic Sales students only.

learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student - Understands the significance of knowledge for organizational performance and the key principles of knowledge management - Knows and is able to explain the key concepts and elements of knowledge management - Recognizes and is able to compare the different approaches of knowledge management - Is able to apply theories and models of knowledge management to examine organizations

learningOutcomes: After the course the student can understand, recognize and define key concepts of leadership. The student can also understand issues related to leading knowledge-intensive organizations, knowledge-intensive work and knowledge-intensive workers. The student understands the role of leadership in these contexts and is able to recognize and solve problematic situations related to leading knowledge-intensive work.
content: The course focuses on history and modern approaches to leadership. The first theme includes development of leadership thinking, feature and behavioral theories, feelings and power, development of leadership in work contexts, problematic situations in work environment, and leadership in change and conflict situations. The second theme of the course relates to leadership of specialist organizations and leading diversity. The course is related to sustainability.

The student is also able to describe and paraphrase theoretical entities that are composed by the association of the basic concepts.
content: Basic concepts and tools of management. Leadership and work community. The basic concepts related to entrepreneurship and different forms of entrepreneurship. The course is related to sustainability.
learningMaterial: 1. Literature assigned by the lecturers. 2. Lecture notes and other material distributed during the course.

name: Economics of Management
learningOutcomes: The student is able to explain how transactions and production costs influence the boundaries of the firm after completing the course. He is also able to analyze the impact of the nature of market competition to the strategic decisions of a firm, and apply this knowledge to study by what kinds of means the firm is able to improve its position in markets and attain sustainable competitive advantage. Moreover he is able to analyze how to set incentives in an efficient way from the point of view of organization of the firm.
content: The horizontal and vertical boundaries of the firm, the impact of competitive structure of decision making, strategic decision making of a firm (e.g. pricing, commitment, entry and exit etc.), attaining and sustaining of competitive advantage, and internal organization and incentives of firm. The evolution of business organizations. Diversification and social context of a firm.
learningMaterial: (1) Besanko D. et al: Economics of Strategy 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th tai 7th ed. (2) Articles on strategy.

name: International and Cross-Cultural Selling

Can identify and select appropriate sales channels, human resources, and potential partnerships for building sales operations in different international environments and industries. Recognizes the cultural challenges of international sales and knows how to operate in different cultural contexts. Understands the basic principles of international customer relationship management.
content: Internationalization strategy and plan (go-to-market strategy). International sales channels, networks, and their management. Technologies and marketing in support of international sales operations. Leading personnel and sales teams in an international environment. Analyzing different cultures and preparing for various business practices. International customer relationship management.

name: International Financial Reporting Standards and Consolidated Financial Statements
learningOutcomes: The course familiarizes students with the obligation, content, and objectives of preparing consolidated financial statements. It provides basic skills for interpreting and analyzing consolidated financial statements. Regarding international accounting standards, the course introduces the requirements of IFRS and develops the ability to compare differences between Finnish regulations and US GAAP. Upon completing the course, the student: Understands the concept of a group (consolidated entity) and can analyze its significance in business Understands the importance of eliminating intra-group transactions and ownership, as well as the role of non-controlling interests, and can apply these principles in practical situations Is familiar with consolidation methods and can justify their use in different scenarios Can interpret the group’s cash flow statement and analyze its relevance for decision-making Understands the background and development of IFRS and can assess its implications Understands the principles of preparing and presenting consolidated financial statements and can apply them in more demanding situations Is familiar with and can apply key accounting standards and assess their impact on corporate reporting Knows the key differences between IFRS, Finnish accounting legislation, and US GAAP, and can analyze the implications of these differences in an international business environment
content: The concept of a group. Regulations on consolidated financial statements. Scope and objectives of consolidated financial statements. Elimination of intra-group transactions. Elimination of intra-group ownership and recognition of non-controlling interests. Consolidation of associated companies and joint ventures. Changes in group structure. Group cash flow statement. IFRS standards. Differences between various accounting standards.
prerequisites: A250A0250 Kirjanpidon peruskurssi, A250A0600 Rahoituksen perusteet and A250A1050 Yritysrahoitus (recommended) or A250A1051 Yritysrahoituksen perusteet.
learningMaterial: Literature: - Englund T., Prepula E., Riistama V. ja Tuokko Y. : Konsernitilinpäätös – kirjanpitolain mukaan. 3. uudistettu painos. WSOY, 2005 ISBN 951-0-30133-7, - Haaramo V.: IFRS-raportointi (internet: fokus.talentum.fi). Other study materials: - Handouts.

name: LUTES Startup Program
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of this course and the accompanying Forward Accelerator program, students are expected to demonstrate the ability to articulate a clear vision and mission for their venture, develop a viable business model, and produce a minimum viable product (MVP) suitable for initial market testing. Students will learn to define and analyze target customer segments, engage systematically in customer-feedback processes, and communicate the value of their business concept to both customers and financial stakeholders. In addition, students will acquire knowledge of startup financing alternatives, understand the role of professional and entrepreneurial networks, and develop the skills necessary to build and leverage such networks. The course also provides structured training in pitching techniques. Each team will be assigned a mentor who will support their progress throughout the program.
content: The course is offered in two formats: a 6-credit and a 10-credit implementation. The credit value corresponds to the duration and intensity of the associated startup program. Both the 6-week and 10-week versions comprise weekly workshops and written assignments addressing central themes in entrepreneurship. Workshops are delivered by professionals with recognized expertise in the field.
learningMaterial: Will be announced before/during the course
evaluationCriteria: Grading scale: 1–5. The final grade is determined by two components: 50 % written plans and reports produced by the founding team, 50 % an individual learning diary. Evaluation emphasizes the quality, coherence, and analytical depth of the submitted materials, as well as the application of entrepreneurial theory—particularly within the 10-week implementation.
workload: Successful completion of the LUTES Startup Program course requires active participation in the Forward Accelerator program organized by LUTES ry. Assessment of completion is based on continuous engagement in accelerator activities, submission of a comprehensive summary report, and inclusion of all design-related documents produced during the course as appendices. Students must also maintain an individual learning diary in which they document, analyze, and critically reflect on their team’s activities using the theoretical frameworks provided during the course. Active participation in all course components and completion of all required assignments are mandatory.

name: Macroeconomics
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: After completion of the course the students are able to: - describe the basic mechanisms and functioning of the modern market economy - explain the basic concepts of macroeconomics and apply them when analyzing the means of economic policy, such as fiscal- monetary-, exchange rate-, and incomes policy - recognize and distinguish alternative economic policy explanations for the relative efficiency of monetary and fiscal policies using the AD-AS model (applied into Finnish conditions) in the closed and open economies. - explain the mechanisms behind unemployment and inflation phenomena and discuss about their background assumptions and analyze the origins of the financial and euro crisis.
content: The goals and means of macroeconomic policy. Keynesian basic model. Business cycles both in the closed and open economies explained by means of the AD-AS- and IS-LM-models. Unemployment, inflation, economic fluctuations, monetary, exchange rate and fiscal policies and their efficiency in different exchange regimes. Ability to understand economic policy-related discussions. The impact of globalization on national economies.
learningMaterial: 1. Lecture notes 2. Mankiw, N. G. Macroeconomics, 4th edition or newer. Chapters 2, 3, 4 1-2., 9, 13, 15, (according to the 7th edition). 3. Separate articles to be distributed.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, written exam 100%.
workload: Lectures 18 h, independent reading of Mankiw’s book, lecture slides, and other materials distributed, preparation for lectures 52 h, written exam and preparation for the exam 90 h. Total workload 160 h.

name: Management Consulting Case Workshop
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing this course, students will be able to: Explain the role, purpose, and key phases of the management consulting process Analyze client needs and translate them into clearly defined consulting tasks and project plans Develop and structure a consulting offer based on a given case Present and justify consulting solutions and proposals in a professional manner Evaluate consulting services from the client perspective and act as an informed buyer of consulting support
content: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of management consulting from both consultant and client perspectives. Students gain an overview of the consulting process, including understanding client needs, defining development tasks, planning projects, creating and pricing consulting offers, and presenting solutions.
prerequisites: This course is for masters' students in business administration, industrial engineering and management and social sciences.
learningMaterial: To be confirmed.
evaluationCriteria: Accepted/Failed. Compulsory attendance on all sessions.
workload: 4 hours of online lectures and seminars, 8 hours of onsite seminars. Preparation for workshop, including reading and written pre-workshop assignment 40 h. Workshop assignment 28 h. Total workload for student ca. 80 h.

name: Managing International Marketing
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to let the students experiment with the strategic planning for international marketing in general and management and execution of international marketing strategies within the context of multinational corporations in particular. The idea is to help the students to develop an understanding of various international or global marketing strategies and critically evaluate their advantages and disadvantages. The assignment [simulation] aims to expose the students to actual management challenges in an international marketing environment. Intended learning outcomes: after completing the course the students should be able to: * analyze international marketing environment, and to develop and carry out properly justified international marketing strategies. * to coordinate and critically evaluate the implemented strategies, by interpreting key indicators of performance; * plan, communicate, and carry out a group research project applied to a firm in a simulation, * work in a multi-cultural team; * be able to interpret new information critically and systematically and be able to develop ideas and projects based on this information; * be able to apply knowledge gained from the course, in addition to that provided by additional reading, analysis and discussion, to the events, activities and/or strategies of an actual firm or organization; * participate in discussion on topics of international marketing interest, and to stimulate and answer questions from a knowledgeable audience; * develop a mindset that fosters sustainability, and global, market and technology orientation in a global business environment
content: The skills and application of critical inquiry into your reading, discussions, and situations and experiences that you encounter with regard to international marketing, both inside and outside the classroom setting. The international business planning process and its content especially related to international marketing. International and global marketing strategies, including e.g. standardisation vs. adaptation, transfer pricing, customer portfolio management, channel strategies, sales management and sustainability. Decision-making, management, organization and control of marketing-related resources, capabilities and knowledge within a multinational corporation. Implementation methods of an international marketing strategy. Real-life firm international marketing strategy and organisation examples (provided by guest lecturers).
prerequisites: A330A0300 Strategic Global Marketing Management, A330A0252 Internationalization of the Firm and Global Marketing or similar courses taken elsewhere.
learningMaterial: Peng, M.W. (2022). Global Strategy (5th edition). Assigned reading (collection of articles). Guide manual for the simulation. Slides from the lectures.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Active class participation 20%. Assignment(s) 30 % exam, 50 % game strategic plan and report. All assignments (including the exam) must be passed.
workload: 2 h introduction lecture, 12h of interactive lectures, and a 2-hour seminar for the simulation training, 1st period. 14 h of interactive lectures and 2-hour simulation reflection seminar, 2nd period. name: Marketing Research with R
learningOutcomes: This course is the foundational prerequisite for advanced studies in the A240A0040 Marketing Analytics. It equips students with essential skills to enhance their digital marketing analytics capabilities using the statistical programming interface of R/RStudio. Participants will gain proficiency in analyzing marketing research data through descriptive and inferential statistics, creating impactful visualizations (e.g., tables, charts, and interactive dashboards), and applying data-driven insights to solve marketing challenges. Key topics include fundamentals of marketing research with R, descriptive statistics, data exploration, and visualization techniques using R, secondary data analysis and experimental research using R, and designing interactive dashboards. The course takes a practice-driven approach, incorporating real-world examples, datasets, and case studies, preparing students for data-driven decision-making. By the end of this course, students will be able to: ILO1: Analyze marketing research data to draw meaningful conclusions for decision-making using the statistical programming interface of R/RStudio ILO2: Create clear and compelling visualizations to effectively communicate marketing insights using R/RStudio
content: Key topics: Fundamentals of Marketing Research with R, Descriptive Statistics and Data Exploration using R, Visualization Techniques using R, Secondary Data Analysis and Experimental Research using R, and Designing Interactive Dashboards using RStudio. Lectures include interactive activities and require active student participation. The online tutorials provide practical, hands-on experience with R/RStudio, using case studies as a foundation for learning.

content: This course is the last course in the Master’s Programme of International Business and Entrepreneurship (6 ECTS credits). The aim of the course is to help students to identify, assess and reflect on how their personal experiences (past and present) ground their attitudes and assumptions about entrepreneurship today. It also aims to aspire students to consider entrepreneurship as their (potential) career path. To achieve this aim, the course supports students in identifying and reflecting on their current entrepreneurial competencies, gives possibilities to further extend these competencies through teamwork during a real-life business development assignment. The course also gives students tools for reflecting on how their potential entrepreneurial career path in the future could look like. After the course, students are expected to understand the entrepreneurial competencies they have, the competencies they still wish to develop, and get a sense of what their potential paths are – and the landscape for an entrepreneurial career with successes and failures – to becoming and being an entrepreneur in a modern and global business environment
