name: MIMIR Fellows
learningOutcomes: On the highest level the students will get a systemic view of the entrepreneurial ecosystem: understanding and identifying the different elements in entrepreneurial ecosystems and their interlinkages, in Finland and beyond. The aim is not to “convert” the students into entrepreneurs, but rather offer them a comprehensive understanding of startups and entrepreneurship as well as a mindset and toolbox that they later can leverage upon, whichever path they choose. The real outcomes of this program are expected to materialize in the next decade. In the shorter term, students are expected to develop an understanding of the requirements for deep tech entrepreneurship, and the logic behind commercializing research. The main focus is to support the students on their own unique learning paths. The diversity of the students will be reflected on their learning paths, and emphasis is put on their personal growth.
content: MIMIR Fellows is a pan-Nordic entrepreneurship program and community run simultaneously in university cities around the Nordics. The program is called after Mímir – a figure in Norse mythology known for his wisdom. The aim is to educate a new generation of entrepreneurs to have the readiness to take deep tech from universities around the Nordics to the market. Guest lecturers and partners will ensure the involvement of industry and investors in our mission to reimagine technology transfer. The MIMIR Fellows Program follows the pedagogical approach of the Aalto University course, Aalto Fellows . First adopted to a Nordic context in 2015, the course was originally modeled on Stanford’s flagship entrepreneurship course – the Mayfield Fellows program , an in-depth, 9 month work/study experience for 12 students. While these preceding courses introduce students to the broader context of the surrounding startup ecosystem, the MIMIR Fellows program will focus on deep tech entrepreneurship and the unique characteristics of research commercialization and academic entrepreneurship. The MIMIR Fellows consists of three parts: i) pre-readings and assignments, ii) one week of intensive lectures, planned for the intensive week at the end of February 2026 iii) students will raise funds for and organize a study trip to an international entrepreneurial ecosystem in the fall 2026. The program provides the students with a comprehensive and systemic view of deep tech entrepreneurship and its context: the intersection between the entrepreneurial ecosystem and the world of academia. The program also aims to bridge academia, i.e. students and participating professors, and the Finnish startup ecosystem, including but not limited to investors, founders, and ecosystem leaders. The students’ personal growth is in focus, and they are supported in formulating their own understanding of how deep-tech startups and the supporting ecosystem function. Up to 12 students are selected through a two-phased selection process. Emphasis is put on diversity, the group including both undergraduate and graduate students with art, science, engineering, and business backgrounds. The selection process is geared towards finding a diverse group of extraordinary students: some may not be at all familiar with the entrepreneurial ecosystem, while others may have worked at the heart of it prior to taking the course. The aim is to prepare the students to work within or with the intersection of academia and the entrepreneurial ecosystems around the world, today and in the future, whether working for a startup, corporation, investment fund, non-governmental organization, or the government. The program is presented to the students as pieces in a puzzle, and the task of assembling the puzzle is left to each of them individually. A systems perspective is emphasized, and curious inquiry rewarded. In addition, one of the 12 students might be selected as a course assistant to ensure the continuity of the program in 2027.

learningOutcomes: The course objective is to familiarize the students with new trends in management, especially regarding sustainable business. content: The course will focus on questions concerning technological advancement, social transformation, and perceptions of nature. It will begin by examining how management as a field is increasingly transdisciplinary and how it advances by connecting to both natural and social sciences, as well as to humanities. The course will then proceed to investigating the questions of responsibility and desires in business, including the potential and perils of technology. It will discuss the requirements of transformation in cultures of growth and the importance of how nature is perceived. Implications to practice are discussed in-class.

name: Organizational Behaviour
learningOutcomes: The goal of the course is to familiarize students with the organizational behavior as a theoretical phenomenon. The course focuses on human behavior, factors affecting human behavior and consequences of human behavior in organizations. After completing the course students should be able to: - define the key concepts of organizational behavior and identify these concepts by definition - understand and describe the key theoretical entities that are composed by the association of the basic concepts.
content: The course focuses on human behavior in organizations, addressing it as a phenomenon at the individual, team, and organizational levels, all of which are interconnected. At the individual level, central themes include personality, psychological capital, values, perceptions, decision-making, attitudes, motivations, and moods/emotions. At the group or team level, central themes revolve around team or group management, group dynamics, power dynamics, politics, conflicts, and negotiation strategies for team behavior. At the organizational level, central themes involve organizational structure, culture, and change management. Since groups and organizations are comprised of individuals, it's crucial to understand individual behaviors, which influence the behaviors of other individuals (groups and organizations) and vice versa. Group and organizational factors also influence individual behavior.
prerequisites: The language of the course is English: all the course materials and assignments are in English.
learningMaterial: 1. Robbins, S.P. & Judge, T. A and Campbell. (2010). Organizational Behaviour. Edition, New Jersey; Pearson/Prentice Hall. 2. Materials announced by the lecturer.

workload: This is a fully online (100%) course. The learning path is structured to foster independent, self-directed learning through individual and group assignments on Moodle. The total workload for students is 160 hours, which includes 86 hours for independent study, including familiarization with the textbook and assignment materials, as well as completing individual and group tasks. Additionally, 74 hours are allocated for the exam and exam preparation, which is conducted electronically.

name: Organizational Learning
learningOutcomes: The objective of the course is to introduce students to the key theories and methodologies of organizational learning and demonstrate their practical application in organizational development and management. By the course's conclusion, students should be able to: Comprehend the fundamental concepts and theories of organizational learning. Understand the facilitators, operational principles, and management strategies related to organizational learning. Acquaint themselves with Problem-Based Learning (PBL). Analyze organizational phenomena through the lens of organizational learning theories. Apply organizational learning theories and methodologies to future work, learning scenarios, and managerial roles.
content: The course is designed to facilitate students' self-directed learning, guided by the principles of student-centered learning and Problem-Based Learning (PBL). The course comprises the following components: Orientation and introduction Individual literature study: Independent reading and essay writing based on assigned course materials (scientific articles) Peer evaluation conducted in pairs or small groups, based on individual literature study Reflection
prerequisites: The course is exclusively for Master’s level students. The course is conducted entirely in English, including all materials and assignments.
learningMaterial: Assigned reading and collection of scientific articles
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, individual literature study 95%, peer evaluation 5%
workload: Total workload for students: 160 hours, comprising 1) introduction to organizational learning (20 hours), 2) individual literature study, involving reading assigned scientific articles and writing an essay (130 hours), 3) peer evaluation based on individual study in small groups (10 hours).

name: Organization Theory
learningOutcomes: Students learn the basics approaches in organization theory and are able to analyze and compare different approaches. In addition, they learn skills in actively participating in discussions, make written reports, and engage in creative and critical thinking.
content: Development of organization theory, different metaphors and perspectives. Organization and its environment. Social and hierarchical structure. Technology. Organizational culture. Power, control, trust and conflicts in organizations. Novel approaches to organization theory.
prerequisites: The course is only for the Master’s level students
learningMaterial: Book and materials selected by the teacher.
evaluationCriteria: Grading 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points. Assignments and other additional tasks.
workload: Seminars 16 h. Individual literature study: independent and intensive reading and reporting of the provided course materials, assignments (individual and group) (144 h). Altogether 160 hours of work.

name: Organizing in Knowledge-Based Networks
learningOutcomes: - Students can describe the key theoretical concepts and theories on knowledge-based organizing and apply them in practical cases - Students can apply the theory and key skills related to working a digital platform to solve real-life complex problems - Students can reflect their individual and team behavior - Students can present effectively their project outcomes to customer - Students can discuss their solution constructively, give & get feedback and document the lessons learned by the project team
content: - Key concepts related to organizing knowledge - New forms of organizing: Ecosystems, digital platforms, collaborative communities and temporary teams
learningMaterial: Articles distributed by lecturers, online-material
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0 – 5. Individual exercises 30 % and group exercises 70 %.
workload: Lectures and interactive seminars 24 h, 1-3. periods. Independent studying online 72 h, Course assignment work (learning diary and real-life sustainability related problem solving in temporary teams on a digital collaboration platform) 64 h. Total workload for student 160 h

name: Orientation to Sustainability Thinking
learningOutcomes: Identify and define central concepts and frameworks related to sustainability. Recognize the interconnectedness of economic, social and environmental sustainability issues. Understand and develop own individual role in driving sustainability.
content: Sustainable development goals, planetary boundaries, sustainable LUT and LAB.
learningMaterial: Online materials and assignments in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Pass-Fail
workload: Online materials and assignments. Total 54 h. Course cannot be completed with previous studies. After the course enrolment in Sisu/Peppi it might take a few days before the course is visible in Moodle.

name: Co-operatives and Sustainable Development
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, student understands the goals, basics and history related to sustainable development goals and understands how cooperation and sustainable development are connected to each other and how different cooperatives can contribute to answering to the challenges related to sustainable development at the international, national and local level in the globalized context. Students are able to analyze the implementation of sustainable development goals as well as their impacts and interconnections to the business of cooperatives.
content: Online course. Investigation and familiarization with the concept of sustainable development, it´s fields and background and how it is connected to the cooperation. Operation of cooperatives are analyzed and viewed comprehensively from the sustainable development goals´s perspective, considering economic, social and ecological perspective. Tasks of the course enable students to focus to the specific field of cooperation (that interests most) from sustainable development perspective. Student can conduct the tasks of the course either in Finnish or in English.
learningMaterial: Brundtland's commission report: Our common future. http://www.un-documents.net/wced-ocf.htm Agenda 2030. https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/post2015/transformingourworld Henrÿ, Hagen (2013) Sustainable Development and Cooperative Law: Corporate Social Responsibility or Cooperative Social Responsibility? in: International and Comparative Corporate Law Journal Vol.10, Issue.3, 2013, 58-75 Hingley, M., Mikkola, M., Canavari, M. & Asiol, D. (2011) Local and sustainable food supply: The Role of European Retail Consumer Co-operatives. Journal on Food System Dynamics, vol 2, no 4. ILO:n and ICA publication: Cooperatives and Sustainable Development Goals, http://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---d_emp/documents/publication/wcms_240640.pdf Peredo, A., M., Chrisman, J. J. (2006) Toward a theory of community-based enterprise. Academy of Management Review, 31(2):309-328. Tenaw, Heinonen, Karhu & Ollila (toim.) (2015) Osuuskunnat ja kestävä kehitys, Pellervo-seura → erityisesti Visa Heinosen artikkeli Osuustoiminnan pitkä linja ja kestävän kehityksen haasteet, http://pellervo.fi/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/osuuskunnat-ja-kestava-kehitys.pdf?cd9ca8 Other literature or materials announced by the teacher.
evaluationCriteria: Evaluation 0-5 grade, independent learning assignment 25 %, Moodle-exam 25 %, independent final assignment 50 %, summary assignment: approved/failed, participation to the online-discussions: approved/failed
workload: Online-lectures 4h. Participation to the online-discussions 15h. Independent learning assignment 25h. Independent final assignment 58h. Independent study 31h and independent summary writing 27h. Total working hours 160h

name: Co-operative Business and Management
learningOutcomes: After completing the course student understands the special characteristics of co-operatives from the management and corporate purpose point of view. Student understands the characteristics of co-operatives and how these influences especially to the governance, decision-making, marketing and management of co-operatives. The student can analyze and report the business of selected case-co-operative from different perspectives in the independent learning assignment.
content: The impact of characteristics of co-operative business model to the firm´s goal, dual-nature, ownership, surplus distribution, governance structure, decision-making and marketing and management. The course focuses especially on consumer co-operatives.
learningMaterial: Tuominen, Pasi (2012:) The Purpose of Consumer Co-operation: Implications for the Management and Governance of Co-operatives. Lappeenranta University of Technology. Available also: http://www.doria.fi/bitstream/handle/10024/86193/-is-bn%209789522653093.pdf?sequence=1 Tuominen, Terhi (2013): The accumulation of financial and social capital as a means to achieve a sustained competitive advantage for consumer co-operatives Väitöskirja. Acta Universitatis Lappeenrantaensis 548. Lappeenranta University of Technology. Yliopistopaino 2013. Available also: http://www.doria.fi/bitstream/han-dle/10024/93983/isbn9789522655103.pdf?sequence=2 Puusa, A., Mönkkönen, K. & Varis, A. (2013) Mission lost? Dilemmatic dual nature of co-operatives. Journal of Co-operative Organization and Management, 1 (1), 6-14 Other material announced by the teacher.
evaluationCriteria: Arviointi 0 - 5. Itsenäinen oppimistehtävä 80 % ja essee 20 % kurssin loppuarvosanasta. Kaikki osuudet suoritettava hyväksytysti. Aalto-yliopiston kauppakorkeakoulun, Itä-Suomen yliopiston ja LUT-yliopiston opiskelijoille hyväksytysti suoritettu lisätehtävä: referaatti artikkelista (+1 op).
workload: LUT students and Aalto-University students choose completion method 1, others choose completion method 2. Online lectures and videos 4 h, Active participation virtually to the course discussions and commentary, 11 h. Independent familiarization with literature (and additional material) 40 h, Independent learning assignment plan 8 h. Independent learning assignment of chosen case-cooperative 52 h. Essay learning assignment, 20 h. Additional assigment (essay of an article) for students at LUT-University, Eastern-Finland and Aalto students, 25 h. Total 160 h.

name: Philosophy of Science
learningOutcomes: The philosophy of science is relevant for doctoral researchers as they contemplate fundamental questions about reality: How do I perceive the world? Where does my research fit within the broader scientific landscape? The completed reading diary from the course serves as a partial foundation for developing the introductory chapter of one’s doctoral dissertation.
content: Definition of Science and the Demarcation Problem Assess: What makes my work scientific? The Historical Nature of Science Understand: The roots of scientific thinking. Exploring Different Schools within the Philosophy of Science Situate : What is my philosophy of science? Recognizing the Structure of an Argument Reason : What is my method and main thesis? Connecting the Philosophy of Science to One’s Own Research Present: My topic and its connection to the philosophy of science.
prerequisites: Master’s degree
learningMaterial: Selected parts from Godfrey-Smith's book Theory and Reality: An Introduction to Philosophy of Science (UCP, 2003), additional reading assigned, and lecture materials.
evaluationCriteria: Active participation, oral presentation ca. 15 minutes and reading diary ca. 10 pages.
workload: Contact teaching, with the option to participate remotely. Lectures, reading groups, guest lectures and oral presentations, including preparation (66 hours). Reading selected chapters from the course book and the assigned material (40 hours). Writing a learning diary (30 hours). Total workload: 136 hours.
equivalentCoursesInfo: Student's who have previously completed the course A210AJ202 Philosophy of Science for Business Studies, can't take this course.

name: Philosophy of Science for Business Studies
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: This course provides students basic knowledge of the philosophy of science in order to equip students for comparing and assessing scientific theories and research methods, and for understanding theoretical and methodological discourse involving business administration. The written assignments for the course give students extensive knowledge of the philosophy of science and allow them to use this knowledge in the evaluation and development of the motivation and argumentation of their own research.
content: Argumentation, theory of knowledge, induction and deduction, main schools of the science of philosophy, scientific explanation and the ethics of science.
learningMaterial: Literature examination: (1) Barker Gillian & Kitcher Philip: Philosophy of science, a new introduction, (2) Lawrence F. et al.: Reading and Understanding Research, 3rd ed. (3) Bryman, Alan ; Bell, Emma: Business Research Methods, 2nd, 3 rd ed. chapters 1, 5 and 24 or 4th ed, chapters 2, 6 and 26, or Bryman, Alan ; Bell, Emma and Harley, Bill: Business Research Methods 5th ed. chapters 2, 6 and 26. (4) Cartwright Nancy & Montuschi, Eleonora (eds.). Philosophy of Social Science, a new introduction, chapters 7, 9 and 15. (5) Responsible conduct of research (RCR), The Finnish National Board on Research Integrity TENK, https://tenk.fi/en/research-misconduct/responsible-conduct-research-rcr
evaluationCriteria: Written exam or written assignments 100%, 0-5.
workload: Independent preparation for written exam or written assignments provided by the course instructor 162 h. Total workload for student 162 h.

name: Philosophy of Science for Technology Post-graduates
learningOutcomes: This course provides students basic knowledge of the philosophy of science in order to equip students for comparing and assessing scientific theories and research methods, and for understanding theoretical and methodological discourse. The written assignments for the course give students extensive knowledge of the philosophy of science and allow them to use this knowledge in the evaluation and development of the motivation and argumentation of their own research.
content: Argumentation, theory of knowledge, induction and deduction, main schools of the science of philosophy, scientific explanation and the ethics of science.
learningMaterial: Course material is handed out in lectures.
evaluationCriteria: Assígnments 100%, 0-5
workload: 16 h of lectures, 16 h of seminar work and 128 h independent work. The course is completed by attending classes and completing the assignments. Lectures are about the general philosophy of science, seminar works handle the philosophy of technology and ethics. The detailed instructions will be sent to students who enroll for the course in spring 2020.

name: Presentation Methods
learningOutcomes: The student is able to - create a visual presentation of a design - facilitate discussion by drawing - create finalized presentation materials and work drawings - explain the possibilities and restrictions of both hand drawn and digital presentation methods.
prerequisites: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching
learningMaterial: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching
workload: Details under the header Teaching

name: Principles of Economics
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to describe the principles of modern market economy. Students will be able to explain the basic concepts of microeconomics and macroeconomics and can apply models of consumer, firm, markets and economy in simple situations. In addition, students can analyse the role and consequences of monetary and fiscal policy.
content: Principles of microeconomics and macroeconomics. Demand, supply and market equilibrium, production and markets for the factors of production, economics of the public sector. Economic growth, unemployment, inflation, economic fluctuations, monetary and fiscal policy.
learningMaterial: The Economy - Economics for a changing world (by the CORE Econ team)
evaluationCriteria: Final Grade 0-5, 0-100 points. For 5 ECTS: Exams 100 points. For 6 ECTS: Exams 100 points, group work (pass/fail).
workload: For 5 ECTS: Contact-teaching on campus (lectures & tutorials) 28h, preparing for lectures and exams 105h. In total 133 hours of work. For 6 ECTS: Contact-teaching on campus (lectures & tutorials) 28h, group work 27h, preparing for lectures and exams 105h. In total 160 hours of work. Business administration students must complete the course with a scope of 6 ECTS credits, and students of social sciences with a scope of 5 ECTS credits.

name: Professional Selling
learningOutcomes: Students will learn - to critically evaluate strategies related to international marketing and sales management - to understand the process of personal selling in industrial marketing - to evaluate the impact of business decisions and administrative practices - to analyze managerial challenges in international marketing environment - to apply relevant business skills
content: This course provides an introduction to personal selling and modern sales management within the international business-to-business (B2B) environment. By the end of the course, students will have honed their personal selling skills, gained an understanding of sales management dynamics in a B2B context, and applied sales strategies in a competitive simulation. The course is structured into two main parts: the first part focuses on personal selling and professionalism in sales, culminating in sales negotiation role plays. The second part focuses on modern sales management, featuring a computer-based simulation game. Students' performance will be evaluated through a combination of assignments (30 %), participation in role-plays (20 %), and a final exam (50 %). The skills and knowledge acquired on this course are directly applicable to careers in sales, marketing, and business management, but also to many other work-life contexts.
learningMaterial: Assigned readings, lectures, and sales management simulation game.
evaluationCriteria: Students will be evaluated on (a) combination of assignments (30 %), (b) team-based role plays and sales-management simulation game (20 %), and (c) an end of the course exam (50 %)
workload: This course is conducted in class-room (contact teaching). There will be a recruitment exercise, role-plays for salesperson-customer interactions, and we will play a team-based sales management simulation game. In class hours (28 hours): 18 hours of lectures, 10 hours of workshops. Out-class hours (132 hours): preparation for role plays 24 hours, and lectures 14 hours, sales management simulation game 16 hours, collaboration with the end of the course project 62 hours, writing a summary of the group work 16 hours.

name: Master's Thesis, Knowledge Management and Leadership
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students should be able to carry out a research project independently and to report the research in written format according to scientific practices.
content: The student applies the knowledge and skills of previous studies to complete an independent Master thesis, and attends the Master's Thesis Seminars covering the specific features of a scientific research process and related requirements.
prerequisites: Approximately 30 ECTS cr. of Knowledge Management and Leadership master's studies.
learningMaterial: Master's Thesis instructions, and lecture notes and other assigned reading during the Master's Thesis Seminar.
evaluationCriteria: Master's Thesis is evaluated on a scale 1-5. All theses submitted for evaluation will undergo similarity check for plagiarism.
workload: Seminar work on 1. - 4. periods. Seminars start in May - June and November. Active participation in research seminars and completion of required seminar assignments. Writing of the thesis and completing the final version of the Thesis. Total workload consisting of research seminars, seminar assignments, research execution and written reporting 800 h. Topic of the master's thesis has to be confirmed as soon as the topic has been decided with the supervisor. Use form 1A in eLUT-portal.

name: Project Course for MSc Students
learningOutcomes: This course is a tool for a student to conduct a company project or take part in business case or business simulation competitions provided by external parties. The learning outcomes of the course are the following. After the course participants should be able to: 1. To assess the focal business situation/phenomena and develop goals and objectives for the project. 2. To analyze data, evaluate information and synthesize knowledge and develop insights for chosen stakeholders in the project context. 3. To apply general working life skills such as, project work, teamwork, report writing, presentation, and problem-solving skills into practice.
content: Course covers concepts and issues affecting business and management within a project context. The student fulfils the requirements of the project agreed beforehand with the course coordinator by participating in the project assigned by the case company (e.g., a market research project) or the business case or simulation competition. By performing the tasks, the student applies previously gained knowledge into practice.
learningMaterial: To be agreed with the responsible teacher.
evaluationCriteria: Pass-Fail based on the course assignment agreed beforehand with the course coordinator (e.g. report, learning diary, presentation, case work).
workload: 80 hours of work (could contain e.g. market research and report writing, learning diary and presentation, or/and participation in a business case competition – the tasks to be agreed with the course coordinator beforehand, before starting the project). The course work can be conducted individually or in a group depending on the goals, objectives, and size of the project. If it were an individual company project this could contain e.g. market research, report writing (progression and results of the project work to the case company) and presentation. There needs also be a diary of the work performed (working hours and tasks, acquired learning). In larger projects or in a business case or simulation competition type of competition this report, and other possible tasks can be compiled in a team.

name: Project Course on Sustainable Business
learningOutcomes: This project course focuses on business sustainability from a chosen case company perspective. Students will learn to assess and analyze sustainability elements of a case company, as well as to create suggestions for improvements and solutions in this regard. The learning outcomes of the course are the following: 1. assess and analyze the sustainability of the business and strategy of a chosen case company. 2. create suggestions for improving the case company’s existing business and strategy toward a meaningfully sustainable long-term strategy. 3. approach and organize their group work as a real-life business/consulting project for the case company.
content: The course is designed around an independent research project, conducted for a case company. Students need to independently find and secure the case company for which the projects are made, from within Finland or internationally. The project involves applying pre-learned theory to practice, data collection and analysis, and creation of concrete solutions for different aspects of sustainable business for the case company. During the course, different frameworks and contexts regarding sustainable business are refreshed, and fresh practical perspectives on sustainability issues are brought from visiting industry lecturers. Students will contact the case companies in small groups in the beginning of the course. During the course, students will work independently, collecting required data from and negotiating the needs and wishes of the case companies. The course assignments are aimed at creating an improved (or new) sustainable strategy proposal for the case company. The course assignments include both individual and group work.
prerequisites: It is recommended that the students have completed a basic course on sustainable strategy or CSR before enrolling (for example Sustainable Strategy).
learningMaterial: Assigned via Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points. Evaluation is based on an individually conducted report (30 points), and the following group submissions: executive report (50 points), presentation (10 points) and peer-review (10 points).
workload: Contacting and finding a case company 20 h, lectures and seminars 28 h, readings 12 h, field research 40 h, writing a project report 60 h. Total hours 160 h.

name: Project Work Course
learningOutcomes: By participating in the project assigned by the case company and performing the tasks, the student applies previously gained knowledge into practice. The student develops general working life skills such as project work, team work and problem solving skills. The student writes a diary of the work performed (working hours and tasks), and reports about the progression of the project work to the case company. The student compiles a well-written report of the work, its results and acquired learning.
content: Applying previously gained knowledge into the project work assigned by the case company, and gaining experience-based knowledge. Organization of the project work and time management skills. Documenting and presenting the results of the project work. Keeping a diary and compiling a report.
evaluationCriteria: Pass / fail, report
workload: Active participation in the project work and performing the tasks according to the case company’s instructions. The student keeps a diary of the work performed (working hours, tasks and meetings). The diary must be attached to the written report (approx. 10 pages). The report must include the following issues: brief presentation of the case company, description of the project and its objectives, student's work tasks and input to the project, learning experiences, benefits for the company and for the student. The report must include a certificate from the case company. The report with appendices will be submitted to the person in charge of the course. Note! Please discuss with the person in charge of the course beforehand. Periods 1-4. Total workload 50-80h depending on the documented working hours.

name: Qualitative Research in Social Sciences
learningOutcomes: The main aim of the course is to familiarize participants with qualitative research and its specific procedures. The course is intended for those interested in how qualitative research is done (i.e., developing the research question, collecting and analyzing data, building theory, writing results, and ensuring rigor). Qualitative research involves an iterative process. During the course the students will have the opportunity to engage in this process. After the completion of the course, the students will be able to design and execute a qualitative research study.
content: The course focuses on the process of doing research and systematic empirical analysis, and builds understanding of various types of qualitative research approaches, data and methods. The course covers the following topics: • Philosophy of qualitative research • Overview of qualitative approaches • Quality and ethics in qualitative research • Research design • Data collection • Data analysis and theorizing • Writing the results
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail, In-class and written assignments 100 %
workload: Seminars (a mixture of presentation, engagement with hand-on exercises and dynamic discussion), total 30 h. Independent learning and course written assignments, 130 h, in total 160 h.

name: Foundations of Finance
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student: can recognize the main parties in financial markets, the structure of financial markets and the most important financial instruments. Understands the time value of money and therefore can draft basic investment calculations, can draft price calculations of different financial instruments and understands the relationship between risk and return. Can draft calculations that are related to financial structure.
content: Financial markets, financial instruments, investments, capital structure, ratios, valuation.
learningMaterial: Niskanen, Jyrki - Niskanen, Mervi: Yritysrahoitus, 2000 or newer Knüpfer, Samuli - Puttonen, Vesa: Moderni rahoitus, 2004 or newer
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation on the basis of 0-100 points, Electronic exam (100%)
workload: Only for students of summer university

name: Financial Markets and Institutions
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course student is expected to be able to: -explain the key functions of the financial markets and their role in the economy -understand the definitions of money and monetary aggregates, and to be able to analyze behavior of interest rates -be able to explain and analyze what factors determine demand for money and supply of money -explain the role of the central bank in the economy and the tools of the monetary policy. -understand the role of regulation and supervision of the financial markets and be able to explain the purpose of the macroprudential analysis and the tools of macroprudential policy.
content: The lecture course gives an introduction to key functions of the financial markets, to financial institutions and to the role of money in economy. The special focus of the lecture course is business and behavior of the financial institutions, financial market equilibrium, demand for money, and determination of interest rates. The lecture course gives also an introduction to the main functions of central banks, to the tools and targets of monetary policy as well as to the regulation and supervision of the financial markets and the macro prudential analysis and policy.
learningMaterial: Mishkin, F.S., 2016. Economics of Money, Banking and Financial Markets, Global Edition, 11th edition. Other material handed out during the course.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points. Electronic exam 100 %.
workload: Lectures 28 h, preparation for lectures and exam 130 h, electronic exam 2 h, 1st period. Total workload for student 160 h.

name: Research Methods in Business Studies
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the participant: Is able to understand and evaluate different research methods in order to approach research questions in business studies. Can execute and report a small scale research project using quantitative and qualitative methods. Has developed skills to critically assess research outcomes.
content: This is a basic-level course on research methods in business studies. Its objective is to advance students' understanding of various principles and practices of conducting qualitative and quantitative research and to improve their readiness to execute a research project. The course covers the fundamentals of the research process, survey development, interview guides, and data analysis, all focusing on issues specific to business studies and emphasizing practical experience with the application of R and NVivo softwares. The main learning outcomes are understanding the uses and limitations of common tools for analyzing data. Students will improve their capacity to interpret and critically assess the methodological execution of empirical business studies. On completion of this course, students are prepared to utilize obtained methodological skills in their bachelor’s theses and/or other research projects.
learningMaterial: 1. Course book: Saunders, M. (2016). Research methods for business students (Seventh edition) . Harlow, Essex: Pearson Education. Other editions work as well. 2. some chapters from: Field, Andy P. 2025. Discovering Statistics Using R and RStudio . London: SAGE Publications. 3. Other materials appointed by the lecturer.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5, 0-100 points: Attendance in teaching 10p; individual assignments 50 points; final exam 40 points. In order to be graded, students need to complete all tasks. Penalties will be applied for late submissions.
workload: Contact teaching on campus (lectures & seminars) 28h, written assignments 92h, preparation for lectures 40h. 160h in total.

name: Responsible International Business
learningOutcomes: The course introduces participants and students of international business and management to the concept of the world as 'VUCA', a volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous, system. Business decisions that we make within organisations (the economic system) are inextricably related to challenges in the societal and environmental system and vice-versa. Resource scarcity (raw materials such as clean water, energy) limits the space within which managers operate and compete successfully. In this context it has been suggested that those firms may sustain long-term success, which engage in responsible stewardship and actively consider external challenges in their business models. When students have completed this course, they will be able to: - Critically understand and discuss the volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous, international business system within which firms operate. - Appreciate and articulate the implications of sustainability decisions within global value chains. - Produce articulate reports that showcase sustainability strategies and their implications. - Analyze firm strategies and associated outcomes, which affect the firms themselves but also the system within which they operate. - Appraise critical social and environmental issues in contemporary business contexts. Furthermore, the behavioral simulation contributes to increased levels of learning in terms of: self-reflection, negotiation abilities, team-work and time-management under pressure as well as self-organization capabilities.
content: The course will focus on the following main topics: - Globalization drivers and ethical issues in IB - Firms and their relationship with the international business environment - Global value chains and international business - Planetary boundaries and circularity - Carbon literacy and net-zero in business
prerequisites: A330A0300 Strategic Global Marketing Management or equivalent basic marketing course or A320A2000 Global Business Environment or equivalent basic international business course.
learningMaterial: Required: Dicken, Peter (2015), Global Shift - Mapping the Changing Contours of the World Economy (7th ed.). London: Sage Publications. (ISBN: 9781446282106). Recommended: van Tulder, Rob and Eveline van Mil ( 2023 ), Principles of sustainable business: Frameworks for corporate action on the SDGs . London, England: Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003098355 Molthan-Hill, Petra, Fiona Winfield, Richard Howarth, and Muhammad Mazhar Eds. ( 2023 ), The handbook of carbon management: A step-by-step guide to high-impact climate solutions for every manager in every function. London, England, UK: Routledge, Taylor & Francis. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003274049 Other readings and assignments to be announced before / in the class
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5. Evaluation 0-100 points: Grade component % - Summative assessments/quizzes (via Moodle), (Individual), 20%; Video presentation (SEC and SUS), Group, 30%; Final exam - part one - Multiple-choice questions, Individual, 10%; Final exam - part two – Sustainability consultant presentation, Individual, 40%;
workload: The course consists of 6 3-hour (online) blocks (see detailed timetable) taken up by lectures and student presentations. Lectures will be conceptually and theoretically informed. However, the style is informal and student participation (questions, comments, and criticisms) are actively encouraged. Student group presentations form an important part of the course unit’s learning process.

name: Risk Management in Supply Chain
learningOutcomes: This course introduces students to supply chain resilience and risk assessment, equipping them with practical methods and tools to evaluate and manage risks effectively. Through hands-on assignments, students will apply these techniques to real-world supply chain scenarios. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: Analyze and enhance supply chain resilience Conduct risk assessments in supply chains Apply relevant tools and methods for risk assessment and resilience Incorporate resilience requirements and risk management principles into decision-making processes within supply chain management
content: The course will cover the following topics: Supply chain resilience and its strategic importance Types of risks in supply management Risk assessment methods, tools, and applications Decision-making in supply chain risk management The role of resilience and risk management in strategic supply chain management
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Econ. ; Bus. Adm.) studies. A310A0101 Strategic Supply ManagementA310A0660 Financial Supply Management. For exchange students B.Sc. studies related to operations management, supply chain management, supply management or similar.
learningMaterial: Course material will be informed later.
evaluationCriteria: The course will be evaluated based on written assignments: case 40%, team work assignment 60%. Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points.
workload: 10 h interactive lectures and case assignment including written report, team work assignment (to be announced before lectures) including written report, intensive course 3rd - 4th period. 18 h for preparing for the lectures, 132 h for preparation the assignment and written report. Total workload 160 h. Moodle is used in this course.

name: Sales Technology
learningOutcomes: This course concentrates on how digitalization is changing the sales function and the customer’s buying process. Over the course you will learn to: 1. Discuss the organizational goals and targets of sales digitalization 2. Analyze challenges in sales processes 3. Describe the benefits of Artificial Intelligence in sales processes 4. Apply and discuss a digital tool in prospecting 5. Understand the human perspective of sales digitalization 6. Understand how digitalization is changing the customers’ buying processes 7. name: Solutions.now
learningOutcomes: Overarching learning goal is being able to mitigate and solve sustainability problems. It comprises of five key competencies to be developed and assessed during the course: 1. Systems thinking competence: -Having completed the course, the student is able to understand structure and dynamics of complex systems related to solving sustainability challenges in a real-life project. - He/she can describe given sustainability challenges from multiple perspectives. 2. Anticipatory competence: - After the course, the student is able to anticipate possible and/or sustainable futures related to solving practical sustainability challenges. - He/she can apply his/her knowledge in order to predict possible outcomes of sustainability projects and compare those with alternative scenarios. - He/she is able to manage expectations and anticipated results of projects. 3. Normative competence: - Having completed the course the student is able to differentiate, justify, and apply values and goals for sustainability. - He/she can approach sustainability challenges from a normative perspective and recognize the different values guiding the project at hand. 4. Strategic competence: - Having completed the course, the student is able to create transition and intervention strategies to enact change. - He/she understands the basic principles of project management and can plan and lead a project from beginning to end. - He/she feels comfortable using different project management tools and understands the basics of working with companies and other stakeholders. - He/she is able to reflect on, and deal with, possible risks. 5. Interpersonal competence: - After the course, the student has developed his/her communicative and collaborative skills. - He/she is able to organize and manage working in a multi-disciplinary team of individuals. - He/she understands the basics of projects’ internal and external communications. - He/she can apply collaborative working methods in his/her work.

name: Sustainable Strategy

Students will learn to discuss and synthesize the relevant academic evidence, examine the links of contemporary topics to previous research and assess the practical relevance of the issues through concrete examples. The learning outcomes of the course are the following: 1. To assess the topic of sustainable strategy in the firm level as well as within the broader institutional context from both academic and practitioner perspectives. 2. To discuss and debate on different and conflicting perspectives regarding sustainability in business. 3. To be able to analyze the practical relevance of sustainable business strategy.

name: Social influence and Negotiations
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the participant: Can define social influence and its key mechanisms. Is able to identify the main methods of persuasion and can critically assess the consequences for themselves and others. Has developed skills to explore their own effectiveness and apply their knowledge to practice. Knows the essential skills for negotiations.
content: The course delves into understanding what social influence is and how to recognize one’s own impact in various social situations. The course content is guided by information processing theories and other key theories of social influence as we explore the cognitive biases that shape our ability to perceive social environments. We also consider the potential downsides of social influence and charisma from both individual and societal perspectives. We will critically assess the ethical dimensions of social influence in sales. Moreover, we introduce key influence techniques identified in sales research. Toward the end of the course, we will focus on persuasive communication, negotiation strategies, and the foundations of successful negotiations. The goal of the course is to provide students with a broad understanding of the psychology of social influence and practical tools to apply research-based knowledge in real-world contexts.

name: Export-Import Operations
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to provide the students with the knowledge of most central issues of firms' exporting and importing functions. After completion of the course the students are able to: - identify the basic theories of international trade and why international trade is conducted - analyze and describe various export and import modes - indicate the most important organizations for export/import assistance. - explain how export and import activities in companies are usually organized - evaluate the export and import readiness of a chosen company in practice and analyze the skills needed for starting and developing international business (market entry) - identify and choose the most suitable payment and transportation modes in a given export/import situation. - explain the role of customs in international trade, and the import / export related official practices between a company and customs - explain the most common documentation related to export/import operations. - conduct project work in teams regarding export/import related matters.

name: Knowledge-based management of individuals
learningOutcomes: After taking the course, the student understands the implications of the changing world of work on employee well-being at work. The student is able to take part in the development of an organization in terms of human resource management and is able to identify the key concepts of knowledge-based management of individuals in innovative business. The student is able to apply self-management practices at individual as well as organizational levels. In addition, the student is able to assess the roles of knowledge sharing and protection in innovative business, knows the concept of confidential knowledge of an organization, knows how to explain the roles of an employment contract and employment relationship in knowledge protection, can identify and assess organization’s knowledge risks in terms of individuals, and knows how to analyze and apply suitable tools for the organization’s needs. The student knows how to work in collaborative project group work in creative problem-solving and knows how to compose written reports and analyze and give constructive feedback on the work of peers.
content: The core areas of the course are 1) well-being at work in innovative business including the concepts of commitment and psychological contract, motivation and rewarding, job crafting and work engagement, as well as self-management and self-leadership, and 2) knowledge sharing and protection in innovative business including the concepts of confidential knowledge, the roles of employment and employment related contracts, as well as personnel-related knowledge risks in an organization. Additional knowledge is individual protection motivation and behavior

The student understands the basics of the entrepreneurial process and the role of entrepreneurial ecosystems along these processes as well the possibilities and challenges associated with supporting entrepreneurship. content: The main themes of the course are the definitions and models of entrepreneurship, the meaning of entrepreneurship to individual and society, theoretical perspectives on entrepreneurship, and entrepreneur-like behavior. name: Modelling and Analytics Applications for Controllers
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will... ...be familiar with some key applications of modeling and analytics tools needed in the work of a business controller. ...understand the importance of analytics and modeling in companies, as well as the fundamental differences and similarities between these techniques. ...be able to use analytics and simple statistical methods and models to support decision-making in companies. ...be able to design and build different types of control and forecasting models for business needs.
content: Course's key content is the adoption of the so-called "controller's workstation" as a tool for data-driven management in companies. The controller's workstation consists of SAS JMP (analytics) and MS Excel (modeling). The course is built around two learning modules, each involving a practical work using designated data. The datasets used in the course change annually, and can be actual company data or open data compiled to address a specific research problem. The purpose of the first module (SAS JMP) is to learn how to utilize analytics and simple statistical methods and models to support decision-making practices. Respectively, the purpose of the second module (MS Excel) is to learn the main principles of creating different types of control and forecasting models.
prerequisites: Good spreadsheet skills (Excel).
learningMaterial: Will be notified at lessons and in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, two data-based practical works (weight: 75 %) and seminar performance evaluation (weight: 25 %).

name: Developing AI Algorithms for Brain Computer Interface Technology
learningOutcomes: The course outcomes will include the development and implementation of a practical machine learning algorithm for the creation of a model, the utilization of the model for real-time processing, and the preparation of one journal publication per group.
content: The content of the course is focused on the developing of machine learning algorithms and using biosignals for rehabilitation applications. In the course, first, students will review the machine learning algorithms and biosignals and relative patterns. This will be followed by practical implementation of the algorithms and mathematics they have learned through hands-on exercises. The course will also cover the recording of biosignal datasets using EEG (Electroencephalogram) and EMG (Electromyogram) devices and analyzing the brain neurons activation and neurons connections using brain map techniques. In the EEG and EMG signal processing, the relative patterns to imagination, intention of movement and real body movements will be presented. The algorithms and developed models will be implemented for real-time processing, and statistical analysis will be used to investigate the achievements. Finally, students will learn how to present their findings in a scientifically rigorous manner through the preparation of scientific papers.

name: Accessibility design and management for people with disabilities
learningOutcomes: The aim in this course is to 1. Draw on disability studies and introduce the students to what disability is (visual, auditory, motor, mobility, and cognitive disability as well as neurodiversity) and how it impacts the life of each disability group 2. Develop the students' capacities in how to work with people with disabilities 3. Introduce the students to some of the common approaches to accessibility and universal design 4. Develop the student’s capacity to critically reflect on society and social practices when it comes to inclusion and disability.
content: Approximately 1 billion people in the world live with some form of disability. This number is only expected to grow due to factors such as aging, natural disasters, and wars. While the term "disability" can be controversial, it's important to acknowledge that no one has perfect abilities or senses all the time. Neurodiversity and emotional disabilities, such as depression and ADHD, also affect a significant portion of society. Disability affects people differently, but it is a common experience that many of us face to varying degrees. It is crucial to understand disability, how to interact with people who have it, and how to promote inclusiveness. Technology is deeply ingrained in our society, affecting nearly every aspect of our lives, from banking to healthcare. However, technology is not always accessible to people with disabilities. Touch screens can be challenging for those with motor disabilities, some offices are not equipped for wheelchairs, and information systems can be inaccessible to those with low vision. It is important to ensure that people with disabilities have equal access to technology and are included in society as citizens, employees, entrepreneurs, and caregivers. The concept of accessibility, universal design, and design for all refers to designing technology in a way that is usable with minimal effort. Ensuring accessibility is both a moral obligation and an opportunity to improve design practices. The purpose of this course is to educate students on disability, how it impacts different groups, how to interact with people with disabilities, common approaches to accessibility, and to encourage critical reflection on society's practices surrounding inclusion and disability.

name: Advanced Finite Element Methods in Solid and Structural Mechanics
learningOutcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to: - Comprehend the fundamental concepts of continuum mechanics. - Understand the mathematical and physical foundations of the linear and nonlinear displacement-based Finite Element (FE) method. - Formulate and analyze mechanical and coupled problems using both MATLAB and commercial FE analysis software. - Evaluate the robustness, accuracy, and efficiency of FE solutions. - Implement finite element analyses for analyzing structural behavior/capacity against different failure mechanisms in steel structures. - Leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) and other AI-based tools to assist in developing and coding a basic FE solver in MATLAB.
content: This course provides an in-depth exploration of advanced topics in finite element analysis (FEA) for solid and structural mechanics. It builds upon fundamental FE principles and extends them to more complex engineering problems. The course covers both theoretical foundations and practical applications through computational exercises using MATLAB and commercial FE software. Topics can cover, but are not limited to: - Introduction to continuum mechanics: Fundamental concepts, stress and strain tensors, constitutive modeling. - Linear and nonlinear finite element methods: Governing equations, solution strategies, and computational challenges in linear and nonlinear FEM. - Material modeling: Elastic, plastic, and viscoelastic material models; hyperelasticity; anisotropic materials; implementation in FEM. - Rigid-flexible body coupling: Interaction between rigid and deformable structures, numerical methods for coupled dynamics, and applications in multibody dynamics, vehicle dynamics, and biomechanics. - Linear thermoelasticity: Finite element formulation for coupled thermal and mechanical problems, steady-state and transient analyses. - Model reduction techniques in FEM: Substructuring methods, modal reduction and reduced-order modeling for computational efficiency. - Parameter identification and optimization in FEM: Inverse methods for material and structural parameter estimation, optimization techniques for model calibration, and uncertainty quantification. - Failure mechanics: Analysis of different failure modes in engineering, including ductile and brittle fracture, buckling, fatigue, within the FEM framework. - Contact mechanics in FEM: Formulation of contact problems, penalty and Lagrange multiplier methods, numerical implementation. The course module provides knowledge about the use of numerical (finite element) methods for analyzing and designing structures for Power-to-X applications.
learningMaterial: Lectures on Moodle. Hakala M.K., Lujuusopin elementtimenetelmä. Rao S., The Finite Element Method in Engineering. Weaver W., Johnston P., Structural Dynamics by Finite Elements.

learningOutcomes: Throughout the course, students will develop the following knowledge and skills: A comprehensive understanding of the potential and development stages of laser made products Detailed knowledge of the suitability of laser systems for production and their restrictions The ability to utilize the advantages of various laser processes in product design Understanding of modeling the processability of different laser processes for varied applications Expertise in product design for laser processes to maximize the product and its sustainability A thorough comprehension of production and design specifications Understanding techno-economic aspects of laser based products and production. By the end of this course, students will possess a strong foundation in laser-based production systems and will be able to apply their knowledge to a range of real-world design problems.
content: This doctoral level course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of advanced photonic digital products and production, with a specific focus on laser-based production technologies and their impact on product design. Course activities include lectures, personal case/project discussions, and undertaking a personal research project. Students will be expected to identify a research question, design a study, collect and analyze data, and present their findings in the form of a scientific article. The course will be delivered in a highly interactive and collaborative environment, with an emphasis on critical thinking and problem-solving. The key requirement for passing the course is the completion of a scientific article that meets the standards of peer-reviewed journals in the field of study and is suitable for submission to an international scientific journal or a peer reviewed conference. By the end of the course, students will have a thorough understanding of production and product design specifications in the context of laser-based production systems, and a publication to further their academic advancement.

content: China has witnessed dramatic changes in science and technology over the past decades. This course aims to provide students with an introduction to a range of the latest and most cutting-edge topics in Science and Technology in China. The topics covered in the course range from History Of Science Development in China to Science and Technology Achievement, from the rapid development of internet to cloud computing , from such new great inventions as CRH, mobile payment, bicycle sharing and online shopping to BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS), from artificial intelligence to 5G network, from smart city to sharing economy.

In the second part of this module we'll see how science, and not magic, can make food appear out of thin air as we are introduced to the start-up company Solar Foods. We'll also see how a range of sustainable agricultural processes have appeared on the technological landscape. In the third part, we'll see how renewable energy and seawater desalination can combine to reduce water scarcity on a global level. This will be followed by a description of the latest efforts to recover a range of other valuable materials from seawater.

content: Module 4 examines the connection between Climate Change and the Sustainable Development Goals. By doing so it brings together a number of the individual elements explored in Modules 1-3 and puts them into a proper social context. The choices we make have a ripple effect upon the world around us. And making significant change in our lives is not only about building a world for the future, but also about wisely deconstructing the world of the past. We need to be sure that the changes we make are not overly disruptive to individuals, systems or societies. A key message in Module 4 is that to create meaningful change, we first need to envision several potential pathways into the future. Then we need to spend some time reflecting on which of those pathways might be possible and desirable from a societal perspective.

name: Disability & Accessibility of technology, games and society
learningOutcomes: 1. Draw on disability studies and introduce the students to what disability is (visual, auditory, motor, mobility, and cognitive disability as well as neurodiversity) and how it impacts the life of each disability group, 2. Develop the students' capacities in how to work with people with disabilities, 3. Introduce the students to some of the common approaches to accessibility and universal design and 4. Develop the student’s capacity to critically reflect on society and social practices when it comes to inclusion and disability.
content: NOTE: IMPORTANT NOTE! for medical reasons, the course will most likely be taught online through zoom lecture for Fall 2025 PLEASE ALSO NOTE: attendance for this course is mandatory and you will be dropped from the course if you miss 4 sessions There are approximately 1 billion individual living with a disability, globally. This is a conservative estimate, and the number is increasing due aging, wars, natural disasters, and so on. The word “disability” is not light and many people, with and without disability, do not relate to it. Yet, how many of us have perfect abilities? Or perfect senses? Do we always have all our abilities and senses or are we all sometimes disabled, for example when we temporarily have a broken arm? How about neurodiversity and emotional disabilities, for example depression or ADHD, how do they impact the people who have it in society? Disability differs between people in terms of severity, impact, effects, and how long it lasts. It is important to understand it since it is something that many of us experience to different degrees. It is also important to know how to interact with people with disability, accommodate them when needed, and how we can foster inclusion wherever we are. When it comes to technology, it has become a part of everything in our society: online banking, work, socialization, entertainment, healthcare, and so on. Yet, technology is not always accessible to people with disabilities. For example, touch screens on phones are difficult to use for many people with motor disabilities, not all offices are wheelchair accessible, someone with low vision can have trouble with their company’s information systems if these systems are inaccessible and a deaf person will find it very hard to participate in zoom calls and remote learning. Yet, people with disabilities are citizens, employees, entrepreneurs, caregivers, and care-receivers. It is important to ensure their equal inclusion in any place that they are and to provide them with equity and access. This is the function of accessibility, universal design, design for all. These are all similar terms that refer to the same idea of designing technology to be usable with the least effort. Accessibility is a moral obligation and an opportunity for us to challenge our design practices and come up with even better and more usable solutions.
evaluationCriteria: To pass, students must score 50% or more
workload: Students must complete a final assessment exam

name: Fiber and Paper Technology; Personal Assignment
Forming and Assembling for Metal Product Design
learningOutcomes: Students who successfully complete the course will demonstrate the following outcomes: The student will understand the principles of forming methods focused for sheet metal components as well as understand design and manufacturing methods of forming tools e.g. for presses. Students also get to know fastening methods for assembling of products. The student will be able to compare the different manufacturing methods in the case when choosing the manufacturing process(es) for a certain product. Understand the meaning of communication between designing and manufacturing and how to design with the product specifications, which allow for efficient, trouble free and economical manufacturing and assembly. Recognize the modern machine shop technologies and it's requirements in generally.
content: Forming processes Presses and tooling systems Design methods: CAD, CAM Mechanical joining and joining techniques Sheet and Plate Metal Engineering Modern machine shop technology etc. DFMA approaches The content of the course is designed from the perspective of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDG's) and its content contributes to the Sustainable Consumption and Production Objectives #9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) and #12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). The proposed concrete actions aim to reduce the adverse environmental impacts of production and consumption by presenting various sustainable solutions to future production challenges. This will ensure both sustainable production and a sustainable value chain in the future, resulting in end-customers receiving sustainably manufactured products. The content of the course is also central to the "Power to X" theme, providing the ability to design and manufacture those parts and products in which formed sheet metal plays a key role.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes, other material and detailed instructions in the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Examinations #1 and #2, grade 0-5. Practical Exercise, grade 0-5. All those three parts of the course must be approved in order for the course to be completed. The final grade (0-5) is based on 70% of the exams and 30% of the Practical Exercise.
workload: NOTE: This course is only for students of the IDE-program or for MSc in Mechanical Engineering students who started before the academic year 2023-2024 and who initially selected the IDE specialisation module in the degree structure! Lectures (self studying material) 27 h. Practical Exercise 40 h (Designing of 3D sheet metal parts using 3D CAD-program, and detailed written report). Independent study 69 h. Total workload 136 h.
