name: Hackathons and ICC events - AHOT fulfillment
Hackathons and ICC events for Bachelor’s - Digital Avatars (6ECTS)
Hackathons and ICC events for Bachelor’s Programs - 1Cr event achievement
Hackathons and ICC events for Masters - Digital Avatars
Hardware and Software of Automated Vehicles
learningOutcomes: After completing this course student will be able to recognize the possibilities and limitations of the autonomous vehicle technology. Discuss various tools to cover safety and security inside and outside autonomous vehicles. Learn how to do basic simulation of vehicle and environment and test control strategies in such environments. Learn about hardware and software used in autonomous vehicles and how it compares to human operated machines.
content: Course comprises of 10 lecture topics: 1. Introduction 2. Sensors and situational awareness 3. Vehicle simulation - part 1 - dynamics 4. Vehicle simulation - part 2 - sensors integration 5. Vehicle simulation - part 3 - predictive control 6. Vehicle simulation - part 4 - high-level control and navigation 7. Autonomous mobility infrastructure 8. External lecture by invited industry or academic specialist - Topic and lecturer will be announced on one of the first lectures in the course 9. Cyber security 10. Cyber security in connected cars: threats, attacks, and protection
prerequisites: The course is cross-disciplinary, and most of the concepts will be introduced from the basic level. Nevertheless, some basic knowledge in software programming is helpful. We recommend, but not require, Matlab courses, Python programming, C, or C++ to understand basic concepts of conditional statements, loops and use of variables. In the course only simple programming will be required to show how control logic can be implemented, so any basic course in programming is enough. Basic Unix/Linux system knowledge is also beneficial as Linux will be used in some exercises.
learningMaterial: Will be provided in Moodle
evaluationCriteria: To pass the course, each lecture topic must be passed. Assesement is based on assignments (100%). Each of 10 lecture topics is worth 10% of the final grade. Minimum points for passing a topic is 30%. To pass the course total points received must be 50% minimum.
workload: Lectures 44 h, exercises 14h, and self-study 79h (solving exercises and reporting - 50 h). Total workload 135 h.

name: Innovation, creativity and arts
learningOutcomes: The Innovation, creativity and arts course has the following objectives: 1.To get familiar with the complexity and variety of innovation management in modern industry, while transferring approaches and techniques from creativity and arts domains. 2.To understand the needs, context and importance of innovation management in an industrial organization and learn up-to-date tools and methods facilitating the effective management of innovation and creativity for sustainable product development. 3.To understand the steps, processes and risks involved in different arts driven innovation projects and their management 4. To enlarge the students’ mindset on imagination, perseverance, observation and risk-taking through the use of specific artistic approaches. 4. To improve both employability and student engagement, creativity, innovation, divergent thinking and transdisciplinary problem-solving skills The innovation challenge solving is expected to contribute to all the objectives by providing real-life experience in applying the students' creativity and innovation skills and knowledge.
content: This Innovation, creativity and arts course provides students with theoretical insights and practical tools aiming at developing innovation and creativity skills for the jobs of the future. Students learn arts concepts and tools for managing innovation (initiating, organizing, planning, and controlling innovation projects) and learn to apply creativity in transdisciplinary product and process innovations. Students also learn how arts and creativity contribute to value creation in general. Engaging with real-life innovation challenges from the EU-funded ArtIST project allows the students to gain relevant practical experience, where they may apply their knowledge and skills, learn the actual issues faced by organizations that seek to benefit from art tools, methods or new innovative solutions and strategies in innovation management. This course covers the fundamental concepts and applied techniques for arts and innovation management. Entrepreneurship and innovation management principles and methodologies are provided with special focus on the impact of music, visual arts, design and theater-based methods. After successfully completing this course, the student will be able to: identify how arts can influence the innovation process; understand arts and comprehend basic tools and techniques to plan, organize and manage arts in an innovation project; approach complex innovation issues with a broad, critical mindset and engage stakeholders.
learningMaterial: Provided by the lecturers before the course starts
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5 based on course participation, class and home tasks and final report (also video presentation and reflection) 70 % report and 30 % home and in-class assignments/group work
workload: Lectures and exercises 40h, course report 40h (includes video presentation), individual work 50h, total 130h. Moodle or other platform is used in this course. Zoom is used as online meetingpoint.

name: Introduction to Life Cycle Costing and Social Life Cycle Assessment
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will be able to have a basic understanding of the of social life cycle assessment (S-LCA) and life cycle costing (LCC) and how they can be used in private/public context apply S-LCA and LCC to different real-world scenarios of products and services life cycles analyze the results of S-LCA and LCC of products and services critically evaluate the results of S-LCA and LCC and develop recommendations for improving the sustainability of products and services
content: 1. The S-LCA development in the last 10 years 2. Goal and scope of S-LCA 3. Social Hotspot Analysis 4. Database and data collection 5. Training on how to use S-LCA software/databases 6. Life Cycle Costing (LCC): definitions 7. Methodologies and indicators for LCC
learningMaterial: Lecture slides and prerecorded videos. Additional reading materials announced in course Moodle environment.
evaluationCriteria: Evaluation: 0-5: Assignment 40%, lecture tasks 30%, quizzes 30%.
workload: Lectures and lecture tasks 14 h, quizzes and preparation for them 12h, assignment and its peer evaluation and presentation: 55 h.

name: Introduction to Life Cycle Thinking and Assessment
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will be able to have a basic understanding of the life cycle thinking and life cycle assessment (LCA) principles and processes, including the different components and stages of the life cycle are familiar with the methods and techniques used to conduct LCA and their application in the development and promotion of sustainable products and services understand how LCA can be used in a business or engineering context, what kind of information it may provide and how it can be useful apply LCA approach to different scenarios of products and services life cycles. analyse the results of LCA in terms of environmental impacts of products and services. critically evaluate the results of LCA and identify opportunities for reducing the environmental load of products and services
content: 1. Life cycle thinking and life cycle sustainability 2. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and its use purposes 3. LCA regulation 4. Different phases on conducting LCA: Goal and scope definition Life cycle inventory Life cycle impact assessment Interpretation Sensitivity and uncertainty
learningMaterial: Lecture slides and prerecorded videos
evaluationCriteria: Evaluation 0-5: Assignment 40%, lecture tasks 20%, quizzes 30%, Moodle exam 10%.
workload: Lectures and lecture tasks 12 h, quizzes and preparation for them 12h, assignment and its peer evaluation and presentation: 57 h.

name: Inventive Product Design and Advanced TRIZ
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to introduce the students to the wide range of existing design methods with a focus on design creativity and innovation. The participants will gain both theoretical competences and practical skills, from the descriptive models for analyzing design processes and behaviors, to the prescriptive tools that provide a structured and multi-disciplinary approach to design. Upon successful completion of the course the learner is expected to be able to: Distinguish conceptual design phase and instruments of it Analyze patent landscape Use ideation algorithms Design a new product and concept of the service on demand Evaluate design concepts from managerial and production perspectives
content: It is a course for all interested in creativity, in systematic tools of ideation. The modules contain basics of TRIZ (Theory for Inventive Problem Solving) and other tools for idea generation and other analytical tools that have proven their efficiency in the industry. Half of the course is devoted to the work on challenges given from real companies. Main course's modules (x means variable part): Introduction Basics of patenting Function definition Ideal final result Function-oriented search and biomimetics Contradictions Function modelling and trimming Cause-effect chain analysis (x) Trends of engineering system evolution (x) Axiomatic design (x) Design for manufacturing and assembly (x) Conclusion There are about 20 case studies and 100+ examples of smart new product design, technology troubleshooting and inventive solutions, many of which are coming from success and failure stories of technological giants.
learningMaterial: Course is heavily supported by study materials in video and textual form. They are all in Moodle, the access is provided during the course.
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0 - 5. Project work 50% and individual work 50%
workload: Lectures and seminars 47 h, group work 85h, individual work and studies 20h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Inventive Product Design and Advanced TRIZ
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to introduce the students to the wide range of existing Design Methods with a focus on Design Creativity and Innovation. The participants will gain both theoretical competences and practical skills, from the descriptive models for analysing Design processes and behaviours, to the prescriptive tools that provide a structured and multi-disciplinary approach to design. The course will also allow experiencing the application of exemplary Design tools within a collaborative design contest.
content: Overall, video tutorials and team-working sessions in electronic domain will develop a comprehensive overview of the aims and scopes of Design Methods, providing the students with theoretical and practical aspects on: - a general framework of design for innovation, - the main classification schemes of Design approaches, - cognitive studies on designing, - design creativity and its influential factors, - current and future challenges of Design Methods, - how to build an exhaustive design specification, - how to stimulate idea generation, - how to select the most suitable design concept among several ones. The course is proposed to be suitable also for doctoral studies.
prerequisites: Preferably, students of engineering major with Bachelor’s degree or M. Sc. in non-technical studies. Basic definitions and tools of inventive thinking are needed (TRIZ).
learningMaterial: Hand outs of lecture notes, internet resources in open access (given), selection of papers (given), videos on the main topics of the course - all available in Moodle and http://triz.thinkific.com/
evaluationCriteria: Final grade 0-5:- Activity on eLearning Platform 30%- Active Participation to team working activities 30%- Presentation of project outcomes (assignment) 40%
workload: Introductory video lectures with exercises equal to 24 h, Team work and a limited project work 20 h, Presentations of the results of the team work/project work 8 h, Independent work, reading 26 h. Total workload 78 h.

name: Knowledge Discovery and Process Data Analysis
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, the student is expected to • Be aware of the effect of digitalization and automation on amount, nature, and quality of data from chemical engineering point of view • have acquired a basic information of the main concept of knowledge discovery process concerning industrial data • be able to apply specified methods and methodology on data • be able to apply management and collaboration skills in implementation of project work.
content: The knowledge discovery is referring to the overall process of discovering useful knowledge from data. The knowledge discovery process is interactive and iterative and involves several steps starting from studying the application domain and ending to use of the information discovered. Process data analysis can be part of this process. Fundamental concepts - such as reliability of data, preprocessing (e.g., de-noising, handling missing data, and scaling strategy), data reduction, choosing methodology, validation, modelling, etc - will be addressed in tutorials, Moodle assignments, and discussions. A project work will be carried out in small groups that will define their working methodology. The course is suitable for distance learning.
prerequisites: Basic skills in Matlab programming and mathematics.
learningMaterial: Tutorial videos, online material distributed or announced in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Numerical assessment (0-5), Project work 39 %, assignments 37 %, discussions in Moodle forum 24 %.
workload: Online tutorials 8 h, online discussions and peer feedback 27 h, Moodle exams, and weekly assignments 40 h. Project work 60 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Laser and Additive Manufacturing Systems
learningOutcomes: After having passed the course, the student will: - understand how laser beams are generated in a laser resonator and what kind of optical arrangements are required for a laser materials processing system - understand the risks, hazards, and regulations involved in laser materials processing and procedures and how these risks are handled in practice - understand the practical aspects of laser material processing of different materials - have an understanding on laser based additive manufacturing systems and their special features - have an understanding of possible manufacturing solutions for the advanced energy sector industry in the future
content: Knowledge on different laser and additive manufacturing (AM) equipment. In laser based systems resonator types, accessories and processing systems and requirements of different ways to process material with a laser beam are presented. Optical components used for laser processing, safety, and quality assurance. Tools for beam forming, guiding, and modification. The principles of systems used for additive manufacturing are introduced focused mainly on laser based processes. Participation in laser processing and AM demonstrations.
learningMaterial: Lecture material in Moodle. Further reading e.g. Steen, W., Laser Material Processing.
evaluationCriteria: Written individual reports 50 %. Evaluation of learning (evaluation is carried out during course in Exam room) 50%.
workload: Lectures 30 h, 3rd and 4th period. Laboratory work 10 h. Laboratory work consists of guided laser process experiment and analysing the results of project work. Reporting of project work 60 h. Individual work on additive manufacturing and reporting 35 h. Total work load 135 h. The course is suitable for on-line learning.

name: Machine Vision and Digital Image Analysis
learningOutcomes: After the course a student is expected to be able to explain the fundamental steps of image processing and analysis, to introduce and compare machine vision applications, to plan a solution to a given object recognition problem, and to implement practical solutions for machine vision problems using Matlab, Python, or other suitable programming language.
content: Digital image processing: digital image, image transforms, image enhancement. Image analysis: segmentation, video foreground detection. Deep learning: Convolutional Neural Network, Graph Neural Network, Graph Convolutional Network, Recurrent Neural Network, Unsupervised Learning, Transfomer networks, Large Language Model, and Multimodal Large Language Models. Hardware, software and applications.
prerequisites: Recommended BM40A0702 Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, BM40A1201 Digital Imaging and Image Preprocessing, BM40A0502 Johdatus laskennalliseen älykkyyteen ja koneoppimiseen.
learningMaterial: References and material published on the course web page.

If the exam score is 0, 1, or 2, the final grade will be the same as exam score. Otherwise, the final grade of the course will be given as the weighted arithmetic mean of the scores, with practices and the exam each contributing 50%. And the practical assignment can add 1-3 extra points to the exam score.
workload: Lectures and seminars 28 h, exercises 12 h, 3rd period. Exercises 6 h, practical assignment 42 h, 4th period. Preparation for the homework exercises, report, and presentations 35 h; lecture preparation, self-studying of taught matters and relevant literature, and preparation for the exam 36 h, 3rd and 4th period. Exam 3 h. Total amount 162 h.

name: Persistent, mobile and toxic organic compounds in the aquatic environment
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, here are the main objectives for the students to achieve after taking this course: (i) Gain knowledge of the occurrence of the persistent (P), mobile (M) and toxic (T) chemicals in the environment; (ii) Describe the terminology of PMT substances, as used across European and international legislations (iii) Comprehend the human health risks associated with the (chronic) exposure to water contaminated with PMT substances; (iv) Gain knowledge about the currently available analytical methods using which these contaminants can be determined; (v) Identify the remediation and removal strategies that can be effective for PMT substances in water systems.
content: Definition of PMT substances; sources and occurrence of PMT chemicals in the environment; human health risk assessment, analytical methods and removal strategies for PMT substances; regulatory measures for controlling PMT substances.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides, scientific articles, e-reports / articles (on course Moodle)
evaluationCriteria: 0 – 5, Lecture/Assignments 30%, Literature review report 30%, Seminar/Presentation (individual) 40%.
workload: Lectures (10 h), Group Activities (22 h), Presentation (3 h), Report Writing (20 h), independent study (80 h)

name: Political Communication, Social Movements and Activism
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will: · Understand the role of political communication, social movements, and activism in society. · Understand the key concepts and research directions in political communication and social movement research. · Be able to identify and examine current phenomena in the field
content: The course focuses on how societal influence is exercised through communication. It examines political communication and its key concepts and theories. Students will also explore social movements and activism as forms of influence. The course will look at current phenomena in political communication and the role of social movements and activism in contemporary society.
workload: Lectures onsite and online, course assingments

name: Postgraduate Course in Laser Based Additive Manufacturing and 3D Printing
learningOutcomes: After having passed the course module the student is able to: - understand features and theoretical backgrounds of different laser based additive manufacturing and 3D printing (AM&3DP) technologies, - know in detail terminology used in field of laser based AM&3DP, - describe, specify and compare the special features of different laser based AM&3DP and how they can be utilized , - develop new process for new case in laser based AM&3DP,, - able to develop new testing procedures for new processes in laser based AM&3DP, - able to do and understand experiments in laser based AM&3DP, - able to analyze and discuss about experimental test results in laser based AM&3DP, - do product design for laser based AMK&3DP, - understand techno-economic points of laser based AM&3DP and - estimate future aspects of laser based AM&3DP.
content: In this course the student will get deep knowledge on laser based 3D printing and factors affecting on processes and design. These include: - parameters and their effect to laser beam – material interaction in laser based AM&3DP. - special features of different laser based AM&3DP techniques, - factors affecting on different laser based AM&3DP processes. - product design for laser based AM&3DP and - techno-economic evaluations of different laser based AM&3DP technologies
learningMaterial: Course material is provided in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Written report 100%.
workload: Lectures 4 h, 1st or 3rd period. Guided group working in teams (3*2h) 6h. Design, execution, analyzing and reporting of case study 260 h. Total work load 270 h.

name: Postgraduate Course in Simulation and Automation of Welding
learningOutcomes: The course will deepen the knowledge of simulation and automation in welding production. After having completed and passed this course, the student will be able to: understand advances in simulation and robotization of welding processes, compare and justify the use of automation solutions and constructions for different welding applications, understand the aspects and demands of simulation for welding robot control and programming, utilize simulation tools to create robot system lay-out and working cycle in different welding applications, plan and outline the implementation of welding robot system.
content: Welding robot mechanics, kinematics and coordinate systems including motion and position control with internal/external sensors and machine vision. Applications of welding automation. Programming and simulation of welding robot and multi-robot systems. Safety of welding automation systems. Future of welding automation and its challenges. Course consists: Exercises related to welding robot simulation. Welding robot programming in practice (laboratory exercises by means of hand programming) + report. Project work, where the student will model a welding robot station, make a welding program and post-process the robot program to a robot controller. Seminar work / academic paper related to welding simulation and automation.
learningMaterial: Teollisuuden robotiikka / The Industrial robot book, Suomen Robotiikkayhdistys Ry Pires, N.J., Loureiro, A., Bölmsjo, G. Welding Robots: Technology, System Issues and Application, 2006, Springer, 180 p. Tarn, T.-J., Chen, S.-B., Chen, X.-Q. Robotic Welding, Intelligence and Automation, 2015, Springer, 640 p. Kah, P. Advancements in Intelligent Gas Metal Arc Welding Systems, 2021, Woodhead Publishing, 416 p.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: pass / fail. Project work, academic paper and exercises.
workload: Welding simulation and programming exercises 50 h. Individual project work 100 h. Independent study, preparation of scientific article and acting as an opponent/reviewer for peer students 120 h. Total workload 270 h.

name: Process Simulation and Monitoring Applications
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the module, the student has the following competencies: Can use statistical data-analysis for process trouble-shooting, and for critical process parameters estimation using MODDE-PRO software. Can set-up experimental data-design using statistical analysis tools, and student is able to analyze data using set of linear equation solvers. Can implement complex process simulation model in ASPEN+ using data-fit correlations describing complex bio/chemical reactions, example water purification plant simulation. Can set-up data reconciliation using mass/energy balances and process measurements. Can use machine learning tools for process based trouble-shooting problems (KNIME).
content: Statistical data-analysis tool for critical process parameters identification using (MODDE-PRO) software: theory&practice, trouble-shooting cases, experimental plan. Water purification plant simulations in ASPEN+: setting up water purification plant for simulating flow parameters such as BOD, COD using plant based process data. Correlations development using MODDE-PRO. Data reconciliation using mass/energy balances and process measurements: theory, data error sources, parameter estimation using data reconciliation. Machine learning in process industries: theory, methods, case examples.
prerequisites: Student must have completed BJ01A5030 Introduction to Process Simulation (Prosessisimuloinnin perusteet) or BJ02A0070 Introduction to Process Simulation, and BJ02A2041 Advanced Process Design. Student also must have completed BJ01A4100 Unit Operations A (Yksikköoperaatioiden mitoitus A) and BJ01A4110 Unit Operations B (Yksikköoperaatioiden mitoitus B), or must have corresponding knowledge. It is strongly recommended that students have taken basic studies in Chemical Engineering or have corresponding knowledge.
learningMaterial: Study material delivered in Moodle
evaluationCriteria: Exam-examination 0-5 grade (30 %), individual assignments 70 % (calculations&report each valued 0-10 %).
workload: Lectures&exercises 20 h (MS-TEAMS or class room lectures), self-study and 7 assignments 115 h. Total work load 135 h.

name: Quality Management and Assurance in Welding Production
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to guide the student to develop, manage, control and ensure the quality and sustainability in welding production. This is related to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of UN and modern technological solutions, such as energy efficient, low-emission and Power-to-X (P2X) applications, which often contain and require high-quality welded structures and components. After having completed and passed this course, the student: understands the meaning of sustainability and quality in welding production, knows how to implement quality assurance systems, knows quality levels and classifications in welding, is familiar with the concept of Welding Procedure Specification (WPS), its development, approval, and implementation, understands welding imperfections and various testing procedures (destructive and non-destructive) of weld joints, knows the basic concepts of weldability tests, is familiar with most important welding quality standards.
content: The course comprises lectures, of which themes are: Concept of sustainability and quality Welding coordination and standards Welding procedure specification (WPS) and welding procedure test Welding defects and imperfections as well as weld classification system and levels Testing methods in welding production Weldability tests Repair welding The course contains laboratory exercises, and some practical case studies based on industrial tasks of a welding engineer, such as: Designing the Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) and performing the welding procedure test according to standards. Identifying welding defects and imperfections from real weldments. Interpreting results of destructive and non-destructive welding tests. Coordination and reporting of the welding procedure test.
prerequisites: Basic understanding and knowledge of welding and welding processes.
learningMaterial: Lectures in Moodle. Welding: Principles and Applications, L. Jeffus, Cengage. The Welding Workplace, R. Boekholt, Woodhead Publishing. Standards related to welding quality and production. Videos of welding quality operations and processes in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exam 50 %, laboratory exercise tasks and WPS report 50 %.
workload: The course is arranged in the form of lectures and practical exercises carried out in laboratory works. Lectures: 28 h, Laboratory exercises and tasks including manual welding in practice, macrographic inspections as well as destructive and non-destructive tests: 20 h, Preparation of WPS and execution of welding procedure test including independent study and report writing: 77 h, Preparation for exam: 10 h. Total workload: 135 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Software and Application Innovation
learningOutcomes: At the end of this course students will be able to: Identify and conceptualize an opportunity for innovation in the selected field Identify the technical possibilities and limitations in the selected field Demonstrate the knowledge and skills of innovation methods in creation of new meaningful software solutions and applications based on some technology Demonstrate good team working skill in developing and presenting the new innovation.
content: Theme of the course changes on a yearly basis. This course combines technology and technology management perspectives for cross-scientific approach in software and application innovation process. Course consists of Basics and use cases of the selected theme and related technologies User-centric needs based design in software and application development Innovation management, idea generation and opportunity identification process (Open) business models and technology commercialization in global markets Product and service development
learningMaterial: Drucker P., The discipline of innovation, Harvard Business Review, August 2002. Buur J., Matthews B., Participatory Innovation, International journal of innovation management, Vol. 12, No. 3, 2008. Technical material focusing on the theme of the year will be announced on the Moodle pages of the course.

name: Software and system architectures
learningOutcomes: The student understands the role of architecture in the development of software and information systems and has the basic skills of how to design and describe architecture. The student can identify architecturally significant requirements and evaluate designed architectures with requirements. The student also understands the challenges of modern distributed architectures and problems of integration.
content: The course centers around software architecture design and meeting the needs of the stakeholders of the system. The contents include basics of software and systems architecture, identifying architecturally significant requirements, designing software architecture with views, and evaluating software architectures. In addition, wider concepts of enterprise architecture and integration are introduced to put architectures in their context. The course includes a large practical design work that goes through these concepts.
prerequisites: Bachelor's thesis or degree completed. Understanding of programming and Internet.
learningMaterial: The course material will be given during the course in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5 Final project report: 36% Final presentation: 25% Learning diaries: 21% Lecture participation: 8% Peer review: 5% Self review: 5%
workload: This course provides a hybrid or blended learning experience. Each lecture week includes also a written learning task.There is a mandatory large project work that lasts through the whole course and a set of readings associated with each phase.Students will present and evaluate their work and the work of others several times during the course.

name: Solid State Detectors and Their Applications
learningOutcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. Understand the historical development and evolution of Solid State Detectors (SSD). 2. Grasp the fundamental physics and principles governing SSD operation. 3. Analyze the design considerations and trade-offs in SSD technology. 4. Consider the many potential uses in various domains. 5. Learn about advanced topics and future directions in SSD research.

name: Strategic Entrepreneurship in an Age of Uncertainty
learningOutcomes: Managing in a knowledge-based economy, Managing by Core Competences, Knowledge intensive firms, Uncertainty. Are they the latest buzz words or another passing managerial fad? Old wine in new bottles? Or perhaps, just perhaps, fundamental means of survival and success for modern day corporations? Given the amount of effort that has been devoted to the topic by both academics and practitioners, it appears worth taking a deep and dispassionate look at the role of entrepreneurial thinking in sustained competitive advantage. The goal is to learn as you go and effectively convert assumptions to knowledge at a low cost. By the end of the course, students will: - be able to identify business opportunities - analyze and assess business ideas and opportunities using different tools of uncertainty management - assess and manage risks in entrepreneurial ventures under conditions of uncertainty and convert assumptions into knowledge - improve analytical and communication skills, lead and manage teams to foster collaboration - understand the main components of different pitches and be able to design and present a pitch
content: During the course students learn to develop and test a business idea following the feasibility analysis, discovery driven planning steps as well as using the uncertainty management tools of Attribute Mapping, Supply Chain Analysis, Differentiation, Quizzing and Market-Busters. The course does not teach business plan writing but rather focuses on opportunity recognition and feasibility assessment. Moreover, it adds the elements of lean startup as well as social entrepreneurship as possible avenues in dealing with entrepreneurial challenges. Entrepreneurial thinking, uncertainty management, strategic entrepreneurship, discovery-driven planning.
learningMaterial: Lectures and additional reading provided in the class. Book: McGrath Rita and MacMillan Ian, (2000). The Entrepreneurial Mindset. Harvard Business School Press., McGrath Rita and MacMillan Ian, (2005). MarketBusters: 40 strategic moves that drive exceptional business growth. Harvard Business Press.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5. Evaluation based on individual assignments 50% and group work 50%.
workload: Lectures 20 h, Seminars 5h, Independent study 77 h, seminar work writing 60 h, Total 162 h

name: Sustainability Assessment in Software and Services
learningOutcomes: Course Aims: The aims of this course are to: ● Educate on how to assess sustainability as a quality concern that software can address directly or indirectly. ● Provide the instruments to embed sustainability into software projects, link sustainability explicitly to the software artifacts responsible for their realization, and associate significant metrics and indicators. Course learning outcomes: ● Apply sustainability analysis to concrete and large-scale software projects. ● Master critical thinking skills. ● Be able to quantify and qualify sustainability impacts and the role of architecture design decisions in an interdisciplinary context.
content: Course contents: After providing a strong theoretical foundation in the multidimensional characterization of sustainability relevant to software engineering and its representation over time and space, the course provides the students with a set of practical tools for designing sustainability into their project of choice. Several hands-on sessions in teamwork provide guidance and support in developing the project and building the necessary skills and competencies. The course aims for the student groups to do various sustainability assessment exercises with companies.

name: Interaction, Participation and Agency in Digital Communication
learningOutcomes: During the course the students gain basic knowledge of theories of interaction, and learn how they are related to the concepts of agency and participation in the context of contemporary digital media. The students learn the core definitions of the concepts of agency and participation, and can connect them to contemporary social, cultural and communication phenomena. Through the project work the students demonstrate their ability to implement their theoretical knowledge into practice while simultaneously learning about presenting their work to others.
content: The course introduces the students to the concepts of interaction, participation and agency in the context of contemporary digital communication. The concepts are discussed through a variety of practical case studies, and the students learn how interaction occurs between individuals and organizations, how different forms of agency are produced through media and communication, and how media technologies both enhance and inhibit participation. Use of AI tools in the course work must be carefully documented according to separate guidelines provided in the course Moodle site.

name: Advanced Course in Strategic Management
learningOutcomes: Strategic management is a widely research topic, that has lead to a rich and many times confusing and even contradictory literature. In order to fully understand the current state of literature, the lens needs to be first turned to the history of different strategic schools. Therefore, the course starts from the roots of strategy management and then builds a comprehensive view to the current status of strategic management literature. After the successful completion of course the student has: 1. Comprehensive picture of the current state of strategic management theory. Understanding reasoning behind different strategic management theories 2. Understanding on the limitations and restrictions in current strategic management theory and their practical implications 3. Holistic view to current new themes linking strategic management theories to other industrial management disciplines
content: 1. Main schools of strategic management The course begins on looking at the development history of main strategic management schools, where the goal is to identify similarities and differences between different literature streams. 2. The challenges and criticism of current strategic management theories Although strategic management theories are widely applied, they are also subjected to wide range of criticism. The second part of lectures focuses on these critical aspects of strategic management. 3. Current development paths of strategic management theory Third part focuses on the various detailed development steps in strategic management literature to counter or point critical points in original theories.

name: Advanced Industrial Mechatronics
learningOutcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Summarize the latest advancements in Industrial Mechatronics. Analyze emerging technologies in automation, control, and intelligent systems. Assess the role of AI, smart sensors, and IoT in industrial applications. Evaluate case studies on modern automation and mechatronic systems. Communicate technical knowledge effectively through presentations and reports.
content: This course explores state-of-the-art industrial Mechatronics, with a focus on: AI in Mechatronics – AI-driven automation, machine learning for predictive maintenance, and AI-enhanced control. Smart Sensors and Actuators – Digital hydraulics, intelligent sensing, and sensor fusion for real-time control. Human-Robot Collaboration – Safety, efficiency, and applications in manufacturing, logistics, and service robotics. Industrial IoT (IIoT) – Connected automation, cloud-based monitoring, and smart factory case studies.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides, tutorial materials, and selected case studies. Research articles on advanced Mechatronics, AI, and IoT applications. Literature Craig, J. J. Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control . Siciliano, B., & Khatib, O. Springer Handbook of Robotics . Bolton, W. Mechatronics: Electronic Control Systems in Mechanical and Electrical Engineering . Selected journal and conference papers on AI, IoT, and automation.
evaluationCriteria: Grading follows a 0–5 scale and is based on multiple components. Student presentations and peer evaluation (30%) assess clarity, depth, and critical thinking in reviewing state-of-the-art Mechatronics topics. Research reviews and written reflections (30%) require students to analyze current literature, ensuring original insights and critical engagement, with documentation of AI tool usage if applicable. Weekly exercises and homework (20%) focus on structured responses to key topics, while in-class quizzes and participation (10%) encourage engagement. The course concludes with a final discussion and self-evaluation (10%), where students reflect on their learning and contributions.
workload: This course has a total workload of 160 hours, including 2 hours of introduction lectures, 20 hours of contact teaching, and 28 hours of weekly exercises analyzing emerging trends in Mechatronics. Students will engage in 34 hours of literature search and research reviews, along with 43 hours of group work for student presentations and peer evaluation. The course concludes with an interactive group discussion (8 hours), complemented by 25 hours of independent study and preparation. This course emphasizes critical engagement with state-of-the-art Mechatronics topics. AI and LLM tools may be used as supportive research aids, but students must document their use, critically evaluate outputs, and demonstrate original understanding and synthesis.

name: Advanced Modelling Tools for Transport Phenomena
learningOutcomes: Transport phenomena are dealing with the heat, mass and momentum transfer in engineering and science. In this course, advanced modeling tools and methods are introduced for students of energy technology and other departments with related background in heat transfer and fluid dynamics. Students will learn how the related computer packages such as FLUENT, COMSOL Multiphysics and MATLAB can be used to solve and analyze heat transfer and fluid flow problems using computational fluid dynamics (CFD). This course provides a mathematical basis for problem formulation, and coding/solving using the above-mentioned computational packages. Students will learn how to solve simple transport problems using their own codes in MATLAB. Then more complex problems will be taught to solve using COMSOL and FLUENT packages. Upon completion of this course, they will be able to start working on various topics in heat and fluid flow engineering for advanced designs or analysis.
content: Introduction to ‘transport phenomena' and related problems, feeding problems into CFD algorithms and methods (discretization of equations and domains, transforming differential equations into algebraic equations etc.), diffusion and convection equations solved by finite difference and finite volume methods, complexities due to property variation, geometry and boundary conditions, application of computational packages (such as MATLAB, FLUENT, COMSOL Multiphysics etc.) in solving transport phenomena problems.

learningOutcomes: The learning outcomes for the course are: (1) that you can describe and understand key concepts and theories, related to soft power, strategic narratives and propaganda (2) that you can describe, compare and contrast different models and theories on soft power, strategic narratives and propaganda (3) that you gain a historical and critical understanding of these models and theories. During the course the participants also get practice in writing academic texts and arguing for their views through their texts. Instructions for writing a reading diary. Reading diary of each article should be ca. 700 words in length (corresponds with ca. two A4 pages with font size 12 and 1.5 spacing). The diaries are submitted in such a way that all 15 reading diaries are put together, one after the other, as one document. Submit your finished diary into Turnitin. The points made and the arguments used must be presented in a manner that is clear to the reader. The main purpose of the reading diaries is to show that you understand what you have read. A reading diary comprises of: •200-300 word summary of the content of the article •400-500 word discussion that offers your take on the article: What did you take away from each reading? What were the core points of the author(s)? How did the reading help shed light on the focal topic? Rewrite the diary in your own words rather than citing sentences from the text. Reflect and analyze but also argue for why you hold a certain position regarding some key claim, insight, theory or concept presented in the article (‘just because’ is not enough). Don’t get too picky with details and limitations – this is not a reviewing exercise or essay. Try to focus on what a study/paper contributes despite its limitations. The use of AI or equivalent is forbidden and will result is rejection of the grade.
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree or alike in an appropriate field in the social sciences or communication sciences that gives eligibility to enroll into the master’s program.
learningMaterial: Literature will be announced in the beginning of the course.
evaluationCriteria: A reading diary. You must write an acceptable quality reading diary of all the 25 articles in order to pass the course, that is you need to get at least 5 points per reading diary. Assessment criteria for reading diaries (max. 10 points per diary): - Understanding of the key message of the article in question (0-3 points) - Clear organisation of own ideas (0-3 pts) - Flow of argumentation (0-2 pts) - Effective introduction and conclusion (0-1 pts) - Clarity of expression (0-1 pts)
workload: This is a literature course that also consists of a final individual discussion to assess a student’s knowledge of the topics covered. name: Advances in Robotics
learningOutcomes: Financing is applied for organizing an Intensive Study Course called CIMO FIRST Intensive Course (3 ECTS cr) to be organized in St. Petersburg in the fall of every academic year. LUT and especially the Engineering master's programs have become known among Russian students and teachers of the high quality education that it offers. From our experience, there was a strong need and interest in innovation training in Russia. The Intensive Course was designed to promote new technologies as a field of study and increase the fruitful co-operation between LUT and LUT partners from students to staff. The aim of this course is to develop the theoretical and practical expertise in the analysis and design of high-tech systems as well as programming and control.The application of new technologies such as robotics, AI, IoT, Big Data covers the a wide area and the course provides a sound base for the study of both Classical and modern techniques.
content: Russia is a significant partner for several higher education institutions in Finland and it also holds a prominent place in different national strategies and programmes. Russia is a longtime bilateral focus country in bilateral higher education cooperation in the Finnish National Agency for Education (EDUFI) and one of the Team Finland Knowledge network’s focus areas. The FIRST+ programme is run by EDUFI and fully financed from Finland. The FIRST+ programme builds on higher education institutions’ network collaboration. FIRST+ networks must involve at least one institution from Finland and another from Russia, but bigger networks are welcome. A Finnish higher education institution or several institutions together establish partnerships with a Russian higher education institution or several institutions in order to implement mobility activities in cooperation with each other. Intensive courses are short study periods which provide students and teachers with an opportunity to work together in a Russian-Finnish group. All intensive courses in the FIRST+ programme should take place in Russia as a joint effort of two or more institutions (at least one Finnish and one Russian partner). The minimum duration is one week (five working days + travel days). There must be an equal number of participating students and teachers from Finland and Russia. Studies completed on an intensive course will be recognised as part of a student’s degree. Intensive courses cannot consist of language studies or research alone. This course introduced latest advances in industrial systems. The analysis of these systems is studied in several domains. Different strategies are introduced, mainly classical with some concepts of modern platforms. But the sign and analysis of these systems will be introduced. During this course, the design, analysis and simulation using different software will be conducted. After the Intensive course, students would know the basics of ControlTheory and had advanced knowledge about Robotic systems. Students will also Concentrate on robot design and have advanced knowledge about design methods. The course (3 ECTS cr) would be evaluated on the basis of research report. The course is suitable for Master's degree students coming from LUT partner and LUT. By organizing the seminar in the fall, it also gives a good opportunity to promote the master's program for Russian students who may apply for the double degree program. It is also Avery a good way to promote student exchange in Russia for Finnish students. The goal of the Intensive course is to teach master's level courses in the master's program. It would also enhance cross-cultural cooperation between students during the entire course and sharing of experiences. In addition to the study courses, the Intensive Course also consisted of practical exercises. The course could be used as part of a major elective study in the LUT's Master's program or as part of a freely elective study at their home university.

evaluationCriteria: The course (3 ECTS cr) would be evaluated on the basis of final report.
workload: The course will be benefited from two lecturers from LUT and two lecturers from LUT partner. In addition, a team of Trainers from industry will hold one day training during the course. All lectures and training will be held in English. The lecture materials and topics are chosen in a way that the training starts from the basics and continues to various valuable lessons in Advanced topics. This is because of pre-arrangements and contacts between course lecturers to avoid any overlap in course subjects, as well as keeping the smooth steady flow of course development from basics to details. The training from industry gives students a valuable live experience on all the lecture topics and is a completion part of the course.

name: Analog Electronics 2
learningOutcomes: Upon completing the course, the student will be able to: Apply the fundamental components of analog electronics and their operating principles in designing practical circuit solutions. Utilize small-signal models and simulation to analyze and troubleshoot the operation of transistor amplifiers. Design amplifiers that incorporate operational amplifiers and specialized analog circuits, and evaluate their performance. Explain how feedback, noise, and distortion affect an amplifier’s performance, and apply feedback techniques in amplifier design. Explain the differences between various classes of power amplifiers (A, B, AB, D) and select an appropriate power amplifier for a specific application. Implement analog circuits in accordance with given design requirements using circuit simulation tools, and compare simulation results with measured values.
content: Analysis of diodes and transistors, biasing of transistor amplifiers, and analysis using small-signal models and circuit simulation tools. Characteristics of practical operational amplifiers and their impact on amplifier design. The principles of feedback and its application in amplifier design. Noise and distortion. Linear power supplies and power amplifiers. Specialized analog circuits and their applications. Design and simulation of analog circuits using a SPICE simulator. The utilization of artificial intelligence in circuit design and documentation. Practical laboratory measurements.

content: From basic building blocks, longer chain hydrocarbons can be produced from little more than air, water and renewable energy. name: Climate Actions for Organizations
learningOutcomes: The aim of this course is to provide students with the knowledge and tools to complete an accurate and transparent assessment of an organization’s climate impact using as well as an ability to direct appropriate climate actions to reduce that impact over time. The main learning objectives of the course are: Provide students with an introductory yet comprehensive understanding of assessing an organization’s climate impact. Introduce tools for analysing and quantifying carbon emissions, with a focus on the GHG Protocol and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Guide students in creating specific climate actions that organizations can take and help them critically assess their effectiveness in real-world contexts. Enable students to communicate findings through a final collaborative case study and presentation on a chosen organization’s climate strategies.
content: The core topics are as follows: · Review organization sustainability report to gather data on GHG emissions according to three Scopes · List any claims the organization makes related to climate neutrality goals · Review general, suggested climate actions proposed by 2050Today · Build a timeline for emissions reductions by the organization · Suggest specific, context-relevant actions that can be achieved over the timeline, possibly in different scenarios · Present solutions to the class for feedback · Adjust proposed solutions accordingly
learningMaterial: GHG Protocol documents and modelling tool access Case study examples and data sets provided by teacher Academic articles and reports on climate actions and sustainability reporting
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail based on successful completion of all assessment items: Class Participation and Engagement (20%) Active participation in discussions, workshops, and peer feedback sessions. Completion of pre- and post-course tasks. Individual Assignments (30%) Two assignments: a short analysis of a company’s carbon emissions report and a report on a specific climate action, assessing its benefits and challenges. Final Group Project and Presentation (50%) Comprehensive case study report and presentation on the chosen organization’s climate actions, using modelling data to support findings and recommendations. Assessment involves peer, teacher and self-evaluation portions.
workload: Contact teaching, 32 h; Reading literature and writing assignments, 12 hours; Group and independent work, 20 hours; Pre- and post-course tasks, 16 h; Total: 80 h

name: Climate Action - The role of Digital Transformation in the Process Industry
learningOutcomes: Module 1: Describe the connection between the process industry and climate change Explain the impact of industrial CO2 waste streams on climate change Recognize the importance of sustainable industrial actions to mitigate climate change Module 2: Explain the process of capturing CO2 emissions from industrial facilities for storage or use Identify the chemical valorization of CO2 as a carbon source to obtain fuels and chemical products Describe alternative chemical routes for manufacturing CO2-based products Module 3: Explain the process of capturing CO2 emissions from industrial facilities for storage or use Identify the chemical valorization of CO2 as a carbon source to obtain fuels and chemical products Describe alternative chemical routes for manufacturing CO2-based products
content: Module 1 examines the past, present and future of global energy demand, the process industry's close relationship with it, and the role of sustainable industrial development. This panorama is linked to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Module 2 highlights industrial CO2 waste streams as a carbon source to replace fossil fuels, viewing them as an asset. The main CO2 capture technologies for large-scale industrial applications and, mainly, trends for its chemical valorization as fuels and chemicals through Power-to-X systems are discussed. Module 3 reviews the industrial revolutions up to the current era of digital transformation. Fundamental elements in the evolution of the fusion of physical and digital worlds in the context of the process industry to current cyber-physical systems are presented, highlighting the role of data-centric decision making. Examples are shown of how digital transformation can support industrial decarbonization in different phases of engineering projects and scales of operation. Company cooperation: Videos recorded with industry experts. Use of AI applications: Information available at https://elut.lut.fi/en/completing-studies/rules-and-regulations/ai-based-tools-policies .

This course aims to introduce students to the present capabilities and future possibilities of computational business analytics tools. After this course student will know: - How to integrate analytics to strategic and operational management of a firm - Possibilities and limitations of different kinds of computational analytics methods in business management

Possibilities created by computational analysis methods in business management a. Possibilities created by network analysis b. Possibilities created by machine learning c. Possibilities in simulation modelling

name: Computer Aided Design of Power Electronic Converters
learningOutcomes: The students will learn how to: -Carry out electromagnetic finite element analyses (FEA) of simple 3D geometries in the ANSYS 3D modelling environment. -Derive reduced-order and state-space models from the results of the 3D analyses and use them in circuit simulation. -Characterize semiconductor device models for circuit simulation with the help of manufacturer datasheets and carry out co-simulations with the models generated from 3D geometry analysis. -Carry out simple thermal studies for 3D structures.
content: Importing 3D models created with SolidWorks or other similar CAD software. Defining and simplifying the imported 3D geometries using ANSYS SpaceClaim and ANSYS Q3D Extractor. Extracting the electrical parameters from the 3D geometries using the Q3D Extractor and producing state-space models for the ANSYS Twin Builder/Simplorer circuit simulator. Creating and running co-simulation models that include the electrical equivalents of the 3D geometries and semiconductor models. Running the ANSYS circuit simulator in co-simulation with the Matlab/Simulink environment. Thermal simulations of simple 3D geometries using ANSYS Icepak thermal simulator.
prerequisites: BL30A1300 Power electronic converters, BL40A1310 Advanced power electronics, BL50A0100 Analogiatekniikka
learningMaterial: To be announced in class
evaluationCriteria: Weekly tasks 40 %, assigment 60 %
workload: Lectures and tutorials 28 h, Weekly tasks 28 h. Assignment work 80 h. Independent study 26 h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Computer Aided Engineering
learningOutcomes: The student will learn, and practice computational methods commonly used in vibration analysis. The special attention will be put to numerical analysis of the rotating systems using 3D solid finite element method. The student familiarizes with the basic theory behind such systems and the numerical methods commonly used to solve them. This will include sparse and dense matrix linear algebra, integration of the equations of motion, eigenvalue analysis, model-order reduction techniques and solution of the nonlinear systems of equations. Good programming practices will be strongly emphasized. The student will learn how to write efficient, clear and manageable engineering code using the high-level linear algebra software Matlab.
content: Numerical modeling techniques for correct and efficient programming using Matlab. Sparse and dense matrix computations, debugging and profiling of the code. Common code mistakes and good practices. Numerical solution of the equations of motion of rotating systems. Eigenvalue analysis of linearized systems. Numerical integration of the ordinary differential equations for analysis of nonlinear systems. Practical modeling and analysis techniques using commercial finite element software.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have completed BK70A0500 Machine Dynamics.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 60%, simulation work including homework 40%.
workload: Lectures 24 h, 1st-2nd period. Teamwork in multi-cultural working environment 30 h, 1st-2nd period. Supervised tutorials 24 h, 1st-2nd period. Independent study 57 h, 1st-2nd period. Total loading 135 h. Moodle is used in this course.

name: Data analytics basics
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student understands: · how to gather data from various internal and external sources · how to organize the gathered data · how to utilize the data in creating useful information for management purposes · how to visually report the information In addition, the student gains a basic understanding about the terminology and theories of data analytics.
content: Students will learn about utilizing data analytics as a part of management in organizations, including operational and strategic business decision-making with the help of data analytics. Tools utilized during the course: Excel basics, Power Pivot, Power Query, Power BI
learningMaterial: Provided via Moodle during the course.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, assignments 100%
workload: Period 3: Lectures and exercises 16 h, independent study 65 h, Period 4: Exercises 6 h, seminar 4 h, group assignment and preparation for the seminar 71 h

name: Democracy, News & AI
learningOutcomes: After completing this course, the students will be able to: understand how strategic narratives are constructed and deconstructed and how soft power works be aware of new forms of influence, soft power and disinformation, for example, around debates on clean air, water & energy and more broadly, around sustainability and green transition. recognise the role of news in sustaining democracy. distinguish new opportunities and challenges posed by AI and new forms of soft power to news and democracy. examine and understand a broad array of theoretical perspectives and approaches related to different forms of influence, and search for recent scientific knowledge and debates on these. independently and critically read and evaluate soft power literature.
content: This course focuses on how various emerging forms of influence, soft power and disinformation are challenging journalistic practices and democratic ideals. These themes are discussed in the context of issues related to for example current topics such as climate change, sustainability and green transition. All use of AI tools for the course work must be carefully documented according to separate instructions provided in the course Moodle site.
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree or alike in an appropriate field in the social sciences or communication sciences that gives eligibility to enrol into the master’s program.
learningMaterial: Literature will be announced in the beginning of the course.
evaluationCriteria: Numerical assessment on a scale of 0–5. Attending lectures and completing group work (25%), weekly reading and reflection assignments (25%) and final essay (50%). Please note that undeclared use of conversational AI-systems in writing the course work, or any part of it, is forbidden and will result in failing the course.
workload: Attending lectures and workshops/seminars (20h), weekly reading and reflection assignments (15 h) final essay (30h), and independent study.

name: Digital Advanced Manufacturing with Lasers
learningOutcomes: After having passed the course, the student will: - understand how laser beams are generated in a laser resonator and what kind of optical arrangements are required for a laser materials processing system - be able to compare and generalize the special features of laser processing systems in production - understand the risks, hazards and regulations involved in laser materials processing and procedures how these risks are handled in practice - understand the practical aspects of laser materials processing of different materials - have skills that are needed to reform technological readiness in different industries - have understanding of possible manufacturing solutions for advanced energy sector industry in the future
content: Knowledge on different laser equipment, resonator types, accessories and processing systems and requirements of different ways to process material with a laser beam. The principles of systems used for production. Optical components used for laser processing, safety and quality assurance. Tools for beam forming, guiding and modification. Practical use of laser processes. Participation in laser processing demonstrations.
learningMaterial: Lecture material in Moodle. Further reading e.g. Steen, W., Laser Material Processing.
evaluationCriteria: Written individual report 50 %. Evaluation of learning (two evaluations carried out during course in Moodle) 50%.
workload: Lectures 30 h, 1st and 2nd period. Guided individual working (5x2h) 10 h. Laboratory work 10 h. Laboratory work consists of guided laser process experiment and analysing the results of project work. Reporting of project work 85 h. Total work load 135 h. The course is suitable for on-line learning.

name: Digitised Design and Production in Welded and 3D-printed Structures
learningOutcomes: Course outcomes: - Overview about whole process chain of plate structures including material selection, structural design, design of manufacturing, manufacturing processes and operations, inspection procedures, monitoring the service and recycling of the final product. - Definitions of the essential phenomena involved in each process phase. - Understanding how the digitalization can be utilized in order to enhance the efficiency of production and how to utilize advantages of modern manufacturing in product design. - Knowledge of advanced and special welding processes and laser based manufacturing. - Understanding various types of weld quality assurance. - Knowledge of welding techniques in automation and digital tools to monitor and trace parts and production. - Selection of suitable manufacturing processes and applications for industrial purposes.
content: Lecture topics: - Introduction: Examples of plate structures for demanding applications (ships, boats, cars, bridges, cranes, booms, beam and frame structures, vehicle frames, process equipment, silos, towers, pipes, chimneys, pressure vessels, shell structures, etc.) - Digitalization of the production chain including material selection, design, manufacturing processes, inspections, and life cycle control. - Material selection based on needs from end users, manufacturing and recycling. - Design for use considering the requirements from manufacturing, transportation, assembly, maintenance and recycling. - Design of manufacturing including pre-treatments, cutting and forming processes of plates, preparing of joints considering welding processes and finishing processes considering the aspect of strength and quality. - Lead time and cost control. - Design and life cycle control of plate structures based on calculation and monitoring. - Welding processes and automation. - Robotic applications in welding. - Optimization of welding application. - Control, sensing and intelligent welding systems (AI). - Case studies of industrial applications. - Laser based production. - Additive manufacturing. - Design for laser based manufacturing. - Traceability and monitoring of parts and manufacturing processes. Homework: - Personal guided exercise concerning the design and manufacturing of structures with documented report: Geometrical design based on life cycle (loading) control and material selection, manufacturing plan including used processes (cutting, forming, welding, 3D-printing, etc.), finishing processes, quality assurance, inspection and recycling plan.
learningMaterial: Lectures in the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Scale of 0 - 5.The grade is based on the quality of the documented report.
workload: Lectures 28 h, writing the report/homework under guiding 70 h, additional individual work 32 h. Total workload 130 h.

name: Dynamics of Adsorption Columns
learningOutcomes: After the module the student understands the fundamentals of adsorption and the propagation of concentration and temperature fronts in adsorption columns. content: Fundamentals of adsorption equilibrium and kinetics. Shock waves and simple waves in adsorption column. Numerical methods to simulate adsorption columns. Industrially relevant process modes.

name: Electric Circuit Analysis (HDD)

learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student is able to solve electrical circuits using systematic methods, define the basic methods used to describe transmission networks, explain the phenomena of change in electrical circuits and calculate changes in electrical circuits. content: Systematic calculation methods for electrical circuits, such as the identification method and the Heaviside method. Laplace transformation and Laplace inverse transformation. Phenomena of change in electrical RLC circuits (voltage or current changes in the circuit). Methods to describe transmission networks.
learningMaterial: Nilsson, Electric circuits (where applicable). Lecture materials in Moodle.
