workload: On-line course. Individual assignments and preparing for Moodle exam, independent work 114h. Group work 48h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Structural and Mechanical System Design
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to - Recognize different failure mechanisms in different type of devices and structures - Understand mechanical behavior of different materials - Define critical design criteria for the different load condition and operational environment - Design and analyze components and structures considering strength of materials - Identify manufacturability aspects in design processes
content: The course deals with the following topics: - Failure mechanisms in structures - Design criterion for different load conditions and structures - Basics of statics - Basics of strength of materials - Strength analysis of components - Consideration of manufacturability in the design process The course module provides knowledge about the structural design process and analysis of mechanical systems used in Power-to-X applications.
learningMaterial: The course material in Moodle. Downling, NE (2018). Mechanical behavior of Materials. 5th edition. Pearson (or older editions).
evaluationCriteria: Moodle Quizzes 50%, Assignment Work and Seminar 50 %
workload: Lectures 14 h, Home work and Moodle Quiz 42 h, Group working and reporting of assignment work 79 h, Total workload 135 h

name: Structural Design and Fabrication for Welded Structures
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to - apply learned theoretical skills comprehensively learned from the previous Steel Structure courses for designing and planning production for welded structures or complete member of such structure - apply theoretical knowledge for practical design and fabrication of welded structure - collect design data and use design tools to create a competitive and fabrication-friendly construction based on requirements set by end-user - design for fabrication (considering the potential and limitations of available fabrication processes), but also understand the background of quality requirements set for the fabrication tolerances - understand the overview on the fabrication costs, and design impacts on them - have encouragement to design and make fabrication plans later in industry, unprompted - apply experience to practical design work in the integrated design & fabrication process (in R&D and workshops)
content: The course deals with the following topics: - Design and analysis procedure of industrial steel structures based on available load information, durability requirements and main boundary conditions given by mechanical system - Use of practical design tools (analytical and numerical) and optimization approaches to design energy efficient constructions - Working as a member of design group, consisting of design/analysis and fabrication experts - Fabrication plans, particularly welding process specifications (WPSs) for a structure, or a complete structural member of it - Methods to take into consideration the available workshop facilities when choosing fabrication processes and evaluating fabrication costs. - Practical interactive process between design and fabrication to find a compromising solution considering strength requirements and fabrication costs of critical structural details. - Documentation of design and fabrication plan. The course module provides knowledge about the design, analysis and fabrication process of demanding structural applications needed in Power-to-X solutions.

name: Sufficiency in Organization and Management Studies
learningOutcomes: On successful completion of the course, the doctoral student will demonstrate enhanced capabilities in three core areas: (1) Knowledge and understanding: • Identify and explain different definitions and understandings of the concept of sufficiency in a social sciences perspective • Describe and thematize contemporary research on sufficiency studies, its implications for organizations, and possible ways forward • Discuss and problematize research on sufficiency (2) Competence and skills: • Critically discuss and analyze social science research questions and problematizations from a sufficiency perspective, vis-a-vis various stakeholders (individuals, corporations, institutions, governments) • Situate one’s own PhD-project within the burgeoning sufficiency discourse • Experience in the design and conduct of academic seminars (3) Judgement and approach: • Reflect on the possibilities and challenges for implementing sufficiency theory and practice. • Problematize ethical aspects of sufficiency theory, in light of other social and political tradeoffs (environmental, economic, political, etc).
content: In this PhD-doctoral course, we take a wide approach to the question of how future researchers in organization and management studies, business administration, and social sciences could and should contribute to constructive sufficiency solutions to contemporary and future challenges. This ambition presupposes a broad view of we who are responsible for change, and assumes that politics, public administration, and scholars as well as private enterprises, civil society, and organizations, all need to contribute, in various ways. Sufficiency cannot be fully dictated from the top down; there must participation and buy-in at all scales. Questions that we will address and discuss in the course include, for example: • How can perspectives from organization and management studies, as well as other academic fields contribute to address the challenges of sufficiency? • How can and should we understand various forms of management and public governance in relation to the new rules of the game that arise from sufficiency demands, and how should society be organized to avert, or to deal with, future crises? • What values are at stake, how should they be prioritized, and what needs to be left behind when dealing with a new era of sufficiency? • What does it mean for organization and management scholars to conduct research in a sufficiency context? • What are the ethics of sufficiency? • How can organizational performance be understood in light of sufficiency? • How should we engage with stakeholders in our research about sufficiency?
prerequisites: Doctoral students, currently registered in a PhD program, are eligible for admission.
learningMaterial: The learning material/reading consists of two types: (1) introductory texts on sufficiency theory that the students are expected to read before the first session, and (2) books and articles assigned by the faculty members for detailed discussion during the daily course sessions.
evaluationCriteria: The course is assessed through: • The production of a paper that is written in preparation for the first seminar, where the student reflects upon their own reading of literature in relation to the sufficiency theme of the course, in relation to their own thesis work; • The production of a final individual paper, where the literature and experiences from the seminars are bound together in relation to the PhD-candidates own thesis work, and that is based upon the course’s learning outcomes; and • The active participation in in-situ workshops and team-based thematic work. A grade Pass (G) or Fail (U) will be given in this course.
workload: The format of the instruction for the course is a seminar.

learningOutcomes: Aim of the course is to demonstrate awareness of the range of modern sustainable manufacturing techniques for composite materials and to select an appropriate manufacturing technique for a given component/use as well as to highlight the developments in the design of energy systems, aircrafts, cars, constructions, etc., which depend critically upon the availability of novel materials. After having completed this course, the student should be able to: apply various manufacturing methods to advanced materials processing, define processing methods based on material selection, define concepts and entities related to composite products, have a good understanding about product range manufactured with various methods, and can solve real-life problems related to the manufacturing of composite products as well as understand and identify possibilities of entrepreneurship in sustainable manufacturing.
content: Introduction to processing technology and overview of manufacturing processes. Usable material forms: fibres and fabrics. Fundamentals of laminate construction. Matrix resins: thermoplastic polymers vs. thermosets. Manufacturing methods: lay-up processes, filament winding, pultrusion, transfer moulding, compression moulding, rotational moulding, injection moulding and extrusion. Composite industry overview: applications for composites, history and current technologies. Applications in energy systems, aeronautical industry, automotive industry, marine industry, and construction industry. Product safety: characterization of material properties. Company cooperation: Technological examples and topics from the companies in the lectures. Use of AI applications: The use of AI applications to support learning is allowed in the course (e.g. for outlining the content of seminar paper or improving grammar in seminar paper) in accordance with LUT's AI policy. The use of AI must be documented in the course assignments.

learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student is familiar with the job application processes of companies and organizations and can prepare the necessary job application documents. content: The student applies to a company abroad for (summer) work, works there as an employee under an employment contract, requests a work certificate, and gets the work approved as work experience for a Bachelor of Science in Technology degree. The work to be approved as work experience must be related to the student's field of study, and the duration of the employment must be at least 4 weeks in a full-time position or an equivalent total number of hours (at least 150 hours). Completing a bachelor's thesis is not accepted as work experience. name: Basics of technical calculation and engineering mechanics Module 2: Matlab basics
learningOutcomes: After completing the module, the student will be familiar with the Matlab environment and the basic arithmetic commands of Matlab, know how Matlab variables and functions work. The student will also be able to use simple Matlab programming structures (loop and conditional structures). In addition, the student will be able to use Matlab to solve simple engineering problems and will learn how to independently obtain information related to the use of Matlab (Matlab help).
content: Data types, symbolic computation, visualization, graphical graphs, functions, reading data, loop and conditional structures, utilizing Matlab in computation.
evaluationCriteria: Grading scale: Pass-Fail, 100 % assignments.
workload: Independent learning and assignments. Total workload 54 h.

name: Basics of technical calculation and engineering mechanics Module 3: Applied Matlab
learningOutcomes: After completing this module the student knows the basic functionality of Matlab and Simulink related to numerical integration, solving initial value problems, optimization and signal processing. The module concentrates on the use of Matlab as a problem-solving tool, but the student has been introduced to the theoretical background of the methods used.
content: Numerical integration, principles for solving initial value problems using the Euler’s method, Runge-Kutta methods and Runge-Kutta-Fellberg methods. name: Advanced Thermodynamics
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: Student can solve different energy conversion processes and study sub-processes such as combustion and gasification related to those. Student understands basic concepts related to chemical reactions and can calculate reaction enthalpy for a chemical reaction. Student can calculate composition of flue gases in combustion process and adiabatic flame temperature. Student can determine equilibrium constant for a chemical reaction and calculate equilibrium composition in a given temperature. Students can determine equilibrium composition of flue gases in combustion or gasification processes. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: mathematics and natural sciences, practical application of theories, working independently, problem solving, and time management and prioritizing tasks.
content: Reacting mixtures and combustion. Reaction enthalpy, reaction heat, heating value of fuels. Chemical thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium, equilibrium criteria, Gibbs function and equilibrium constant, heterogeneous reactions, electrolysis and fuel cells. Equilibrium for simultaneous reactions, combustion and gasification reactions. Course includes Power-to-X themes.
prerequisites: BH20A0750 Engineering thermodynamics
learningMaterial: Online material on Moodle, “Thermodynamic tables” handout, enthalpy and entropy chart for steam. The relevant parts of Moran, M.J. & Shapiro, H.N.: Fundamentals of Engineering Thermodynamics, 5th ed. 2004 or later.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Examination 60 %, quiz-assignments 40 %.
workload: 3rd period: 12 h of lectures, 12 h of tutorials. 30 h of self study in online learning environment and answering to multiple choice (Quiz) assignments, 24 preparation for the examination, 3 h examination. Total workload 81 h.

name: Theory and Modelling of Multiphase Flows
learningOutcomes: This course gives a preliminary insight into the theories and formulations for modeling of two-phase flows. Different types of flows in multiphase systems are discussed and calculational methods from simple (1D flows) to complex (3D flows) models are taught.
content: 1) Fundamentals of Continuum Mechanics 2) Problems in Continuum Mechanics - Navier-Stokes equations for 1-phase fluid flows - Basic principles and definitions in two-phase flows - Conservation equations in two-phase flows - Homogeneous Flows - Separated Flows 3) Flow Regimes in Two-Phase Flows 4) Mathematical Formulation of the 'Mixture Model' for Multiphase Flows 5) Suspensions of solids in fluids.
learningMaterial: Available in Moodle
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail. Assignments plus 2 course projects.
workload: Virtual sessions in Zoom with recorded videos available for all sessions.

name: Theory and Simulation of Dispersed-phase Multiphase Flows
learningOutcomes: The theory behind the analysis and modeling of multiphase flows with a dispersed phase is the main aim of teaching this course. These flows are vastly found in various industrial applications from spraying processes to metal cutting by pressurized water. This course will provide the theoretical knowledge on these systems and how to prepare to model them.
content: - Introduction (Industrial applications and theoretical study) - Basic properties of dispersed phase flows, size distribution definitions - Particle-fluid interaction model - Particle-particle interaction model - Continuous phase equations - Droplet-particle cloud equations - Numerical modeling: 1. Dilute flows (Lagrangian models) 2. Dilute flow (two-fluid model) 3. Dense flows (Lagrangian approach) 4. Dense flows (Eulerian approach) - Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation techniques 1. Event-driven algorithms 2. Soft-sphere or Discrete Element Method (DEM)
learningMaterial: Available in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail. Class work + 2 Course projects.
workload: Virtual teaching via Zoom and recorded videos are available for all sessions.

name: Thermal Design of an Electric Device

content: Heat transfer mechanisms, cooling methods of electronic devices, the effect of operating temperature on the performance of an electronic device, thermal resistance networks, analytical thermal calculations, and cooling methods of electrical machines.
learningMaterial: Lecture materials are available in Moodle. The course is based on selected parts of the following books: Incropera, DeWitt, Fundamentals of heat and mass transfer; Hagen, Heat transfer with applications; Cengel, Heat transfer: A practical approach, and Pyrhönen, Jokinen, Hrabovcova: Design of Rotating Electrical Machines.
evaluationCriteria: 0–5, EXAM electronic examination 100 %.
workload: Lectures 14 h, exercises 14 h, exam 2 h, indipendent studies 51 h, 3rd period. Course is suitable for distance learning. Total workload 81 h.

Apply transition theories to analyze developments in key industries and sectors. Outline the roles of various actors and policy instruments in sustainability transitions. Describe and explain the principal regulations of the global and national logistics sector. Analyze various mobility and transport models and theories.

name: Trends in Innovation and Technology Management
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: 1. understand technologies theories, concepts, and tools to contribute meaningfully to business success. 2. explain the concepts of disruptive innovations, and disruptive technologies, and discuss disruptive technologies’ recent trends and their impacts on contemporary business and management practices 3. explain and interpret the taxonomies of digital business models and how to reinvent traditional business models for digital transformation. 4. analyze platform revolution; how to design, market, and monetize platforms 5. reflect a deeper understanding of all three-course modules by preparing a seminar to present it in front of an audience.
content: This course has three sections, in the first section, this course aims to discuss technology theories, disruptive technologies, and disruptive innovations. This course will introduce business students to recent technological trends, such as Cloud Computing, to enhance their understanding of how these technologies are influencing contemporary businesses. In the second part, this course intends to develop learners’ understanding of digital innovation and transformation, reinventing business models for digital strategy, and creating digital products and services. In the third section, this course unpacks recent platform revolutions to explore their designing, marketing, monetizing, and strategy elements. It will help students to understand technology-oriented markets and business models (platforms) that are revolutionizing the traditional way of doing business.
prerequisites: Recommended to have taken The Core of Innovation Management courses.
learningMaterial: Selected Sections from the following books will be included in the Course: Tidd & Bessant (2018) Managing Innovation: Integrating Technological, Market and Organizational Change, 6th Edition Scott Shane, Technology Strategy for Managers and Entrepreneurs Geoffrey G. Parker, Marshall W. Van Alstyne, and Sangeet Paul Choudary, PLATFORM REVOLUTION, How networked markets are transforming the economy— and how to make them work for you Other material appointed by the lecturer

name: Wind power and solar energy technology and business
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. model the process from wind energy into company turnover at the principle level, 2. identify and describe the key technologies related to wind power, the core business principles, environmental issues, energy policy and their development trends, 3. describe the mutual effects of wind power and electric power systems, 4. identify and describe the technologies related to solar power., 5. describe the basic principle of photovoltaic cells, 6. estimate the performance and profitability of a PV plant.

name: User Interfaces and Usability
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course the student will be able to: 1. Understand what good usability is, how user experience relates to it, and which factors contribute to both. 2. Know about the evolution of interfaces and how they led to current practices. 3. Design interactive systems that provide a good usability. 4. Understand the most common usability techniques and evaluation methods. 5. Design and conduct a small user study using basic HCI research methods. 6. Use the findings of a user study to create a conceptual design of an interactive system. 7. Apply design knowledge to most common contemporary interactive environments, such as mobile and web. 8. Realize the designs using a current front-end programming language.
content: Design principles of web and mobile interfaces. Human-centered design process. Understanding users through basic HCI research methods and applying this knowledge in design. Design techniques, such as use cases, prototyping, story-boarding, and usability evaluation. Usability and user experience as concepts. Usability standards in interface design and usability testing. Design patterns and considerations of designing interfaces for modern software systems. Basics of front-end programming for user interfaces.

name: Vector Analysis
learningOutcomes: - Understanding of vector fields. - Concepts of scalar and vector potentials. - Multidimensional integrals. - Line and surface integrals. - Application of various coordinate transforms in multidimensional problems. - Divergence and rotor. - Understanding of Green's, Gauss's, and Stokes' theorems. - Numerical implementations of the above.

Differential calculus: Partial derivatives, differentiability, gradient, divergence, curl, chain and product rules, changes of coordinates, Taylor series and approximation. Integral calculus: Riemann integral, Fubini's theorem, line integral, surface integrals, divergence theorem, gradient theorem, Green's and Stokes' theorem. Numerical implementations, applications and examples.

name: Current issues in communication sciences
learningOutcomes: After the course, the students are familiar with current issues in communication sciences and can independently search for peer-reviewed academic literature related to a topic of their interest. By writing a literature review, the students deepen their skills in academic writing and conducting research in communication sciences, such as formulating a research question and selecting the source materials. The course provides the students with skills needed to write their bachelor’s thesis.
content: This course is a soft introduction to doing research in communication sciences. During the course, the students explore current and timely issues in the broad field of communication sciences, revisit some elements of academic writing, and familiarize themselves with conducting a systematic literature review on a topic of their personal interest.
evaluationCriteria: Assessment will be on a scale of 0–5. Review article 80%, peer feedback 20%.
workload: The course requires participation to lectures and writing the literature review based on literature chosen by the students themselves. The literature review is written according to a process writing method, where the text is worked on together during the classes and in small groups and based on feedback both from other students and the teacher. The final version of the review is handed in after the last lecture.

name: Applied Thermodynamics Laboratory Course
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to 1. measure in practice a centrifugal pump and a turbocompressor 2. calculate performance of a centrifugal pump and a turbocompressor, 3. perform uncertainty analysis 4. design a centrifugal pump. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Know-how on own field, mathematics and natural sciences, Written, oral and visual communication, team working skills.
content: Laboratory measurements: Centrifugal pump performance measurements: capacity, head, rotational speed and shaft power. Valve and variable speed control. Data acquisition is performed via Labview. Screw compressor (5.5 kW) measurements: mass flow rate, rotational speed, electrical power, pressures and temperatures. Valve and variable speed control. Data acquisition is performed via Labview. Assignment: Design of a centrifugal pump. Use of specific speed, specific diameter (Ns, Ds) -chart. Drawing with CAD a 3D picture of impeller.
prerequisites: Recommended: BH40A0201 Pumps, Blowers, Fans and Compressors.

In addition, the student knows how to apply the presented theories to solve simple problems and is able to evaluate the reasonableness of the result of the problem he/she has solved.

name: Water Pollution and Treatment
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course, it is expected that students - are aware of the main issues related with global water scarcity - are able to describe reasons that cause water pollution - are able to list pollutants that wastewaters may contain - are aware of what kind of legislative factors are related to water purification - are aware of water treatment techniques that can be utilized to fulfill the legislative requirements
content: This course is designed to provide students basic information of water scarcity together with possible challenges and solutions related to it. This course will cover the following topics: - Global water resources - Pollutants in wastewaters, including nutrients, metals, emerging pollutants - Legislation related with purification of wastewater - Purification techniques for different types of wastewaters, including conventional and advanced techniques

name: Welding and Laser Processing of Metals
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to familiarize the student with the welding metallurgy and weldability of metal materials as well as different laser processing methods and applications on metals. After having completed and passed this course, the student will be able to: identify the composition and classification of metal materials, explain the physical characteristics and mechanical properties of metals, demonstrate heat effects and treatments on metals, identify fundamental principles and practices of welding metallurgy, predict and analyze macrographs and microstructures of metal samples and welded joints, apply the knowledge of material behavior in welding for different applications in practice, understand the basic concepts of weldability tests, compare laser materials processing processes and knows special features of different processes, identify what are the theoretical basis affecting in different laser processes and how they affect the possible applications based on them, understand how laser processing parameters affect the quality of the process / part.
content: The course comprises lectures and laboratory exercises, of which themes are: Basic metallurgical principles of both metal materials and welding of them Principles of heat treatments / effects and metallographic examination procedures on metals Different metallurgical analyzing procedures in practice Weldability tests Laser beam material interaction, transmission, reflection and absorption Effect of laser-based heating, melting, vaporization and ablation on material Formation of keyhole and related phenomena Most common laser processes, such as laser welding, laser-hybrid welding, cutting, marking, drilling, engraving, laser-based additive manufacturing and surface treatment Combined theoretical and practical cases and applications
prerequisites: Basic understanding of welding processes and materials sciences. BK10A3500 Materiaalitekniikka / BK10A5900 Materials
learningMaterial: Lectures and course material in Moodle. Welding: Principles and Applications, L. Jeffus, Cengage. Welding Metallurgy, S. Kou, John Wiley & Sons. Introduction to the Physical Metallurgy of Welding, K. Easterling, Butterworth-Heinemann. Modern Welding Technology, H. B. Cary, S. C. Helzer, Pearson. Welding Metallurgy and Weldability, J. C. Lippold, John Wiley & Sons. Applied Welding Engineering: Processes Codes and Standards, R. Singh, Elsevier. Laser Material Processing, W. Steen, J. Mazumder, Springer. Laser Processing of Engineering Materials, J. Ion, Elsevier.

name: Welding Quality and Economy
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to guide the student to develop, manage, control and ensure the quality and sustainability in welding production as well as get knowledge and familiar with the welding work and its economy. After having completed and passed this course, the student: understands the meaning of sustainability and quality in welding production, knows how to implement quality assurance systems, knows quality levels and classifications in welding, is familiar with the concept of Welding Procedure Specification (WPS), its development, approval, and implementation, understands welding imperfections and various testing procedures (destructive and non-destructive) of weld joints, is familiar with most important welding quality standards, knows special welding process variations for enhancing productivity, has a knowledge regarding the production chain of welded structures, understands economics, costs, and productivity of welding production, understands welding networks and supply chains, has a general overview of production management systems and methods, is familiar with welding safety and health hazards.
content: The course comprises lectures, of which themes are: Concept of sustainability and quality Welding coordination and standards Welding procedure specification (WPS) and welding procedure test Welding defects and imperfections as well as weld classification system and levels Testing methods in welding production Repair welding Welding productivity improvement methods Economics and cost accounting of welding procedures and investments Welding work indicators Welding networks and supply chains Welding safety aspects in workshop production Case examples from practical welding industry work The course contains laboratory exercises, some practical case studies based on industrial tasks of a welding engineer and assignments related to productivity, economy, profitability and safety of welding work, such as: Designing the Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) and performing the welding procedure test according to standards. Identifying welding defects and imperfections from real weldments. Interpreting results of destructive and non-destructive welding tests. Coordination and reporting of the welding procedure test. Modifications and developments of welding processes. Cost calculations of welding operations. Different levels of welding production chains. Evaluating the safety risks of welding production and workplaces.
prerequisites: Basic understanding and knowledge of welding and welding processes.
learningMaterial: Lectures in Moodle. Welding: Principles and Applications, L. Jeffus, Cengage. The Welding Workplace, R. Boekholt, Woodhead Publishing. Standards related to welding quality and production. Videos of welding quality operations and processes in Moodle. Additional material (e.g., laboratory demos) in Moodle. Case materials from welding industry.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exam 50 %, exercises, tasks and project works 50 %.
workload: The course is arranged in the form of lectures, practical laboratory exercises and project works. Lectures: 28 h. Laboratory exercises, tasks and analyses including manual welding in practice, macrographic inspections as well as destructive and non-destructive tests: 20 h. Preparation of WPS and execution of welding procedure test including independent study and report writing: 67 h. Exercises and tasks concerning welding investment calculations: 10 h. Preparation for exam: 10 h. Total workload: 135 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Welding Work and Economy
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to guide the student to get knowledge and familiar with the welding work and its economy. After having completed and passed this course, the student: knows special welding process variations for enhancing productivity, has a knowledge regarding the production chain of welded structures, understands economics, costs, and productivity of welding production, understands welding networks and supply chains, has a general overview of production management systems and methods, is familiar with welding safety and health hazards.
content: The teaching method of the course is full digi. The course includes also practical exercises in the welding lab. However, if you can't attend, an extra assignment related to the topics is done compensate the lab exercise. The course comprises lectures with following themes: Welding productivity improvement methods. Economics and cost accounting of welding procedures and investments. Welding work indicators. Welding networks and supply chains. Welding safety aspects in workshop production. Case examples from practical welding industry work. The course contains case studies and exercises related to productivity, economy, profitability and safety of welding work: Modifications and developments of welding processes. Cost calculations of welding operations. Different levels of welding production chains. Evaluating the safety risks of welding production and workplaces. The course promotes UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) by increasing health and safety for welders working conditions by increasing knowledge of hazards, utilizing devices and automation of welding process to reduce the risk of any health issues. The knowledge also pursues good training for the welders in order to improve the safety and sustainability of the production (for example reducing waste and requirement for rework). Utilizing virtual technologies and automation as well as knowledge of health, safety and ergonomics increases equality in the means of creating a cleaner and more sustainable environment of the welding production. This also creates whole welding production more attractive to all people and further pursue equality. The sustainability aspect of the production is consisted of each lecture and training to support innovational thinking, responsible production as well as responsible choices in welding production. Thus, in a wider perspective reduces the impact on the climate and environment. This course supports P2X development from the manufacturing point of view. With correctly planned manufacturing and sustainable choices in production, the devices of P2X can be created better in terms of longer life cycles as well as operating with higher efficiency.
prerequisites: Basic understanding and knowledge of welding and welding processes.
learningMaterial: Lectures in Moodle. Additional material (e.g. laboratory demos) in Moodle. The Welding Workplace, R. Boekholt, Woodhead Publishing. Case materials from welding industry.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exercises and exam 50 %, project work 50 %.
workload: The course is arranged in the form of lectures, practical exercises and project work. Lectures: 28 h, Exercises and tasks concerning welding networks, costs, safety and productivity enhancement methods: 20 h, Laboratory exercises regarding special welding process variations: 10 h, Preparation and execution of project work including independent study and report writing: 67 h, Preparation for exam: 10 h, Total workload: 135 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Wireless Communications
learningOutcomes: After the course, the student will acquire the basic understanding of wireless communication systems, namely: 1) Ways to handle the challenge of multiple access of the shared wireless medium; 2) Principles of layering and slicing based different network functionalities and application services; 3) Fundamentals of digital communications: modulation, coding, and fundamental limits; 4) Roles of time, frequency and space in wireless communications; 5) Performance analysis of communication systems; 6) Wireless connectivity as an enabler of cyber-physical systems.
content: 1) Access of shared wireless medium; 2) Layers for different network functionalities and slices for different application requirements; 3) Digital modulation, communication channels, demodulation, and coding: designing principles and fundamental limits; 4) Time, frequency and space in wireless communications: orthogonality, propagation, and multiple antennas; 5) Performance analysis of communication systems using ns3 simulator; 6) Wireless communications as an enabler of cyber-physical systems. Note: The use of generative tools (the so-called artificial intelligence or simply AI) are discouraged as the proposed tasks are designed for human learning; nevertheless the so-called AI applications can still be used according to general LUT policies.
prerequisites: digital signal processing (Fourier transform), probability theory (random variables) and scientific computing (python)
learningMaterial: Textbook, simulations in python and ns3 produced by the teachers and other suggested materials.
evaluationCriteria: Grade range: 0-5 based on: six assignments (60%) + two presentations (20%) + final work with presentation (20%).
workload: Total workload 216 h (online course). Theory via recorded videos 14 h (14 x 1h). Recorded video tutorials using python or ns3 - 28 h (14 x 2h). Textbook readings - 46 h. Assignments - 50 h. Presentations - 20 h. Final work - 30 h. Independent studies - 28 h.

name: Work experience in Bachelor's Degree abroad
learningOutcomes: On completion of the course, the student knows from personal experience what is paid work what it is like to work for an employer what are the basic rules of working life from the employee's point of view, and how to work in a work community.
content: The student applies for a (summer) job in a company or other organisation, works there as an employee in an employment relationship, applies for a certificate of employment and has the work accepted as a work experience for the Bachelor of Social Sciences degree. To be accepted as an work experience, the duration of the employment relationship must be at least 4 weeks full-time or the equivalent total number of hours (minimum 150 hours). The completion of a candidate's thesis is not accepted as a work experience. name: Unit Operations A

name: Creating real-world impact: Entrepreneurial mindset in doctoral careers
learningOutcomes: The course helps doctoral researchers identify, articulate, and apply their scientific competences beyond academia. It fosters a mindset shift, enabling participants to convey the relevance and broader significance of their research to diverse audiences, including industry, funders, and society, and to recognize opportunities to make meaningful impact outside the university. 1. Apply entrepreneurial thinking to their own research projects to identify impact potential. 2. Distinguish between invention, innovation, and entrepreneurship in a research context. 3. Understand the challenges of research commercialization. 4. Identify impact and commercialization opportunities across diverse industry sectors and society. 5. Assess uncertainty, risk, value creation and capture in innovation projects. 6. Understand business models, market segmentation, and competitive positioning. 7. Communicate research value effectively to non-academic stakeholders. 8. Demonstrate awareness of Intellectual property (IP) management, commercialization pathways, and institutional support at LUT.
content: This course introduces doctoral researchers to entrepreneurial mindset and various career pathways from research to impact. Participants will explore how scientific ideas can evolve into market-ready innovations, learn to evaluate commercialization potential of their own research ideas and/or projects, and understand the processes, challenges, and opportunities of science-based value creation and capture. Through lectures, case studies, group work, and experiential activities, students will gain practical insights into innovation, intellectual property, opportunity recognition, and value creation, while developing transferable skills in communication, creativity, and problem-solving. · From Lab to Market : Innovation types, PhD as a project, valley of death · Skills & capabilities : Intellectual property (IP), team formation, creativity, technology readiness levels (TRL), design thinking · Opportunity recognition : Disruptive innovation, product development, market readiness · Role Models & Case Studies : Successes and failures in tech ventures · Value Creation & Capture : Business models, strategy, market adoption · Communicating value : Research communication for non-academic audiences · LUT Innovation Ecosystem : Intellectual property (IP) protection, Technology Transfer Office (TTO) services, Research-to-Business (R2B) projects · Prototyping & Practice : Site visit Jamie Hyneman Center (JHC), group presentations
prerequisites: LUT Doctoral students, Master's degree
learningMaterial: · Pre-recorded lectures and expert guest talks · Readings: Business Model Canvas, Deep Tech Opportunity Navigator, selected case studies · Templates and tools for market validation, financial planning, and executive research summary/value-centred pitch · Workshop resources for prototyping and Research-to-Business preparation
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Active participation, completion of given assignments (weekly tasks), engagement with the required readings. A detailed description of the assessment criteria is available on the Moodle platform of the course.

name: Life-Cycle Costing of Sustainability Related Investment Projects
learningOutcomes: After passing the course, students will be able to: 1. Explain what is an investment appraisal, why investment appraisals are needed and differentiate different investment appraisal types from each other. 2. Demonstrate skills on investment appraisal analysis 3. Use investment appraisal methods in sustainability / circularity context for basic life-cycle costing analysis, in proper situations 4. Demonstrate the knowledge and skills within the life cycle costing terminology in sustainability context, specially in long term perspective
content: Main content: Investment proposal. Life-cycle of investment project, life-cycle costs and profits, capital costs, initial investment and working capital, classification and selection of projects, uncertainty and risks. Evaluation methods introduced: net present value, internal rate of return, return on investment, payback period, benefit-cost ratio and profitability index. Supplementary content: Investment process, timing and financing of projects, public-private partnership, life-cycle models of machine replacements, evaluation of projects from the perspective of sustainability.
prerequisites: Recommended engineering / business school bachelor level degree OR equivalent knowledge base

name: Software development with the C-programming language for international programs
learningOutcomes: This comprehensive course introduces learners to the fundamentals of software development using the C programming language. Through a structured hands-on approach, students will gain a solid understanding of software development in C, covering topics such as data representation, memory management, control flow, functions, and data structures. In the second period, students will undertake a larger programming project independently, applying the skills learned throughout the course. name: Working capital management of value chains
learningOutcomes: Identify how to calculate the cash conversion cycle Discover understanding of a company’s operational working capital structure Identify how to manage working capital to increase profitability Apply financial value chain analysis method Establish and explore basic knowledge of Working Capital Management strategies/models Analyze collaborative working capital management potential.
content: Objective of the course is to give students modern insight to working capital management of value chains. Practical examples of three different industries are used. The course contents basics and role of working capital management (WCM) as a part of supply chain finance. Working capital components, financial value chain analysis method, flexible asset management, WCM connection to profitability and WCM models/strategies are presented. Figures of automotive value chain is compared to other industries and data of individual companies are used for demonstrations of the models. Future of collaborative WCM and effect of digitalization are outlined.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge on cost and supply chain management.

content: During this course, students apply all the software engineering skills they have acquired from their earlier courses to practice. Students form teams that run a real software project in collaboration with a customer, from requirements to implementation and delivery to the customer. Topics for the projects are generated by real customers. The focus of the course is on the process and project management issues, especially customer collaboration and efficient teamwork. Delivery of the solution to the customer is required for the successful completion of the course.

learningMaterial: Materials listed on the course moodle page.

name: Complex Systems
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, students will be able to: describe complexity, know basic phenomena of complex systems understand principles of complex systems use simulation to model complex systems investigate the evolution of complex models use NetLogo software for agent-based modelling
content: We learn the language that scientists use to understand complexity in systems. Students design their own chaos, fractals, various types of popular optimization algorithms like ant or genetic algorithms, simulate behavior of complex communities, participate in interactive prisoner dilemma game and more. We witness the birth of complexity in every topic: how extremely simple rules of interaction between elements can result in intelligent behavior of the whole system. Topics: Theory of complexity System dynamics and chaos Fractals Information theory Genetic algorithms Cellular automata Models of biological self-organization Models of Cooperation in Social Systems
prerequisites: Basic programming skills. Familiarity with the basics of system modelling is welcome
learningMaterial: Course materials are given in Moodle together with lectures, quizzes, assignments, additional materials. The course uses teaching materials of Santa Fe Institute (USA) licensed for LUT use.

Gain hands-on experience applying AIOps tools for monitoring, troubleshooting, and optimization. Design end-to-end pipelines integrating AI, DevOps, and regulatory/ethical considerations. Explore real-world challenges and solutions through industry guest lectures.
content: This course aims to make students understand the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI), DevOps practices, regulatory operations (RegOps), and AI Operations (AIOps). Students will learn to integrate AI-driven tools and techniques into DevOps workflows to enhance automation, efficiency, compliance, and ethical considerations. Students will learn to innovate responsibly in the rapidly evolving software industry through lectures, hands-on assignments, guest talks, and real-world case studies.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Active Participation (10%), Assignments (30%), Group Project (30%), Final Exam (30%).

name: Corporate entrepreneurship
learningOutcomes: This course aims at developing critical understanding on the importance of an entrepreneurial attitude in individuals and organizations. This course discusses the concept of corporate entrepreneurship/intrapreneurship and why it is beneficial for employees and organisations. After the course you will be able to assess yourself as an entrepreneurial actor and understand what it takes to create and manage entrepreneurial mindsets and organisations.
content: corporate entrepreneurship/intrapreneurship, entrepreneurial skills, entrepreneurial behaviour, innovativeness, new venture development
learningMaterial: Study materials will be lecture slides, scientific articles and reports. Materials will be announced in the beginning of the course and be available in Moodle.

name: Creating science-driven ventures: Turning scientific knowledge into business
learningOutcomes: The course enables participants to develop, validate, and implement research-based ventures. Equipping participants to apply their scientific expertise strategically with business acumen, create value across industries and communities, and communicate the impact of their work to diverse stakeholders. 1. Develop and articulate a clear vision, mission, and value proposition for a science-based venture. 2. Apply advanced technology-market matching and business modelling tools to identify opportunities. 3. Conduct stakeholder mapping, value chain analysis, and ecosystem strategy development. 4. Validate market potential and customer needs through surveys, interviews, and market research. 5. Design commercialization strategies including pricing, revenue streams, and market entry. 6. Apply strategic financial literacy and understand funding/venture capital considerations. 7. Pitch a science-based venture to potential investors confidently and persuasively.
content: This project-based course supports doctoral researchers in transforming their scientific work into viable business ventures. Participants will work on their own research project, startup idea, or Research-to-Business (R2B) initiative. Through workshops, hands-on exercises, and feedback sessions, students will iteratively develop their venture ideas and prepare investor-ready presentations. Key topics include: · Technology–market matching · Business model innovation · Customer profiling and value creation · Value chain and ecosystem analysis, stakeholder mapping · Financial planning and commercialization strategy Investor pitching and venture readiness
prerequisites: LUT Doctoral students, Master's degree
learningMaterial: · Pre-recorded lectures o Covering entrepreneurship theory, innovation processes, business models, Intellectual property (IP), and communication. · Guest talks o Invited entrepreneurs, industry experts, and role models sharing experiences. · Readings, selected chapters o Thomas et al. (2020) Capabilities of the Science-Based Entrepreneur . o Christensen (1997) The Innovator’s Dilemma. o Osterwalder & Pigneur (2010) Business Model Generation (BM Canvas). o Academic articles on Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs), disruptive innovation, and opportunity recognition. o Case studies on successful and failed ventures. · Supportive materials : Market Opportunity Navigator tool, Business Model Canvas templates, Intellectual property (IP) guidelines from LUT.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Active participation, completion of given assignments (weekly tasks), engagement with the required readings. A detailed description of the assessment criteria is available on the Moodle platform of the course.
workload: Lectures, guest lectures, oral presentations, office-hours, including preparation (45 hours). Reading selected articles and the assigned material (12 hours). Preparing, writing and commenting blog/forum posts (24 hours). Total workload: 81 hours.

Futures thinking in complex environments
learningOutcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to apply futures thinking as a strategic approach to anticipate and shape future scenarios. Students will gain expertise in futures research and foresight methods, enabling them to navigate uncertainty in complex organizational environments. Students will also develop the skills and confidence needed to influence the future and take on leadership roles in a rapidly changing world.
content: Through a combination of theoretical learning and practical exercises, students will explore various futures research methods and develop the skills necessary to implement them effectively in organizational development contexts. The core content of the course includes: Understanding the complexities of organizational environments Introduction to futures research and foresight Understanding the role of strategic foresight in organizational planning Developing the ability to think critically about long-term development Application of futures research methods in organizational development Engaging in experiential learning and practical testing and implementation of futures research methods

content: The Interdisciplinary course on Sustainable Finance aims to bridge the gap between engineering and business students to develop transdisciplinary skills necessary to solve sustainable finance issues. name: Systematic Creativity - TRIZ Basics
learningOutcomes: After having completed the course, the student should be able to: Recognize the role and place of creativity and inventing in innovation process/business, identify inventive problems in the complex process of product development Apply several tools for systematic idea generation (Function modelling, Ideal final result, Function-oriented search, Con-tradiction analysis, biomimetics) Actstep-by-step, systematically when creative and out-of-box ideas are needed
content: Introduction: creativity, invention, innovation. Creativity obstacles and supporters. Place of creativity in modern economy. Invention and Innovation. Basic institutions of invention: know-how, patent, public good (paper). Thinking inertia and other invention killers. Tools for creativity support and place of TRIZ among them. Biomimetics. Definition of Function. Function Oriented Search. Axiom of Ideal Final Result in TRIZ. Formulation, examples. Operation time, operation zone. Invention as contradiction elimination. Engineering contradictions and elimination standards. Altshuller Matrix. Physical contradictions and elimination standards. Separation principles. About 200 creative problems, case studies, examples and projects are discussed/solved through the course. The course is proposed to be suitable also for doctoral studies.

name: The core of Innovation Management
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course, students will be able to: 1. Develop a familiarity with important topics in innovation management, such as open innovation, business model innovation, and disruptive innovation. 2. Use tools to explore innovation and evaluate alternative solutions for improved performance, and creativity in the organizations. 3. Critically appraise different sources of innovation to generate creative ideas and utilize them. 4. Understand how to structure an organization for improved innovation and create novel products and services. 5. Evaluate the role of innovation management for improved organizational performance.
content: Innovation management is vital for an organization to gain and sustain a competitive advantage in today’s dynamic environment. Moreover, innovation is acknowledged as a key antecedent for achieving higher growth, better financial and environmental performance, and outperforming competitors, however, managing innovation is an upheaval task, especially in today’s dynamic and disruptive environment. Managers struggle to introduce creative ideas and convert them into successful innovations or they can build on emerging creative tools to collaborate, generate creative ideas, and train their employees to introduce competitive products. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental of innovation management, tools used to enhance employees’ creativity, developing an innovative culture in the organization, designing an innovation strategy for creative products and services, and capturing the business value of innovation

content: The Master's thesis is the final project of the degree of Master of Science (Technology). Usually it involves a development project commissioned by a company and takes about six months. name: Creativity in Innovation Processes TUDI
learningOutcomes: After the course student understands creativity and its components in innovation. He/she recognizes people as creative actors. He/she is able to understand collective creativity and creativity systems. He/she can combine artistic and engineer creativity. He/she understands principles of multi-actor innovation and creativity processes. The course develops following skills: creative personality, creative thinking skills and methods, creative will and motivation, as well as skills to act as innovation promotor in open innovation processes.
content: As basic competence level student can use practical creativity methods and methods enhancing group dynamics. Further on, he/she is able to avoid association obstacles and lock-ins in creative processes. As special expertise student can enhance intellectual gross-fertilization in innovation sessions.

name: Software Quality Management
learningOutcomes: By completing the course the student knows the most common quality assurance (QA) models, measurements and tools applied in the software processes. The student has the capability of doing QA tasks independently, or design and implement quality control tools to measure quality as a part of larger process organization. Student knows how quality assurance is done and how the QA and software development are associated.
content: Software quality-related models and measurements. Software quality and quality control-related tools and the common documents. Software quality assurance as an organizational activity, improvement of software quality. Quality-related standards and certifications, Quality assurance and quality control in practice.

name: Work Experience in Bachelor's Degree in Finland
learningOutcomes: After completing obligatory internship, 2 cr, the students will be able to: understand the disciplines of doing paid work in a company or as an entrepreneur understand the main principles of working life from an employee's or an entrepreneur's viewpoint perform as a member of a work community After completing optional internship, 1-6cr, the students will be able to: perform on a work position and work environment related to his/her own study field apply the studied issues and gathered knowledge in practice
content: The student applies the (summer)job, works as a paid worker, applies for the reference on the job and gets an approval for work internship. The duration of 4 weeks of full-time work is worth of 2 cr. Bachelor thesis work is not relevant for work internship. Discretionary, employment before the beginning of the studies can be approved as work internship, in the case that they are not accepted as work internship in the previous degrees of the student. Working as an entrepreneur is also valid for applying work internship.
evaluationCriteria: Pass / fail. Internship application and written report 100%
workload: Obligatory internship, 2cr: Applying for job and recruitment 10 hours, issues related to the work initiation (orientation, employment and workplace principles) 15 hours, notification of work community courses of action alongside own work (organization of work/ production, management, work community and team work, social intercourse) 24 hours, written report 5 hours (length 2-3 pages, please use the template). Total 54 hours. Optional internship, 1-6 cr: working in a job in the field of industrial engineering and management, written report (length 2-3 pages, please use the template), total 27-162 cr. Instructions from eLUT.

name: Supply Chain Risk Management
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to familiarize students with risk assessment in supply chains. During this course, students apply methods and tools of risk assessment in practical assignments. After completing the course, students will - understand the fundamentals and concepts of supply chain risk management - knows methods and practices in supply chain risk assessment and can evaluate those - is able to utilize risk management in supply chain planning, assessment and decision-making
content: The course will cover the following topics: Basics of supply chain risk management, supply chain risk management process, different types of supply chain risks, identification and assessment of supply chain risks, risk management tools and methods in supply chains, decision making in supply chains, uncertainty in supply chain risk management, supply chain visibility.
learningMaterial: In Moodle
evaluationCriteria: Assignment and report 100 %

name: Supply Chain Management TUDI
learningOutcomes: After completing the course the student is able to: • define the basic concepts of supply chain management • distinguish between supply chain types with different characteristics and objectives • assess the causes and effects of different phenomena in supply chain management • analyze the costs and service factors of the supply chain • assess the suitability of the supply chain management principles and theories in different operating environments • apply material flow control models in supply chain
content: Core: The basic concepts and typical tasks of supply chain management. Methods for controlling and analyzing inventories. Controlling material flow in the supply chain environment. VMI. Supply chain dynamics, bullwhip effect and its management. Supply chain structures, principle of postponement, pooling effect. Planning the distribution network. Strategic starting points and competitive factors for supply chain planning and control. Company cooperation In one of the assignments, you will independently explore the practices of a company of your choice.

name: Basics of database systems
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course the student will be able to: 1.Design and model relational databases 2.Understand how the evolution of relational algebra led to SQL databases 3.Model real world problems with ER and transform the ER model to relational databases 4.Understand and solve issues related to relational database design, such as optimization and normalization 5.Implement relational databases in practice and embed them in applications
content: Database systems. Database design. Object-centric modeling and ER-modeling. Specifying relational models. SQL and object languages. Perspectives into database design: How database is designed, how data is modeled, and what are data storage structures and access methods. Transforming ER models to relational models, and then to relational databases. Basics to database programming: queries and other operations, database management, such as triggers. Implementing databases in practice and how to use SQL databases from other programs.
prerequisites: Introduction to Programming or equivalent.
learningMaterial: Beynon-Davies, P.: Database Systems, Palgrave Macmillan, Third Edition, 2004. Foster, Elvis, C.: Database Systems A Pragmatic Approach, Apress, 2014. name: Basics of Linux

name: Distributed Systems
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course students will be able to Explain what a distributed system is, and what the desired properties of such systems are. Apply the basic theoretical concepts of distributed systems. Design and implement simple distributed system. Examine how modern distributed systems meet the demands of contemporary distributed applications.
content: The course introduces the concepts of distributed systems including (but not limited to) processes, communication, naming, synchronization, and consistency. After the introductory part, design principles underlying the development of distributed systems are discussed followed by more advanced concepts such as fault tolerance and security. Students will also be familiarized with some of the main architectural paradigms in distributed systems: object-based systems, file systems, web-based and coordination-based systems. On the completion of the unit, students will understand the fundamentals of distributed computing and be able to design and develop distributed systems and applications.

name: Environmental Sustainability of Logistics
learningOutcomes: Sustainability of conducting business has become a central concern. After all, who is there left to enjoy of the profits if the planet and its inhabitants are gone. In addition, majority of modern businesses cannot produce value anymore if natural resources are depleted. Logistics practices are focal part for running business operations and furthermore supply chains act as a backbone enabling modern societies. However, transportation of goods is responsible for approximately quarter of all greenhouse gases produced globally, not to mention other pollutants that are adverse to animal and human health. Recently global (Paris agreement), regional (EU's decarbonization goals) and national targets have been established to reduce greenhouse gas and air pollutant emissions. This course offers learning in emission measurement methods, emission related policies and their effect to businesses, as well as state-of-the-art technologies in emissions reduction.
content: Lectures, exercises with openly available real-life data and written report
prerequisites: Courses completed or professional background in logistics and supply chain management are recommended.
learningMaterial: Jaccard, M. (2006). Sustainable fossil fuels: the unusual suspect in the quest for clean and enduring energy. Cambridge University Press. McKinnon, A., Browne, M., Whiteing, A., & Piecyk, M. (Eds.). (2015). Green logistics: Improving the environmental sustainability of logistics. Kogan Page Publishers. Hilmola, O. P. (2018). The Sulphur cap in maritime supply chains: environmental regulations in European logistics. Springer. Elkington, J. (1997). Cannibals with forks. The triple bottom line of 21st century, 73.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Exercises 25 %, written report 75 %.
workload: First time in 2023-2024 (2nd year studies). Lectures 30 h, exercises 30 h (results are discussed in the classroom), written report 100 h (contains planning, literature review, data gathering). Total 160 h.

name: Full Stack Development
learningOutcomes: Upon completing the course, the students (1) will be able to conceptualize full-stack applications for all platforms including web, mobile and desktop; (2) will be able to reflect on development practices related to full-stack development; (3) will be able to demonstrate full-stack development practices use no/low code services; (4) will have hands-on experience of diverse full-stack development technologies, programming languages and tools; (5) will be able to outline the benefits of full-stack development
content: The course Full Stack Development covers the holistic development of web, mobile and desktop applications from front-end to back-end. The course will focus on the technologies and frameworks that are currently used in industry, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and React for web, Swift and Kotlin for mobile and Electron for desktop, just to name a few. Students will learn how to design and implement full-stack applications for all platforms including user authentication and authorization, data storage, and server-side rendering. Additionally, students will learn about software development best practices, such as version control, testing, and deployment, as well as serverless applications. The course will also include an overview of no-code or low-code platforms and frameworks, which allow for the rapid development of applications without writing code, and how to integrate these into traditional full-stack development workflow. Furthermore, it will cover the concept of microservices. The course will include both lectures and hands-on coding exercises to give students practical experience in building full-stack applications. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to design, implement, and deploy full-stack applications to production for all platforms including web, mobile and desktop.

name: Fundamentals of smart systems
learningOutcomes: Students will be able to explain the nature of artificial intelligence and smart in the case of software and systemsStudents will be able to apply concepts of artificial intelligence and data analytics to software engineeringStudents will be able to develop rudimentary smart systems incorporating smart featuresStudents will be able to identify and classify value in data and apply data-driven methods to smart systems developmentStudents will be able to distinguish between interactive and non-interactive smart systemsStudents will be able to apply concepts, theories, and methods of smart systems to develop software
content: The aim of Fundamentals of Smart Systems is to introduce the broad spectrum of smart and intelligent systems, especially from a software engineering aspect. This includes mostly non-physical systems such as conversational agents, robotic process automation, prediction, and detection systems but also basics on how cyber-physical systems work and rely on data and sensors. Therefore, this course mostly uncovers the software side of smart systems, as software is crucial to make the systems "smart", by combining and analyzing data, for example from sensors.

name: Holistic Digital Service Development
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the students (1) will gain a comprehensive understanding of the process of developing digital services, from ideation to implementation; (2) students will develop their teamwork and communication skills through working in close collaboration with industry mentors and partners; (3) students will have the opportunity to apply the theoretical concepts learned in class to real-world projects, strengthening their understanding of the subject (4) students will gain hands-on experience in developing innovative digital services that address real-world challenges faced by companies; (5) students will develop valuable professional skills such as project management, critical thinking, and problem-solving, preparing them for careers in the digital service development industry.
content: Holistic Digital Service Development is a project course that combines theoretical learning with hands-on practical experience. In this project-based course, students work in teams to develop innovative digital services in close collaboration with industry partners. Each team is guided by a mentor from the partnering company, who provides valuable insights into the company's business model, needs, and portfolio. The goal of the course is to enhance the value creation of the company through the development of new digital services or the improvement of existing ones. This course offers a unique opportunity for students to apply their knowledge in real-world settings and develop valuable skills in digital service development. In this course, students apply their knowledge of cloud-based services, infrastructure, service design, and intelligent and smart systems.

name: Industrial Project Management
learningOutcomes: 1.To get familiar with a variety of industrial projects, multi-project environments and project management principles 2.To understand the needs, context and importance of PM in an industrial organization, and learn up-to-date tools and methods facilitating the effective planning, productivity and project workflow processes control 3.To learn resource-planning (people, time and costs) and budgeting as the foundation of project planning and control 4.To understand the steps, processes and risks involved in different industrial projects and their management 5.To understand the roles and responsibilities of HR manager, project leader and project manager.
content: Industrial Project Management Course provides Master's students with theoretical insights and practical tools aiming at developing project management skills. Students revise the PM concepts and tools for organizing, planning, and controlling projects (PERT, Gantt, critical path, critical chain) using the software (MS Project) and learn to apply the work breakdown structures and networks for planning and scheduling the projects and project portfolios. Students also learn how to estimate the status of projects and how to finance technology development projects. Engaging with real projects analysis allows the students to gain relevant practical experience, where they may apply their knowledge and skills, benefit from project management tools, methods or new innovative solutions and strategies in project management. This course covers the fundamental concepts and applied techniques for cost effective management of both long-term development programs and short-term projects. Project management principles and methodologies are provided with special focus on planning, controlling, and managing projects. After successfully completing this course, the student will be able to: identify the elements of the PM lifecycle: plan, control, organize and allocate the resources; understand PM processes and comprehend basic tools and techniques to plan, organize and manage a project; optimize results while managing the constraints and stakeholder communications.
learningMaterial: Kerzner, Harold R. (2013). Project Management: A Systems Approach to Planning, Scheduling, and Controlling. Wiley, New Jersey. Eppinger, Steven D. ; Tyson R. Browning (2012). Design Structure Matrix Methods and Applications. MIT press, Boston.
