name: Introduction to Corporate Social Responsibility
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, the students will be able to: · define and apply key concepts and perspectives regarding CSR · identify relevant issues and analyse the challenges related to corporate responsibility in selected industries · describe the role of CSR in business and in relation to wider international political and economic issues · describe the different aspects through which organizational practices can be CSR-oriented · apply key concepts of CSR in their daily work. In addition, the students will be able to analyse CSR literature, organise their work independently and work in a virtual environment.
content: · Central concepts in CSR o CSR and sustainable development o Definitions of CSR o Why CSR matters – the business case o Stakeholder salience · Working with stakeholders o Political CSR o Cross-sector partnerships and CSR o Multi-stakeholder initiatives and CSR o CSR and human rights · CSR in company operations o Human resource management (HRM) and CSR o CSR and supply chain o CSR and sustainable consumption o CSR – minimum wage and living wage · Examples of CSR o CSR and communication o CSR and corruption o CSR and leadership o CSR and responsible investment CSR and social entrepreneurship
learningMaterial: The link to primary reading materials will be provided on the learning platform.
evaluationCriteria: Grading on a scale from 1 to 5. The grade is composed of: - weekly assignments/ short essays (60 %)- case analysis: final assignment (40%)
workload: Weekly assignments: There are four weekly assignments in the course; one for each week for the first four weeks of the course. The weekly assignments are done individually. Final assignment: The final assignment can be completed in a group or individually. The final assignment needs to be submitted by the end of the seventh week of the course. The course instructors provide guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence applications during the course.

name: Introduction to M.Sc. Studies in Computational Engineering
learningOutcomes: The course provides information on studying at LUT in the specific degree programme. The course supports the student to organize and schedule her/his M.Sc. studies. In practical level, three main subjects are addressed: A) The course provides the student with basic knowledge of studying at LUT in general and particularly in his/her degree programme. The course supports the student to plan and complete a personal study plan and to follow the progress of his/her studies according to the personal study plan. B) Student will learn how to find electronic material from the Academic Library services, collections and databases. Students will learn to use needed digital services and different distance learning applications. C) Student will get familiar with the information security issues in general and specifically related to studies at LUT.
content: The Orientation Days activities. Practical study-related information, degree requirements. Planning of Master's studies. Preparation of the electronic personal study plan at the ePSP workshop. Getting familiar with the support in monitoring the progress of the studies. Use of digital services in studies. The Academic Library collections and databases. Information security training.
learningMaterial: Material given during the orientation Days, Study Guide, Information retrieval course in Moodle, the Academic Library collections and databases. Information security training in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Active participation, assignments. ePSP, assignment on information retrieval, and assignment on information security training completed.
workload: Participation in the Orientation Days activities. Library introduction lectures, library use, information sources, information retrieval, and assignments. Assignments on general information about Master Studies. Using Moodle. ePSP workshop, meetings with the Academic Director and Study Councellor. Independent study. Information security training. Total workload 27 h, 1. period.

name: Laboratory Course in Electrical Engineering
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: work safely on practical tasks in electrical engineering and manage electrical risk in the workplace identify typical electric, electronic and installation components use multimeters and oscilloscopes design and implement test setups and analyze the operation of electric devices based on measurements read and produce technical reports Use of AI applications: Artificial intelligence applications can be used according to general policies of LUT for example for improving the language of written reports.
content: Electrical safety, first aid, professional working attitude and practices in different laboratory environments at LUT, multimeter and oscilloscope in typical measurement tasks, measurement of electrical power, measurement automation and data acquisition, measurement uncertainty and typical error sources, typical components in electrical engineering and electronics, various practical design and measurement tasks.
learningMaterial: Materials are based on accepted industrial and scientific documents and will be delivered for students in Moodle. Literature: Sedra, A. Smith, K. 2009. “Microelectronic Circuits”, Kirja, Oxford University Press, USA, ISBN: 978-0-19-532303-0 (Luvut 6.1-3 ja 7.1-4) Veṅkaṭeśa, Vī. Electrical Engineering. 1st ed. Oxford, England: Alpha Science International Ltd., 2014. Print.
evaluationCriteria: 0–5. Moodle assignments, laboratory work, demonstration test and reports 100 %. All the assignments on the course have to be completed with a passing grade. The laboratory sessions will be organized in the LUT Lappeenranta campus, in laboratory rooms 6316 and 6318. As the laboratory sessions require attendance, the course cannot be completed remotely.
workload: Moodle, laboratory work and reports, 1st – 4th period. Independent study 61 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Laboratory Course in Electrical Power Engineering
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. plan and execute measurements in laboratory on electric drives, motors, power electronics and/or electric networks, energy storages and hydrogen economy. 2. analyse measurement results, 3. analyse databases of electric networks, 4. write good-quality technical reports, 5. participate in electrical measurement activities in laboratory environments.
content: Laboratory works on electric drives, motors, power electronics and/or electric networks and markets, energy storages and hydrogen economy. Design, measurements, simulations, analysis and reports. Electrical safety. Use of AI applications: AI applications can be used for understanding concepts and searching for information, taking into account the constraints of the AI in source criticism. Students have to provide the answers in laboratory works by own produced text. Students are not allowed to present AI-generated text or figures or any other material as their own.
prerequisites: Basics of electrical engineering. Basic laboratory courses of electrical engineering. Electrical safety.
learningMaterial: Materials based on accepted industrial and scientific documents are given in each specific laboratory work. Laboratory work instructions are delivered for students in Moodle. Additional material: Mohan, Ned. Undeland, Tore M. Robbins, William P. Power Electronics: Converters, Applications, and Design. John Wiley & Sons. Pyrhönen Juha, Hrabovcová Valeria, Semken, R. Scott. Electrical machine drives control. P.C. Sen, Principles of electric machines and power electronics. Leander, W., Matsch, Late, J., Derald, Morgan, Electromagnetic and electromechanical machines Bessarabov, D. G. et al. PEM Electrolysis for Hydrogen Production: Principles and Applications. Armand, Michel et al. Lithium-ion Batteries - Current state of the art and anticipated developments.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, measurements, laboratory work and reports in groups of three persons (personal grades) 100 %.
workload: Introductory lecture 2 h, 1st period on M.Sc. (Tech.) at Lappeenranta campus. Laboratory work, computer-aided work, writing of preliminary reports and measurement reports. 1st-4th period on M.Sc. (Tech.) 1, 1st -2nd period on M.Sc. (Tech.) 2 at Lappeenranta campus. The lecturers responsible for the course give further information about the laboratory assignments and prerequisites of each assignment. Measurements and working in laboratory 18-xx h. Independent study: Measurement analysis and report writing 60-xx h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Laboratory Course in Electrical Power Engineering

learningMaterial: I

name: Laboratory Course in Electronics 2
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will: be able to carry out advanced measurements using the basic instruments (oscilloscope, multimeter, power source) in the laboratory. be able to carry out common measurements using an impedance analyzer and a spectrum analyzer. be able to design a circuit board, taking into account typical electromagnetic and thermal effects, and the limitations imposed by the manufacturing process. be able to to account for the limitations and non-ideal properties of prototyping boards, measuring instruments, passive components, operational amplifiers and digital circuits in development and testing tasks of electronics. identify the value of documenting laboratory work, and be able to routinely keep a log of measurements or laboratory journal.
content: Electronics laboratory work and challenging measurements. Design and manufacturing process of a printed circuit board. Non-ideal properties of components. Differential pairs and balanced lines. Use of AI applications The use of AI tools for almost all aspects of this course is encouraged. Use AI to help you write code, understand circuits, improve your writing, etc. Make sure your use of AI doesn't violate LUT policies. Exception to the above: laboratory notebooks must be an accurate record of what you did and observed in the laboratory. These notebooks must be done manually by you. Use of AI for laboratory notes without prior permission from the teacher is considered cheating. Remember that you are still responsible for what you turn in for each assignment, even if you used AI to do it. You are expected to understand everything that you have had AI do for you. For example, if you are unable to explain why a specific circuit was designed the way it was, it will count negatively towards your grade, even if the circuit was correct.
prerequisites: The student should already be able to: Carry out common measurements using multimeters and oscilloscopes. Identify passive components used in electronics and understand the markings on them. Build electronic circuits on prototyping boards and to carry out measurements and tests on them. Explain the functionality of the most common electronic components, especially that of resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, operational amplifiers and logic ports; design simple circuits with these components; and to interpret and draw circuit diagrams and to report measurement results. Write simple programs for embedded microcontrollers and use interrupts Design simple analog and digital filters and describe the properties of them
learningMaterial: The Art of Electronics by Paul Horowitz and Winfield Hill, 3rd edition, 2015 Microelectronic Circuits by Adel S. Sedra and Kenneth C. Smith, 5th edition, 2004 Signal Integrity: Applied Electromagnetics and Professional Practice by Samuel H. Russ, 2nd edition, 2022. Supplementary material may be available via Moodle. Students are also expected to independently look up material for certain exercises.
evaluationCriteria: 1–5. Continuous assessment based on laboratory tasks and other assignments.
workload: Laboratory exercises in electronics, and related pre-lab assignments and reports. 1.–4. periods. Laboratory work 98h, other work 64h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Laboratory Course in E-Mobility
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. plan and execute measurements in laboratory, 2. analyse measurement results, 3. write good-quality technical reports.
content: Laboratory works on electric drives and machines, grid converter and calorimeter. Design, measurements, simulations, analysis, and reports. Electrical safety. Use of AI applications: Artificial intelligence applications can be used according to general policies of LUT.

evaluationCriteria: 0-5, measurements and reports in groups (personal grades) 100 %.
workload: Introductory lecture, 1 h, 3.period. Laboratory work, computer-aided work, writing of preliminary reports and measurement reports, 3st-4th period on M.Sc. (Tech.) 1. name: Laboratory Course of Heat Transfer (HDD)
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to 1. apply the theories of heat transfer in practical engineering and develop calculation models for the thermal analysis of applications, 2. write a technical report on the application oriented thermal design and the analysis related to laboratory tests, 3. analyse experimental results and evaluate their reliability, 4. apply heat transfer related theoretical and experimental information, available from the teaching of and literature on heat transfer, and the principles of the thermal design of most typical heat transfer cases in an application oriented way, 5. practice of project and team work. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Know-how on own field, Knowledge of the research of own field, Mathematics and natural sciences, Practical application of theories, Written communication, Oral communication, Digitalisation and utilisation of data, Leadership skills, Team working skills, Social skills, Working independently, Problem solving, Information retrieval, Project management, Time management and prioritizing tasks, Developing own skills in working life, Critical thinking skills, Analytical thinking skills.
content: Student participates to three projects that are done in groups dealing with conduction, convection and radiation in different heat transfer applications.
prerequisites: Engineering Thermodynamics and Fluid mechanics completed. Engineering Heat Transfer completed or studied at the same time.
learningMaterial: Incropera, De Witt: Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer. Saari, J.: Design of Heat Exchangers. Literature Incropera, De Witt: Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer Saari, J.: Design of Heat Exchangers Bergman, T.L.: Incropera's principles of heat and mass transfer Holman J.P.: Heat Transfer Cengel: Heat Transfer, A Practical Approach
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, based on three projects
workload: 1st project 19 h: planning of project and measurements 3 h, measurements 1 h, analysis and reporting 13 h, peer review 2 h. 2nd project 31 h: planning of project 2 h, theoretical background 5 h, design calculation 13 h, reporting 8 h, peer review 3 h. 3rd project 31 h: planning of project 2 h, theoretical background 5 h, design calculation 13 h, reporting 8 h, peer review 3 h. Total workload 81 h.

name: Laboratory Safety Course
learningOutcomes: After the course the student - Recognizes the risk in laboratory work and can take into account them when working in laboratory - Understands the meaning of safety in laboratory work and how to put it into practice - Understands the whole chemical chain and is able to handle chemicals safely - Can choose the proper protection to work in the laboratory - Knows what to do in emergency or exceptional situation - Understands the roles, tasks and responsibilities of different persons, learns to work in group. Knows basics of good laboratory practices in laboratory working.
content: In the course it is told how to work safely in laboratory and which risks you should notice. In addition the chemical handling chain is explained and material safety data sheets are read. Different personal protection equipment are shown and how to choose them. The action in emergency and exceptional situations are handled as well as the roles and responsibilities of personnel in organization are discussed. During laboratory days there is practical exam and training of basic laboratory practices.
prerequisites: Course is only for students attending any master program (biorefineries, chemical engineering for energy transition, food processing technology, water technology, SBBE) which include laboratories during the same study year.
learningMaterial: Materials given in Moodle. e.g slides, videos, material safety data sheets.
evaluationCriteria: Passed/Failed
workload: Laboratories 16 h, practical exam 3 h, self study 21 h. Total workload 54 h.

name: Organizational Perspectives on Sustainability Communication
learningOutcomes: After completing this course, the students will be able to: - explain the central theories of corporate responsibility and sustainability communication - empirically evaluate sustainability and political communication and their organizational and societal implications -create communication plans for organizations in the context of sustainability and corporate responsibility
content: The course covers current theories of corporate responsibility and sustainability communication, including greenwashing. In addition, it introduces theoretical approaches to organizations as political actors in the context of such communication. The course discusses also sustainability reporting, stakeholder analysis and engagement from the perspective of different organizations and actors. Use of AI applications AI applications can be used for idea generation in the group work.
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree or alike in an appropriate field in the social sciences or communication sciences that gives eligibility to enrol into the master’s program.
learningMaterial: O’Connor, A. (Ed.). (2022). The routledge handbook of corporate social responsibility communication . Taylor & Francis. A set of articles given at the beginning of the course. Literature will be announced in the beginning of the course.
evaluationCriteria: Numerical assessment on a scale of 0–5. Group work (50 %) and an independent learning assignment (50 %).
workload: The course is completed by attending the lectures and returning group work and an independent learning assignment.

name: Overview of China
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: Enrich themselves with the tradition and modernization of China; Understand the philosophy, policies and behavioral patterns that have shaped China into what it is today; Comment on the story of China with sound argumentation and reexamine the ties between China and the world with fresh perspectives; Find new opportunities to get involved in the collaboration between their home nations and China.
content: The course introduces students to a panorama of China through a task-based learning approach. Students will read recommended materials, discover related official websites, attend lectures, write video reviews and accomplish team projects to obtain a better understanding of the given topics like but not limited to below, Land of opportunities: leading Chinese cities with their unique characteristics You must see it: cultural heritages and tourist attractions in China A gourmet paradise: Chinese food and drinks Cultural kaleidoscope: local customs and folk arts in China Profound changes in Chinese society: life style and technological advancement Oriental wisdom: essence of Chinese traditional philosophy
prerequisites: Students should have an interest in the traditions and modern life of China.
learningMaterial: 1.Peng Guo, Long Cheng, China Panorama, Beijing, Higher Education Press, 2012 2.Xiaowei Zang, Understanding Chinese Society (Second Edition), New York, Routledge, 2016 3.Aimin Cheng, Understanding China, Shanghai: Shanghai Foreign Languages Education Press, 2018 4.Handouts and online resources from a variety of official websites
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Lecture attendance (10%), Reading Report (25%), Tutorial Participation (15%), Group Project Plan (10%), Group Project progress Report (15%), Final Project (25%)
workload: Lectures 28 h, small group planning meetings 28 h, project design and construction 52 h, Total workload 108 h.

name: P2X Laboratory course
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the module, the student: - is familiar with basic P2X Laboratory equipment and processes - knows the experimental methods in the field - is capable of operating with relevant analytical methods
content: The course includes a literature review and P2X-related laboratory experiments to study gas purification and processing into other compounds. The exact work topics and their number might vary yearly. Laboratory work including experiments, analyses, and reporting will be conducted in small groups.
prerequisites: COMPULSORY PREREQUISITES Students, who have not studied their bachelor's degree in LUT have to take course BJ02A0061 Laboratory safety course before taking this course.
evaluationCriteria: 0–5, reports and laboratory work
workload: Laboratory experiments (50 h), pre-reports (30 h), result analysis and final reports (55 h). Total workload 135 h.

name: Postgraduate Course in Finite Element Method
learningOutcomes: The student will be able to: Grasp the fundamental concepts of continuum mechanics. Construct displacement-based nonlinear finite elements for structural and solid mechanics applications using MATLAB. Evaluate the robustness, accuracy and efficiency of the FE solutions.
content: Fundamentals of finite element analysis for structural and solid mechanics, including both linear and nonlinear finite element methods. This encompasses updated and total Lagrangian schemes, derivation of structural and continuum elements, numerical solution methods, convergence requirements, and the application of finite elements in large displacement dynamics. *** The course is related to UN's Sustainable Development Goals (SDG): 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, 12 Responsible consumption and Production, 13 Climate Action, 17 Partnerships for the Goals
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have basic skills in the Finite Element Method (FEM).
learningMaterial: Lectures notes in the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 50 %, simulation works 50 %.
workload: Lectures 14 h. Exercises in computer class 14 h. Simulation works 128 h. Total loading 156 h.

name: Postgraduate Course in Packaging Technology
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to deepen the doctoral students’ knowledge and know-how in packaging technology related topics. Emphasis will be put on research methodology, sustainability, manufacturing machinery, processes and materials related to packaging technology and converting of materials in general. The doctoral students will deepen their knowledge, improve and focus on their skills in scientific research methodology, as well as presenting scientific results related to their field of study.
content: The course consists of a seminar-based structure with written reports and presentations. Emphasis will be put on modern packaging technology, manufacturing technologies and novel materials with a sustainability point of view, especially related to SDG's 12 and 13 (Responsible consumption and production, climate action). Aspects of scientific research related to packaging technology as well as other converting methodology in the field of mechanical engineering will be covered.
prerequisites: M.Sc. degree in (Mech.Eng.)
learningMaterial: Textbooks will be selected individually for each student and the content will be discussed during the seminar. Examples include: Niskanen K, Mechanics of Paper Products, Conference proceedings: International Conference on Flexible Automation and Intelligent Manufacturing (FAIM) and IAPRI World Packaging Conference.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Written exam 50 % and seminar 50 % or individual research project 100 % or teamwork 100%.
workload: It is possible to perform the course either by participating to conventional lectures and seminars during the 1st and the 2nd period or by carrying out an individual research project during periods 1-4.

name: Postgraduate Course in Production Engineering
learningOutcomes: Doctoral students will be familiar with how to form and apply analytical, statistical and stochastic models to support production analysis and development together with the tools of sustainability analysis. Students will get to know how to use different analysis methods to solve technical problems in production. Depending on the number of students on the course, course includes seminar, which focus on the approaches and methodologies of scientific research.
content: The aim of the course is to deepen students' knowledge and understanding about the aspects of modern production engineering and manufacturing technologies, especially the future trends, development aspects of sustainability issues including processing of novel materials, and the results of scientific research dealing with production in mechanical engineering.
learningMaterial: Will be available on Moodle on requests, and dependent on frame of student's interests.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Seminars 50 %, Oral exam 30 %, Written exam 20 %.
workload: All actions below during 4 periods

name: Postgraduate Course in Real-Time Multibody System Dynamics
learningOutcomes: To provide the theoretical and practical skills for doctoral students in the field of real-time multibody system dynamics. To improve the ability of doctoral students to model and simulate multibody systems in real-time.
content: Formulation used of real-time multibody system dynamics. Time integration schemes for real-time multibody system dynamics. The course module supports the following UN Sustainable Development Goals: #9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes, Javier Garcia De Jalon, Eduardo Bayo, Kinematic and dynamic simulation of multibody systems: the real-time challenge, Springer Science, 1994.
evaluationCriteria: Examination 50 %, seminars and simulation exercises 50 %.
workload: Lectures 10 h, seminars 34 h, computer class exercises 16 h. Personal modeling and simulation exercises 56 h. Independent study 40 h. Total workload 156 h.

name: Postgraduate Course in Rotor Dynamics
learningOutcomes: To deepen the theoretical skills of doctoral students in the dynamic phenomena of rotating machinery. To give the doctoral students the ability to model and analyze the dynamic behavior of the rotor-bearings systems. To give the doctoral students the ability to reflect the research work of other doctoral students within a research group. Ability to carry out review of other researchers' work and participate in academic debates.
content: Rigid and flexible rotor equations, bearing types and their modeling, solution of rotor dynamic system equations, free-free vibration modes, critical speeds and modes, whirl speeds, steady state responses and transient response. Individual or group work on selected structure/component, implementation it's analysis into computer code and seminar presentation of the results.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes. Selected chapters from the following text books: 1. Chen, W. J. and Gunter, E. J., 2005, Introduction to Dynamics of Rotor-Bearing Systems, Trafford Publishing, Victoria. 2. Krämer E. Dynamics of Rotors and Foundations. Berlin: Springer-Verlag, 1993 3. Friswell M, Penny J, Garvey S et al. Dynamics of Rotating Machines. New York: Cambridge University Press, 2010 4. Lalanne, M., and Ferraris, G., 1998, Rotordynamics Prediction in Engineering, 2nd Edition, John Wiley ; Sons, West Sussex.
evaluationCriteria: PASS/FAIL. Evaluating is based on seminar presentations and personal modeling and simulation exercises.
workload: Lectures 4 h, Seminars 36 h. Personal modeling and simulation exercises 58 h. Independent study 58 h. Total work load 156 h.

name: Postgraduate Research Course in Welded Metal Structures
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to · Plan and conduct research in the field of metallic materials · understand how to efficiently utilize research facilities and equipment · interpret research results in a scientific way · collaborate with researchers in a similar field with good research ethics · write a scientific paper related to the procedure and results of experimental research for welded structures · proceed with publication process(es)
content: During the course, the student will become familiar with scientific research. This comprises: · Planning scientific research and finding suitable publication channels for research work, considering student-specific content · conducting extensive literature reviews supporting scientific work · performing metallurgical investigations (macro- and micro-level analyses, hardness measurements, etc.) for in the studied field · carrying out mechanical testing, and analyzing and reporting experimental results · peer-support and problem solving on research topics · presenting research topics in clear and understandable way to scientific community. The course module provides knowledge about the experimental methods and studies to investigate the performance of structural components used in Power-to-X applications.
prerequisites: M.Sc Degree in (Mech.Eng.)
learningMaterial: The course content is adjusted as per registered students and their research background. Consequently, no specific learning material is not followed/recommended.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail, according to quality of presentations in seminars and activity on working on case studies.
workload: Lectures (8*2h) 16h in periods 1-3. Case studies on field of welded metal structures 39h. Design, execution, analyzing and reporting of studies 80 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Power Electronic Converter Design
learningOutcomes: Upon completion, the student will be familiar with working in a group and execute the following project tasks: 1. contribution of essential information for specification purposes from the area of interest, 2. apply design skills acquired in previous courses to analyse, simulate and realize a system 3. document and present the analysis and project results.
content: Design work for a system prototype in a group. Specification making. Analysis and simulation of the design options and reporting analysis and simulation results. Identification of possible technical challenges in operation and in production. Reporting of design documents for the final design ready for production and tests. Use of AI applications: AI applications can be used for understanding concepts and searching for information, taking into account the constraints of the AI in source criticism. Students have to provide the reports by own produced text and figures. Students are not allowed to present AI-generated text or figures or any other material as their own.
prerequisites: Basics of Power Electronics. Basic laboratory courses of electrical engineering. Electrical safety. Master studies of 1st year attended. Specific interest in some of the following research areas: electronics or power electronics, control systems, electric machines, or smart grids. This course is meant for students of 2nd year in Master studies.
learningMaterial: Materials are based on accepted industrial and scientific practices related to the topic of the project work and will be disseminated via Moodle and in the lecture.

name: Power Electronic Converters
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. demonstrate good general knowledge of the selected different basic main circuits in modern power electronics, 2. describe the features and functions of selected rectifiers, switch-mode converters and inverters, 3. calculate and simulate typical design tasks of the aforementioned circuits, 4. describe the joint operation of power electronic converters and loads as well as some network interferences caused by converters and some alternatives to reduce these interferences.
content: Operation of the main circuits of different power converters: rectifiers (single and three-phase), DC-DC switch mode converters, inverters (single and three-phase). Characteristics and operation. Pulse width modulation (PWM). Harmonic components. Simulation of power electronic circuits.
prerequisites: Recommended: BL30A0000 Electric Circuits. Integration and derivation (esp. sine and cosine functions). FFT. Laplace transforms. Basic software skills with Excel, Word, Matlab/Simulink.

content: Working with various data structures (multidimensional arrays, cell arrays, etc.) and variable types (numeric, logical, textual, etc.), Matlab symbolic functionality, conditional statements (if-else, switch-case), loops (for and while), using built-in functions, handling external data, 2-D and 3-D plotting, writing user-defined functions.

name: Project Course in Electric Transportation Systems
learningOutcomes: Aim of the course is to get the students familiar to the project type working in electrical transportation. Project work in groups.

After having completed this course, the student should be able to: ability to build up material selection route from end product and manufacturing methods to raw materials ability to work in a project organisation in certain role can act and communicate in groups and networks.

Sub- areas for project can be following: material optimization, selection of manufacturing method, testing, production planning, scheduling and inventory optimization, capacity utilization, lead time reduction, quality improvement and control, new product development process, effective maintenance, energy usage, layout floor planning, inter-departmental effectiveness, feasibility study in to a new technology, market approval, sales, marketing and business strategy, new markets, products, company strategies, competitors and routes to market.

name: Project Course in Mechatronic Systems
learningOutcomes: The design of modern, automated mechatronic systems requires expertise across multiple disciplines, such as mechanical design, electrical design, control design, and software development. Thus, commonly, a diverse team of engineers works on the design of mechatronic systems. This project course is meant to replicate a full design process of a mechatronic system meant for automation, from conceptualization to realization in hardware and on-board software. In this course, students will learn to work in an interdisciplinary team in which each person has a different focus area analyze an automation task and conceptualize a mechatronical solution as a team formulate design goals in a measurable and structured manner Depending on their individual focus area in the team, students will learn to design the mechanical and electrical components of the devised solution, develop automation software on an embedded level using version control, assemble and/or manufacture a hardware prototype, validate whether the design goals are met by the developed solution, conduct hardware testing to ensure reliable operations, document the designed solution in a report written in LaTeX, present the designed solution and its validation and test performance in an oral presentation, supported by slides and, as far as feasible, live hardware demonstrations. The course workload and credit points are determined at the outset by the instructors, based on the scope of the tackled fields and the expected effort per student.
content: The course starts with one or multiple initial physical sessions, introducing the goals of the course, the depth of tasks expected, and the project scope. Students are partitioned into groups by the teachers based on the results of a questionnaire assessing their skills and interests. Automation problems tackled are either proposed by the teachers, by partner companies, or suggested by students, subject to instructor approval. The number of credit points is set at the outset of the project by the responsible teachers, depending on how many fields are tackled in detail and on the expected workload per student. Regardless of the specific project, each team must consider all steps, within budgetary feasibility, including problem analysis, conceptualization, system and component design, validation, testing, documentation, and presentation.
prerequisites: Students are expected to have prior knowledge in the following areas: Mechanical design (CAD/CAE) Electrical design Control design Embedded programming (C and/or C++) Scripting (Python, MATLAB, or similar)
learningMaterial: Materials from the students' other courses in their Mechatronics program, as they provide the theoretical basics for this course.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5: Criteria are the quality of the developed solution (50%), the quality of the documentation (20%), quality of the presentation (10%), knowledge of the students as exhibited when questioned during presentation (20%).
workload: The course requires a certain amount of presence, for instance for the initial event(s) as well as for the final presentation. Moreover, work with hardware will require physical presence.

name: Project work in Materials Characterisation
learningOutcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: Independently design and execute a research project focusing on the compositional, microstructural, and/or crystallographic characterisation of metallic samples. Select and apply appropriate materials characterisation techniques, such as energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic/magnetic force microscopy (AFM/MFM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and/or electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Perform comprehensive material characterisation and critically interpret experimental data to draw meaningful conclusions about the properties of their chosen samples. Effectively document and communicate research findings through a technical report and oral presentation.
content: This course provides students with an opportunity to apply their previously acquired knowledge of characterisation techniques in an individual experimental project. Students will analyse metallic samples—either their own or those provided by the instructor—by first defining research objectives, selecting appropriate characterisation techniques, designing experimental procedures, preparing samples, conducting measurements, post-processing the experimental data, and critically interpreting the results. Throughout the course, students will work independently under the supervision of the teachers for guidance and feedback. Ultimately, each student writes a comprehensive technical report that includes methodology, results, discussion, and conclusions and presents their findings to their fellow students.
learningMaterial: Course materials include: Instructional guides and manuals for analytical instruments. Supplementary reading materials and research articles, provided via course Moodle. Access to software tools for data analysis, such as crystallography programs. Regular consultations with supervising teachers for guidance and feedback on project progress.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, experimental project work 100%
workload: Lectures 6h, project planning 10h, data collection and analysis 70h, report writing 64h, discussions with the guiding teacher 10h, presentation 2h. Total amount 162h.

After having completed this course, the students will be able to: understand the potential of recyclable materials define technical processes for utilization of recyclable materials can put new ideas into action
content: The course will cover the following topics. What are recyclable materials? Waste policy and waste hierarchy in EU and globally. EoW legislation. Pre-treatment and sorting methods for recyclable materials. Potential manufacturing and production methods for recycled materials. Recycled end products. Company cooperation Technological examples and topics from the companies in the lectures. name: Research methods in circular economy
learningOutcomes: Learning goals: Upon completion of the course the student is expected to be able to: 1. Name a number of research methods commonly used within the field of circular economy 2. Explain the basics of the research methods introduced in the course 3. Name some of the benefits and limitations of each of the methods 4. Identify (an) appropriate research method(s) in accordance with an identified research question 5. Explain the implementation steps of one of the selected research methods 6. Use references in an appropriate and scientific matter. 7. Write a well structured essay/report
content: Many different research methods are used within the context of the circular economy. The course “Research methods in circular economy” will give you an introduction to some of these methods. Each lecture will focus on one of these methods and will be introduced by an expert working with the methods within his or her research. Both quantitative and qualitative methods will be covered. You are expected to attend the lectures and read additional reading material given. You will be asked to perform tasks after each lecture based on the lecture content and the reading material, participate to the final seminar (mandatory), and complete an assignment at the end of the course. In the final lecture/seminar you will present you work within small groups to other students and discuss your findings together. You will need to pass your final assignment with a pass in order to pass the course. Use of AI applications You are not allowed to present AI in any of your assignments as if it was your own. However, you are encouraged to ask help from AI to create ideas or get a general overview of the topic (similar as in the use of an encyclopedia) . We, however, expect you to be aware of the outcomes of AI, as they are generic and not always accurate, and its content will not be sufficient to complete your assignments successfully. We expect you to go deeper into your assignment topics by going through scientific literature, among others. Working life skills The aim of the course is to provide you with the knowledge on different research methods and how they can help you tackle questions related to sustainability and the circular economy. Additionally, you will develop your writing skills and learn how to reference in an appropriate manner. These will be important skills to have in your future profession. We additionally hope to develop critical thinking by means of feedback to other students and your own.
prerequisites: Bachelor's thesis or degree completed.
learningMaterial: Lectures, scientific articles and blog posts that can be found from Moodle

name: Selection Criteria of Materials
learningOutcomes: After having passed this course module the student is able to: * apply and develop systematic material selection methods and tools to solve cross-technological material selection tasks * define and analyse the properties, strengths, weaknesses and application areas of the main groups of engineering materials for different types of applications * justify and build generalized models to solve the material selection task by taking into account the functionality, manufacturability and environmental aspects in addition to the total costs of the product * evaluate and utilize recent results and documents of material science * take into account the UN's sustainable development goals (SDG) during the materials selection process. * apply systematic material selection tools to select structural materials that can be used in Power-to-X (P2X) technologies. * derive analytical models based on the principles of LCC's, LCA's and MIPS-factors in material selection.
content: During the course the student will become familiar with the properties and application areas of different engineering materials. The recent scientific results dealing with material science and technology will be discussed. Aspects of selecting and comparing different materials are discussed from the viewpoints of functionality, manufacturing aspects, costs and environmental aspects of the product. Future trends in materials science are discussed briefly. Metallic alloys, polymers, ceramics, composites, adaptive materials and nanomaterials will be considered. Environmental aspects of material selection from the viewpoint of LCC and LCA and the basics of MIPS calculations. Innovative solutions of the material selection tasks will be discussed. Principles to formulate and solve the materials selection tasks based on analytical and systematic approaches and means to develop models to support the selection process staring from the product's requirement list will be discussed in detail. Considering and accounting for the UN's sustainable development goals (SDG) during the materials selection process will be discussed. Selection criteria for structural materials that can be used in Power-to-X (P2X) technologies will also be discussed. Project work focuses on selecting engineering materials for industrial applications, including P2X technologies.
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Mechanical Engineering) or B.Sc. (Materials Engineering)
learningMaterial: Mangohon, P., The Principles of Materials Selection for Engineering Design. Ashby, M., Materials Selection in Mechanical Design. Strong, A. B., Plastics: Materials and Processing. Kalpakjan, S. and Schmid, S., Manufacturing Engineering and Technology. Lectures and exercises in Moodle. For Finnish students and distance learning: Eskelinen ; Karsikas, Vihreän teknologian näkökulmat konstruktiomateriaalien valinnassa, ISBN 978-952-265-457-1.

name: Solving Societal Challenges with Data
learningOutcomes: After completing this course, the students will: know where and how they can obtain open data, be able to assess the quality and restrictions of data sources, be aware of the opportunities of multidisciplinary collaboration, be familiar with planning projects solving societal challenges.
content: Massive amount of data is generated every day by public and private organizations around the world. Digital footprints are collected as part of people’s everyday lives and their everyday activities, for example when shopping online, browsing the internet, or using social media. Big data collected has attracted increasing attention over the recent years, and increasing amount of survey, register, and other traditional type of data are openly available. Much of this data remains unutilized, even though powerful analyses for solving societal challenges become possible. This course explores the opportunities and challenges of open data and the benefits of multidisciplinary approach to problem solving.
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree or alike in an appropriate field in the social sciences or communication sciences that gives eligibility to enrol into the master’s program.

name: Start-up Challenge
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, students will be able to: - understand a start-up culture and operate in a start-up setting - recognize and evaluate start-up challenges - apply creative problem-solving techniques - manage creativity in an international, cross-disciplinary team - plan, manage and execute challenge-based, short-term projects - understand and apply the principles of agile, lean and social start-up - develop and pitch a client-oriented solution
content: Are you an entrepreneur? Are you considering an entrepreneurial career or work in a small, agile and rapidly growing firm? Would you like to get a sense of what it feels to be a part of a start-up team and deal with start-up challenges on a daily basis? In all these cases, this course is for you! Despite the rising popularity of entrepreneurship, start-up culture brings its own unique set of challenges and problems that its leaders must commit to addressing. A number of challenges await a start-up already at the stages of product/service development, proof of concept and prototyping. Furthermore, multiple managerial issues constantly emerge - dealing with limited resources and fierce competition, a need to build external relations being a small firm, a need in a constant change and agility along with a mission to grow rapidly. The course is designed in a way that every student gets a chance to get a deep dive into the challenges of a real start-up and help the company in solving these challenges. Just like in a real-life situation, the real start-up firms invited to participate in this course combine managerial and strategic business challenges (business strategy, innovation, and new venture management), to be solved by the course students with the help of experienced mentors. The students form teams to solve a complex start-up challenge of their choice. The course encourages lean start-up entrepreneurship principles in dealing with entrepreneurial challenges.
prerequisites: Recommended, but not required: A370A0001 Johtamisen ja yrittäjyyden perusteet; A370A0401 Case-Course of Business; A380A6050 Introduction to International Business and Planning; A130A0550 Introduction to Organizational Behavior
learningMaterial: Lecture materials, additional readings, start-up challenge’ materials
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points; challenge solution 100 % (plan, presentation and report).
workload: Lectures 16 h, 1st and 2nd period. Pitching sessions 4 h, 2nd period. Independent project 140 h, 1st-2nd periods. Total workload 160 h.

name: Sustainability Challenge Project Work
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to act as an active member of an interdisciplinary project team in different roles. Depending on her/his rolein the project, the student can: 1. describe the outline of the project plan and apply different methods to divide the project into subtasks and to schedule the project, 2. prepare a budget for the project and monitor it, 3. document the group's and her/his project work results both orally and in writing, 4. reflect her/his actions as a member of the team and assess the outcome ofthe project and the other team members' work, 5. recognize the key elements in project risk management, 6. apply knowledge and skills acquired in other courses to complete the project
content: Varying themes according to the project.
learningMaterial: Case-specific
evaluationCriteria: 1-5. The course is evaluated based on the work done in the project and its appropriate documentation, by student self-assessment and by teachers and peers. Comprehensive documentation, monitoring and reporting on the projectare key elements in the evaluation.

Working in a project as a member of a project team in different roles and tasks e.g. related to generating ideas, planning, dimensioning, construction, manufacturing, measuring and testing documentation, management and negotiations. Continuous self-assessment, evaluation of the project group work and the outcome of the project e.g. with alearning and/or project diary.

name: Sustainability in Socio-Technological context
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: 1) Explain the core idea and thinking behind sustainability, and outline the different dimensions of sustainability; ecological, social, economic and cultural, 2) Explain the interaction between the environment, society and business and the relationships, of various actors in these fields and their impacts on the society and the environment , 3) Understand the importance to limit or decelerate environmental damages and improve our quality of life while pursuing a more sustainable lifestyle and business within the planetary boundaries, 4) Apply practically the learned principles and concepts of sustainability in relation to current production and consumption habits, 5) Reflect on sustainability principles and gain basic understanding of sustainability transitions.
content: The general objective of the course is to provide a comprehensive overview of the concepts of sustainability, sustainable business, and sustainable transition generally and especially in the socio-technological context. The course introduces the global sustainability challenges that the planet and societies are facing and understands the need for a sustainability transition. A future negotiation-learning approach is applied in the course. Key themes: - Sustainability and society - Socio-technical systems - Sustainability transitions
learningMaterial: Will be provided in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Individual assignments 20%, pair work 50%, group work 30 %.
workload: 1st period: 2*2 h lectures, 2*3 h seminars, independent digitalized studies including individual (approx. 92 h) and group assignments (approx. 61 h). Total workload 162 h.
equivalentCoursesInfo: BH60A4400 Introduction to Sustainability

name: Sustainable Cities
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course, students will be able to: Summarize the driving forces behind the city sustainable development Name the measurements of sustainable cities with the three-pillar model Explain the main operations of a city from an environmental point of view Access the environmental, economic and social challenges related to city’s sustainable development Identify the resources for the cities to develop the sustainable solutions Apply One Click LCA (life cycle assessment) software to assess the life cycle environmental impacts for buildings
content: The course explores the basic terminologies, needs, challenges, opportunities, and guidance in the development of sustainable cities. It focuses on available resources and approaches to develop integrated sustainable solutions for cites. Emphasis is placed in the field of engineering and natural science, including energy, environmental impact, urban planning, and infrastructure. This course contributes UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) - SDG11 (Sustainable cities and communities) in particular.
prerequisites: This course is intended for 3rd year students (Non-qualified students will be moved out in the 1st week of the course). Environmental Technology students can take this course also in 2nd year if needed. Exceptions may be considered on an individual basis. Please contact the responsible teacher directly for enrollment details.
learningMaterial: Mega, Voula. Human Sustainable Cities: Towards the SDGs and Green, Just, Smart and Inclusive Transitions . Springer Nature, 2022. Other materials will be provided in each Lecture through Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Three tasks: 1. Quiz 20%, 2. Group or individual work 50% (report and presentation), 3. One Click LCA-modelling report 30% ( total workload: 156 hours)
workload: Course intro, 7 Lectures, 2 Tutorials and 1 individual guidance

name: Technical Computing Software
learningOutcomes: After the course, the student is an elementary-level user of some computational development environment and is familiar with finding its documentation and implementing numerical methods using the development environment. The student has been introduced to software engineering and can define and solve simple computational problems using the development environment or a spreadsheet program. The students can use and produce technical information and assess information produced by themselves and others. The student may be introduced to use of AI tools in problem-solving and writing assistance.

In addition, Simulink and a spreadsheet program is used for problem-solving. Basic applications in numerical analysis, such as root finding, optimization and solving simple differential equations, with examples for engineering. Documenting the development process and writing formulas using LaTeX. Company cooperation The course project may be done for a company. Use of AI tools AI tools can be used to assist in problem-solving and writing. As an optional topic, you may train your own AI to solve a simple problem.

name: Bachelor's Thesis in Electrical Engineering
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. work independently and in a goal-oriented manner, 2. delineate a narrow research problem, 3. select research methodology suitable for the study, 4. set her/himself goals for results and time management, 5. search source material in a systematic way, assess the quality and credibility of sources, and use and analyze source material in her/his study, 6. write a report according to scientific practices with a special reference to electrical engineering.
content: Bachelor's thesis is a written thesis for the Bachelor's degree, by which the student shows familiarity with the topic of her/his study. The student defines a narrow research problem, selects suitable research strategy and methodologies, and writes the Bachelor's thesis. The emphasis of the Bachelor's thesis is on a literature review, which can be complemented by practical elements where applicable. Fundamentals of scientific work and good scientific conduct. Information searches and analysis skills. Scientific thinking and communication.

Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: working independently, information retrieval, problem solving, written communication, know-how on own field, knowledge of the research of own field, time management and prioritizing tasks.
content: The Bachelor’s thesis is the final thesis of the Bachelor’s degree, with which the students show that they are able to apply their knowledge and skills to solve a research problem related to their field of study. name: Internationalization of the Firm and Global Marketing
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: After completing the course the student will be able to: - understand and evaluate benefits and costs of internationalization of the firm - justify and recommend how to enhance international competitiveness of the firm - analyze and justify the key management decisions related to internationalization of the firm: whether to internationalize, which markets to target, and how to enter selected markets - apply relevant theories and frameworks to explain and facilitate internationalization of particular firms
content: - Must know: internationalization motives and barriers; chain of strategic decisions related to internationalization of the firm; risks assessment in international markets; internationalization theories (OLI, Uppsala model, Network approach, Born Global); firm's international competitiveness; international market selection process; factors influencing entry mode choice; characteristics of various entry modes (export modes, intermediate entry modes, hierarchical modes). - Should know: concept of the value chain in internationalization; comparison of SMEs and LSEs in internationalization; global market research; sustainability in internationalization of the firm; the integration-responsiveness framework; organizing strategies - Nice to know: transaction cost analysis; principles of decision-making; functional strategies of an international firm

name: Internet of Things – Introduction
learningOutcomes: The main goal of this course is to give a comprehensive introduction into the state of IoT in the modern world and familiarise a student with key concepts of the subject. Student will learn about different types of data and their possible impact on communications between devices. At the end of this course student will be able to identify the applications for IoT systems and perform basic analysis of such systems. As this course is only an introduction one of the goals is to spark interest in students for further studies of the subject. 1. Understand definitions of IoT, data, information, system; 2. Understand types of networks and their features; 3. Familiarise student with IoT as a subject for further studies.
content: This course will introduce the role of IoT in modern life as well as basics of concepts that are necessary to understand IoT systems. The definitions and explanations for the terms System, Information, and Network will be considered in the first part of this course. Later we will learn about applications of theoretical concepts in some practical cases. The course is designed for people who want to understand what role IoT systems play in Fourth Industrial Revolution known as Industry 4.0 and to help them find relevant applications for these technologies in their work and studies. The course is divided into 4 chapters, each has theoretical part and a short assignment in a quiz form at the end, as follows: 1. Introduction; 2. Systems, Information, and Networks; 3. Probability and Game Theory; 4. Applications of IoT systems.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes and other material in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail; Quizzes 100%.
workload: Videos (4h); Reading assignments (8h); Quizzes (4h); Independent studies (11h). Total: 27 h.

name: Introduction to Materials Engineering
learningOutcomes: Aim of the course is to introduce possibilities of Material Engineering to students. Diverse possibilities of different materials is taken into consideration when optimizing the variable possibilities in Product Designing. After having completed this course, the student should be able to: understand the influence of material selection to the product design recognize the variable possibilities of different materials show creative and innovative expertise in the field of Materials Engineering.
content: Basics of Materials Engineering and Product Design. Principles of materials selection and introduction to materials selection procedures. Choice of fabrication techniques including case studies related to different materials. Selecting polymers and composites as raw materials: structure, properties, processing characteristics and applications for the commercially important polymers including general classes of polymers: commodity, engineering and specialty thermoplastics, thermosetting resins and rubbers. Introduction to specific metals, alloys and minerals: metallurgy, properties, applications and potentialities of metals, alloys and minerals in a wide variety of engineering environments. Wood materials. Introduction to engineering ceramics. Properties and manufacturing of carbon based materials. Recycled Materials as a raw material source.
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle. Other literature to be announced during lectures.
evaluationCriteria: Examination 70 % (Exam), seminar 30 %.

name: Transformation of Media and Changing Media Logic
learningOutcomes: The course provides the students with an understanding of how media technologies have developed both in the Finnish and international context. The course provides the students with the ability to assess critically the historical development of media and allows them to see possible paths for future development.
content: The course tackles how media technologies have changed over time, and how these changes have reverberated through society, communities, and everyday lives of ordinary people. The course studies social impact of development and change of media technologies and seeks to highlight the processes that have led to the current media landscape. Use of AI tools in course work must be carefully documented according to separate guidelines available in the course Moodle page.

name: General Chemistry Laboratory Works
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will be able to: work safely in laboratory environment prepare simple solutions perform a gravimetric analysis and an acid-base titration write reactions of the most common ions explain the basics of solubility in qualitative analysis name molecules set up simple synthesis apparatuses employ the main laboratory techniques in organic chemistry (refluxing, distillation, extraction, crystallization, drying etc.) and explain the essential theory related to them perform a multi-step organic synthesis with the required purification and separation steps evaluate the quality of the synthesis product and report the results use spectrometric methods in the analysis of organic compounds.
content: The course consists of 2 sections: inorganic chemistry and organic chemistry. In the inorganic chemistry section, the most common ion reactions in inorganic solution chemistry are covered, and qualitative and quantitative analysis methods are introduced. In the laboratory, the reactions of different ions are studied, and experiments are conducted using basic chemistry methods such as gravimetry and titrimetry. The experiments also introduce the students to analytical and safe working methods in the chemistry laboratory. In the organic chemistry section the following topics are covered: Safe laboratory work considering the specific characteristics of organic chemistry. Construction of simple synthesis apparatus. Key laboratory techniques in organic chemistry: refluxing, distillation, extraction, crystallization, recrystallization, drying, determination of melting and boiling points. Implementation of multi-step synthesis. Separation and purification of the product and assessment of its purity. Reporting of results. Spectrometric methods in quantitative and qualitative analysis.
prerequisites: Course: BJ01A0020 Safety in laboratory must be passed. General chemistry Laboratory course starts after Laboratory safety course is finished (both courses are starting at same period).
learningMaterial: Laboratory guides
evaluationCriteria: 100% lab work
workload: Introductory lectures 3 h. Laboratory work 84 h. Self-study 21 h. Inorganic lab work (periods 1 and 2), organic lab work (periods 3 and 4).

Can calculate steam boiler efficiency, heat flows to heating surfaces and do combustion calculations. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: mathematics and natural sciences, working independently, problem solving, and information retrieval.
content: Characteristics of fuels. Combustion calculations. Functioning of the water-steam system. Engineering design, ability to calculate boiler efficiency, heat loads to surfaces and combustion calculations. Types of boilers. Combustion methods and equipment. Gasifiers. The effect of different fuels and combustion mechanisms on emission formation.

name: Project Work in Engineering Mathematics 2
learningOutcomes: The student advances their knowledge of mathematical theory or gains practical knowledge from applying mathematical skills in analyzing, modelling or optimizing a problem related to their field of studies. The course prepares the student for advanced studies leading up to the writing of an M.Sc. thesis or doctoral studies and scientific research. The student gains insight into the role of digitalization and mathematical models, including AI tools, in the future life, society and business.
content: A specific project is done as either a theoretical study, laboratory experiments or in a suitable commercial co-operator. The project is planned with the supervisor and may consist of laboratory work, literature research and/or theoretical studies, reporting, article writing or problem-solving in industry. The course underlines the importance of understanding the computer models of the student’s field that are driving much of industry and business and the role of digitalization in changing business models. Company cooperation The project work may be done for a company. Use of AI applications AI applications are an example of the "computer models" and may optionally be used or studied in the project.

name: Pumps, Blowers, Fans and Compressors
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to: 1. define the operational principle and structure of pumps, blowers, fans and compressors, 2. choose the appropriate type of pumps, blowers, fans and compressors for different applications, 3. demonstrate sufficient knowledge of pumps, blowers, fans and compressors for economical optimization and for sale or purchase meetings, and 4. design their principal dimensions.
content: Different types of pumps and their operating principles, calculation of centrifugal pumps and their characteristics in pipe network. Different types of compressors and their operating principles, calculation of radial compressors. Different types of blowers and their operating principles. Process applications, selection criteria and control. Expertise and skills: Know-how on own field, mathematics and natural sciences SDGs: 9 industry, innovation and infrastructure, 13 climate action
prerequisites: Recommended: BH40A1400 Fluid Dynamics I and BH20A0750 Engineering Thermodynamics.

name: An Introduction to RF and Microwave Circuits
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. apply transmission line theory to practice: to analyse how the waves act on a transmission line, and solve simple design problems requiring transmission line analysis, 2. apply the obtained knowledge of the behaviour of electromagnetic waves, 3. handle passive components and transmission lines on the Smith chart and apply it to the design of a simple L-section matching circuit, 4. apply simple expressions related to antennas to solve for example the received signal power level in an antenna, 5. explain the principles and applications of modulation in signal processing.
content: Introduction to radio and microwave circuits, radio waves, transmission line theory and S-parameters. An overview of passive RF and microwave components. Basics of radio wave propagation, antenna theory and antennas, signal analysis of analog and analog/digital systems.
prerequisites: Recommended BL30A0300 Sähkömagnetismi (electromagnetism).

Heating systems; boilers, district heating (consumer appliances), heat pumps (ground and air source heat pumps), solar energy systems, electric heating. name: Chemical Kinetics

content: Basic principles of chemical kinetics. Rate equation and determination of its parameters from experimental data. Mass balance of a batch reactor. Effect of temperature on reaction rates. name: Smart Materials and Nanotechnology
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: understand structures, properties and some applications of the actuator and sensor materials, characterize properties of selected smart materials in laboratory exercises, know how selected smart materials are manufactured using 4D printing, understand how micro- and nanotechnologies can be utilized in adaptronics, design own smart material device and demonstrate its workability (not required for passing the course), and understand the importance of the smart materials technology for conserving material and energy resources.
content: The course introduces smart materials technology (adaptronics) that integrates actuator and sensor functions into materials and structures so that the adaptronic system can react to environmental stimuli. The goal is to create an intelligent and simple construction that replaces separate machine parts in a way similar to how semiconducting materials replaced separate electronic components. In the course, it is taught how adaptronics can be miniaturized into a micro- and nanoscales through the integration of separate functional components and how smart materials structures can be manufactured using 4D printing.
learningMaterial: Lecture material available in Moodle (slides and videos).
