name: Structural Dynamics
learningOutcomes: The student will learn theories and practices of mathematical modeling and structural dynamics, and knows how to apply the knowledge in the design of machine systems. The student is able to utilize simulations as an integrated tool of product design and can utilize these skills to generalize the theories of engineering design to solve multidisciplinary design tasks. The student is able to compare and justify the use of different constructional solutions for linear and rotating motion mechanism based on their static, kinematic and dynamic analysis. Some of the practical examples and assignments used in the course are real-life cases arising from co-operation with industrial companies. The student is able to carry out individual scientific work to simulate mechatronic machines.
content: PART-1: Principles of multibody dynamics and the use of Lagrangian equation. Constraint equations and Lagrangian multipliers. Inertia of rigid bodies. Numerical integration of the equation of motion. Individual utilization of simulation software, which includes also the principles of how to apply previous mentioned mathematical theories into handling and solving abstract and multidisciplinary problems. PART-2: Multiple degree-of-freedom vibrations, solution and interpretation of natural frequencies and modes. Response to the harmonic and general force excitation. Derivation of the equations of motion of the system and solution in the frequency and time domain. Introduction to rotor dynamics. The course module supports the following UN Sustainable Development Goals: #9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have basic skills on matrix algebra and dynamics. Experience or basic studies of Finite Element Method (FEM) is also recommend, but not required.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes. Shabana, A. A.: Computational Dynamics, John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 1st edition, 1994. ISBN 0-471-30551-0. Inman, D. J.: Engineering vibration, 3rd ed., Pearson Education Inc., New Jersey, 2007. ISBN 0-13-228173-2.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, two mid-term examinations (online), simulation work, weekly homework.
workload: Lectures 32 h, Periods 3-4. Supervised tutorials 16 h, Periods 3-4. Homework 40 h, Periods 3-4 Independent study 47 h, Periods 3-4. Total loading 132 h. Moodle is used in this course.

name: Thermal Design of Steam Boilers
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to 1. use the “Systems Engineering” method for the definition of initial data in energy system projects, 2. describe the implementation phases of a component of the energy system projects, and 3. demonstrate practical skills for the planning, management and implementation of a component in energy system projects and for the estimation of the systems' total costs. Understand how large industrial products are designed by dividing design to parallel tasks. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: practical application of theories, team working skills, problem solving, and time management and prioritizing tasks.
content: Students develop their own system product component (steam boiler for power plant) through team and project work. During the course, students apply the “Systems Engineering” method, which consists of the following: the definition of the requirements for the product, testing, validation, the assessment and comparison of alternatives, the management and specification of subentities, risk assessment, reliability analysis, the optimisation and documentation of implementation. The student assumes one of the roles for the team: project manager, technical engineer, mechanical engineer, cost engineer. Project planning and execution. Cost analysis. Mechanical design. The use of computer software as a planning aid. Skills, problem solving, and time management and prioritizing tasks.
prerequisites: Recommended: BH50A0200 Introduction to Power Plant Engineering and BH50A0800 Steam Boilers.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Written report of the planning assignment 70 %, oral presentation 30 %.
workload: 3 period: 10 h of lectures and planning tutorials. 4 period: 8 h of lectures and planning tutorials and 2+2 h of seminar. Independent study approximately: Written assignment 80 h. Presentation preparation 14 h. Studying given material 46 h. The planning assignment is carried out in a team. Total workload 162 h.

name: Digital skills for university life
learningOutcomes: Opiskelija ymmärtää kuinka voi hyödyntää digitaalisia työkaluja yliopisto-opiskelun tukena ja tuntee kurssilla käsiteltyjen työkalujen perusteet. Opintokokonaisuuden suoritettuaan opiskelija osaa myös hakea itsenäisesti lisätietoa häntä kiinnostavista työkaluista tai kysyä neuvoa sitä tarvittaessa.
content: Digitaidot yliopistossa -opintokokonaisuus suoritetaan omatoimisesti verkkokurssina. Opintojaksolla opiskelija tutustuu opiskelua tukeviin digitaalisiin työkaluihin ja niiden käytön perusteisiin. Kurssilla tutustutaan muun muassa Office-työkaluihin (erityisesti Word, PowerPoint ja Teams), ja muihin opiskelijalle hyödyllisiin digityökaluihin. Kurssilla harjoitellaan muun muassa oman esityksen tekemistä ja jakamista muille, projektinhallinnan työkaluja sekä oman puheen ja esiintymisen nauhoittamista. Käymme läpi myös LUT:n ohjeistukset tekoälytyökalujen käytöstä.
evaluationCriteria: Hyväksytty - hylätty
workload: Opintokokonaisuus suoritetaan omatoimisesti verkkokurssina Moodlessa syyslukukauden aikana. Opiskelija pääsee kurssin Moodle-alustalle automaattisesti sen jälkeen, kun ilmoittautuminen Sisussa on hyväksytty. Erillistä kurssiavainta ei tarvita.

name: Discrete Models and Methods
learningOutcomes: Kurssin jälkeen opiskelijan odotetaan tuntevan diskreetin matematiikan peruskäsitteitä, osaavan muodostaa yksinkertaisia diskreettejä ongelmia kuvaavia malleja sekä ratkoa niitä.
content: Perusteita seuraavista aiheista: Logiikka, propositiot ja ehdolliset propositiot, induktio. Relaatiot, relaatioiden laskutoimituksia, ominaisuuksia ja ekvivalenssi- sekä järjestysrelaatio. Kombinatoriikka, graafiteoria, polut ja syklit, lyhimmän polun menetelmä. Graafien matriisimuotoinen mallinnus. Päätöspuut ja kuljetusongelmat.
prerequisites: Suositellaan Matematiikka I (tai Taloustieteiden matematiikka) ja Matematiikka II -kurssien käymistä ensin.
learningMaterial: Dossey, Otto, Spence, Vanden Eynden, Discrete mathematics, Pearson 5th edition, 2006Richard Johnsonbaugh, Discrete mathematics, Prentice hall, 6th edition, 2005.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises 14 h, individual work 21 h, preparation for exam and examination 18h. Total workload 81 h.

name: Discourses and Society
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student understands the basics of discourse studies and is able to examine language use as a social activity from a research perspective. The student is able to apply the techniques of discourse studies in analyses.
content: The course focuses on the basics of discourse studies and the theories behind it. Through the course literature, the student delves into language as a social activity through the concept of discourse. Through literature, concepts closely related to discourse, such as representation, genres and narratives, are also examined.
learningMaterial: Pietikäinen & Mäntynen, (2019). Uusi kurssi kohti diskurssia. Tampere: Vastapaino. ja Jokinen, Juhila & Suoninen, (2016). Diskurssianalyysi — Teoriat, peruskäsitteet ja käyttö. Tampere: Vastapaino.
evaluationCriteria: Arvosana 0-5.
workload: Kurssi suoritetaan kirjallisuusesseellä.

name: Electricity Market (FiTech)
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. describe the characteristics of the different business sectors in the Nordic electricity market, 2. identify the elements affecting the electricity price formation, 3. describe the operation principle of the power exchange, 4. identify and describe the products of the power exchange, 5. describe the right risk management methods for electricity trade, 6. identify the tasks of the different parties in an electric power system in maintaining technical and commercial power balance, including demand side management, 7. describe the motivations and principles of electricity market deregulation.
content: The restructuring of the electricity markets, power exchange, electricity trade, balance management.
evaluationCriteria: Pass-/fail.
workload: Weekly assignments. Total workload 54 h.

name: Energy Economics for EnTeDI
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to utilise energy economic calculation methods and to calculate the additional cost in the energy production costs caused by emission trading. Students will be able to describe the basic concepts of Finnish energy economics and explain the structure of energy taxation in Finland, and calculate the energy taxes of fuels. Students will understand the structure of energy tariffs, and will be able to compile a duration curve of the consumption curve of energy. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: sustainable development, basics of business operations, know-how on own field, knowledge of the history and development of own field, written communication, working independently, information retrieval, critical thinking skills
content: Use of energy statistics. The variation in energy demand and duration curves. Calculation methods for energy production costs. Profitability calculations of energy projects. Environmental impacts in energy production, especially carbon dioxide emissions. Energy and fuel markets. The effect of emission trading on the price of electricity, and energy tariffs. Energy taxation and the pricing system of natural gas. Energy economics in Finland and EU. The need for investments in electricity production. National energy and climate strategy. Fuel economics. Energy scenarios.
learningMaterial: Study materials, including the lecture material, will be listed in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Evaluation is based on exercises and homework in Moodle 100%, Pass/Fail.
workload: Independent studies in Moodle, Homework based on lectures and exercises in Moodle. Total workload 135 h.

name: Energy Efficiency
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. determine actions for the energy efficiency of the energy conversion process, 2. estimate the overall energy efficiency of the energy conversion system, 3. identify applications of electric energy usage and apply methods that can be used to improve the energy efficiency.
content: The course provides the student with an introduction to the significance and development potential of energy efficiency in energy production, transmission, distribution and end use. The focus is on electric energy and systems approach. The lecture topics are the efficiency of energy production processes, the efficiency of electricity transmission and distribution and the efficiency of energy end use. The course is arranged as a series of lectures delivered by experts. The lecture topics may vary from year to year.
learningMaterial: The learning material is based on the latest research and is distributed to students in Moodle. Additional material: Amory Lovins, Reinventing Fire - Bold Business Solutions for the New Energy Era.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, EXAM electronic examination 100%. In addition, 50 % of individual assignments have to be passed. It is also possible to receive additional points to the exam based on the individual assignments./Ed. 20.10.25/ml
workload: Lectures 12 h, individual home works 93 h, EXAM electronic examination 3 h. The course is suitable for distance learning, however exam will be in electronic exam room. Total workload 108 h./Ed. 20.10.25/ml

name: Green Fibre Materials
learningOutcomes: After having passed this course, the student will be able to: - estimate different fiber resources available - define concepts and entities related to fiber usage - determine and explain what properties fibers have in relation to the growth and functions of fiber cells - compare structures and properties of fiber materials and their effects on the most important practical applications
content: Fiber resources. Practical principles of managing fiber resources. Fiber procurement. Macroscopial and microscopial structure of fiber materials and functions of fiber cells. Physical and mechanical properties. Empirical methods for defining strength properties. Modeling of relations between physical/mechanical/end use properties. Introduction to fiber based composites. The course is related to sustainability.
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle. Wood Handbook, Wood as an Engineering Material. Forest Products Laboratory, 2010.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Assignments 100 %.
workload: Individual assignments. Individual work 130 h. Total workload 130 h.The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Individual Project Work of Laser Technology
learningOutcomes: After having passed the course module the student: - apply comprehensively the learned skills of previous courses for laser based processes, systems and products - understand how to perform research project in field of laser engineering / processing - apply theoretical knowledge in practical R&D work - have skills to collect existing data and use it for determining solutions - know how to design and run experiments in field of laser processing - select and design a laser system for industrial case. - knows how to select right laser process and optimize the process for different materials - is able to develop processes for different applications
content: During the course student will become familiar with: - basic phenomena of laser - material interaction in specific case i.e. transmission, reflection, absorption - the features affecting on performing the experimental work to define the limitations and potential of ways to apply laser for manufacturing - the effect of potential of laser in design and how to apply that into product and its manufacturing. - reporting the tests carried out in an efficient effective way both in writing and orally. - principles how to design and run a research project - principles in writing scientific peer review publication
prerequisites: BK30A1301 Laser Based Manufacturing for Design or BK30A1201 Laser Materials Processing passed or equivalent understanding shown in oral exam.
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle.Further reading e.g. Steen W., Laser Material Processing, Ion, J., Laser Processing of Engineering Materials.
evaluationCriteria: Project plan 15 %, Written report 55 %, Oral presentation 30 %.
workload: Lectures 2 h. Guiding discussion with supervisor 15 h. Design, execution and reporting of project work 113 h. Total workload 130 h.The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Individual Research Project I
learningOutcomes: After finishing the course successfully the course students are able to: - Plan and carry out an industrial project and write both the project plan and report according to IMRAD structure - Conduct an academic research literature review on focused topic - Integrate practical project management tools and scientific approaches to solve and handle industrial design engineering tasks especially about ID research focus area - Integrate different fields of engineering to support cross-technological problem solving in industrial design engineering, to achieve sustainable product development goals
content: - Give the students a deeper understanding on Industrial design engineering in a subgroup area (i.e. product design, furniture design, interaction design, packaging design etc.) and alongside with research focus of the IDE group such as circular design or human centered design and design thinking. - Give support for conducting an in-depth scientific research project in the field of design with academic perspective. - An individual project will be carried out possibly in collaboration with industrial company or external collaborators of the university. - The project is planned together with the supervisor (lecturer) and the company, and the topic may focus especially on problem solving tasks in industry. - In some exceptional cases the content of the project could consist of laboratory work or collaboration with one of the mechanical engineering laboratories or other laboratories in LUT. - Prepare the students to apply both practical project management tools to take care of an engineering project and apply scientific approaches. - The project is supporting students for their upcoming master thesis in regard of scientific viewpoint, structure, identification of focus area.
learningMaterial: Reading material, assignments and case studies, will be supplied via Moodle
evaluationCriteria: Grading 0-5, exercises , development progress of the project , Final report
workload: NOTE: This course is only for students of the IDE-program or for MSc in Mechanical Engineering students who started before the academic year 2023-2024 and who initially selected the IDE specialisation module in the degree structure! Teams meetings with the teacher, project plan, individual project work and a written report, Total workload 135 h including discussion sessions and checkpoints (1 ECTS cr is about 27 hours work)

name: Individual Research Project II
content: - Give the students a deeper understanding on Industrial design engineering in a subgroup area (i.e. product design, furniture design, interaction design, packaging design etc.) and alongside with research focus of the IDE group such as circular design or human centered design and design thinking. - Give support for conducting an in-depth scientific research project in the field of design with academic perspective. - An individual project will be carried out possibly in collaboration with industrial company or external collaborators of the university. - The project is planned together with the supervisor (lecturer) and the company, and the topic may focus especially on problem solving tasks in industry. - In some exceptional cases the content of the project could consist of laboratory work or collaboration with one of the mechanical engineering laboratories or other laboratories in LUT. - Prepare the students to apply both practical project management tools to take care of an engineering project and apply scientific approaches. - The project is supporting students for their upcoming master thesis in regard of scientific viewpoint, structure, identification of focus area.
learningMaterial: Reading material, assignments and case studies, will be supplied via Moodle
evaluationCriteria: Grading 0-5, exercises , development progress of the project , Final report
workload: NOTE: This course is only for students of the IDE-program. Teams meetings with the teacher, project plan, individual project work and a written report, Total workload 135 h including discussion sessions and checkpoints (1 ECTS cr is about 27 hours work)

name: Introduction to Energy Technology for EnTeDI Students
learningOutcomes: After passing the course, the student: understands the basics of power plant engineering, and how the most common power plants work, is able to calculate the most common power plant process and operating parameters, is able to describe the Finnish power system, understands how electricity is produced in Finland and elsewhere, is able to interpret energy scenarios and compare them. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: sustainable development, know-how on own field, knowledge of the history and development of own field, mathematics and natural sciences, written communication, oral communication, team working skills, social skills, problem solving, information retrieval, project management.
content: Fundamentals of power plant engineering: solar power, wind power, and fuel cells, hydropower, thermodynamics, steam power plants, gas turbine power plants, combined cycle power plants. Energy production and consumption and future energy scenarios in Finland and elsewhere: energy resources, electricity generation, energy storage, energy scenarios.
learningMaterial: The learning material is based on the latest research and is distributed to students in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Exercises and homeworks 50%, group work 25%, peer evaluation 5%, electronic exam 20%.
workload: On-line lectures, contact teaching days, Moodle lectures and exercises, homeworks, self-studies, group assignment, periods 1 and 2. Total workload 108 h.

name: Introduction to MSc Studies in Biorefineries
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student has an understanding of the goals and modes of study in Biorefineries Programme. knows about learning theories and can reflect on their own learning strategy. has defined their personal goals. knows their fellow students.
content: On this course, the student will learn about modern learning theories, effective on-line learning strategies and tools for personal goal setting. The course includes group activities.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail.
workload: Total workload 27 ECTS.

name: Introduction to Water Treatment Technologies
learningOutcomes: By the end of the course, it is expected that students will be able to: · recognize the challenges facing humanity and the environment from water pollution sources (drinking water supplies and municipal/industrial wastewaters) · identify the limitations of conventional water treatment procedures and justify the need for advanced technologies. · be acquainted with the main advanced water treatment technologies (components’ fabrication and/or assembly, operating and action modes, targeted pollutants and related regulations). · solve problems by selecting suitable technology(ies) to remediate specific water pollution cases and be able to justify their decision. · recognise, and later promote, the important role of advanced water treatment in the implementation of the emerging sustainable concepts of bioeconomy and circular economy in general, and biorefineries in specific.
content: Learning the various kinds and properties of conventional and advanced water treatment technologies, including, but not limited to, membrane technology, advanced oxidation processes, nanotechnology, electro-chemical processes, adsorption, ion exchange, etc. Knowing the pros and cons, and R&D prospects for each advanced technology. Reinforcing the acquired knowledge with “catchy” case studies from the biorefining and water treatment industries, targeting efficient municipal/industrial water/wastewater treatment and resources recovery. Including the economic factor and the environmental footprint of those advanced technologies, to their pollution removal efficiency. Providing the necessary tools to effectively deal with various environmental issues and industrial challenges using advanced water treatment technologies, in single or integrated approaches.
prerequisites: COMPULSORY PREREQUISITES Students, who have not studied their bachelor's degree in LUT have to take course BJ02A0061 Laboratory safety course before taking this course. RECOMMENDED PREREQUISITES Chemistry knowledge. Chemical engineering knowledge.
learningMaterial: Videos, lecture presentations, recommended literature and additional material (Moodle).
evaluationCriteria: Exam 50% (50% minimum to pass de course), quizzes 15%, presentation 25%, laboratory report 10%=100 points. To pass the course and get the grade all tasks related to evaluation must be completed. A minimum of 55 points are required for passing the course.
workload: Lectures 11 h; company day 4 h; quizzes, laboratory lessons, laboratory report, presentations, 55 h; independent study 65 h. Total workload 135 h
equivalentCoursesInfo: Replaces the course BJ03A1010 Introduction to Advanced Water Treatment, 5 ECTS

name: Laser Materials Processing
learningOutcomes: After having passed the course module the student is able: - to compare laser materials processing processes and knows different processes special features - identify what are the theoretical basis affecting in different processes and how they affect the possible applications based on them - to know how to select and optimize proper process and processing procedure for different materials - understanding how processing parameters affect the quality of the process / part - to define what kind of lasers and laser systems can be applied in various processes and applications and how they could be applied - is able to develop processes for different applications - is able to work as expert to develop laser based processes for industrial applications - have research skills that are needed to reform technological readiness in different industries - have understanding of possible manufacturing solutions for advanced energy sector industry in the future
content: Contents of this course includes e.g.: - laser beam material interaction, transmission, reflection, absorption - the features of different materials and laser beams affecting on phenomena - the effect of laser based heating, melting, vaporization and ablation on material - behavior of molten material and heat transfer mechanisms. - formation of keyhole and phenomena connected - knowledge on existing ways to process material with laser beam and the effect of laser beam material interaction on that - knowledge on most common laser processes like laser welding, laser hybrid welding, cutting, marking, drilling, engraving, micro processing additive manufacturing and surface treatment and the lasers and laser systems used for carrying them out - practical cases, applications will be combined to theory
prerequisites: BK30A0803 Digital Advanced Manufacturing with Lasers passed or equal level of understanding shown with oral exam.
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle. Further reading e.g. Steen W., Laser Material Processing. Ion, J., Laser Processing of Engineering Materials.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, written project work report 80 %, oral seminar presentation 20 %.
workload: Lectures 28 h, guided team working 3x2 h. Design, execution and reporting of project work in teams 95 h. Laboratory work 6 h. Laboratory work consists of preparing, carrying out the experimental study and analysing the results of project work. Total workload 135 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Understanding and Managing a Business as a Dynamic Whole - Business Simulation Game
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, students will be able to: · describe how different areas in business studies are connected in the entity of enterprise functions and in making a profit · apply various methods of collaboration in a virtual team and to become aware of the key regularities in the collaborative business environment · apply different business analysis tools in planning and managing a business and understand the essential role of strategy in the process. A central part of the course is the optimisation of a business as a whole with respect to both various business functions and goals; students will understand why it is not practical to optimise single functions separately and why the management needs to have a holistic perspective of the company that simultaneously takes into account social, ecological and financial responsibility.
content: · The foundation for this course is a decentralised and collaborative business simulation exercise in which students work in teams and collaborate with other teams. Besides engaging in real-time decision-making during the simulation days, the students will complete assignments that relate to various business sciences and analyse the actions taken in the simulation outside the simulation days. · Participation takes place in small virtual groups, the members of which come from different universities. · The thematic core for the simulation is the entity formed by the different functions of a company and the responsible agency of the company in a network of enterprises. The relevant themes include several areas of cross-company functions (purchasing, project management, distribution and customer relationships) and the reporting related to these topics. The course emphasises the entity of business operations from the perspective of responsible management. · During the course, students are introduced to the dynamics of business networks where the students’ company is part of a network of competitors, suppliers and customers. · The theoretical material and the exercises distributed on the course are related to the thematic core for the simulation and for other LITO learning themes.
prerequisites: The course serves as a capstone, bridging together the other modules in the LITO entity. The course provides an overall picture of business dynamics and explains how the different fields of business studies are related to it. Various tools and services outside the LITO learning platform may be used in the analyses during the course. It is recommended that before taking this course, the student has taken at least the following LITO courses: ‘Introduction to Accounting and Financial Management’ and ‘Basics of Management and Organisations’. Alternatively, the student must possess sufficient previous knowledge in these fields in order to be able to analyse a business as a whole.
learningMaterial: The literature includes: simulation game instructions, a description of the simulation environment, learning videos, a course hand-out and a selection of other articles (to be announced).
evaluationCriteria: The evaluation scale of pass/fail is used. Performance will be rated based on the assignments given out during the course.
workload: The course includes a compulsory preliminary assignment that has to be completed successfully by a pre-defined date. : The course assignments are related to both the planning of the simulation company operations and the analysis of materialised operations, as well as being related to the development of the core metaskills needed in working life. An essential part of the course is also a review of the core metaskills needed in working life. Related to this, the course assignments include exercises related to team grouping, as well as evaluation and analysis of team and personal activities. The students complete the assignments both individually and as group work.

name: Measurement Technology
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course a student will be able to: 1. apply fundamentals of measurement, 2. apply analog and digital signal conversions, 3. apply digital signal filtering and data transfer.
content: 1. Static properties of measurements 2. Measurement accuracy and uncertainty 3. Dynamic properties of measurements 4. Signal conversions with AD and DA conversions 5. Digital and analog signal I/O connections 6. Digital filtering of measured signals 7. Digital measurement and control with machine vision and RF tag´s 8. Applications of digital and wireless measurement and control
prerequisites: BL40A0110 Measurement and Automation Technology, Introduction. Basics of differential equations
learningMaterial: Lecture material in Moodle, John P. Bentley 'Principles of measurement technology'
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, weekly assignments 100 %
workload: Independent distance learning and weekly assignments. Total workload 54 h.

name: Orientation to M.Sc. Studies
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student - is familiar with the formal requirements of his/her studies and with the campus services and their appropriate use during his/her studies - know the importance of sufficient study skills in university studies - is aware of information security issues - possesses ability for information searching - know how to refer scientific literature - is able to write a literature review - is aware of job hunting procedure.
content: During the course the student will learn about the relevant instructions affecting his/her studies and how to generate a personal study plan. The student will familiarize him/herself with the relevant staff of his/her degree programme and with the services provided by e.g. the Library and Study Services. The student will write a short literature review on the given topic.
learningMaterial: Moodle material
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail. After completing the course assignments acceptably, the student passes the course.
workload: Lectures 6 h, independent assignments 15 h, self-study 6 h. Total workload 27 h.

name: Process and Plant Design
learningOutcomes: After the module the student can - name and explain most common steps of process and plant design - use the most common methods of process and plant design - read and compile basic documents of process design (process flowsheets, equipment definitions, drawings and equipment lists) - perform process calculations, especially mass and energy balances - make preliminary material selections - estimate cost and profitability of the process - do a small project work in group
content: Initial information of design. Fundamentals, methodology, steps and content of process design. Process synthesis and analysis. Process flowsheets. Equipment design. Basis of material selection. Layout design. Cost and profitability calculations. Project work. Company collaboration Company visit
learningMaterial: Coulson J.M. et al. Chemical Engineering, Vol 6 (selected chapters).
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Exam examination 30 %, home assignments 40 %, group work 30 %.
workload: Lectures, seminars and exercises 28 h, 1st period. Group project work 30 h, home assignments 20 h, self-study 30 h. Total workload 108 h.

name: Smart Grids
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to 1. Label the key elements and functionalities of the smart grid system 2. Analyze the impacts of the smart grid elements on electricity distribution system and electricity markets 3. Document and present orally the results of the seminar work 4. Provide both written and oral peer review.
content: Smart grid concept, demand side management, energy storage, distributed generation, microgrids, communications in smart grids. In addition, annually changing topical subjects.
prerequisites: Attending the course BL20A0500 Sähkönjakelutekniikka (Electricity distribution) OR BL20A0401 Electricity Market OR BL20A0400 Sähkömarkkinat (Electricity Market)
learningMaterial: Study materials handed out in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. The course is evaluated based on seminar work (written and oral presentation), Moodle quizzes, and student’s work as a reviewer and an opponent.
workload: Lectures 14 h, Moodle quizzes 7 h, independent seminar work 105 h. Presentation of the seminar work 2 h, peer review of a written seminar work 5 h and working as an opponent in seminar 2 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Solid-Liquid Separation in Biorefining
learningOutcomes: After completing the module the student can: - know the fundamental phenomena insolid-liquid separation - name different methods and equipment used for solid-liquid separation - select and size suitable equipment for separation processes based on suspension properties and data from laboratory tests - explain the effects of the characteristics of the solid material and the liquid on the separation and post treatment processes - define different filter media used in filtration and make a preliminary selection of a medium for different cases - perform an experimental test in laboratory scale - write a scientific report.
content: The topics are as follows: Fundamentals of solid-liquid separation, filtration methods, operation of filters, cake formation and washing, deliquoring, design and modeling of filters and scale-up. Filter media and blinding. Experimental design in filtration test work.
prerequisites: Knowledge of the fundamentals of particle characterization and mechanical separation methods. Recommended literature: Fundamentals of Particle Technology by Richard Holdich, Chapters 1–8.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Moodle exams and home assignments 60%, laboratory work 20%, literature review 20%.
workload: Lectures 18h, exercises 18 h, filtration laboratory work + report 20 h, literature review 20 h, Self-study 59 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Electricity Market

name: Electricity Distribution Technology
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. perform technical and financial calculations related to electricity distribution networks: voltages, currents, losses, fault currents, reliability, investment, outage and maintenance costs, 2. compile long-term strategic development plans related to electricity distribution networks, 3. carry out techno-economic dimensioning of an electricity distribution network, 4. explain the targets and principles of the use of electricity distribution networks, 5. use the distribution automation applications in the operation of a distribution network and design short circuit and earth fault protection in electricity distribution networks. 6. Have an understanding of economic regulation and Smart Concepts and their impact on the electricity distribution business.
content: Network technology and planning, operation of distribution system, protection and automation of distribution networks, information systems of distribution companies, Smart Grids, industrial networks. Company co-operation The course includes guest lectures. Use of AI applications: AI can be used to understand concepts and retrieve information during the course. However, it is important to consider AI's limitations regarding source criticism. The student must provide answers independently in the learning tasks (assignment and exam). The student must not present text created by AI tools as their own.

learningMaterial: The learning material is based on the latest developments in the industry and the most recent research. The material consists of lecture slides and recordings, as well as a lecture book. The lecture slides, videos, and assignments will be shared with students on Moodle. Lakervi, E. ; Partanen, J.: Sähkönjakelutekniikka (Otatieto, moniste 609).
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 100 % (paper exam in Lappeenranta campus and EXAM electronic examination). Satisfactorily completed assignment required giving some extra points to exam evaluation.

Background survey on the student's personal background and goals related to the course. 42 h of lectures, 28 h of tutorials, 3rd and 4rd period. Assignment 60 h. Written examination 3 h. Independent working 83 h. The lectures focus on the core learning objectives in the topic. Successful completion of the course requires student’s active independent work. The course is suitable for distance learning. Total workload 216 h.

name: Technical Documentation and 3D-modelling
learningOutcomes: Opintojakson suoritettuaan opiskelija osaa: - käyttää 3D-mallinnusohjelmaa (SolidWorks) tekniikan eri sovellusalueilla ja mallintaa erityyppisiä geometrioita. - mitata olemassaolevien kappaleiden perusmittoja työntömitalla. - hyödyntää voimassa olevia standardeja teknisiä dokumentteja laadittaessa. - suorittaa kappaleen toleranssimitoituksen ja selittää, mitä eri toleransseilla tarkoitetaan. - merkitä pinnanlaatua koskevat vaatimukset dokumentteihin ja määritellä, mitä nämä vaatimukset tarkoittavat. - laatia tuotteen valmistuspiirustukset, ml. hitsauspiirustukset, voimassa olevien standardien mukaisesti. - laatia kokoonpanon tekniset dokumentit, tunnistaa niistä eri koneenosat, ja löytää kokoonpanon kriittiset kohdat laitteen toiminnan varmistamiseksi. - tuottaa, vertailla ja valita eri käyttötarkoituksiin parhaiten soveltuvat tietokoneavusteiset tuotteen esitys- ja mallinnustavat. - tulkita yleisesti käytettyjä teknisiä kaavioita. - työskennellä suunnittelutyötä tekevässä työryhmässä.
content: - Perustiedot teknisten piirustusten laadintaa käsittelevistä standardeista, tiedon käsittelystä ja tiedonsiirrosta. - Tuotteen valmistuspiirustukset ja niissä käytettävät symbolit ja merkinnät (tolerointi, pintamerkit, hitsausmerkinnät) ja valmistusystävällisyys ja kestävä suunnittelu huomioiden. - Kokoonpanopiirustukset ja 3D-räjäytyskuvat. CAD-sovellusten vertailun perusteet. - CAD/CAM -integroinnin perusteet. - Tietokoneavusteisen suunnittelun tehokkuuden lisääminen parametrisen, olioperusteisen ja piirrepohjaisen mallinnuksen avulla. - Tuotteen visualisoinnin perusteet.
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, harjoitukset: 30%, ryhmätyöt: 40%, suullinen palautus: 30%

name: Science, Technology and Society
learningOutcomes: After the course student will be able to: - understand the interplay between science, technology and society - analyze the themes presented in the course from different viewpoints - present a justified opinion on the effects of technology on society and connect his/her views to the larger societal debate - discuss societal issues within his/her professional area with public with a non-technical background - ground the argumentation on scientific research and other reliable sources.
content: Course discusses the interplay between science, technology and society from several different angles through six specific themes. The themes for academic year 2025-26 are: new labor, technology for sustainable growth, technological democracy, technological equality, autonomous technology, and artificial intelligence - a threat or an opportunity.
learningMaterial: The course material is based on the teacher’s expertise, scientific publications and other material that provides insight in to the themes of the subject area. Each of the sisxthemes include current materials (3-4 separate articles, podcasts, or videos). More detailed information is distributed in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Weekly learning tasks 60 %, end of course assignment 40 %
workload: Course is an online-course with following learning tasks: 1) familiarizing oneself with learning materials related to each theme area (podcasts, videos and written materials) 2) completing the weekly learning tasks, and 3) the end of course assignment compiling the themes. The workload of the course is divided as follows: weekly materials and learning tasks 60 h, end of course assignment 48 h. Total workload 108 h.

name: Big Data in Business
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: Describe the application types of big data in business Understand the CRISP-DM process model of big data analysis in business Preprocessing the big data and dealing with the different data features. Understand 7-8 algorithm procedure among top 10 algorithms Select suitable algorithms for practical big data analysis problems Develop and test the big data models with Python Evaluate the performance of big data analysis, and explain the knowledge obtained from the big data model.

The course module provides substantial knowledge about the high-strength steels that can be used in Power-to-X applications

name: Digital Electronics
learningOutcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Explain the fundamental concepts of digital number representation and Boolean algebra. • Design and analyze combinational logic circuits consisting of basic components like gates, multiplexers, and decoders. • Explain the principles of sequential logic consisting of flip-flops and counters. • Explain the basics of processor operating principles, architecture, • Explain embedded systems, including common peripherals and memory types. • Describe programmable logic devices and their applications. • Design, simulate, and implement simple digital systems.
content: Digital representations and number systems. Logic circuit implementation, gates, sequential logic. Memory and processor architecture basics. Embedded systems with microcontrollers and I/O interfaces. Programmable logic devices.
prerequisites: Basic Electronics
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle. Literature: Thomas L Floyd, “Digital Fundamentals”, 9 th Edition, Prentice Hall Publication, 2006.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, written examination 50 %, individual assignment 20%, group assignments 30%
workload: Period 1 Lectures 14 h, exercises 14 h, exam 3 h after the first teaching period, Period 2 Lectures 14 h, exercises 14 h, individual & group assignments 6 h, individual study 16 h . Total workload 81 h, Lectures will be only in Lappeenranta campus.

name: Digitalization
learningOutcomes: After completion of the course, students will: understand the various concepts related to digitalization and socio-technological systems. be familiar with the processes and effects of digital transformation, understand the significance of digital security and data protection in society, recognize various e-citizen services and citizen involvement in a digital society, and be familiar with the planning socio-technological digital systems.
content: This course explores the phenomenon of digitalization, examining its definition and key components, such as the Internet of Things and artificial intelligence, along with related processes like datafication and platformization. It also traces the progression of digital transformation and its impact on how we work, live, and produce. Additionally, the course explores the environmental and labor dimensions of digitalization, as well as its broader consequences, including the need for digital security and the expansion of e-citizen services. To structure these discussions, a political economy approach to socio-technological digital systems will be introduced, along with other perspectives on governance, regulation, and different societal implications of digitalization.
learningMaterial: Neugebauer, R. (2019). Digital transformation. Berlin: Springer. Srnicek, N. (2016). Platform Capitalism. Cambridge, UK: Polity. Zuboff, S. (2019). The Age of Surveillance Capitalism: the Fight for a Human Future at the New Frontier of Power. London: Profile Books. Other material and literature specified in lectures or in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Final essay (60%), individual assignments (40%)

name: Doctoral seminar in the social sciences
learningOutcomes: After taking this course, the students will: - be familiar with typical argumentation patterns in discussions on social science research, - have experience in giving and receiving feedback on research manuscripts, and - be able to review manuscripts for scientific journals.
content: Research in the social sciences is often subjective, usually open to interpretation, and always in need of discussion. Therefore, well-rounded researchers in the social sciences do not only need to be able to conduct research – they also need to be able to participate in the discourse around their research. The skill to connect a text to the wider scientific debate is as important as the skill to spot weak spots in a study design. Moreover, the researchers need to be able to present their comments in a logical and constructive way. This seminar introduces doctoral students to the practices, strategies and vocabulary of discussions on social science research. Please note that the seminar content is different in each term. Therefore, PhD students can take this seminar twice in two different terms.
prerequisites: Master’s degree
learningMaterial: Announced in the beginning of the course
evaluationCriteria: quality of the discussion participation
workload: This course has 7 course days. Attendance of at least 6 complete course days is mandatory. The students will (a) present at least one of their own draft manuscripts and open it for discussion, (b) be the discussant for at least one another draft manuscript, and (c) comment on the other manuscripts discussed.

name: Introduction to Electrical Drives
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to describe the principles of electric motors and frequency converters and recognize terms in the field of electric drives. The student can solve simple calculation problems in the field of electric drives.
content: Operation of electromechanical and electromagnetic devices, current vector, torque. Basic types and operation principles of rotating electrical machines: general rotating field machine, DC machine, asynchronous machine, synchronous machine, reluctance machine. Energy efficient electric motor drives. Control principles: scalar, vector and direct torque control (DTC). Applications. Electrical energy storages.
prerequisites: Recommended: BL 10A0102 Basics of Electrical Engineering, BL30A0000 Electric Circuits completed and BL30A0300 Electromagnetism attended.
learningMaterial: The study materials are based on research and distributed to students in Moodle. Including lecture and exercise materials. Recommended to follow also additional material. Juha Pyrhönen, Tapani Jokinen, Valeria Hrabovcova: Design of Rotating Electrical Machines. John Wiley & Sons.

searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule

name: Partial Differential Equations
learningOutcomes: After the course, the student is able to solve simple partial differential equations analytically and numerically with MATLAB. Student knows different functions spaces related the analysis of partial differential equations. Student is familiar with the basic properties of harmonic functions. Student reaches the analysis knowledge required to advance to Master's level courses on modelling of partial differential equations.
content: First and second order simple PDEs: analytical solutions and existence and the uniqueness of the solutions. Special emphasis on the second order linear elliptic PDEs and harmonic functions. Numerical methods: basics of finite differences. Basic Euclidean topology, Hölder spaces and analytic functions.
prerequisites: Recommended: BM20A8000 - Differential Equations, BM20A4102 - Vector Analysis, BM20A8701 - Matrix Calculus.
learningMaterial: Finnish and English lecture notes.
evaluationCriteria: 0–5. Grade is determined by exam.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises 21 h, independent practice 83 h and exam 3 h. Total 135 h.

name: Political Economy of Digital Transformation
learningOutcomes: After completing this course, the students will: Understand the core socio-economic processes in the context of digitalisation Know the key concepts of political economy and critical social science analysis of digitalisation Understand the key processes of emergent social dynamics of the digital economy Understand the dimension of power and inequality in digital transformation Understand how digital transformation reconfigures economic activities and changes the social and economic relationships between different groups and classes

name: Brand Management
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to familiarize the students with the management of 'brand equity', which is clearly an issue of major strategic importance. Few would deny the importance of brands as valuable assets and potential source of sustainable competitive advantage. Brands provide a shortcut for customers when making a purchasing decision, seeking to avoid risk and obtain value for money. Brands provide a relevant, exciting experience. Brands connote a certain life style, values or attitude. Brands can become objects of affection: 'Lovemarks', even. Buying a brand is an integral part of an individual's quest for identity and meaning. After completing the course the students should be able to: - have a deep understanding on how companies manage 'brand equity' - critically evaluate and compare different brand management strategies - analyze and explain reason, affect and decision-making related to brands - assess the social meaning and cultural rooting of brands - identify and explain current trends and issues in branding - work in a multi-cultural team - compile academic reports about branding - apply knowledge gained from the course, to the events, activities and/or strategies of an actual firm or organization
content: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to strategic brand management, covering such areas as the building of brand equity, brand identity, brand extension, brand portfolios etc. in national, regional and global markets. Indicative and subject to change topics include: 1. Introductory session - branding exercise. Brand basics. 2. Brand overview - Dyson: the man, the brand, the product, the market. Understanding codes, discourses and the potential for renewal and disruption. Sponges and hedgehogs. Mums, kids and washing liquid. The importance of consumer insight: Got milk? Fathers and whiskies 3. More about brands and how we relate to them: reason, affect and decision-making. Brand personality, brand archetypes. Brand endorsement and meaning transfer. 4. Branding people and experience. Service and experiential branding: Starbucks case study + the Apple Store 5. Brands in context. The social meaning of brands. What consumer studies and anthropology teach us. 6. A diamond is forever, beer is for men: the cultural rooting of brands. How brands become icons. Case study: Reviving an iconic brand – Levi's in the 80s 7. Brands & communities: Harley Davidson and Jones Soda. Tribal marketing & social networks. 8. Brand placement, brand content, brand events 9. Conclusion: current issues in branding
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree, A330A0300 Strategic Global Marketing Management, or equivalent basic marketing course

learningOutcomes: Upon completing the course, the student will be able to: 1. Synthesize electronics theory and practical skills and apply them to design challenges in industrial electronic systems. 2. Apply, analyze, and evaluate the technical design process—from requirements specification to validation—taking into account risk analysis, quality assurance, and customer requirements. 3. Collaborate effectively as a responsible member of a multidisciplinary product development team by employing project management methods and professional communication skills. 4. Evaluate the impact of their work within a technical project by considering schedules, budgets, and quality criteria, and produce technical documentation. 5. Justify their technical design solutions by researching, analyzing, applying, and creating information in design work.
content: The course covers the fundamentals of project planning and management, including requirements specification, documentation, and preparation of presentations. The technical content varies annually according to the client requirements and student roles, including practical properties of electronic components, electronics design, embedded system implementation and programming, practical thermal dimensioning, EMC, power electronics applications, device protection, and mechanical design for electronics. Projects are based on industry needs, and students evaluate costs and make component choices considering economic aspects. The student project team is responsible for implementation, project management, organization, and results. Assessment emphasizes technical quality (60%) and project management (40%). Students are evaluated according to their specific roles, but all are required to demonstrate both technical and project management competencies.

learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. Identify the constraints and potentials of all relevant energy resources in a global context. 2. Analyse the principal structure of future energy systems on the basis of energy resource characteristics. 4. Describe the special relevance of wind energy and solar energy in the ongoing energy transition.
content: The course will cover the following topics. 1. Provide an overview of the availability of energy resources and related emissions and the techno-economic maturity of related energy conversion technologies, which induces a fundamental structure for the future energy system and the related energy transition pathway. 2. Comprises the main energy resources for the current and future energy system: crude oil, natural gas, coal, uranium, hydro power, bioenergy, solar energy, wind energy, geothermal energy, and ocean energy. 3. Provide an overview of different theoretical, technical and economic potentials as well as geographic variations in availability of these energy resources. The resources also differ considerably in the impact of the emissions related to the respective energy conversion technologies being relevant for the degree of sustainability. A broad variety of energy conversion technologies at different levels of maturity are used for utilising the resources.

name: Energy Scenarios
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. Describe the sustainability requirements of future energy systems as the major guard rail for the energy transition. 2. Analyse and model energy transition scenario for a chosen country and identify the key technologies and setups for sustainable energy progress. 3. Describe the energy transition in all sectors, the major technologies, the required transition period and entire system cost optimisation. 4. Describe the special role of power technologies in the energy transition. 5. Recognise the difference between standard levelised cost of energy and total societal cost of energy. 6. Use EnergyPLAN software for energy system analysis for a chosen country.
content: The course will cover the following topics. 1. Key elements for describing energy scenarios: demand, supply, cost, constraints. 2. Provide an overview of energy demand which includes power, heat, cooling, mobility, agriculture, and industrial energy demands. The demand must be matched with supply of energy fulfilling sustainability criteria, safety requirements and societal acceptance for the least cost. 3. A complete set of demand curves, technical characteristics of all major technologies, current and projected technology costs and emission factors are taken into account for sustainable energy transition pathway formulation. 4. The special relevance of wind energy and solar photovoltaics, the increasing relevance of power technologies, the role of storage technologies and the necessity of societal cost of energy are discussed in detail. 5. Real scenarios for Finland, Europe and the world are used as references. 6. Finally, the knowledge gained will be applied to a chosen country using EnergyPLAN software to do a techno-economic analysis of a future fully sustainable energy system.

content: The course deals with the following topics: - Design principals to avoid fatigue failure of mechanical engineering components and structures - Introduction to fatigue in micro and macro scale, deformation of structural materials, stress concentrations and fracture mechanics - Design of structures based on stress-life approach, strain-life approach and linear elastic fracture mechanics. name: Steam Boilers
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to 1. demonstrate considerable knowledge to understand the requirements of the fuel on the combustion technology and equipment, 2. describe the most typical boilers burning biomass, 3. dimension the heat delivery surfaces of boilers and understand the scaling of the boilers, 4. perform thermal and fluid dynamical dimensioning of the combustion and flow equipment of boilers, 5. understand the fundamentals of the manufacturing and mechanical structure of the pressure vessel, 6. describe the main controls of boilers, 7. describe the most typical auxiliary equipment of boilers, and 8. recognise the most typical problems from the perspective of the boiler operation.
content: The characteristics of power plant fuels in relation to the boiler. The chemical balance, reaction kinetics and the imperfection of combustion. A theoretical examination of the ignition phenomenon. The stability of the flame. The factors affecting the efficiency of the boiler. Engineering design, dimensioning principles of the furnace, superheaters and pre-heaters. The burner technology and equipment for gaseous, liquid and solid fuels. Emission formation. Emission reduction during combustion and by using flue gascleaning methods. Fouling of heating surfaces, corrosion and erosion of the heating surface. Soot blowing. The control of the boiler. Kraft recovery boiler, heat recovery boiler and new boiler technologies.
prerequisites: Recommended: BH20A0300 Fundamentals of Heat Transfer. BH50A0500 Introduction to Combustion and Boiler Technology.

content: The aim of this course is to: - Give the students a deeper understanding on mechanical engineering in a specialized area, e.g. industrial design engineering and related topics, design of welded metal structures, laser processing and additive manufacturing to support innovative product design, mechatronics, machine dynamics, material selection in modern engineering and industrial design or sustainable production including applications of packaging technology - Give support for solving practical problems in industry and industrial design and give also a vision about entrepreneurship - Prepare the students to apply both practical project management tools to take care of an engineering project and also apply scientific approaches - Prepare students to start their coming M.Sc. thesis smoothly A specific individual project will be carried out preferably in an industrial company or in exceptional cases in one of the laboratories of the department of Mechanical Engineering at LUT. The project is planned together with the supervisor (lecturer) and the company and the topic should focus especially to problem solving in industry. The course module highlights the aspects of entrepreneurship. In some exceptional cases the content of the project could consist of laboratory work and literature research together with reporting and article writing. In some exceptional cases the project can be completed also as teamwork.

name: Introduction to Particle Physics
learningOutcomes: After this course, the students should be able to: 1. Explain the basic theoretical and experimental concepts in particle physics (in writing) 2. Calculate the rate of a particle interaction or decay process and explain their thought process clearly (by pen and paper) 3. Analyse a set of experimental data (with a computer) These ILOs cover the basic professional skills of experimental and theoretical particle physicists, who need to be able to analyse data with both theory knowledge and computing skills, and be able to discuss the results in context using the specific concepts of particle physics.
content: This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of particle physics, bridging both theoretical foundations and experimental analysis. Students will explore the core principles of special relativity and quantum mechanics as they apply to particle interactions and decays, while gaining hands-on experience in data analysis using Python or similar programming languages. Topics include decay rates, cross-sections, the Dirac equation, Feynman diagrams, and deep inelastic scattering, providing a strong foundation for further studies in experimental and theoretical particle physics. Underlying concepts [special relativity, quantum mechanics] Decay rates and cross sections [Lorentz-invariance, matrix element] The Dirac equation [relativistic QM => spin + antimatter] Interaction by particle exchange [Feynman diagrams] Electron-positron annihilation [calculations in perturbation theory] Electron-proton elastic scattering [form factor] Deep inelastic scattering [Bjorken x, PDFs] (*Symmetries and the quark model)
prerequisites: Special relativity, classical quantum mechanics and introduction modern physics and structure of matter. For the experimental analysis, Python or another similar programming language.
learningMaterial: Course book is "Modern Particle Physics" by Mark Thomson. This course covers chapters 1-8. Additional material will be made available in the form of slides and self-study videos/quizzes. More recommended literature: F. Halzen, A.D. Martin, Quarks and Leptons , John Wiley & Sons 1984. D. Griffiths, Introduction to elementary particles , John Wiley & Sons 1987. M. Peskin, D. Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory , Westview Press 1995. I. Aitchison, A. Hey, Gauge Theories in Particle Physics , Taylor & Francis 2004. A. Seiden, Particle Physics: A Comprehensive Introduction , Addison-Wesley 2004. O. Nachtmann, Elementary Particle Physics , Springer-Verlag 1990.
evaluationCriteria: Grading is from 1 to 5. Theory exercises (25%) and experimental analysis (25%) - exam (50%) - minimum of 45% required to pass
workload: Lectures, workshop and exercise sessions 42 h, Exercise assignments and contact session preparation/follow-up 56 h, preparation to exam 30 h, Exam and peer review 7 h. Total workload 35 h.

name: Inverse Problems
learningOutcomes: The student learns - how to recognize an inverse problem, - the main challenges related to them (instability, non-uniqueness) and - knows the main computational approaches to solve them.
content: Inverse problems appear in several fields, including medical imaging, image processing, mathematical finance, astronomy, geophysics, nondestructive material testing and sub-surface prospecting. Typical inverse problems arise from asking simple questions "backwards". For instance, the simple question might be "If we know precisely the structure of the inner organs of a patient, what kind of X-ray images would we get from her?" The same question backwards is "Given a set of X-ray images of a patient, what is the three-dimensional structure of her inner organs?" This is the inverse problem of Computerized Tomography, or CT imaging. Usually the inverse problem is more difficult than the simple question that it reverses. Successful solution of inverse problems requires specially designed algorithms that can tolerate errors in measured data.
prerequisites: Bachelor level studies in mathematics. Completion of the course BM20A7300 Functional analysis or a similar course is a recommended prerequisite.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes based on various materials. Recommended reading includes Kirsch: An Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of Inverse Problems, Springer 2011.
evaluationCriteria: Written examination with grading 0-5. Home exercises provide additional points towards the course grade.
workload: Lectures 14 h, period 2. Virtual learning material 14 h, period 2. Supervised tutorials 14 h, period 2. Homework 41 h, period 2. Independent study 52 h, period 2. Total workload 135 h.

name: Manufacturing of Metal Products
learningOutcomes: Manufacturing of metal products is a complex and precision-driven process that requires the use of many different methods and tools. The process starts with product design and technical analysis, where the dimensions, materials, mechanical properties and manufacturing methods are determined. Modern design philosophy includes two main areas: manufacturing and assembly. The aim is to design products so that their manufacturing and assembly is as simple and error-free as possible. Selected manufacturing methods, however, play a key role in the industrial production process. Correctly chosen manufacturing methods can significantly reduce production costs. For example, automation can reduce labor costs and improve productivity. Manufacturing methods also have a direct impact on product quality. Accuracy and repeatability are important factors in ensuring that each product meets the required quality standards. Flexible manufacturing systems (FMS) allow a rapid response to market changes and customer needs. This can include, for example, adaptive production lines that can manufacture different products without major changes. Environmentally friendly manufacturing methods can reduce waste and energy consumption, which is important for sustainable development. This can also improve a company's reputation and attract environmentally aware customers. The introduction of new manufacturing methods can lead to innovative products and a competitive advantage in the market. In addition, efficient and optimized manufacturing processes reduce production lead times, allowing products to be produced more quickly and profitably. The course is a direct continuation of the course "Principles of Industrial Manufacturing Processes" (BK10A3800), which provides students with the basic knowledge necessary for the manufacturing of metal products ("machining" and sheet metal working). This course focuses on the management of the whole production chain of metal products and on specific selected manufacturing techniques. Approved completion of the course will provide students with the competences: Manage manufacturing-friendly design principles for different components using modern software (DFMA principles and methods, CAD/CAM). Analyze and develop production organization and production efficiency in factories manufacturing different product groups (LEAN tools, production organization and facilities, production control). Estimate the production costs of components and the variables affecting them. Manage production automation in factories manufacturing metal products (storage systems, FMS, robotics, automated transporters). Evaluate the profitability of investment in machine tools. Understand the environmental impact of metal product manufacturing processes. Manage the processes and support functions used in the manufacture of metal products. Know the most common safety hazards in manufacturing companies, risk mitigation and supervisor responsibilities.
content: The content of the course focuses on four (4) topics, themes. These themes are designed to benefit the student in working life according to the chosen study orientation. The topics focus on the manufacture and manufacturability of metal products so that students gain a comprehensive understanding of the metal products industry. The course will cover topics such as advanced and automated manufacturing processes, trends and visions, materials and quality issues. The numerous case studies used in the course are drawn directly from the real world. The different course modules use the content of the themes in a selective way, so that the students can acquire the knowledge they need after successfully completing the course. The topic of sheet metal technology: Presses Press tool systems Deep drawing process and tools, stretch forming Special sheet metal forming processes. Mechanical joining methods without additional elements Storage systems for sheet materials and semi-finished components Quality issues in the manufacture of sheet metal products Rapid prototyping Machining theme: CAD/CAM Machine tools for various machining operations CNC machining for machining centres, CNC machining centres, CNC machining centres for machining operations Workpiece handling Zero point fixturing systems Production development Production and competitiveness Production planning The production and productivity theme: Production systems Robotic automation Production management and organization at factory level Production efficiency and its improvement Production costs and investments The Metal Products theme: Design and manufacturability aspects of metal products (DFMA) Modularization and standardization Simulation of production and digital manufacturing Surface treatment of metal products Safety at work
