name: Master's Thesis
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student is expected to be able to: 1. define a research problem, 2. choose and apply research methods relevant to the research problem, 3. search for suitable reference material, and assess the quality and reliability of the material and the information it contains, 4. use and interpret reference material correctly and diversely, 5. report on his or her work in writing, taking into account language and layout requirements, and 6. give a concise oral presentation on the content and results of the work.
content: The thesis is a research or a planning project. Students must demonstrate the ability to complete the project independently and following a plan. A report is prepared following the instructions for the Master's thesis.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Master's Thesis 100 %.
workload: The presentation of the thesis will be arranged with the supervising professor. There will not be a separate seminar. Total workload approx. 780 h.

name: Mathematical Modelling
learningOutcomes: Student understands the applicability of mathematical models to solving different real-life problems, and is able to formulate models and assess their suitability, and acquire knowledge and skills for studying more demanding applications. Student understands the modeling process, knows types of models and conservation principles. He/she is able to formulate models using differential equations, discrete, probabilistic and fuzzy concepts. The student knows how to use data and perform parameter estimation and understands the ideas of approximation and scales.
content: Mathematical applications, stages of the modelling process. Different types of models. Conservation principles and basics of models. Differential equations and systems theory. Discrete models. Models, data and parameter estimation. Equilibrium models and stability. Approximation and scales. Probabilistic models. Case examples.
prerequisites: Recommended: BM20A1401 Statistics I BM20A1601 Matrix Calculus, BM20A6700 Mathematics I, BM20A6800 Mathematics II, BM20A6900 Mathematics III, fysiikan 1. vuoden opinnot.
learningMaterial: Course material is in internet, web-address will be announced via Moodle when course starts.
evaluationCriteria: 0.5, exercises 60 %, project work 40 %.
workload: The course is organized on on-line learning environment in form of weekly video lectures and exercises and project work. On-line learning and independent study, 135 h. 1. and 2. period.

name: Measurement and Control Systems
learningOutcomes: Student can 1. evaluate the applicability of measurement equipment to the given application based on available information and estimate the equipment measurement uncertainty, 2. choose components for a measurement system and do a measurement plan, 3. form differential equations based models from simple dynamic systems, 4. form the state space representation from the differential equations of the system 5. form transfer functions from differential equations and 6. study the stability of dynamic systems using commonly applied methods, 7. evaluate dynamic properties of (1st and 2nd order) systems and tune these using simple controllers.
content: Basic terms describing the static and dynamic properties of measurement systems. Measurement accuracy, uncertainty, sensors, and digitizing of measurement signals. Dynamic models of linear systems. Transfer functions. Laplace domain. Basic concepts and analyses of control engineering. Compensators and controllers. Duality of time and frequency domains. Analytic tuning of a controller. State space models. Use of Matlab/Simulink programs in control problems.
prerequisites: Basics of differential equations, basics of complex numbers.
learningMaterial: Lecture material in Moodle
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Assignments 50% and examination 60%.
workload: 14 h of lectures, 14 h of tutorials, 1st period. 14 of lectures, 14 of tutorials, 2nd period. Practical assignments 34 h. Independent study 30 h. Total workload 130 h.

name: Mechanics and Wave Motion
learningOutcomes: After the Mechanics part of the course the student should be able to understand translational and rotational motion and static equilibrium and to apply Newton's laws and principles of conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum in different motion and static equilibrium problems. After the Wave Motion part of the course the student should be able to understand and solve problems in harmonic motion, damped and forced oscillations and harmonic waves (mechanical and electromagnetic waves) in different physical systems, propagation of waves in medium (reflection and refraction), detection of waves (intensity, decibel scale, Doppler effect), superposition of waves (standing waves, beats, interference), diffraction and polarization of waves.
content: Mechanics part of the course: Basics of translational and rotational motion, Newton's laws, principles of conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum. Wave Motion part of the course: Mechanical oscillations (harmonic, damped and forced oscillations), harmonic waves, mechanical and electromagnetic waves, interference, diffraction and polarization.
learningMaterial: Study materials in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, exercises, midterm exams and final exam.
workload: Completion method: 1st and 2nd period, Lectures 28 h, exercises 42 h. Independent studing 40 h. Examination and preparation for it 25 h. Total workload 135 h.
equivalentCoursesInfo: BM30A2600 Mekaniikan perusteet 4 op, BM30A2900 Aaltoliikeoppi 3 op ja BM30A3100 Johdatus yliopistofysiikkaan 6 op.

name: Microelectronics
learningOutcomes: The properties of silicon and other semiconductors will be used to explain the behavior of a variety of semiconductor devices such as light emitting diodes, sensors, bipolar transistors and field effect transistors. A device widely used in integrated circuits is the MOSFET (metal oxide semiconductor field effect transistor).
content: We study classical Microelectronics based on Silicon technology by considering p-n junctions, diodes, and transistors (bipolar junctions and MOSFET). The course includes also computations and simulations performed in MATLAB. These tasks help to visualize the working principle of devices and allow a better understanding of the lectures. We will also discuss the Moore's law and beyond.
prerequisites: Recommended BL40A1711 Johdanto digitaalielektroniikkaan and BL50A1400 Analogiaelektroniikka.
learningMaterial: Fonstad, Clifton G. Microelectronic devices and circuits . McGraw-Hill, Inc.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 100 %. Satisfactorily completed assignment required.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises and tutorials 28 h, assignment 40 h, preparation for exam 60 h. Assignment and its presentation. Written examination.

name: Modelling of Unit Operations
learningOutcomes: After completing the module, the student is able to describe steady-state and transient unit operations with mathematical models, to verify and validate models and to estimate their parameters from experimental data, to apply models in process development and design, including sizing, optimization, and scale-up, and to use mathematical and simulation software (MATLAB).
content: Basics of chemical reaction system Description and derivation to model chemical reactions system into ordinary differential equations (ODEs) based on the stoichiometric balance of reacting components Solve the derived ODEs in computational software such as MATLAB using odesolver e.g. ode45 and ode15s Model development and validation Compare the assumed developed model to experimental data. Apply curve-fitting or optimization tools to validate assumed models, using tools such as “Fminsearch”, and “lsqr” via defined objective functions (e.g., standard square error of model and experimental data) to validate the developed model. Application of model development Model material and energy balances in chemical engineering processes based on steady- and dynamic-state Develop model for batch, semi-batch, and continuous (e.g., CSTR and plug flow reactor) based systems based on ODEs and Partial differential equations (PDEs) Solve and curve-fit the derived ODEs in MATLAB using odesolver as well as optimization tools Apply appropriate boundary conditions and solve the derived PDEs in MATLAB using odesolver via methods of lines, i.e. converting the PDEs into ODEs.
prerequisites: Either the Finnish course Johdatus tekniseen laskentaan or Principles of Technical Computing, or corresponding skills in MATLAB programming, as well as a knowledge in reaction chemistry and kinetics (i.e., stoichiometric balance, elementary reaction kinetics)
learningMaterial: Lecture notes and links to supplementary material are given in Moodle
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Grade is determined by weekly exercises, home assignment and Exam-examination
workload: Lectures 24 h, exercises 14 h, 2nd period. Home assignments 68 h, self-study 25 h, examination (Exam). Total workload 135 h.

name: Modern Welding Processes
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to widen the knowledge about the various aspects of industrial modern welding processes. After having completed and passed this course, the student: has a knowledge about the welding processes and their variations that are used in industry, can compare and evaluate different welding processes and automation levels from productivity, usability and profitability point of view, can choose the most suitable welding process and automation level for manufacturing different type of products, understands the relationship between the welding process, quality and costs, has a general overview of utilizing welding standards relative to welding production, safety and quality management, knows the different sensor techniques used in welding.
content: The course comprises lectures, exercises and obligatory laboratory tutorials to make the student familiar with industrial welding processes and practices. Lecture topics are listed below: The concept of weldability in terms of materials, structure and manufacturing. Essential parameters, productivity, usability, and efficiency of major welding processes. Welding preparations (e.g. groove cutting and beveling methods) and post-weld treatments. Automation levels of welding (manual / mechanized / robotized). Sensor technologies and jig systems used in welding. Adaptive welding. Cost accounting of welding procedures and investments. Quality, sustainability and safety aspects in a welding workshop. Each lecture has an exercise, which consists of multiple-choice / open questions, and some practical assignments based on the industrial tasks of a welding engineer. Additionally, the course has an obligatory seminar, which is a report of 10-20 pages written by the student for the whole duration of the course.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge related to welding processes.
learningMaterial: Lectures in Moodle. Modern Welding Technology, H. B. Cary, S. C. Helzer, Pearson. Standards related to welding. Videos of industrial welding operations and processes given during the course.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exam 50 %, laboratory exercises and seminar work 50 %.
workload: The course is delivered in a form of lectures with interactive questions and discussions with students. The course includes also practical laboratory exercises. Weekly assignments will be carried out in Moodle and the final exam will be conducted as an electronic exam. Lectures 28 h. Weekly assignments 20 h. Seminar work and presentations 40 h. Laboratory exercises including mechanized and robotized welding as well as different sensor technologies 14 h. Independent study and preparation for exam 28 h. Total workload 130 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Diverse Interaction Skills
learningOutcomes: The student will be able to - perform with confidence, assurance and purpose in different languages, taking into account the requirements of the communicative situation and environment - discuss and argue convincingly in interaction situations - work as a member of multicultural groups - use a wide range of basic principles and techniques of spoken communication.
prerequisites: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching
learningMaterial: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching
workload: Details under the header Teaching

name: Nanophysics
learningOutcomes: The objective of the course is to make information about the rapidly evolving areas of nanoscale science and technology available to a wide range of students. Upon completion of the course, students will clarify the principal difference between physical phenomena in macro-scale and nano-scale. Students will be able to: - develop their understanding of bio-, physical and chemical systems, - characterize the systems related with Materials science and Metrology, - recognize the difference in prevailing forces in different size scales, - explain many practical observations and anomalies found in their experimental research activity, - apply this combined knowledge in practice. After taking the course, students should become capable to operate safely with nano-systems, considering their hazardous aspects. The course helps to systematize the fragmented information about nano- related phenomena and knowledge from physical and chemical disciplines studied before.
content: Nanoethics, Forces in the Nanoworld, Scaling Laws, Nanomaterials and Nanocomposites, Nanomechanics, Nanothermodynamics, Nanofluidics, Nanochemistry, Tribology, Nanooptics of Metals and Semiconductors, Nanoelectronics, Spintronics, Nanomagnetism, Nanocarbon, Nanolithography.
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Tech) studies.
learningMaterial: Lecture handouts
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, examination 50 %, exercises 25 %, presentation 15 %, laboratory works 10 %.
workload: Lectures 42 h, exercises 28 h, preparing for exercises 36 h, preparing for the presentation 8 h, preparing for laboratory works 6 h, preparing for the examination 40 h, 1st-2nd period. Total workload for student 160 h.

name: Nuclear Power Plant Engineering
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to explain the functional principles of nuclear power plants and perform engineering design of main heat transfer and power conversion processes. The student will learn elements of engineering design of light water reactor plants process components (excluding the reactor core) and radiation shielding. The student understands nuclear fuel cycle and related technologies, can manage nuclear waste and apply nuclear safety principles. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Written communication, Oral communication, Team working skills , Time management and prioritizing tasks
content: Nuclear reactor as heat source. Power conversion in light water reactor power plants. Main process systems and safety systems of light water reactors, both large and small (SMRs). Health effects of ionising radiation, radiation protection. Nuclear fuel cycle, nuclear waste management. Nuclear safety in design, major nuclear accidents.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Written examination 70 %, assignment and presentation 30 %.
workload: Completion method 1. Exam: Lectures 14 h, tutorials 14 h, presentation 25 h, independent study 25 h, 3rd period. Lectures 14 h, tutorials 14 h, assignment 25 h, independent study 28 h, 3 h, 4th period. Total workload 162 h.

name: Nuclear Reactor Physics Methods
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to derive the neutron transport equation from the basic physical phenomena, understand the concepts of neutron flux and current, and use simple numerical calculation methods for the neutron flux solution with diffusion approximation. Students will understand solution process of core simulator to obtain flux distribution and multiplication factor of reactor. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Know-how on own field, Practical application of theories, Problem solving, Analytical thinking skills.
content: The transport equation for neutrons. The diffusion theory and simple numerical solutions. Two-group diffusion theory. Numerical solution of multiplication factor. Solution process of reactor core simulator. Expertise and skills: Know-how on own field, Practical application of theories, Problem solving, Analytical thinking skills.
prerequisites: BH30A0201 Nuclear Reactor Design and BH30A2105 Nuclear Reactor Dynamics.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes. Additional information: Reuss: Neutron Physics. Duderstadt, Hamilton: Nuclear Reactor Analysis. Stacey: Nuclear Reactor Physics. Hébert: Applied Reactor Physics.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, assignment 100 %.
workload: Lectures 14 h, tutorials 14 h, computer exercises 4 h, assignment 49 h. Total workload 81 h.

name: Numerical Methods in Electromagnetism
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to model and analyse electrical machines using commercial finite element based calculation software.
content: The fundamentals of the element method, boundary conditions, modelling of materials, post-processing of results. Iron loss models. Eddy current problems, utilisation of circuit model in calculation.
prerequisites: BL30A0500 Introduction to Electrical Drives and BL30A0400 Design of an Electrical Machine.
learningMaterial: Course material in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Course requirements: participation in tutorials and a satisfactorily completed assignment. 0-5, assignment 100 %.
workload: 28 h of supervised tutorials. 3rd period. Self study: assignment and report 80 h. Total workload 108 h.

name: Numerical Simulation
learningOutcomes: Throughout the course, students will gain practical hands-on experience in using MATLAB for problem-solving in linear algebra, differential equations, optimization, and statistical analysis parameter estimation results. The emphasis will be on both theoretical understanding and practical application, equipping students with the skills needed for technical problem-solving in diverse fields.
content: • Linear Algebra: – solving systems of linear equations (using both matrix form and symbolic math toolbox). – Singular value decomposition (SVD) with applications in, for instance, image reconstruction, solving linear equations, data compression, etc. • ODEs and DAEs: – Solving ODEs analytically and numerically (using both symbolic and numeric methods); – Solving DAEs numerically. – Applications in various dynamical systems. • Optimization: – Description of the general form of a model. – Linear least squares estimation in Matlab (using Matlab backslash) – Parameter estimation for nonlinear models using Matlab fminsearch optimizer – Specific purpose alternatives: lscurvefit and polyfit – Various applications with both dynamic models and algebraic models. • Statistics: – Basics: sample statistics – Statistics for linear models: Covariance of estimates using coefficient matrix, t-values, Rsquare value, crossvalidation. – Statistics for nonlinear models: Covariance of estimates by computing the Jacobian matrix (analytically and numerically) – Alternative ways to obtain the statistics of parameter estimates: Adding noise to data, Bootstrapping – Various applications with both dynamic models and algebraic models. The course is related to UN's Sustainable Development Goal (SDG): 4 Quality Education.The course is related to industry and employment: Research and Development.
prerequisites: Knowledge of the basic usage and programming syntax of Matlab and some level of Mathematical background for instance, calculus, ordinary differential equations, and optimization.
learningMaterial: Lecture material available in Moodle
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, assignments and exam
workload: Lectures 12 h, computer class exercises 24 h, independent study 65 h, preparation for exams 34 h, 1st period. Total 135 h.
equivalentCoursesInfo: Replaces the course BM20A9000 Principles of Technical Computing for MSc Students,

name: Cyber Security of Software Systems
learningOutcomes: The objective of the course is to introduce the fundamental aspects of the cyber security and cyber security thinking to the student, especially from the viewpoint of software engineering and the entire software organization. After the course, the student identifies and understands how the cyber security is related to the software development, what are the most common security threats from the viewpoint of software, and how they are usually managed.
content: Fundamental concepts of cyber security. Threats and vulnerabilities. The common attack and prevention techniques. The fundamentals aspects and objectives of cyber security-related activities. The effect of security policies. Cyber security from the viewpoint of software engineering.
prerequisites: CT60A0202 Introduction to Programming, CT60A4002 Software Engineering or equivalent knowledge.
learningMaterial: Schneier, B.: Secrets and Lies, Wiley, 2000.Mead, N. R., ; Woody, C.. Cyber Security Engineering: A Practical Approach for Systems and Software Assurance. Addison-Wesley Professional, 2016. Other materials provided by the lectures.
workload: 3 ECTS cr course for the Software and Systems Engineering (Lahti) programme, only. First time in the academic year 2022-2023 (2nd year studies).

name: Open Science
learningOutcomes: - Understanding the principles of Open Science and what could it mean to one's own research - Implementing LUT open science principles to one's own research - How to prepare oneself for possible challenges related to Open Science
content: Open science and research culture, open publishing, open data and open education
learningMaterial: The course material will be available in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: learning assignments and feedback

name: Optoelectronics
learningOutcomes: This course gives a comprehensive understanding of optoelectronics and photonics devices. It provides a necessary background to deal with optical data communication tools, construction of wave guides using total internal reflection and working principles of light emitting diodes (LEDs), LASERs and photodetectors.
content: The course begins by summarizing Maxwell equations for the electromagnetic field and the wave equations. Then the lectures discuss optical planar waveguides, linear optical fibres, propagation of linear pulses, LEDs, LASERs, detectors and photovoltaic devices. Some exercises with MATLAB will be given so that students can start their own numerical experiments.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge about optics.
learningMaterial: Kasap SO. Optoelectronics and photonics. Prentice Hall; Wartak, Marek S. Computational photonics: an introduction with MATLAB . Cambridge University Press.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 100 %.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises 14 h, preparation for exam 114 h, 1st period. Examination.

name: Pressure Equipment

learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will know: the fundamentals related to pressure equipment legislation, the principles of the pressure equipment dimensioning, and the general standards related to pressure equipment. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life:
content: Pressure Equipment Act, related decrees, and Pressure Equipment Directive (PED). The requirements for the use of pressure equipment. Pressure equipment design, manufacture and conformity assessment. Pressure equipment inspection and control. Pressure equipment manufacturer, owner and holder responsibilities.

name: Service Process Management

name: Photonics
learningOutcomes: After the course a student: 1. knows the basic properties of waves and wave motion, 2. understands the material polarization phenomenon as the ultimate source of light, 3. knows the basic properties and physics of laser action, 4. knows the ideas and applications of ultrafast optics, 5. knows the basic physics and applications of nonlinear optics, 6. knows the Fresnel-equations, and understand accordingly the physics of light reflection and refraction, 7. knows the basics of light polarization, the corresponding applications and the Jones matrix formulation, 8. understands the meaning of spatial and temporal coherence of light, and their implications for the technical applications, such as FTIR spectroscopy, 9. knows the ABCD-matrix formulation for geometrical optics, 10. knows the basics of laser imaging: one- and two-photon confocal microscopy, spectral imaging, and fluorescence nanoscopy, 11. understands the physics of producing slow and fast light, and knows their applications, 12. understands diffraction of light, and its applications.
content: 1. Wave motion and wave equations, 2. Maxwell equations and electromagnetic spectrum, 3. Lasers, 4. Ultrafast lasers, 5. Fresnell equations, 6. Polarization and optical activity, 7. Geometrical optics, 8. Coherence, 9. Interference and diffraction, 10. Nonlinear optics, 11. Optical microscopy and nanoscopy, 12. Slow and fast light, THz-optics, 13. Attosecond optics, 14. Coherent control.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have completed a basic course in physics.
learningMaterial: Lecture material available in Moodle (slides and videos), based partly on textbooks: 1. Eugene Hecht, Optics, 4th edition (Addison-Wesley, 2002). 2. G. R. Fowles, Introduction to Modern Optics, 2nd edition, (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, New York, 1976). 3. R. W. Boyd, Nonlinear Optics (Academic Press, San Diego, 1992). 4. Y. R. Shen, The Princples of Nonlinear Optics (Wiley, New York, 1984).

name: Basics of Polymer Chemistry

name: Postgraduate Course in Fiber Composites

name: Power Exchange Game for Electricity Markets

name: Principles of Industrial Manufacturing Processes
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: Manufacturing process fundamentals: Identify, describe, and compare various manufacturing processes, including machining (turning, milling, etc.), sheet metal production (cutting, bending, forming, joining), additive manufacturing, common welding processes, and packaging. Machining Expertise: Master the fundamentals of machining, including parameters, cutting tools, forces, fluids, chips, fixtures; manufacture machined products or manage their procurement; analyze cost structures; and understand/mitigate waste generation. Sheet metal production: Understand the complete sheet metal product process, including cutting, punching, bending, forming (including special methods), and joining techniques. Composites fundamentals & materials: Define composite materials, differentiate between types (particle, fiber, structural, bio, and WPC), explain the advantages/disadvantages of natural vs. synthetic fibers, and describe key chemical/physical properties of natural fibers (cellulose, lignin, aspect ratio, moisture) and common thermoplastics used in WPCs (melting point, mechanical properties). WPC manufacturing processes: Describe and understand the steps involved in key WPC manufacturing techniques, including compounding, extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, and 3D printing. Applications and scope: Identify a wide range of applications for WPCs and natural fiber composites across various industries. Understand the packaging industry and its context : Define the fundamental roles and functions of packaging, encompassing product protection, preservation, communication, convenience, and environmental considerations. Explain packaging from diverse perspectives, incorporating materials science, machinery, printing/converting, product knowledge, and the influence of business models, consumer behavior, environmental issues, and regulations Describe packaging materials and manufacturing processes : Describe common packaging materials, including fiber-based materials, various plastic types, metal, and glass, outlining their properties and applications. Explain the manufacturing and converting processes for various packaging types. Design and manage packaging production : Comprehend key factors in designing new packaging lines, such as production volumes, cost analysis, efficiency, and the crucial role of material runnability. Explain various maintenance paradigms for packaging equipment, including reactive, preventive, and predictive maintenance, analyzing their benefits and drawbacks. Master the laser fundamentals and technologies: Understand the core principles of photonic digital manufacturing, including additive manufacturing (3D printing) and laser-based processes, and classify the various AM technologies. This includes identifying system components, understanding process parameters, and differentiating between various laser types and their applications. Analyze industrial applications and impact in AM: Evaluate the practical applications of photonic digital manufacturing across industries, with a particular focus on the automotive sector. This includes analyzing case studies, assessing the impact on product design, supply chains, business models, and understanding the economic, lifecycle, and environmental considerations. Explore advanced concepts and future trends in additive manufacturing: Investigate advancements in photonic digital manufacturing, including new materials, automation, simulation-driven design, large-scale additive manufacturing, and quality assurance techniques. Define welding concepts: Understand core welding terminology and processes(MMA, GMAW, FCAW, SAW, GTAW, Plasma). Assess HS/UHSS weldability: Identify challenges and considerations for welding high strength/ultra-high strength steels and understand relevant welding standards for them Apply welding design principles : Design welded structures using HS/UHSS, accounting for strength and distortion. Describe welding production processes: Outline the steps in welding production and quality control. Explain supply chains in welding: Understand the importance of collaboration in the welding supply chain. Recognize digital impact : Appreciate the role of digital technologies in modern welding. Safe work in welding : Know safe work methods in welding.
content: This course covers a wide range of manufacturing and engineering topics, including the fundamentals of sheet metal fabrication, material selection, basic processing operations (cutting, punching, bending), and traditional joining methods. Cutting and machining are explored, detailing steel fabrication, cutting parameters, tool wear, and common machining operations like turning, milling, and drilling. Sustainable manufacturing highlights strategies for improving product sustainability. The study of composite materials delves into fundamental principles, classifications, and the advantages/disadvantages of natural fibers, with a specific focus on Wood-Plastic Composites (WPCs), including their chemical composition, properties, manufacturing processes, and applications. Packaging engineering and technology encompasses the entire packaging value chain, material types (fiber-based, plastic, metal, glass), manufacturing processes, environmental impact, and regulatory compliance. Laser and additive technologies are covered in depth, including the principles of photonic digital manufacturing, various additive manufacturing (AM) technologies (especially for metals), industry standards, system components, process parameters, laser types, applications (particularly in automotive), case studies, economic/environmental considerations, and cutting-edge advancements. Welding is examined, covering terminology, processes (MIG/MAG, TIG, SAW), joint types, weld characteristics, the challenges and advantages of welding High-Strength/Ultra-High-Strength Steels (HS/UHSS), design for welding (considering static/fatigue strength, distortion, tolerances), manufacturing and quality control (production planning, inspection, work instructions), the role of digital supply chains, real-world case studies, and safety considerations. The course includes a reverse engineering group project. Topics covered: Sheet metal: Sheet metal materials Basic sheet metal processing operations like cutting, punching, bending, and folding. Traditional mechanical joining methods (with additional elements). Cutting and machining: Steel fabrication processes. Basics of cutting parameters and tool selection. Tool Wear Basic machining operations, such as external and internal turning, milling, drilling, sawing, grinding Sustainable Manufacturing: Strategies for improving the sustainability of products through manufacturing processes. Composite materials: Fundamental principles of composite production, including reinforcement and matrix phases. Classification of composites (particle-reinforced, fiber-reinforced, structural). Advantages and disadvantages of using natural fibers in composites. Chemical composition and properties of natural fibers (cellulose, lignin, etc.). Types of thermoplastics used in WPCs and their properties. Compatibility issues between fibers and polymers and methods for improvement (e.g., coupling agents). WPC manufacturing processes: compounding, extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, and 3D printing. Mechanical and physical properties of WPCs, including weathering and durability. Applications of WPCs in various industries. Packaging engineering and technology: Overview of the packaging industry, covering the entire value chain from material production to end-of-life considerations. Key topics include: the functions and requirements of packaging (with a focus on food packaging); analysis of the global packaging market and industry trends. In-depth study of fiber-based, plastic, metal and glass packaging materials Detailed examination of manufacturing processes such as converting, forming, filling, and sealing; and the design, operation, and maintenance of packaging lines. Environmental impact, sustainability, logistics, and regulatory compliance Laser and additive technologies Understand the core principles of photonic digital manufacturing, including additive manufacturing (3D printing) and laser-based processes. Understand the different AM technologies suitable for metal. Classify the various AM technologies according to industry standards (ISO/ASTM 52900:2015). Identify system components, understanding process parameters, and differentiating between various laser types and their applications. Evaluate the practical applications of photonic digital manufacturing across diverse industries, with a particular focus on the automotive sector. Analyze case studies, assessing the impact on product design, supply chains, business models. Understand the economic, lifecycle, and environmental considerations of these technologies. Investigate the cutting-edge advancements in photonic digital manufacturing, including new materials, automation, simulation-driven design, large-scale additive manufacturing, and quality assurance techniques. Welding: Terminology, processes (MIG/MAG, TIG, SAW, etc.), joint types, weld characteristics. HS/UHSS: Advantages, challenges, and the impact of welding on these materials. Design for Welding (HS/UHSS): Static/fatigue strength, distortion, tolerances. Manufacturing & Quality: Production planning, inspection, and the role of work instructions. Digital supply chain: Optimization through digital tools, data, and real-time monitoring. Case Studies: Real-world applications and problem-solving. Safety in welding.

name: Principles of Thermal Gas-Liquid Processes
learningOutcomes: Student understands distillation, evaporation and gas scrubbing technologies, including equipment structures and sizing principles. Student can design gas-liquid contactors by hand, is able to form mathematical calculation models, and can apply equations for computer simulation.

Distillation process (trays, reboiler, condenser, reflux), distillation efficiencies, thermodynamics. Mass balances, phase equilibrium calculations (MATLAB). Pxy-diagram, Flash distillation, Bubble temperature calculation, dew temperature calculation, Txy-diagram formulation, Batch distillation simulation program development (MATLAB). name: Reliability Engineering
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course students will be able to calculate the reliability parameters for separate components and simple systems, formulate and solve fault and event trees for systems, and estimate the effect of human factors. content: The course will cover the following topics. 1. Focussing on the conversion technologies related to different renewable energy resources. 2. All technologies are classified with respect to their applications, efficiency, maturity, economics, industrial scaling and expected relevance for the ongoing energy transition.

name: Solar Economy
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. Identify the constraints and potentials of all relevant energy sources in a global context. 2. Describe the major characteristics of renewable energy (RE) technologies, in particular applications, efficiency, economics, industrial scale and future prospects. 3. Analyse the need for storage technologies and their different fields of application based on their key technical and economic features. 4. Describe the sustainability requirements of future energy systems as the major guard rail for the energy transformation. 5. Analyse energy transformation scenarios and identify the key technologies and setups for sustainable energy progress. 6. All aforementioned aims are specially highlighted for solar energy.
content: The energy transformation has to fulfil a broad set of different requirements beyond technical and standard economic considerations. The course provides an overview of the resource basis of the current and future energy system through applying relevant guard rails. RE technologies in focus on the course are solar photovoltaics, wind energy, battery storage, and power-to-X technologies. Further technologies are considered according to their relevance to energy scenarios. Technologies are discussed in light of their technical characteristics, but also with reference to applications, sustainability criteria, and current and future economics. The special relevance of wind energy and solar photovoltaics, the increasing relevance of power technologies, the role of storage technologies and the necessity of societal cost of energy are discussed in detail. Solar energy is in particularly highlighted.
prerequisites: Previous studies either in economics, electrical engineering, environmental engineering or energy engineering are recommended.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes and other materials distributed during the course by email.

name: Statistical learning

content: Statistical learning refers to a field of machine learning drawing from statistics and functional analysis. Statistical learning focuses on developing and studying methods, algorithms, and models for making predictions or decisions based on data. Statistical learning is widely applied in various domains, including finance, healthcare, natural language processing, computer vision, and bioinformatics. We will discuss the algorithms for classification and regression such as SVM, Nearest Neighbor, Regularization Methods, and Kernel Methods.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge on probability theory
learningMaterial: Lecture notes.

name: Statistical Parameter Estimation
learningOutcomes: Bayes theorem, hierarchical models, stochastic processes, MCMC, Kalman and particle filters
content: - Preliminaries of stochastic processes: Brownian motion, fractional Brownian motion, and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. - Simulation of the processes, additive noise processes and postulating the statistical parameter estimation problems as Bayesian statistical estimation problems. - Bayes’ theorem: Solutions of the parameter estimation problems as a posteriori distributions, e.g. estimate the a posteriori probability density of Hurst parameter and variance scaling parameter of the fractional Brownian motion. - Drawing estimators from the posterior distribution with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods (Metropolis-Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) and optimisation-based methods (quasi-Newton). This includes also uncertainty quantification of the parameters. - Applications in science, finance and industry. The course is related to UN's Sustainable Development Goal (SDG): 4 Quality Education. The course is related to industry and employment: Research and Development.
prerequisites: Basics of statistics, linear algebra, and differential equations.
learningMaterial: Andrew Gelman, John Carlin, Hal Stern, David Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 2021. Simo Särkkä, and Arno Solin, Applied Stochastic Differential Equations, 2019. Simo Särkkä, Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing, 2013. Christian P Robert, and George Casella, Monte Carlo Statistical Methods, 2004.

name: Steel Structures 2
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, students can design welded structures for demanding applications, also considering fabrication requirements. This signifies that students are able to: - choose and apply purposeful analyzing methods for fatigue assessment of welded joints - design plate (welded and cold-formed) structures considering stability - design structures and joints using the plastic limit state method - evaluate risks for the brittle fracture in structures, particularly for arctic applications - design beams considering multiple load configurations, such as normal forces, torsion, warping, distortion, and shear lag. - optimize structures, particularly considering the potential in the use of high and ultra high strength steels - design of mechanical (bolted) connections
content: The course involves the following topics: - Theoretical background and applications for the fatigue design of welded joints. - Plasticity theorems of beams, frames and plates (yield line method). - Analytical and numerical methods for analyzing of brittle fracture considering the material properties of welded joints. - Theoretical background and design methods (based on Eurocode 3, EC3) for buckling of plates, columns and beams. - Theory of thin-walled structures - Practical design methodologies for designing and multi-objective optimizing welded structures, considering global structural behavior, joint details, and material strength effects - Failure modes of mechanical (bolted) joints. The course module provides knowledge about the design, fabrication and analysis of demanding structural applications that can be used in the Power-to-X solutions.

name: Sustainable.now
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students: 1) Understand the intersectional, partly contradictory, goals and interdimensionality of the climate challenge and the challenges of sustainable development. 2) Are familiar with the multidisciplinary links between climate change and different goals of sustainable development, and will identify different tools for solving problems. 3) Outline the importance of positivity and solution orientation both through the global responsibility of individuals and through the transformation of existing structures.
content: Sustainable.now is a basic course for anyone interested in sustainable development and climate change. The principles of sustainable development will be linked to the 1.5 degree climate target. - Ecological sustainability - Social sustainability - Economic sustainability - Cultural sustainability The course provides a solid knowledge package on the concept of sustainable development and its ecological, social, economic and cultural dimensions, as well as the connections and tensions between them. The ethical perspective that runs through the course provides a basis for considering sustainable development also as a political and normative concept. The course also emphasizes the importance of agency and the different roles of the individual. Students will be given the opportunity to look at the sustainability of their own lifestyle in terms of individual choices, but on the other hand, sustainability and climate challenges will also be presented as a structural and systemic problem.
learningMaterial: Material and Literature specified in MOODLE course overview.

name: Sustainable Sheet Metal Product Fabrication
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will be able to: - identify and compare different production methods in the industrial manufacture of sheet metal products. - identify and compare different types of sheet materials and coatings used in sheet metal products (pre-coated materials, surface treatment processes used in sheet metal products). - manage the manufacturing processes and machine tools, including tooling systems, used in the production of sheet metal products in the following areas: Cutting and punching of thin sheet materials (shears, punches, laser cutting machines, water jet cutting machines). Bending of thin sheet materials (edging presses, plate benders and automatic bending machines). Forming of thin sheet materials (presses) Special forming methods (high pressure forming, electro-hydraulic and magnetic pulse forming, pressure forming, rotary forming). Joining of thin sheet materials (mechanical joining methods with and without additional elements). - manage the manufacturing-friendly design of sheet metal products using modern software (DFMA principles and methods, CAD/CAM). - analyze and develop production organization and production efficiency in sheet metal manufacturing plants (LEAN tools, production organization and facilities, production control). - assess the costs of sheet metal products and the variables affecting them. - manage the automation of production in sheet metal product factories (storage systems, FMS, robotics, AGV). - evaluate the return on investment in machine tools - be aware of the environmental impact of sheet metal manufacturing processes.
content: This course focuses on fabricating and manufacturability of sheet metal products in such a way that the students will reach a comprehensive understanding of sheet metal industry. The course covers traditional and automated sheet metal fabricating processes, trends, and visions, as well as materials and quality issues. Numerous case examples used in this course are straight from the real world. The course is related to sustainable development. Lecture topics: Sheet metal materials Cutting sheet metal materials Punching sheet metal materials and special punch press operations Bending sheet metal materials Folding sheet metal materials Presses Press tooling systems Deep drawing process and tools, stretch forming Special sheet metal forming processes. Total of 5 lectures from this topic. Surface treatment processes Mechanical joining methods with additional elements Mechanical joining methods without additional elements Storage systems for sheet metal materials and semi-finished components Manufacturing systems Robot automation Quality issues in sheet metal product fabricating Production costs and investments Production management and organizing in factory level Rapid prototyping Production efficiency (DFMA, LEAN)
prerequisites: Not required.
learningMaterial: Course material will be published during the Course on the Moodle website. A textbook to complement the course material, where applicable, is Manufacturing Processes for Engineering Materials in SI Units (Edition:6) by Kalpakjian, Serope; Schmid, Steven. ISBN13: 9781292254418, ISBN13s: 978-1-292-25441-8. The link to the electronic textbook can be found on the course Moodle page.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5; Moodle-exam 25 %, seminar work 75 %.

name: Sustainable System Transition
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: 1) Describe and analyze complex sustainability challenges, 2) Interpret and analyze system transition, 3) Assess and apply theoretical concepts related to sustainability transition, 4) Utilizing Backcasting-method as part of multidisciplinary group, 5) Produce a scientific report on the desired sustainability transition and present findings at a seminar.
content: This course provides analytical and conceptual tools to understand and analyze system transitions towards sustainability. The course also provides advise for applying diverse theoretical concepts in research and solution seeking. The central concepts related to the system transitions are discussed in groups and reflected individually in one essay. Group work conducted during the course is presented orally in the seminar and completed in the written report. - Systems thinking - Sustainability transitions - Backcasting methodology
prerequisites: BH60A4402 Sustainability in socio-technical context OR BH60A5600 Kestävyysmuutos ja johtaminen OR BH60A5300 Introduction to Sustainable System Transition must be passed before taking this course.
learningMaterial: Course book: Advanced Introduction to Sustainability Transitions. Other course material will be announced during the lectures in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Evaluation 0 - 5. Group work, seminars 50%, individual assignments 50%.
workload: 8x2h lectures and 5x2h tutorials (26h), seminars (12h), independent work 124 h. Total workload 162. Independent work consists of group project work (50%), including seminar presentations. Individual learning (50%) is assessed on the basis of the response papers and other individual assignments.

name: Sustainable Traffic Systems
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student is expected to be able to 1. comprehend basic vehicle and transportation systems and technologies 2. comprehend aspects that impact on transportation energy consumption 3. comprehend energy production methods for the transportation sector 4. apply methods for assessing energy production for the transportation sector 5. apply methods for reducing energy consumption in the transportation sector 3. apply methods to assess sustainability of transportation systems and transportation energy production
content: Energy production for transportation, vehicle and transportation systems and technologies, possibilities to reduce energy consumption in the transportation sector, sustainability perspectives of transportation systems and transportation energy consumption. Sustainable transport fuels including Power-to-X routes.
learningMaterial: Course materials will be delivered via Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Examination 50 %, assignment(s) 50 %.
workload: 20 h of lectures and exercises, 3rd - 4th period. Independent work (approx. 114 h):Assignment, approx. 80 h, Examination and preparation for the examination, approx.56 h. Total workload 156 h.

name: Sustainable Water Use
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, the student is expected to be able to define the key concepts of water pollution control apply risk analysis methods related to water issues implement different methods for water footprint calculation recognize the main factors affecting water footprint and sustainability of water use explain the operation of essential process technology and equipment related to the control of water pollution compare and give grounded proposals for water treatment methods and processes applicable to different situations recognize means to protect groundwater and reduce an environmental load of surface waters understand methods for the environmentally friendly management of side-product flows from water treatment analyze the sustainability of water management systems
content: Sustainability challenges of water use. Water footprint. Water risk assessment. Water supply, water use in different sectors and loading of water systems. Wastewater treatment in industry and municipalities. Sludge treatment. Production of drinking water. Protection of groundwater deposits. Legislation on water quality and sludge treatment. Economic efficiency of different water treatment methods.
prerequisites: BH60A0001 Ympäristötekniikan perusteet (Basics in Environmental Engineering) or equivalent knowledge. Recommended: BJ01A1010 General Chemistry or equivalent knowledge
learningMaterial: Handouts provided by the lecturer, course environment on Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Examination and Moodle quizzes 50%, assignment 50%
workload: 1st - 2nd period: 14 h of lectures. 1st - 2nd period: tutorials and independent exercises 20 h. 1st - 2nd period: Assignment approx. 64 h. 1st - 2nd period: Moodle quizzes and examination including preparation for them approx. 64 h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Sustainable Welding Production
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to guide the student to develop, manage, control and ensure the quality and sustainability in welding production. After having completed and passed this course, the student: understands the meaning of sustainability and quality in welding production, knows how to implement quality assurance systems, knows quality levels and classifications in welding, is familiar with the concept of Welding Procedure Specification (WPS), its development, approval, and implementation, understands welding imperfections and various testing procedures (destructive and non-destructive) of weld joints, knows the basic concepts of weldability tests, understands economics, costs, and productivity of welding production, is familiar with most important welding standards, understands welding networks and supply chains, is familiar with welding safety and health hazards.
content: The course comprises lectures, of which topics are: Concept of sustainability and quality Welding coordination and standards Welding procedure specification (WPS) and welding procedure test Welding defects and imperfections as well as weld classification system and levels Testing methods in welding production Weldability tests Economics, costs, and productivity Welding networks and supply chains Welding safety The course contains laboratory exercises, and some practical case studies based on industrial tasks of a welding engineer, such as: Designing the Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) and performing the welding procedure test according to standards. Identifying welding defects and imperfections from real weldments. Interpreting results of destructive and non-destructive welding tests. Cost calculations of welding operations. Evaluating the safety risks of welding production and workplaces.
prerequisites: Basic understanding and knowledge of welding and welding processes.
learningMaterial: Lectures in Moodle. Welding: Principles and Applications, L. Jeffus, Cengage. The Welding Workplace, R. Boekholt, Woodhead Publishing. Standards related to welding quality and production.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exam 50 %, laboratory exercise tasks and WPS report 50 %.
workload: The course is arranged in the form of lectures and practical exercises carried out in laboratory works. Lectures 28 h. Laboratory exercises and tasks including manual welding in practice, macrographic inspections as well as destructive and non-destructive tests 20 h. Preparation of WPS and execution of welding procedure test including independent study and report writing 72 h. Preparation for exam 10 h. Total workload 130 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: System Engineering Project Work
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student is prepared to work in a R&D team as a system engineer. The student is able to manage the project scheduling and project roles, and share responsibilities among group members. The student can produce a technical documentation.
content: The students will analyze and design a selected electrical energy conversion system in the field of industrial electrical drives, renewable energy conversion or a motion control system. The topics are linked to an on-going research or industrial co-operation in the above-mentioned fields. The project work includes several partly alternative system engineering tasks, such as project planning, preliminary system design, dynamic modelling and simulation, component dimensioning, electrical dimensioning, control design, automation design, control software design and project documentation. The tasks are project dependent and will be defined in the project plan. Introduction to a system engineering approach in technical projects. Project documentation, different tasks in project work, project planning and implementation, example projects, execution of system engineering tasks, project documentation and presentation. The main result of the project work is technical project documentation including an overall description and the results of agreed system engineering tasks.
prerequisites: A majority of the M.Sc. (El. Eng.) studies should be completed before participation.
learningMaterial: One lecture and project related material.Jürg Kuster, Eugen Huber, Robert Lippmann, Alphons Schmid, Emil Schneider, Urs Witschi,Roger Wüst. Project Management Handbook, ISBN 978-3-662-45373-5.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Project work that includes management of the project, system design, problem solving, designs, documentation and presentation.Also the project phases from setting the goals to the design, implementation and utilization are graded.
workload: Introductory lecture, independent group working (3-5 students in one group), subgroup or individual tasks within the group work, 3-5 project group meetings with supervisors, writing project documentation, project presentation and demonstration. The project work topics will be defined in detail at the beginning of the course. Total workload 162 h.

name: Electricity Market
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. describe the characteristics of the different business sectors in the Nordic electricity market, 2. explain electricity price formation and model electricity consumption, 3. explain the operation principle of the power exchange, 4. identify and describe the products of the power exchange, 5. select the right risk management method for electricity trade, 6. describe the tasks of the different parties in an electric power system in maintaining technical and commercial power balance, 7. conduct the balance settlement, 8. price the products of electricity trade and distribution, 9. describe why and how electricity distribution business is regulated.
content: The development of electricity markets, loads on the electricity network and load forecasts, power exchange, electricity trade, balance management, the fundamentals of pricing, electricity distribution business and related regulation methodology.
learningMaterial: Lecture book, ppt-presentations and lecture video. All available in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, Moodle examination 100 %.
workload: 28 h of lectures, 14 h of tutorials, 1st period. Independent studies. Written examination. The lectures focus on the core learning objectives in the topic. Successful completion of the course requires student’s active independent work. The course is also suitable for distance learning.Total workload 130 h.

name: Protection of Electricity Networks
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. explain the properties of the protection relays and the general criteria for the design of the relay protection of the electricity network, 2. design the relay protection schemes for the short circuit and earth fault protection of the electricity distribution network and for the distance relay protection of the electricity transmission network, 3. recognise the impacts of the distributed generation to the relay protection of the electricity distribution network, and to consider these impacts in the planning of the protection schemes, 4. name the most common differences in the principles of the relay protection of different types of electricity networks, 5. recognise the most important properties of current and voltage transformers and circuit breakers from the relay protection perspective, and perform basic dimensioning of these components.
content: Basic principles of the fault protection of electric power networks. Different protection relays, overcurrent relays, distance relays, differential relays, arc protection, over voltage protection. Insulation co-ordination. Protection of network lines, cables and transformers. Planning of the relay protection.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have completed BL20A0700 Sähköverkkotekniikan peruskurssi, and participation in courses BL20A0500 Sähkönjakelutekniikka and BL20A0600 Sähkönsiirtotekniikka.
learningMaterial: Elovaara, Haarla: Sähköverkot II (Otatieto), Mörsky: Relesuojaustekniikka (Otatieto, moniste 540) material handed out in class. Aro, Martti et al.: Suurjännitetekniikka. Otatieto Oy, 2003.
workload: Lectures 21 h, calculation exercises 14 h, 4th period. Active teaching (lectures and exercises) every second year (odd years). Passive teaching = independent studying (slides and videos in Moodle) is every second year (even years). Examination. The lectures focus on the core learning objectives in the topic. Successful completion of the course requires student’s active independent work.Total workload 135 h.

name: Radiation Protection
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will have knowledge and understanding of the use and effects of ionizing radiation, the fundamental principles of radiation protection and the radiation legislation and regulations in Finland. The students will be able to identify, evaluate and minimize risks involved in the use of radiation, adopt safe working procedures and apply safety regulations in practice. Poossible to get a radiation safety officer's certificate. Completing the course supports the development of the following general working life skills: mathematics and natural sciences, independent work, problem solving, schedule management and prioritization of tasks.
content: Lectures on radiation protection and safety. Basics of radiation physics, biological effects of radiation, dosimetry, radiation detection and measurements, sealed and unsealed sources, x-ray appliances, industrial radiography, radiation protection in nuclear power plants, radiation safety of workers, legistlation. Basics of pollution calculations. Possibility to get radiation safety officer's certificate.
prerequisites: BH30A0001 Introduction to Nuclear Energy.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes. Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority, Finland: Säteily- and ydinturvallisuus, where applicable, as well as the valid legislation and the related radiation safety regulations.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Examination 100 %. Possible to raise the grade by tutorials.
workload: Lectures 28 h, tutorials 14 h, laboratory work 8 h, assignment 17 h, preparation for the examination 11 h and written examination 3 h. Total workload 108 h.

name: Work experience in Bachelor's degree in Finland
learningOutcomes: After the work internship, the student will be able to define and explain what is involved in working for an employer and what the basic rules of the world of work are from the employee's perspective, and further, how to act in a working community. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Developing own skills in working life, career management aspects.
content: The student obtains a (summer) job in a company, works there as an employee, requests for a certificate of employment and applies for the approval of the work experience for the Bachelor's degree. A full-time employment relationship of at least four weeks can be approved as work experience. The completion of the Bachelor's thesis is not accepted as work experience. An employment relationship preceding the studies can be approved, provided that it has not been accepted and included in any other previous degree.
learningMaterial: Instructions and application and report forms in eLUT portal: https://elut.lut.fi/en/completing-studies/work-internships
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Report 100 %.
workload: Practical work experience of min. of 4 weeks. Written report including a description of working environment, tasks of the student and their contribution to the goals and operation of the company. First 2 ECTS credits: applying for a job and recruiting 10 h, tasks connected to starting an employment relationship 15 h, observing (while working) how the working community operates 24 h, a written report 5 h (2-3 papers), total 54 h. Next 1-4 ECTS credits: having different tasks in a company 27-108 h. (1 ECTS credit/27 h). Total workload 54-162 h. Work experience can be added to the free elective studies of the Bachelor's degree.

name: Work experience in Bachelor's degree in Finland
learningOutcomes: After the work internship, the student will be able to define and explain what is involved in working for an employer and what the basic rules of the world of work are from the employee's perspective, and further, how to act in a working community. The completion of the study module supports the development of the following general working life skills: working independently, developing own skills in working life, career management aspects.
content: Applying for a job and recruiting, tasks connected to starting an employment relationship (e.g. orientation, the rules of the employment relationship and the work place), observing (while working) how the working community operates (e.g. how work/production is organised, supervision, the working manners of the working community/teams, the social environment of the work place), practical training in a company.
learningMaterial: Instructions, as well as forms for work internship application and report available in LUTE portal.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Internship report 100 %.
workload: Practical work experience of min. of 4 weeks. Written report including a description of working environment, tasks of the student and their contribution to the goals and operation of the company. First 2 ECTS credits: applying for a job and recruiting 10 h, tasks connected to starting an employment relationship 15 h, observing (while working) how the working community operates 24 h, a written report 5 h (2-3 papers), total 54 h. Next 1-4 ECTS credits: having different tasks in a company 27-108 h. (1 ECTS credit/27 h). Total workload 54-162 h. Work experience can be added to the free elective studies of the Bachelor's degree.

name: Work Experience in Bachelor's Degree in Finland
learningOutcomes: After having collected work experience in mechanical engineering, the student will be able to define and explain what mechanical engineering paid work is, what is involved in working for an employer and what the basic rules of the world of work are from the employee's perspective, and further, how to act in a working community.
content: The student obtains a (summer) job from mechanical engineering company, works as an employee, requests a certificate of employment and applies for the approval of work experience for the Bachelor's degree. A full-time employment relationship of at least four weeks can be approved as work experience. The number of admitted credits 0-10 cr depends on the content of the work and the length of the employment relationship. The completion of the Bachelor's thesis is not accepted as work experience. The content of the work should be in tight connection with mechanical engineering and the work experience should be collected during the Bachelor’s degree studies.
learningMaterial: Guidelines available in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail, internship report 100 %.
workload: Applying for a job and recruiting 10 h, tasks connected to beginning of an employment relationship (e.g. orientation, the rules of the employment relationship and the workplace) 15 h, observing (while working) how the working community operates (e.g. how work/production is organized, supervision, the working manners of the working community/teams, the social environment of the workplace) 22 h, a written report about work experience 5 h (2 - 3 pages). It is recommended to collect the work experience in mechanical engineering summer job between the second and the third year of study. The content of the work experience should support the studies of mechanical engineering. The maximum number of credits is 10 ECTS credits (1 ECTS cr = 27 h). The credits should be included to the elective studies of the degree

name: Work experience in Bachelor's degree in Finland
learningOutcomes: After the work internship, the student will be able to define and explain what is involved in working for an employer and what the basic rules of the world of work are from the employee's perspective, and further, how to act in a working community.
content: Applying for a job and recruiting, tasks connected to starting an employment relationship (e.g. orientation, the rules of the employment relationship and the work place), observing (while working) how the working community operates (e.g. how work/production is organised, supervision, the working manners of the working community/teams, the social environment of the work place), practical working in a company.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail, report 100%.
