name: Machine Dynamics
learningOutcomes: The student will learn theories and practices of structural dynamics and knows how to apply the knowledge in the design of machine systems. He/she is able to model dynamic machine systems, solve the equations of motion in frequency and time domains and analyze the results from simulations and measurements. The student knows the basics of vibrations measurements and experimental modal analysis. The student is able to review and interpret his/her student mate's simulation results resembling the tasks in the later career. Some of the practical examples and assignments are real-life cases arising from co-operation with industrial companies.
content: Multiple degree-of-freedom vibrations, solution and interpretation of natural frequencies and modes. Response to the harmonic and general force excitation. Derivation of the equations of motion of the system and solution in the frequency and time domain. Vibration measurements and experimental modal analysis. Introduction to rotor dynamics. Torsional vibrations.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have basic skills on Dynamics. Experience or basic studies of Finite Element Method (FEM) is also recommend, but not required.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, online examination or online mid-term examinations 50 %, homework and laboratory exercises 50 %.
workload: Lectures 28 h, periods 1-2. Online tutorials 24 h, periods 1-2. Laboratory work or analysis of measurement results 4 h, homework 79 h, periods 1-2. Total workload 135 h. Lectures, tutorials and lab sessions are possible to follow online.The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Master's Thesis
learningOutcomes: This course aims at developing problem-solving and project management skills including: research problem formulation, independent research and learning, problem specification and solution and reporting the results of the project. After successfully completing this course you should be able to: 1. Identify and formulate relevant thesis, problem or research question. 2. Define the goals and scope of the research problem and systematically outline a plan for solving the problem. 3. Apply appropriate resources associated with a particular problem. 4. Gain in-depth understanding of the relevant research or engineering problem by using literature and other resources. 5. Analyze, specify, design, and implement a solution to the selected problem including all aspects of the project like risk and time management. 6. Report the outcomes of the project by means of written presentation in a scholarly style with appropriate referencing.
content: A research-based thesis course that offers students the opportunity to work on a comprehensive, individual project that demonstrates mastery of the specializations of software engineering or digital transformation. Topic to be agreed in consultation with a supervisor. The project will be of suitable complexity for results to be published for an expert audience. Students are expected to complete thesis in a single semester, but exceptions are accommodated only after seeking academic advice. The purpose of this course is to develop the student's research and problem-solving skills. The course involves the specification, development and evaluation of an individual research project on a specific topic or problem within the broad fields of software engineering. The student is expected to systematically plan and manage the project, and to clearly present the work and its contribution in context of the current literature and prior state of the art. Beginning with the thesis assignment will not be permitted until a project is allocated and the supervisor has agreed that the project is suitable. An independent thesis done in the field of information technology, according to the instructions given. In the beginning a student must contact the responsible professor. The starting and finishing point of the thesis vary. Before the thesis is returned for grading it must be checked with the Turnitin programme in the moodle page of the course. Topic of the master's thesis has to be confirmed as soon as the topic has been decided with the supervisor. Use form 1A in UNI-portal.
prerequisites: Completed Bachelor's thesis or degree and 30 ECTS cr of the MSc program including courses CT10A9512 Research Design and Methods or CT10A9511 Research Methods in Software Engineering.
learningMaterial: There are no set textbooks for this course. Students will be advised on appropriate learning resources by their supervisors but there is also an expectation that students will seek out information for themselves in the spirit of independent learning and research.• The course Moodle site provides access to required and recommended resources, instruction videos regarding the work process, and information regarding relevant events for the thesis workers. Example works and expert databased are available via LUT Library services• Anytime registration, no separate scheduled teaching events, material handouts and upcoming events accessed from the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5 Grade 100%Definition of research problem and objectives and delimitations 0-5 The relationship to previous research 0-5Research approach, methods, and material 0-5Systematic and responsible execution of project 0-5Coherence and reliability of the interpretation of results and the conclusions 0-5Utility of the results 0-5Readability, language, and layout of the report 0-5
workload: It is the student's responsibility to contact the reponsible professor for this course before finding an appropriate topic and supervisor. Students with their own ideas for a project should consult a potential supervisor in a similar subject area. Should a student wish to involve an external supervisor (from a company or other school) who may even take on the primary role of driving and directing the project, they must also find an main supervisor from the SWE domain who will ensure that the academic goals of the project are not overlooked, and that project administration is handled in accordance with LUT policy.Master’s Thesis, total 780 h.

name: Materials Science and Engineering B
learningOutcomes: To understand the behaviour of materials: electrical properties.
content: Lattice vibrations and phonons, electrons in crystal, Fermi energy, energy bands, basics of semiconductors, basics of magnetic properties, basics of superconductors and nanotubes.
prerequisites: BM30A0910 Materiaalifysiikka A
learningMaterial: Lecture handouts
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 100 %.
workload: Lectures 18 h, exercises 8 h, preparing for exercises 16 h, preparing for the exam 36 h, 4th period. Total 78 h. Examination.

name: Mathworks Self-Study Courses
learningOutcomes: The course deepens students' understanding of the specialized topics in matlab through a set of online courses. There are three possible modules for student to do. Module ‘Financial applications': By the end of the module student will be able to become familiar with the main features of matlab integrated design environment and its user interfaces. Work with vectors and matrices. Automating command with scripts. Handle dates and times in data set. Perform conditional data selections. Work with missing data. Writing functions. Fitting models to empirical data. Module ‘Data processing and visualization' By the end of the module student will be able to import tabular data. Preprocess data. Handle graphics formatting Functions. Import data from multiple files. Analyze group within data. Import unstructured data. Module ‘Matlab programming techniques' By the end of the module student will be able to use development tools in Matlab to assist in understanding, debugging and optimizing code. Creating a test framework to determine if the application is behaving as expected. Writing functions that can handle flexible user input values and display relevant error messages when appropriate. Reviewing of selection of Matlab data types. Organizing data in Matlab through the use of various data types. Modifying the structure of code files. Writing better and more efficient code. Sharing applications using toolboxes.
content: Module ‘Financial applications' Working with the matlab user interface, perform mathematical calculations on imported vector data, and create basic visualizations. Extract a subset of vector data, perform statistical calculations and customize plots. Perform various mathematical operations on matrices. Query and combine multiple matrices. Import date and time data interactively. Creation and modification of variables representing dates and times. Computations on date and time data. Custom plots using date and time durations. Extract and analyze subsets of data that satisfy given criteria. Typical data pre-processing and analysis tasks in matlab, including locating missing values and working with them. Linear regression, employing distribution fitting to determine quality of the model and creation of monte carlo simulations from the model. Module ‘Data processing and visualization' Module consists of importing column oriented data files that contain a mixture of data types. Handling missing value and categorical data. Creating sophisticated visualizations using matlab graphics objects. Reading large data stored in multiple files. Identifying groups within data and analyzing them. Plotting irregularly spaced data. Importing blocks of data into matlab. Module ‘Matlab programming techniques' Utilize development tools. Verifying Application Behavior. Creating robust applications. Review of data types. Structuring data. Structuring code. Performance and memory. Creating a toolbox.
learningMaterial: Matlab documentation files. The material of the specialization topic depends on the selected module.
evaluationCriteria: Passed/Failed, discussions with the supervisor. A set of accepted matlab online courses 100%.
workload: Personal study of the selected specialization topic(s). Course can be done at any point of studies and execution is based on the discussions with the person responsible of the course. Total workload is agreed before execution and can be 26-78 h.

name: Engineering Mechanics I
learningOutcomes: Students who successfully complete the course will demonstrate the following outcomes: - An ability to make difference between a particle and a rigid body - An ability to construct free-body diagrams and to calculate the reactions necessary to ensure static equilibrium in 2D. - A knowledge of internal forces and moments in members - An ability to calculate kinematics and kinetics for particles - An ability to use Newton's second law and energy and momentum methods for particles - An ability to calculate kinematics and kinetics for rigid bodies - An ability to use Newton's second law and energy and momentum methods for rigid bodies - A knowledge of basics of vibrations (1 DOF)
content: Equivalent Systems of Forces, Moment of a Static Force and a Force Couple, Equilibrium of Particles and Rigid Bodies in 2-D, Kinematics of Particles, Force and Acceleration, Work and Energy, Impulse and Momentum Methods for Particles and Rigid Bodies. Impact Loadings. Frictionless Eccentric Impact. One Degree of Freedom Harmonic Vibration, Platform Stimulus, Rotating Unbalance. In general: 2D statics and dynamics.
learningMaterial: Lecture material. Source materials include: Hibbeler R.C, Engineering Mechanics, Statics. (Whichever edition.) Hibbeler R.C., Engineering Mechanics, Dynamics, 9th ed. Chapters 12-15 and 16-19.
evaluationCriteria: Weekly exercises 20 %, Individual exercises 30 %, Examination 50 %. Paper exam. Grade scale 0-5.
workload: Lectures 42 h. Weekly guided exercises 28 h. Finalizing weekly exercises 28 h. Individual exercises 50 h. Preparation for exam and examination 14 h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Engineering Mechanics II
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: -fluently express forces and moments in vector form and perform statics calculations using vectors -construct free-body diagrams and to calculate the support reactions necessary to ensure static equilibrium in 3D -analyze friction forces and equilibrium states of mechanisms -interpret internal force and moment distributions in beam structures -summarize the basics of the strength of materials -evaluate the strength of simple parts, structures and pressure vessels
content: Equilibrium in 3D, Moments of forces in vector form, Space trusses, Internal loadings in 3D structures. Friction. Virtual work. Definition of normal and shear stress. Mechanical properties of materials. Axial, torsional and bending stress. Simple shear vs transverse shear. State of stress resulting from combined loadings. Stress hypotheses.
prerequisites: BK80A4000 Engineering Mechanics I or BK80A5800 Engineering Mechanics 1 recommended.
learningMaterial: Lecture material. Source books include: Hibbeler R.C, Engineering Mechanics, Statics. (Whichever edition.) Hibbeler, R.C., Mechanics of Materials. Ugural A.C. and Fenster S.K., Advanced Strength and Applied Elasticity, 4th ed. Ugural A.C. Mechanics of Materials. Hibbeler, Structural Analysis.
evaluationCriteria: Weekly exercises 20 %, Individual exercises 30 %, Examination 50 %. Paper exam. Grade scale 0-5.
workload: Lectures 42 h. Weekly guided exercises 28 h. Finalizing weekly exercises 28 h. Individual exercises 50 h. Preparation for exam and examination 14 h. Total workload 162 h.

name: Engineering Mechanics III
learningOutcomes: After the course, the students should possess the needed skills to: -Dimension different beam-, column- and frame structures according to elasticity theory both in serviceability limit and ultimate limit states -Dimension axles subjected to both torsion and bending according to elasticity theory -Examine the fatigue limit and fatigue life of a structure using simple tools -Define strength parameters for hybrid structures -Understand the differences of plane stress and plane strain states and perform strength analysis using both state assumptions -Define the principal stresses of the structure also in 3D-state -Apply different stress hypotheses
content: Standard profiles for beams, dimensioning of a beam, beam deflection, curved beams, hybrid beams. Dimensioning of a column, Euler buckling. Dimensioning of an axle. Fatigue limit and fatigue life Haigh-Goodman-diagram, S-N-curve. Ortotropic material. Plane stress and plane strain. Principal stresses in 3D state. Stress hypotheses. Thick-walled pipes and pressure vessels.
prerequisites: BK80A4000 Engineering Mechanics I and BK80A4010 Engineering Mechanics II studied. (Not necessarily passed yet, but participated on these courses.)
learningMaterial: Lecture material in Moodle. Source book authors include but not limited to: R.C. Hibbeler, Pennala, Ylinen, Ugural.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Weekly exercises 20 %, individual exercises 30 %, examination 50 %.

name: Cyber Security of Software Systems
learningOutcomes: The objective of the course is to introduce the fundamental aspects of the cyber security and cyber security thinking to the student, especially from the viewpoint of software engineering and the entire software organization. After the course, the student identifies and understands how the cyber security is related to the software development, what are the most common security threats from the viewpoint of software, and how they are usually managed.
content: Fundamental concepts of cyber security. Threats and vulnerabilities. The common attack and prevention techniques. The fundamentals aspects and objectives of cyber security-related activities. The effect of security policies. Cyber security from the viewpoint of software engineering.
prerequisites: CT60A0202 Ohjelmoinnin ja data-analytiikan perusteet, CT60A4002 Ohjelmistotuotanto, Computer networks and Internet (or equivalent knowledge) Basic information how web-protocols work.
learningMaterial: Schneier, B.: Secrets and Lies, Wiley, 2000.Mead, N. R., ; Woody, C.. Cyber Security Engineering: A Practical Approach for Systems and Software Assurance. Addison-Wesley Professional, 2016. Other materials provided by the lectures.
evaluationCriteria: Pass / fail
workload: Independent study, project assignments and learning diary 108h.

name: Organizational Learning
learningOutcomes: The goal of the course is to give extensive general knowledge about organizational learning as a theoretical phenomenon and utilization of it in development and management of organizations. By the end of the course, students will be able to: - Familiarize themselves with the state of the art literature on organizational learning - Understand basic concepts and theories of organizational learning - Understand enablers, functioning principles and management of organizational learning. - Apply Problem Based Learning (PBL) approach in organizational problems - Analytically evaluate organizations from the perspective of organizational learning - Apply organizational learning theories and methods to future work, learning situations, and management.
content: The course is self-learning course grounded by Problem Based Learning (PBL) and will be conducted via Moodle learning space. The course consists of the following parts: 1) Individual learning phase (iStudy): Independent literature study by utilizing PBL. Individual learning phase comprises intensive reading and writing based on the provided course materials (scientific articles), 2) Social learning phase: Participation in a group work assignment that comprises of utilization of PBL method in case analysis, applying relevant organizational learning theories to case analysis, and writing group work report.
prerequisites: No
learningMaterial: Assigned reading and collection of scientific articles
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5, evaluation 0-100 points, individual study 50% and group work 50%.
workload: Individual learning phase (50%): virtual introduction (8 hours), Independent self-managed reading assigned articles and writing a study report (80 hours), Social learning phase (50%): Group work, introduction to PBL and PBL case analysis, written group work report, (80 hours). Total workload for the student 160 hours.

name: Organizing in Knowledge-Based Networks
learningOutcomes: - Students can describe the key theoretical concepts and theories on knowledge-based organizing and apply them in practical cases - Students can apply the theory and key skills related to working a digital platform to solve real-life complex problems - Students can reflect their individual and team behavior - Students can present effectively their project outcomes to customer - Students can discuss their solution constructively, give & get feedback and document the lessons learned by the project team
content: - Key concepts related to organizing knowledge - New forms of organizing: Ecosystems, digital platforms, collaborative communities and temporary groups The course is related to entrepreneurship and sustainability.
learningMaterial: Articles distributed by lecturers, online-material
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0 – 5. Individual exercises 30 % and group exercises 70 %.
workload: Lectures and interactive seminars 24 h, 1-3. periodsIndependent studying online 72 hCourse assignment work (real-life sustainability related problem solving in temporary teams on a digital collaboration platform) 64 hTotal workload for student 160 h

name: Principles of Industrial Manufacturing Processes
learningOutcomes: Students should be able to identify the principles of machining products, sheet metal production, additive manufacturing, common welding processes, and packaging processes after completing this course module. In this course, students learn to describe the characteristics that describe the manufacturability of various materials and measures of quality, as well as aspects of efficient use of natural resources, sustainable production, and manufacturing. Students will also be able to seek out scientific information, evaluate it critically, and use it in their own writing in addition to writing technical and scientific reports.
content: The course examines on the most common industrial processes in manufacturing technology and ways to improve the sustainability of products through manufacturing. In addition, aspects of production management are considered. The course includes reverse engineering task for a group work.
learningMaterial: Course material is available in the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, exam 40 %, seminar 60 %, final presentation and working as an opponent. Participation in seminar.
workload: Period 1: Lectures 28 h, Grouping and initiation of group work 4 h, Self-study 32h. Period 2: Seminar lecture 4 h, Group seminar work and working as an opponent 63 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Principles of Technical Computing for BSc students
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course students: - get a good understanding of Matlab syntax and programming, - gain fluency in principles of technical computing, converting tasks into basic algorithms - are able to apply the skills to basic mathematical and engineering problems (the skills are applicable in big part to Octave and R programming, too).
content: Working with various data structures (multidimensional arrays, cell arrays, etc.) and variable types (numeric, logical, textual, etc.), Matlab symbolic functionality, conditional statements (if-else, switch-case), loops (for and while), using built-in functions, handling external data, 2-D and 3-D plotting, writing user-defined functions.
prerequisites: Basic university calculus required. Recommended first year university calculus necessarily including matrix calculus.
learningMaterial: Lecture material available in Moodle (slides and videos), based partly on textbook: Gilat, A.: An Introduction to Matlab with Applications.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, EXAM-examination 100 % or Continuous evaluation: 40% weekly assignments, 60% Moodle-exams
workload: Lectures 12 h, computer class exercises 24 h, independent study 38 h, preparation for exams 34 h, 1st period. Total 108 h.

name: Project on Product and Process Design
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the module, the student will be able to: Apply chemical engineering knowledge to realizable product and process design. Perform technical and economical design calculations. Solve real design problem starting sometimes from limited and incomplete initial information. Seek and create novel solutions to design problems.
content: The projects are carried out in groups of five students. The topics are mainly from industry and the design work is done under supervision of industrial partners. The main focus is on energy transition related processes, i.e. carbon capture and utilization, hydrogen economy, and Power-to-X processes, but topics from chemical industry in general, waste treatment and processing, bioprocesses, metal processing, and circular economy, are also possible. A typical topic starts with product analysis covering a brief market survey, comparison of process alternatives, preliminary process design (process flow diagram, mass and energy balances, sizing of main equipment, lay-out, cost and profitability estimation). Different aspects are emphasized in different projects, depending on the topic.
prerequisites: BJ01A5020 Prosessi- ja tehdassuunnittelu (process ; plant design) or equivalent passed.BJ02A2041 Advanced Process Design or equivalent passed.
learningMaterial: Course Materials in Moodle. Additional materials. Tuunila, R., BJ01A5020 Process&Plant Design (In Finnish), course material, 2015. Branan, C., Rules of Thumb for Chemical Engineers, 3rd ed., Elsevier, USA, 2002. Walas, S.M., Chemical Process Equipment Selection and Design, 3rd ed., Elsevier, USA, 2012. http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/book/9780123969590 Towler, G., Sinnott, Principles, Practice and Economics of Plant and Process Design, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2012. Peters, M.S., Timmerhaus, K.D., Plant Design and Economics for Chemical Engineers, 4th ed., McGraw-Hill, Singapore, 1991. Loh, H.P., Process Equipment Cost EstimationFinal Report, US Dept. of Energy, 2002
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, design reports 100%.
workload: Lectures and exercises 18 h, project meetings, 1st and 2nd period. Design and project work 252 h, 1st-2nd period. Total workload 270 h.

name: Project Work 1
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: • apply knowledge gained from course work to practice • use critical thinking and problem-solving skills • collaborate effectively in a multicultural environment • develop creative ideas and solutions • design and implement a product or service • use tools and other resources to develop a prototype • present to a real audience of peers and corporate mentors • give and receive feedback on the effectiveness of project activities
content: The course introduces students to the concept of challenge based learning through a learning-by-doing approach. Students will be engaged in solving a real-world problem or answering a complex question related to one of the core areas of expertise (Electrical engineering, Energy technology, Mechanical engineering, Environmental Technology). In the end, they will demonstrate new knowledge and skills by developing a useful product or service and presenting it to a real audience. Students will receive some background instruction on the nature of challenge based learning, and then apply this knowledge to the project work. First steps will involve defining the question, problem or challenge that will serve as the basis of the project work. This will be followed by the design and construction of a prototype product or service. Throughout the project work, students will give, receive and use feedback to further improve their process and prototypes. After refinement, the prototype will be explained, displayed and presented to peers and possible corporate partners. Students participating in the Lahti Venture Program or Lahti Summer School course in Co-design Better Urban Living and Well-being – Planetary Health can submit their certificates as equivalent to this course.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes to be provided during the course on Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Progress presentation (10%), Project plan (25%), Presentation/Poster (20%), Demonstration/Video (10%), Self-assessment report (10%), Final report (25%). Students who submit certificates for the Lahti Venture Program or Lahti Summer School will be graded on a Pass/Fail scale.
workload: Contact teaching sessions 10 h, small group planning meetings 20 h, project design and construction 80 h, preparation of and participation in final presentations 25 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Project Work 2
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: • apply knowledge gained from course work to practice • use time management, critical thinking and problem-solving skills • collaborate effectively in a multicultural environment • develop creative ideas and solutions to real-world problems • design and implement a product or service • incorporate end-user or customer needs into prototype design • use tools and other resources to develop a prototype • present to a real audience of peers and corporate mentors • give and receive feedback on the effectiveness of project activities
content: The course enhances experience in challenge based learning through a learning-by-doing approach. Students will be engaged in solving a specific real-world problem or answering a complex question related to one of the core areas of expertise (Electrical engineering, Energy technology, Mechanical engineering, Environmental Technology). In the end, students will demonstrate new knowledge and skills by developing a useful product or service in cooperation with corporate mentors and presenting it to a real audience. Students will receive extended instruction on the nature of challenge based learning, and then apply this knowledge to the project work. First steps will involve defining the question, problem or challenge that will serve as the basis of the project work. This will be followed by the design and construction of a prototype product or service. Throughout the project work, students will give, receive and use feedback to further improve their process and prototypes. Corporate mentors will also provide feedback throughout the project. After refinement, the prototype will be explained, displayed and presented to peers and possible corporate partners.
prerequisites: LES10A060 Project Work 1
learningMaterial: Lecture notes to be provided during the course on Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Progress presentations (15%), Project plan (20%), Presentation/Poster (20%), Demonstration/Video (10%), Self-assessment report (10%), Final report (25%)
workload: Contact teaching sessions 22 h, small group planning meetings 30 h, project design, construction and refinement 80-188 h, preparation of and participation in final presentations 30 h. Total workload 162-270 h.

name: German 1 for exchange - los geht's!
learningOutcomes: Student - understand slow and clear speech related to the topics of the course - can communicate orally and in writing in simple and routine every day and student situations - can identify some of the specific features of the target culture - can master some of the most common basic structures - creates a basis on which to build learning, both in guided and in everyday situations in the exchange destination
prerequisites: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching
learningMaterial: Details available in Completion methods under the header Teaching

name: Service design
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the students (1) will be able to explain the differences and commonalities of services and products; (2) will be able to critically reflect on common theories of product- and service dominant logic; (3) will be able to demonstrate the concepts of digital services and software related services; (4) will be able to identify and classify value in interaction and value in use of services; (5) will be able to interpret and outline the different facets of design; (6) will be able to apply concepts, theories and methods of service design and design valuable services.
content: The aim of Service Design is to show the broad spectrum of services and their relevance, especially in the field of software engineering. Basic theoretical definitions, as well as comparisons with the product-dominant logic, are discussed and current perspectives such as the service-dominant logic and servicification are elaborated. The value, which can be generated by a service, i.e., the value in use and value in interaction is covered when talking about why services take such a significant role in our economy. Based on this, digital services, and aspects such as software-as-a-service will be discussed. To successfully design services, the topic of design and its various facets will then be covered. Above all, human-centeredness is an essential point, which is then concretized with methods of service design and practical exercises.
prerequisites: The course has no specific prerequisites
learningMaterial: Gummerus, J., Mickelsson, J., Trischler, J., Härkönen, T., & Grönroos, C. (2021). ActS–Service design based on human activity sets. Journal of Service Management. Vink, J., Koskela-Huotari, K., Tronvoll, B., Edvardsson, B., & Wetter-Edman, K. (2021). Service ecosystem design: Propositions, process model, and future research agenda. Journal of Service Research, 24(2), 168-186. Stickdorn, M., Schneider, J., Andrews, K., & Lawrence, A. (2011). This is service design thinking: Basics, tools, cases (Vol. 1). Hoboken: Wiley. Clatworthy, S. (2017) Service design thinking. In Marika Lüders, Tor W. Andreassen, Simon Clatworthy, and Tore Hillestad (Eds). Innovating for Trust. Cheltenham: Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. pp. 167-182.
evaluationCriteria: Grade 0-5. To pass the course, a student needs to receive at least 50 % from the maximum points of mandatory assignments. To achieve the highest grade, 90 % of the maximum points is needed. The grading is linear between these ends.
workload: Lectures 24h, exercise classes 24h, independent reading, research and assignments 40h, project work 48h, preparing for oral exam and learning portfolio 26h. Total 162 h.

name: Digital Signal Processing I
learningOutcomes: The course acquaints the student with fundamentals of digital signal processing. Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. analyse discrete-time systems in time, z- and frequency domain, 2. design simple digital filters by using pole-zero placement and apply the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) to signal analysis and explain how it is related to other transform methods.
content: Principle of sampling. Discrete-time signals and systems. z-transform and its application to the analysis of linear time-variant systems. Frequency analysis of signals and systems. Discrete Fourier transform (DFT).
prerequisites: Basics of complex arithmetic, basics of series calculation, theory of continuous-time signals.
learningMaterial: Kosonen, A.: Signaalien digitaalinen käsittely (lecture notes). Lecture slides and exercises.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5 (0-100 p.). Two mid-term examinations (max. 30 p./exam.), assignment (max. 40 p.). In addition, accepted home works, from which is possible to get additional points (max. 5 p.).
workload: 14 h of lectures,14 h of tutorials and 7 h of homeworks, 1st period. 14 h of lectures, 14 h of tutorials and 7 h of home works, 20h of assignment, 2nd period. Two mid-term examinations in Moodle. Independent study 14 h.Total workload 104 h. Applicable for distance students.

name: Simulation, Laboratory Course
learningOutcomes: The student will learn the advanced theories and practices of the mathematical modelling and computer simulation of machine systems. The student will be able to utilise advanced simulations to solve a practical design assignment. The student will be able to verify and evaluate the accuracy of simulation models. The student will be able to conduct individual scientific work to analyse the dynamics of machine systems.
content: Spatial kinematics, modelling of flexible bodies in multibody applications, modal reduction methods, real-time simulation, embedded systems, contact modelling, multibody dynamics on failure analysis, vehicle modelling, model verifications, practical measurements. The course module supports the following UN Sustainable Development Goals: #9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure.
prerequisites: Recommended: BK70A0001 Simulation of a Mechatronic Machine completed.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes. Shabana, A. A.: Dynamics of Multibody Systems, Cambridge University Press, 3rd edition, 2005. ISBN 0-521-85011-8.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 45 %, simulation work 45 %, in class quizzes 10 %.
workload: Completion method 1. Exam: Lectures 22 h, periods 3-4. Teamwork in a multi-cultural working environment 32 h, periods 3-4. Supervised tutorials 36 h, periods 3-4. Independent study 40 h, periods 3-4. Total workload 130 h.

name: Smart Grids
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to 1. Label the key elements and functionalities of the smart grid system 2. Analyze the impacts of the smart grid elements on electricity distribution system and electricity markets 3. Document and present orally the results of the seminar work 4. Provide both written and oral peer review.
content: Smart grid concept, demand side management, energy storage, distributed generation, microgrids, communications in smart grids. In addition, annually changing topical subjects.
prerequisites: Attending the course BL20A0500 Sähkönjakelutekniikka (Electricity distribution) OR BL20A0401 Electricity Market OR BL20A0400 Sähkömarkkinat (Electricity Market)
learningMaterial: Study materials handed out in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. The course is evaluated based on seminar work (written and oral presentation), Moodle quizzes, and student’s work as a reviewer and an opponent.
workload: Lectures 14 h, Moodle quizzes 7 h, independent seminar work 105 h. Presentation of the seminar work 2 h, peer review of a written seminar work 5 h and working as an opponent in seminar 2 h. Total workload 135 h. NOTE: Not lectured in 2021-22.

name: Solid Waste Management Technology
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student is expected to be able to 1. explain the most important generation mechanisms, properties, and collection and treatment systems of solid waste, 2. explain the operation of essential process technology and equipment, 3. compare and give grounded proposals for treatment methods and processes applicable to different situations, 4. calculate process parameters related to composting, digestion and energy utilization, 5. apply waste management legislation, 6. apply what he/she has learned to the environmental treatment and utilization of waste, and 7. describe the operation of regional waste management.
content: Generation of solid waste and waste management in different parts of the world, properties of waste, legislation concerning waste management, source separation, collection and transport, pretreatment, composting, anaerobic digestion, waste-to-energy, landfilling, regional waste management, treatment of polluted soil.

name: Strategic ownership
learningOutcomes: The courseintroduces the student with the phenomenon of entrepreneurship, ownership, andfamily firm. The course aims to enhance students' understanding of thecharacteristics, contributions, and issues surrounding family business. Throughcase studies, student research and guest speakers, we consider questions ofownership, succession, conflict resolution, sibling rivalry, compensation,attracting and retaining both family and nonfamily talent, estate planning, andfinancing the family owned enterprise. After the course, students should beable to define and understand the conceptual special characteristics and thecentral theories of these phenomena. In addition, students learn to applydifferent theories in the analysis of practical cases as well as aboutways to manage the transitional processes such as family business succession. Itcombines rigorous learning with practical group works. The course willappeal to those who are interested in starting up their own business, as wellas those interacting with small firms and family businesses as advisors,managers and policy-makers.
content: Course explores the unique challenges and opportunities involved in managing a family firm. The course will address a wide variety of topics, including: the strengths and weaknesses of a family firm, the dynamics of family interactions, family business culture, conflict resolution in a family firm, transferring ownership of a family firm, planning for a family firm's growth and continuity, effective leadership and communication, and planning for succession.
learningMaterial: 1.Ernesto J. Poza (2010). Family Business, South-Western, Cengage Learning. 2.Materials indicated during lectures 3.Cases and articles delivered during the course.
evaluationCriteria: Individual exercise 50 %, group exercise 30 % moodle exam 20 %

name: Sustainability in Socio-Technological context
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: 1) Outline the different dimensions of sustainability; ecological, social, economic and cultural, 2) Explain the interaction between the environment, society and business and the relationships, of various actors in these fields and their impacts on the society and the environment , 3) Explain the core idea and thinking behind sustainability and its importance in order to limit or decelerate environmental damages and improve our quality of life while pursuing a more sustainable lifestyle and business within the planetary boundaries, 4) Apply practically the learned principles and concepts of sustainability in relation to current production and consumption habits, 5) Analyze environmental impacts of a product within a selected system, 6) Know and be able to apply different value-adding activities and tools that promote sustainability; and 7) Reflect on sustainability principles and desirably in thinking and lifestyles.
content: The general objective of the course is to provide a comprehensive overview on the concepts of sustainability, sustainable business, and sustainable transition. The course introduces global sustainability challenges that the planet and societies are facing due to human activities and natural causes. Sustainability challenges and their interconnections are learnt and understood in order to realize the need for the sustainability transition.
learningMaterial: Will be announced in Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Individual assignments 30%, group work 40%, examination 30 %.
workload: 1st period: 2*2 h lectures, 2*3 h seminars, independent digitalized studies including individual (approx. 92 h) and group assignments (approx. 61 h). Total workload 162 h.

name: Sustainable System Transition
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: 1) Understand and analyze complex sustainability challenges, 2) Understand and analyze system transition, 3) Assess and apply theoretical concepts, 4) Elaborate transition themes in written assignments, 5) Work on multidisciplinary group 6) Produce a scientific written report and to present findings at a seminar.
content: The course provides analytical tools to to understand and analyze complex sustainability challenges, and apply learned theoretical concepts in solution seeking. The central concepts related to system transitions are discussed in multicultural groups. Solutions for sustainability transition developed during the course are reported and presented orally in the seminar and completed in the written report. Course includes Power-to-X themes: innovative solutions for sustainable transition such as Power-to-X solutions SDGt: 1 No Powerty, 2 Zero Hunger, 3 Good Health and Well-Being, 7 Affordable and Clean Energy, 8 Decent Work and Economic Growth, 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, 10 Reduced Inequalities, 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, 12 Responsible Consumption and Production, 13 Climate Action, 14 Life Below Water, 15 Life on Land, 16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions, 17 Partnerships for the Goals

learningOutcomes: After completing this course, the students will: Understand major processes and institutions of sustainable water use governance Know how power relations, inequality, and security relate to water use governance Understands water infrastructure and governance Understand the role of stakeholder dialogues and public participation in water governance Be able to explain major conceptual frameworks related to water governance

name: System modelling

Economic/ financial/ demographic/ logistic systems are supposed to be used as the application.

These keywords should ring a bell: eigenvalue, complex number, polynomial roots, differentiating and integrating of basic scalar functions, linear time-invariant differential equation (of 1st and 2nd order), autonomous and non-autonomous solution (Duhamel integral), Matlab and Simulink.

name: Electromagnetism
learningOutcomes: After completing the course, the student will be able to: explain Ampère's, Biot-Savart's, Faraday's, Gauss's and Lenz's laws, Poynting's theorem and the Lorentz force using examples and tell why these equations are needed in electrical engineering. explain the material's conductivity, permeability, permittivity effect to the propagation of the electromagnetic wave and the speed of light, explain the force effects of electric and magnetic fields and use them to describe the operating principles of key electromechanical devices, explain in your own words the main generation mechanisms of electromagnetic radiation and the propagation of an electromagnetic wave in a medium, and name the most important antenna types, explain the operation of key electromagnetic devices and basic components (inductance, capacitance, transformer, antenna, transmission line) using the theories of electromagnetism, form analytical equations/calculate using basic equations the field strength and magnetic flux, e.g. in the case of a straight conductor and a simple loop, creates a model describing the transmission line using distributed parameters, identify the reflection phenomenon in the line and make simple calculations to fit the transmission line.
content: electromagnetic waves, plane waves, the force effects of electric and magnetic fields, waveguides, transmission line, applications of Maxwell's equations in electrical engineering, magnetic materials, and magnetic circuits.

name: Electrical Safety
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student possesses the information required of a professional in electrical engineering about the electrical safety regulations, the main standards and procedures related to the electrical safety (e.g. SFS 6000 Series and SFS 6002). Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. understand the physiological effects of electricity on human beings, 2. act in the event of electrical accidents, 3. describe the structure and properties of the electricity distribution systems in buildings and in public distribution, 4. is familiar with the safety regulations and the related standardisation, 5. describe safe electrical working practices, 6. select the electrical equipment based on ambient conditions and perform the dimensioning for the supplying electricity distribution system, 7. describe and choose the protection methods for protection against electric shocks as well as the effects of overcurrent and voltage, 8. perform the dimensioning for the devices used for fault protection, overload and short-circuit protection as well as verify the operation of the protection in a TN system with calculations, 9. list the special characteristics of small-scale generators, power electronic converters and electrical drives pertaining to electrical safety, 10. design the electrical installation in a building and document the plan, 11. describe the contents of commissioning and certification inspections of electrical systems.
content: Electrical safety regulations and standards, safety at electrical work, electrical safety in building and utility grid installations, control of electrical safety and related inspections. The effects of electric current on human beings, electrical accidents, risk reduction, and emergency guidelines. Electrical safety requirements for electrical equipment and installations, and for electrical work. Supervision of electrical works and operations, supervision of electrical installations. Structures and characteristics of electric systems in buildings and public distribution networks. Electrical installation methods, ambient condition classifications and installations in different conditions. Protection methods for buildings and public low-voltage distribution networks. Dimensioning of the equipment, conductors, cables and protection of an electric system. Fundamentals of the design of building grids and electrotechnical documentation of the plans. Requirements for and contents of commissioning, verification and periodic inspections of electric systems. The course focuses on the regulations and relevant standards in electrical engineering in the scope required for the electrical safety examination (2). The course includes generic training on safety at electrical work. Use of AI applications AI applications can be used for understanding concepts and searching for information, taking into account the constraints of the AI in source criticism. Students have to provide the answers in assignment by own produced text. Students are not allowed to present AI-generated text as their own. Company cooperation No company cooperation included.
prerequisites: Recommended: BL10A0101 Basics of Electrical Engineering, BL30A0001 Electric Circuits
learningMaterial: Study materials are based on relevant electrical safety legislation and standards (Contents of SFS handbooks 600-1-1 and 600-1-2, SFS 6002 standard, applicable parts of the SFS 6001 standard). Study material includes lecture slides and recordings.
evaluationCriteria: The course is graded on a scale 0–5. Assignment and Moodle-quizzes are graded on a scale 0–5 and training on safety at electrical work on a scale pass/fail. The assignment’s share of the total grade is 70% and Moodle-quizzes 30%. To pass the course, completion of the assignment, Moodle-quizzes and the training on safety at electrical work, are required.
workload: All teaching is given in Finnish. Period 1: Lectures 22 h and tutorials 6 h at Lappeenranta campus. Period 2: Lectures 14 h and tutorials 14 h at Lappeenranta campus. Moodle-quizzes related to the topic after each lecture. An assignment completed in groups during the periods 1 and 2. The assignment work is guided and partly done during tutorials. Traning SFS 6002 Safety at electrical work and examination. Independent workload of the assignment, Moodle-quizzes, peer-review of the assignments and safety at electrical work training, in total 79 h. Successful completion of the course requires active independent work. Total workload 135 h.

The wholistic nature of IT- and analytics investments and differences between different business models and business architectures and strategic planning regarding these is being understood and the student is able apply these concepts in strategic planning of their home organization.

name: Engineering Thermodynamics
learningOutcomes: After completing the course students are familiar with basic concepts in energy technology, such as temperature, state properties, systems and processes, control volume analysis,different forms of energy and fundamental laws of thermodynamics. Students are able to use different charts and tables to find thermodynamic properties of different substances. After completing the course students can formulate the equation for the conservation of energy for an open control volume. Students are able to calculate heat, work and entropy change in ideal gas compression.Students understand the working principle of a heat engine and importance of Carnot-efficiency as a limit for the theoretical maximum efficiency of any heat engine. Students can apply fundamental laws and equations of thermodynamics for studying different processes (especially related to energy and environmental technology). Students are able to calculate basic heating and air conditioning processes. Students understand working principle of heat pump and refrigeration systems and can calculate operational values of such processes. Students understand working principle of different energy conversion process es and can solve simple internal combustion engine, gas turbine and steam power processes. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: mathematics and natural sciences, practical application of theories, working independently, problem solving, and time management and prioritizing tasks.

Expansion and compression work for isothermal, isentropic and polytropic processes. The second law of thermodynamics, Carnot-process, heat engines, isentropic efficiency. Thermoeconomics, exergy. Ideal gas mixtures, heating, ventilation and air conditioning processes, refrigeration and heat pump systems, energy conversion processes: internal combustion engine, steam power plant, gas turbine process. SDGs: 7 Affordable and Clean Energy, 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, 13 Climate Action

name: Welding and Laser Processing of Metals
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to familiarize the student with the welding metallurgy and weldability of metal materials as well as different laser processing methods and applications on metals. After having completed and passed this course, the student will be able to: identify the composition and classification of metal materials, explain the physical characteristics and mechanical properties of metals, demonstrate heat effects and treatments on metals, identify fundamental principles and practices of welding metallurgy, predict and analyze macrographs and microstructures of metal samples and welded joints, apply the knowledge of material behavior in welding for different applications in practice, understand the basic concepts of weldability tests, compare laser materials processing processes and knows special features of different processes, identify what are the theoretical basis affecting in different laser processes and how they affect the possible applications based on them, understand how laser processing parameters affect the quality of the process / part.
content: The course comprises lectures and laboratory exercises, of which themes are: Basic metallurgical principles of both metal materials and welding of them Principles of heat treatments / effects and metallographic examination procedures on metals Different metallurgical analyzing procedures in practice Weldability tests Laser beam material interaction, transmission, reflection and absorption Effect of laser-based heating, melting, vaporization and ablation on material Formation of keyhole and related phenomena Most common laser processes, such as laser welding, laser-hybrid welding, cutting, marking, drilling, engraving, laser-based additive manufacturing and surface treatment Combined theoretical and practical cases and applications
prerequisites: Basic understanding of welding processes and materials sciences. BK10A3500 Materiaalitekniikka / BK10A5900 Materials
learningMaterial: Lectures and course material in Moodle. Welding: Principles and Applications, L. Jeffus, Cengage. Welding Metallurgy, S. Kou, John Wiley & Sons. Introduction to the Physical Metallurgy of Welding, K. Easterling, Butterworth-Heinemann. Modern Welding Technology, H. B. Cary, S. C. Helzer, Pearson. Welding Metallurgy and Weldability, J. C. Lippold, John Wiley & Sons. Applied Welding Engineering: Processes Codes and Standards, R. Singh, Elsevier. Laser Material Processing, W. Steen, J. Mazumder, Springer. Laser Processing of Engineering Materials, J. Ion, Elsevier.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exam 50 %, laboratory exercises and project works 50 %.
workload: The course is arranged in the form of lectures, practical laboratory exercises and project works. Lectures: 28 h. Laboratory exercises and analysis work: 20 h. Preparation and reporting of project works and independent study: 77 h. Preparation for exam: 10 h. Total workload: 135 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Welding Automation
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to widen the knowledge about the various aspects of industrial welding digitalization, automation and adaptivity. Further, welding robotization and offline programming are the main focus of the course. After having completed and passed this course, the student: · has a knowledge about the welding automation processes and their variations that are used in industry, · can compare and evaluate different welding processes and automation levels from productivity, usability and profitability point of view · can choose the most suitable welding process and automation level for manufacturing different types of products, · understands the relationship between the welding process, automation, adaptivity and quality · has a general overview of utilizing welding automation methods relative to welding production and quality management · knows the different sensor techniques, data analysis methods and virtual/digitalized tools used in welding · will be able to use offline robot simulation software to model a robot welding station, simulate its operation and make programs for the welding robot cells
content: The course comprises lectures, simulation exercises and laboratory exercises to make the student familiar with welding automation, processes and practices related to the welding automation field. Course themes are listed below: · The concept of weldability in terms of automation and adaptivity. · Automation levels of welding (manual / mechanized / robotized). · Essential parameters, productivity, usability, and efficiency of mechanized and robotized welding processes. · Robot Programming methods · Multi-robot stations · Welding robot off-line programming · Welding preparations (e.g. groove cutting and beveling methods) and post-weld treatments as an automated welding production point of view. · Sensor technologies and jig systems used in welding. · Adaptive welding · Possibilities of Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality and Mixed reality in welding production The simulation exercises consists of basic operations of the welding robot off-line programming. Laboratory exercises consists of welding robot manipulation, welding operations as well as seam finding and tracking possibilities. The final exam consist of questions related to all the lecture material and laboratory exercise contents.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge is required from the welding processes and manufacturing. BK10A3601 Valmistus- ja tuotantotekniikka or BK10A7400, Production Engineering 1 (or similar knowledge) is recommended to be passed before attending the course.
learningMaterial: · Lectures in Moodle(Echo360) and face-to-face lectures (will be recorded also). · Teollisuuden robotiikka / The Industrial robot book, Suomen Robotiikkayhdistys Ry · Modern Welding Technology, H. B. Cary, S. C. Helzer, Pearson. · Modeling, Sensing and Control of Gas Metal Arc Welding, D. S. Naidu, S. Ozcelik, K. L. Moore, Elsevier.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Moodle Exam 30 %, Welding simulation exercises 10%, Project assignment 60 %.
workload: The course is delivered in a form of lectures. The course includes also practical laboratory exercises, simulation software exercises and a project assignment, where student models a welding robot station and creates process paths. • Lectures: 28 h • Weekly assignments: 28 h • Simulation exercises: 26 h • Project Assignment: 45 h • Laboratory exercises: 8 h • Total workload: 135 h.

name: Nuclear Engineering Fundamentals
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will understand the basic concepts of reactor physics, cross section and neutron flux, working principles of nuclear reactors, nuclear fission and light water reactor core, prerequisites for the criticality of an infinite reactor and elements of heat transfer in nuclear fuel. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: know-how on own field, mathematics and natural sciences, practical application of theories, working independently. Only organic intelligence will be used on this course.
content: Neutron induced nuclear reactions, especially nuclear fission, and fission products. Fundamentals of reactor physics: cross sections, neutron flux, reaction rate, critical reactor and reactivity. Composition and operating principle of a nuclear reactor. Heat transfer from fuel to coolant.
prerequisites: BH30A0001 Introduction to Nuclear Energy attended.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides, lecture videos, lecture notes
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Quizzes 20 %, examination 80 %.
workload: Lectures 14 h, tutorials 14 h, independent study and preparation for the exam 50 h and final examination in Exam 3h. Total workload 81 h.

name: Basics of university level physics
learningOutcomes: Opiskelija hallitsee lukion laajan fysiikan kursseja ”FY3: Energia ja lämpö”, ”FY4: Voima ja liike”, sekä ”FY6: Sähkö” vastaavat sisällöt pääpiirteittäin. Yksityiskohtaisemmat osaamistavoitteet: Opiskelija syventää ymmärrystään energiasta fysiikan keskeisenä käsitteenä, osaa tutkia aineen termodynaamiseen tilaan ja olomuodon muutoksiin liittyviä ilmiöitä, osaa soveltaa termodynamiikan käsitteitä ja malleja energiantuotannon ratkaisujen tarkastelussa. Opiskelija ymmärtää voiman, liikkeen sekä säilymislakien merkityksen fysiikassa. Opiskelija osaa solveltaa voimaan ja liikkeeseen liittyviä käsitteitä arkielämän sovelluksissa. Opiskelija ymmärtää sähköön liittyviä ilmiöitä, osaa käyttää kentän ja potentiaalin käsitteitä sähkökentän kuvaamisessa, tuntee sähkölaitteisiin ja sähköenergian siirtoon liittyviä näkökohtia.
content: Ydinaines: Energiaan ja lämpöön liittyvät peruskäsitteet, kuten mekaaninen työ, lämpötila, paine, energian säilyminen ja siirtyminen, lämpömäärä, olomuodon muutokset ja ideaalikaasu. Voimaan ja liikkeeseen liittyvät peruskäsitteet, kuten Newtonin lait, liikeyhtälö, paino, kitka, liike- ja potentiaalienergia, liikemäärä, impulssi. Sähköön liittyvät peruskäsitteet, kuten sähkövirta, jännite ja resistanssi, Ohmin laki, Joulen laki, Kirhoffin lait, akut ja latauspiirit, Columbin laki, homogeeninen sähkökenttä ja sen potentiaali ja energia, kondensaattori, puolijohteet. Täydentävä tieto: Peruskäsitteiden syvällisempi ymmärtäminen, käsitteiden soveltaminen mekaniikan ja energiatekniikan yhteydessä, sähköturvallisuus.
prerequisites: Ei ole.
learningMaterial: Luentomateriaalit. Vapaaehtoisesti myös sisältöä vastaavat lukion laajan fysiikan kurssikirjat.
evaluationCriteria: Arviointimenetelmät: kotitehtävät ja välikokeet (2kpl, Moodle). Arviointiskaala 0-5.
workload: Suoritustavat. Luennot 14h, Laskuharjoitukset 14h, välikokeet 4h, omatoiminen opiskelu ja kotitehtävätyöskentely 22h. Kokonaismitoitus 54h.

name: Environmental Permits and Measurements
learningOutcomes: After completion of the course the student is expected to be able to 1. Identify emission sources. 2. list measurable pollution parameters. 3. Describe measurement methods (sampling and sample handling, analytical methods). 4. Explain the operation of the most common laboratory measurement methods and equipment. 5. Calculate basic parameters about different types of emissions and present the results in the correct units. 6. Evaluate the uncertainties and reliability of measurements. 7. Discuss EU legislative requirements. 8. Interpret environmental permit decisions. 9. Apply environmental measurement methods according to standards. The completion of the study module supports the development of the following general working life skills: mathematics and natural sciences, written communication, problem-solving, time management, and task prioritization.
content: Topic information: determination of emission concentration, mass flow and volume flow. Measurement methods (sampling, sample handling, analysis methods and equipment). Measurement for wastewater, ambient water, airborne particles, gases and noise measurements. Supplementary information: legal obligations, environmental permits. Special knowledge: calibration of measurement devices, result traceability, measurement reliability, total uncertainty and quality assurance.
learningMaterial: Online material on Moodle. Ministry of the Environment's websites. The relevant parts of Heikki Torvela: Measurement of Atmospheric Emissions, Springer London, 2013.
evaluationCriteria: 0 - 5. Written assignment 50 %, returned excercices 27 %, quiz questions 20 %, lectures 3 %.
workload: Lectures 14 h, exercises 12 h, independent work: quiz questions and homeworks 21 h, written assignment in pairs 34 h. Total load 81 h.

name: Digital Control, an Introduction
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the student will be able to: 1. write the state equations of the system and use them to analyse the behaviour of the system, 2. discretise the state model and the transfer function model and explain the pole mapping from continuous to discrete plane, 3. analyse the properties of the discrete system and examine its stability and behavior using Bode diagram, Nyquist diagram or root locus, 4. design a continuous time controller that meets the given specifications and discretise it by using an appropriate approximation, 5. discretize the given specifications and design directly a discrete controller, 6. program a digital controller and system model.
content: Basics of sampling theory and discrete modelling, discrete transfer function, continuous time and discrete state model. Basics of state equation techniques. Methods of analysis of digital control circuits, discrete frequency response, stability of a discrete system. Basic digital control algorithms and their tuning. Practical aspects of implementing a digital controller.
prerequisites: BL40A0200 Säätötekniikan perusteet A.
learningMaterial: All course material in Moodle including edited lecture videos. Presentation slides and matlab scripts in Moodle. One book from the following list is recommended.Ioan D. Landau and Gianluca Zito, Digital Control Systems, Design, Identification and Implementation.Franklin, Powell, Workman, Digital Control of Dynamic Systems.Åström, Wittenmark, Computer Controlled Systems.Kuo, Digital Control Systems, 2nd edition.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination 80 % small assignments 20%. Satisfactorily completed main assignment required.
workload: Lectures and demonstrations 10 h, exercises 10 h small assignments 8h, 3rd period. Lectures and demonstrations 10 h, exercises 10 h and assignments 8h, main assignment, 4th period. Examination. Total workload 104 h. NOTE: in 2022-23 only in Finnish, starting from 2023-24 implementations both in Finnish and in English..

name: Fluid Mechanics II
learningOutcomes: After this course student is able to 1) perform dimensional analysis in field of fluid mechanics 2) calculate drag and lift of common geometries 3) understand fundamentals of compressible flow and 4) basics of computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Know-how on own field, mathematics and natural sciences
content: Dimensional analysis, physical quantities and units. The Pi theorem. Modeling and similarity. Dimensionless numbers, e.g. Reynolds, Mach, Froude and Strouhal numbers. The differential equations of mass conservation and linear momentum. External flow: flat plate, sphere and cylinder. Lift and drag. Compressible flow: Mach number relations, normal shock waves, oblique shock waves, expansion waves. Introduction to computational fluid dynamics (CFD).
prerequisites: BH40A1400 Fluid Dynamics I or BH40A1401 Fluid Mechanics I attended.
learningMaterial: Course textbook: Cengel Y.A., Cimbala J.M. (2019). Fluid Mechanics: Fundamentals and Applications. Alternative textbooks: White, F.M. (2005). Fluid mechanics. Munson B.R., Young D.F., Okiishi T.H. (2002). Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics. Bohl W. (1988). Teknillinen virtausoppi. (Technische Strömungslehre).
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, laboratory work 16%, week assignments 12%, home assigements 10% and quizzes 12%.
workload: Lectures 12 h, Exercises 12 h, 4. Period. Laboratory work 1 h + 3 h. Home and week assignments and quizzes 50 h. eEXAM 3h. Total workload 81 h.

name: Sustainability transition of food systems
learningOutcomes: After completion of the course, students will be able to: Understand the aspects of food processing. Recognize the critical factors for process intensification for increased sustainability. Economic considerations in sustainable food manufacturing. Understand the elements of the sustainability transition in food systems. Recognize the different actors in the food system and their capacities in sustainability transition. Recognize justice issues and various ethical perspectives on food systems and sustainability transition.
content: During the course, students will gain an understanding of sustainable food manufacturing and current food system transitions. The intensive course provides a holistic view of food systems, considering critical aspects such as processing, environment, economics, and social factors and their roles, capacities, and approaches in the sustainability transition. The course is preceded by an independent study of the topic through literature. It starts with introductory lectures, which are followed by thematic group work. At the end of the course, the group work results will be presented and discussed in a seminar. Finally, an individual essay on one of the course themes will be written. The course covers the following topics: Food processing for increased palatability and preservability. Sustainability in food manufacturing and transition aspects of food systems. Economic factors in sustainable food systems. Systemic approach to food studies, including global and local food systems perspectives. Actors and their roles in the food system. Justice transition and ethical perspectives. Issues include power relations, food security, poverty, and inequality in food systems.
prerequisites: No formal prerequisites.
learningMaterial: Selected journal articles and book chapters are provided as readings Literature related to lectures and seminar topics
evaluationCriteria: Passed/failed. To pass, students should participate in all teaching activities.
workload: Individual reading work, Introductory lectures, Group work and presentations, Individual essay writing

Connect IO to PLC system. 3. use the analog and digital communication techniques applied to automation, 4. apply fieldbuses, 5. construct controllers and models of dynamic systems using IEC61131-3 and C programming languages, 6. work in a group solving automation and control problems.

name: Basics of database systems
learningOutcomes: At the end of the course the student will be able to: 1.Design and model relational databases 2.Understand how the evolution of relational algebra led to SQL databases 3.Model real world problems with ER and transform the ER model to relational databases 4.Understand and solve issues related to relational database design, such as optimization and normalization 5.Implement relational databases in practice and embed them in applications
content: Database systems. Database design. Object-centric modeling and ER-modeling. Specifying relation models. SQL and object languages. Perspectives into database design: How database is designed, how information is modeled, and what are information storage structures and access methods. Transforming ER models to relation model, and then to relation databases. The use of different file formats in different environments. Perspectives to database programming: queries and other operations, database management, e.g. triggers. Implementing databases in practice and how to use SQL databases from other programs.
prerequisites: Introduction to Programming.

name: Computer Aided Engineering
learningOutcomes: The student will learn, and practice computational methods commonly used in vibration analysis. The special attention will be put to numerical analysis of the rotating systems using 3D solid finite element method. The student familiarizes with the basic theory behind such systems and the numerical methods commonly used to solve them. This will include sparse and dense matrix linear algebra, integration of the equations of motion, eigenvalue analysis, model-order reduction techniques and solution of the nonlinear systems of equations. Good programming practices will be strongly emphasized. The student will learn how to write efficient, clear and manageable engineering code using the high-level linear algebra software Matlab.
content: Numerical modeling techniques for correct and efficient programming using Matlab. Sparse and dense matrix computations, debugging and profiling of the code. Common code mistakes and good practices. Numerical solution of the equations of motion of rotating systems. Eigenvalue analysis of linearized systems. Numerical integration of the ordinary differential equations for analysis of nonlinear systems. Practical modeling and analysis techniques using commercial finite element software.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have completed BK70A0500 Machine Dynamics.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, examination or mid-course examinations 60%, simulation work 20%, in class quizzes 10%, homework 10%.

name: Digitalised Design, Simulation and Production Tools and Applications
learningOutcomes: The student will learn theories and practices of digital methods and tools that are applied in the different phases during the product life cycle. They get an understanding how the digital methods can enhance the operational actions in the industrial working environment. Additionally, they have the capabilities to start working on with the digital tools i.e. basic understanding of the features and characteristics of the software that are used in the field of mechanical engineering decreasing the step to start using the software at the later stages of the studies of in working life. The majority of the case studies are real-life examples from the industry.
content: The content cuts through the product processes that are related to mechanical engineering during the lifecycle of a product. The content touches subjects such as design, analysis and simulation of machines that is typically related to design phase of the products. The course path flows towards digital methods in manufacturing taking into consideration different manufacturing methods ranging between conventional machining and the most advanced, modern 3D printing initiatives. Additionally, the content includes the aspects of sustainability, after sales services, recycling and rebirth enabled and supported by digital methods in mechanical engineering.
prerequisites: Students are recommended to have basic skills and understanding of mechanical engineering.

Besides studying anddiscussing a selection of academic articles, students will be actively involvedin the entrepreneurial process through practical cases. After the course,students should be able to: Prove evidence of a comprehensive knowledge of the concepts and theories used in the course Prove evidence of (research and case-based) empirical knowledge regarding the different topics covered by the course Be able to link theoretical knowledge with empirical insights and apply it to practical cases, in particular: Be able to analyze a business case and critically assess the quality of entrepreneurial strategies and tactics based on theoretical and practical insights Be able to find and evaluate relevant literature and empirical evidence to support the analysis of specific topics covered by the course Be able to critically assess the validity of statements based on empirical research

name: Steam Boilers
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to 1. demonstrate considerable knowledge to understand the requirements of the fuel on the combustion technology and equipment, 2. describe the most typical boilers burning biomass, 3. dimension the heat delivery surfaces of boilers and understand the scaling of the boilers, 4. perform thermal and fluid dynamical dimensioning of the combustion and flow equipment of boilers, 5. understand the fundamentals of the manufacturing and mechanical structure of the pressure vessel, 6. describe the main controls of boilers, 7. describe the most typical auxiliary equipment of boilers, and 8. recognise the most typical problems from the perspective of the boiler operation.
content: The characteristics of power plant fuels in relation to the boiler. The chemical balance, reaction kinetics and the imperfection of combustion. A theoretical examination of the ignition phenomenon. The stability of the flame. The factors affecting the efficiency of the boiler. Engineering design, dimensioning principles of the furnace, superheaters and pre-heaters. The burner technology and equipment for gaseous, liquid and solid fuels. Emission formation. Emission reduction during combustion and by using flue gascleaning methods. Fouling of heating surfaces, corrosion and erosion of the heating surface. Soot blowing. The control of the boiler. Kraft recovery boiler, heat recovery boiler and new boiler technologies.
prerequisites: Recommended: BH20A0300 Fundamentals of Heat Transfer. BH50A0500 Introduction to Combustion and Boiler Technology.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes. Teir, Sebastian: Steam Boiler Technology, 2nd ed. 2006. Poltto ja Palaminen, 2nd edition, IFRF - Finnish Flame Research Committee. Vakkilainen, Esa, Steam generation from Biomass, 2016. Moodle.

The university may also accept as a licentiate thesis a) a number of scientific publications or manuscripts accepted for publication it deems sufficient, or a summary of such publications or b) a work that meets equivalent scientific criteria. The publications may also include collective publications if the doctoral candidate has independently and demonstrably prepared a part of it.

name: Fundamentals of Heat Transfer
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students are able to 1. understand the fundamental principles related to heat conduction, convection and radiation, and the physical laws behind the phenomena, 2. apply the general solutions for heat transfer and different calculation models when analyzing engineering heat transfer problems, 3. estimate thermally performance of most common heat exchanger types. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Know-how on own field, Knowledge of the research of own field, Knowledge of the history and development of own field, Mathematics and natural sciences, Practical application of theories, Written communication, Working independently, Problem solving, Time management and prioritizing tasks, Critical thinking skills, Analytical thinking skills.
content: Fundamental concepts and terminology of heat transfer. Stationary heat conduction, fin theory, free and forced convection, heat exchanger analysis, fundamentals of radiation heat exchange.
