name: MIMIR Fellows I
learningOutcomes: On the highest level the students will get a systemic view of the entrepreneurial ecosystem: understanding and identifying the different elements in entrepreneurial ecosystems and their interlinkages, in Finland and beyond. The aim is not to “convert” the students into entrepreneurs, but rather offer them a comprehensive understanding of startups and entrepreneurship as well as a mindset and toolbox that they later can leverage upon, whichever path they choose. The real outcomes of this program are expected to materialize in the next decade. In the shorter term, students are expected to develop an understanding of the requirements for deep tech entrepreneurship, and the logic behind commercializing research. The main focus is to support the students on their own unique learning paths. The diversity of the students will be reflected on their learning paths, and emphasis is put on their personal growth.
content: MIMIR Fellows is a pan-Nordic entrepreneurship program and community run simultaneously in university cities around the Nordics. The program is called after Mímir – a figure in Norse mythology known for his wisdom. The aim is to educate a new generation of entrepreneurs to have the readiness to take deep tech from universities around the Nordics to the market. Guest lecturers and partners will ensure the involvement of industry and investors in our mission to reimagine technology transfer. The MIMIR Fellows Program follows the pedagogical approach of the Aalto University course, Aalto Fellows . First adopted to a Nordic context in 2015, the course was originally modeled on Stanford’s flagship entrepreneurship course – the Mayfield Fellows program , an in-depth, 9 month work/study experience for 12 students. While these preceding courses introduce students to the broader context of the surrounding startup ecosystem, the MIMIR Fellows program will focus on deep tech entrepreneurship and the unique characteristics of research commercialization and academic entrepreneurship. The MIMIR Fellows I consists of three parts: i) pre-readings and assignments, ii) one week of intensive lectures, May 2024 iii) a paid 2–3 month summer internship at a startup or venture capital firm The program provides the students with a comprehensive and systemic view of deep tech entrepreneurship and its context: the intersection between the entrepreneurial ecosystem and the world of academia. The program also aims to bridge academia, i.e. students and participating professors, and the Finnish startup ecosystem, including but not limited to investors, founders, and ecosystem leaders. The students’ personal growth is in focus, and they are supported in formulating their own understanding of how deep-tech startups and the supporting ecosystem function. Up to 12 students are selected through a two-phased selection process. Emphasis is put on diversity, the group including both undergraduate and graduate students with art, science, engineering, and business backgrounds. The selection process is geared towards finding a diverse group of extraordinary students: some may not be at all familiar with the entrepreneurial ecosystem, while others may have worked at the heart of it prior to taking the course. The aim is to prepare the students to work within or with the intersection of academia and the entrepreneurial ecosystems around the world, today and in the future, whether working for a startup, corporation, investment fund, non-governmental organization, or the government. The program is presented to the students as pieces in a puzzle, and the task of assembling the puzzle is left to each of them individually. A systems perspective is emphasized, and curious inquiry rewarded. The course will be organized as a collaborative effort between LUT and MIMIR Fellows Oy. In addition, one of the 12 students will be selected as a course assistant to ensure the continuity of the program in 2025.
prerequisites: Successful completion of this course requires completed Internship for Master's Programmes course.
learningMaterial: Students will be provided with an extensive reading list with materials spanning 6 categories: i) venture capital ii) startups iii) creativity iv) entrepreneurial ecosystems v) technology transfer vi) readings on the study trip destination The reading list is designed to be quite extensive and familiarize the students with the pace and nature of the course and entrepreneurial endeavours. Students will be instructed to spend approximately 40 hours on it focusing on topic areas that they are not familiar with in order to provide common ground for the group prior to the intensive lecture weeks.
evaluationCriteria: The MIMIR Fellows I consists of four parts: i) pre-readings and assignments, ii) one week of intensive lectures, May 2024 iii) a paid 2–3 month summer internship at a startup or venture capital firm The program provides the students with a comprehensive and systemic view of deep tech entrepreneurship and its context: the intersection between the entrepreneurial ecosystem and the world of academia. The program also aims to bridge academia, i.e. students and participating professors, and the Finnish startup ecosystem, including but not limited to investors, founders, and ecosystem leaders.
workload: Pre-assignments (60h), Lectures (42h), Reflection essays (43h), Workshops (15h). Total workload 160 h.

name: Numerical Methods for Partial Differential Equations
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: Answers to the following questions What is a partial differential equation (PDE)? How are PDEs used in science and technology? When is a PDE well-posed? How can we approximate a solution to a PDE using finite elements? How can big matrices be stored and matrix-vector systems be solved in the computer?
content: Basics of partial differential equations Modeling with PDEs The stationary diffusion–advection–reaction equation Existence and uniqueness of weak solutions Construction of the finite element method Meshes Test and trial functions Transformation of finite elements Obtaining the system of linear equations Analysis of the finite element method Consistency, error orthogonality, and best approximation Error estimates in the energy norm Error estimates in Lebesgue norms Condition numbers of finite element matrices Direct methods for sparse linear systems of equations LU decomposition without pivoting Data structures Bandwidth reduction Iterative methods for systems of linear equations Linear stationary iterative methods Gradient and conjugate gradient methods Preconditioned conjugate gradient method
prerequisites: Analysis in integer dimensions notion of a (classical, continuous) derivative, a gradient, a divergence, and a Laplacian not mandatory: notion of a weak derivative Lebesgue integration (also on manifolds) Gauss's divergence theorem and integration by parts Linear algebra notion of a matrix, a vector, and a point solve a matrix-vector system using Gaussian elimination and LU decomposition Linear functional analysis notion of a vector space, a Banach space, and a Hilbert space not mandatory: notion of a Sobolev space properties of Lebesgue spaces
learningMaterial: The course heavily relies on the content of the following monographs. They are ordered according to their influence on the course's manuscript. P. Knabner and L. Angerman. Numerical Methods for Elliptic and Parabolic Partial Differential Equations: With contributions by Andreas Rupp . 2nd ed. Vol. 44. Texts in Applied Mathematics. Computational Science and Engineering . Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, 2014. doi: 10.1137/1.9781611973617 A. Ern and J.-L. Guermond. Finite Elements . 1st ed. Vol. 72–74. Texts in Applied Mathematics. See Manuscript for details. Springer International Publishing, 2021

name: Introduction to Programming
learningOutcomes: On completion of this course student should: • be able to use standard Python. • be able to develop simple algorithms and implement them using the standard control structures. • be able to use existing libraries and user defined functions when writing programs • be able to write programs that promote code reuse. • be able to write programs that correctly manipulate standard data and text files • be able to handle exceptions thrown and writing own exception classes. • be able to develop python programs that can read and update CSV files, for data analytics-based tasks at basic level. • follow good coding guidelines devise strategies to test the programs developed.
content: Programming theory: History and background, terminology; user need and program; libraries and the benefits of reuse; quality assurance, testing; data analytics from the programmer point of view; programming styles; program performance, algorithms, pseudocode, recursion, compiler and interpreters; data representation formats, ASCII and other tables, binary and hexadecimal numbers and their conversions; user interfaces, documenting, visualization, graphical and command line user interfaces; good programming style. Practical programming in Python: I/O including formatted output, datatypes, variables, roles of variables, data type conversions, calculations, strings; selection structure, conditional code, branches, code blocks, logical operators, menu-based program; repetition structures for and while; program structure, functions, parameters, name spaces; file handling, member variables and methods; structured data structures, list, class, dictionary, tuple; libraries; exceptions, errors, debugging.
learningMaterial: LUTin Python ohjelmointiopas (in Finnish, https://lutpub.lut.fi/handle/10024/162088), lecture material, other material announced on lectures.

name: Role of Software in Societies
learningOutcomes: After completing this course you will: - understand how software impacts different aspects of society - can reflect on the role of software development in different aspects of contemporary life - recognise how questions of society and communication are related to themes in software engineering - understand also the dark side of software engineering learn to handle data to provide additional information

prerequisites: Bachelor's degree or alike in an appropriate field in the social sciences or communication sciences that gives eligibility to enrol into the master’s program.
learningMaterial: Literature will be announced in the beginning of the course.
evaluationCriteria: Learning diary and project work. You must write an acceptable quality learning diary of all the lectures in order to pass the course, and present about your project work together with your group. Instructions for writing a learning diary. One learning diary of each lecture and related literature should be ca. 300 words in length (corresponds with ca. one A4 page with font size 12 and 1.5 spacing). The diaries are submitted in such a way that all diary entries are put together, one after the other, as one document. Submit your finished diary into Turnitin. The course will have project work where group of students focus on a specific topic, write an article (around 20 pages) about that and present their work. The work is peer-reviewed by another group, which then gives feedback and let the group to improve their work before final submission. Students also individually improve Wikipedia by writing some course related topic to Wikipedia. Grading: learning diary 30%, group work 40%, presentation 10%, peer-review 10%, improvement of Wikipedia 10%.
workload: Attending lectures, reading related literature, writing a learning diary and doing a case study (group work) on a selected topic

name: Selection Criteria of Materials
learningOutcomes: After having passed this course module the student is able to: - apply and develop systematic and analytical means and tools of systematic material selection approaches into solving cross-technological material selection tasks - define and analyse the properties, the strengths, the weaknesses and the application areas of the main groups of constructional materials for different types of applications - is able to justify and build generalized models to take into a count both the functionality and the manufacturability aspects in addition to the total costs and environmental aspects of the product in solving the material selection task - is able to evaluate and utilize recent results and documents of material science - derive analytical models based on the principles of LCC's, LCA's and MIPS-factors in material selection.
content: During the course the student will become familiar with the properties and application areas of different constructional materials. The recent scientific results dealing with material science and technology will be discussed. Aspects of selecting and comparing different materials are discussed from the viewpoints of functionality, manufacturing aspects, costs and environmental aspects of the product. Future trends in materials science are discussed briefly. Metals and their alloys, polymers, ceramics, composites, wood materials, adaptive materials, nanomaterials. Environmental aspects of material selection from the viewpoint of LCC and LCA and the basics of MIPS calculations. Innovative solutions of the material selection tasks will be discussed. Principles to formulate and solve the materials solution tasks based on analytical and systematic approaches and means to develop models to support the selection process staring from the product's requirement list will be discussed in details. Multi-language teaching environment will be utilized during the project work. Project work focuses to selecting structural materials for industrial applications.
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Mech.Eng.).
learningMaterial: Mangohon, P., The Principles of Materials Selection for Engineering Design. Strong, A. B., Plastics, Materials and Processing. Kalpakjan, S. ; Schmid, S., Manufacturing Engineering and Technology. Lectures and exercises in Moodle. For Finnish students and distance learning: Eskelinen ; Karsikas, Vihreän teknologian näkökulmat konstruktiomateriaalien valinnassa, ISBN 978-952-265-457-1.

Can formulate and calculate simple probabilities 3. Can define statistical problems and solve them with the methods taught in the course, such as hypothesis tests and statistical inference.
content: Calculating probabilities, random variables, and common probability distributions. Data and descriptive statistics. Basics of statistical inference. Basics of Bayesian inference. Parameter estimation. Hypothesis testing. Use of calculator, handbooks and tables to solve problems.
prerequisites: Recommended: Yliopistomatematiikan perusteet or similar basic mathematics course.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides, lecture videos, handbooks and possibly other materials are announced on the course page.
evaluationCriteria: Paper exam 100%. In order to get a permission to go to exam, a student must do at least ~25% of exercises.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises 14 h, individual study work 50 h, exam and preparation for exam 16 h. Total workload 108 h.

name: International Study Module
learningOutcomes: After completing the module, the student understands and is able to apply the knowledge gained in the thematic lectures within an international learning environment to their own organization, as well as to the development of their personal leadership and managerial interaction skills.
evaluationCriteria: Active attendance and participation in the contact teaching days, and an approved reflection on the learning content of the international module.
workload: articipation in the contact teaching days (three contact study days) and a reflection on the learning content.

name: Basics of university level physics
learningOutcomes: Student acquires deeper understanding on thermodynamics and energy as key concepts of physics. The relationship between thermodynamics and energy conversion processes is also covered. Student will understand the role and apply in practical calculations the concepts of force, kinematics, and conversation laws of physics. Student will understand electricity-related phenomena such as electric field and potential. Student knows the basics of electrical instruments and electricity transmission.
content: Key concepts of energy and heat such as temperature, pressure, energy conservation and transport, phase changes and ideal gas. Concepts related to force and kinematics such as Newton’s laws, gravitation, kinetic- and potential energy, momentum and impulse. Electricity-related concepts such as electric current, voltage, resistance, Ohm’s law, Joule’s law, Kirchoff’s laws, accumulators, Coulomb’s laws, homogonous electric filed and potential, capacitors and semiconductors.
prerequisites: Ei ole.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides. Students can use their own physics textbooks from college as support material.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Homeworks and Moodle-exam.
workload: Lectures 14h, Exercises 14h, mid-term test 4h, independent study and homework 22h. Total 54h.

name: Bachelor's Thesis
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: • use different research methods and tools related to future studies of a Master of Science degree and write a research report according to IMRAD structure • combine theoretical and practical knowledge • integrate theoretical information to practice • carry out a project independently and follow a plan • set goals that are related to results and time scheduling • acquire information and use electronic scientific databases, etc. • critically evaluate one's own or another's technical scientific reports and give constructive feedback • modify found information and use cross references to write a scientific text
content: Bachelor's thesis is final thesis for bachelor's degree, which the student prove familiarity with his/her thesis topic. Bachelor's thesis is done to major subject. On bachelor's thesis the emphasis is on literature review, which may be supplemented with the practical part. Bachelor's thesis can also be done in groups, but in this case each student's work must be clearly visible.

name: Bachelor's Thesis Seminar
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: • show the main content and results of his/her bachelor's thesis orally in a seminar • participate in a scientific discussion • provide feedback on another student's bachelor's thesis • objectively analyze the main scientific outcomes and contribution of a B.Sc. thesis • compose an elevator speech highlighting the practical results of the research
content: Student will learn the basics skills of the scientific work and ways of working. The student selects a suitable thesis topic and the appropriate research strategy and suitable research methods. Students will practice to solve the scientific problem and the correct scientific reporting. The student makes information searches related to their work and practicing proper citation practices and know how to correctly refer to sources. Student is also aable to modify the found information and use cross references. In the end of the course, the students present their work orally and answer the questions. The course is linked to sustainable development.
prerequisites: Student can take part to bachelor’s thesis seminar when he/she has gain at least 110 ECT. Prerequisites will be define by specialization subject.
learningMaterial: Lecture material in the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: Elevator speech pass/fail. Lectures pass/fail. Lecture exam pass/fail.
workload: Lectures 4 h (compulsory participation in 3rd period). Lecture Exam in Moodle 1 h. Elevator speech when thesis is ready.Total workload 52 h.

name: Basics in Material Physics
learningOutcomes: Student understands the structure of matter on atomic scale and the changes in structure during phase changes. Students gets familiar with nanostructures, polymers and composites. Student understands what kind of atomic-level structural changes are related to aging of materials. Manufacture and life cycle of different kinds of materials are also covered. Student learns about properties of recycled materials.
content: Core contents: The basic nature of matter, stomic scale structure of material in different phases (liquid, gas, solid and plasma), phase changes, aging of materials, industrial processes related to materials processing, life cycle of materials, basics of recycling. Additional contents: nanomaterials, polymers, composite materials, adaptive materials and recycled materials.
prerequisites: Ei ole.
learningMaterial: Lecture slides and additional material from the teacher.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5. Homeworks and Moodle-exam or only an exam.
workload: Lectures 14h, Exercises 14h, exam 3h, independent study and homework 23h. Total 54h.

name: Linear Optimization
learningOutcomes: In the end of the course the student should - know how formulate various linear programming models - know how to solve different kinds of linear programming problems - understand the principles of solution algorithms and be able to analyze the results - know how to use optimization software.
content: Introduction to operations research. Examples of formulating LP models. Solving LP problems with the simplex method and analyzing the solution. Introduction to integer programming. Transportation problem and algorithm. Some network problems and algorithms. Introduction to multiple objective linear programming. Application of linear optimization software.
prerequisites: Recommended BM20A6700 Mathematics I, and BM20A6900 Mathematics III , or A130A0600 Mathematics for Business and Economics
learningMaterial: Lecture slides (in Finnish). Hillier, F.S., Lieberman, G.J.: Introduction to Operations Research, McGraw-Hill, 1990. Taha, H.A.: Operations Research, An Introduction, Prentice-Hall, 2007.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, exam 100 %. Assignment.
workload: Lectures 28 h, exercises 28 h, 3rd period. Assignment 50 h. Self study and exam 56 h. Total work load 162 h.

name: Electronic Equipment and Systems Design
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, the student is able to: 1. Write requirements for an electronic system or equipment, 2. Apply the knowledge of electronics design gained from previous courses to the design of an electronics prototypes and systems, 3. Identify the key differences between prototype design and production version design; and take these differences into account in their designs, 4. Apply their design skills to electronic equipment from circuit scale to system level, 5. Analyze the technical concepts, solutions and manufacturability of electronic equipment. 6. Document and present their projects in an understandable way to other people.

Most importantly, the student should have an interest in device design, device building and ability to work as a part of a team.

Line integral of a vector field, Green equation, surface integral of a scalar field, gradient, divergence and rotor, Gauss equation, Stokes equation, vector potential.

learningOutcomes: Student can by hand and numerically with MATLAB - solve linear and nonlinear equations and groups of equations, initial value problems for differential equations and groups of differential equations - calculate the integral of function of one variable - make linear and nonlinear fittings to given data.

Solving equations and systems of equations: Newton's method method and fixed point method. Integration: midpoint rule, trapezoid rule, Simpson's rule. Differential equations: Euler's method, midpoint method, Heun's method and Runge–Kutta methods.
prerequisites: Recommented: BM20A7800 Basics of university mathematics/A130A0600 Mathematics for Business and Economics, BM20A7900 Differential calculus, BM20A8000 Differential equations.

content: Statistical inference: hypothesis testing, two sample tests. Nonparametric tests. Basics of analysis of variance, time series analysis and multiple regression models. Introduction to nonlinear regression. Introduction to factor analysis.

Identify the societal impacts of sustainability transformation, climate change and biodiversity loss on issues such as justice, ethics, inequality and climate refugees Understand theoretical and conceptual approaches and historical developments Understand historical developments and identify key social science theories and concepts (such as fossil capitalism, path dependence, ecological modernism, anthropocentrism)

name: 5G - A Friendly Introduction

Brief introduction of the main technologies and methods like millimetre waves, beam forming, and network slicing will be discussed to give a good foundation for further research. At the end of the course the student be able to understand basics of technologies used in 5G and understand the impact they bring to energy, transportation and other industries. This will allow the student to better understand how 5G can be used in their field of work and study and spark interest for further research on this topic.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/fail, quizzes 100%. In order to pass, the student needs to score at least 20 out of 25 points in ALL quizzes.

name: AWARE on Basics of Waste Management. Current Development on Russian and Finnish Daily Waste Management
learningOutcomes: After passing the course, students will be able to: 1. Explain what are the current basic structures in waste management both in Russia and Finland. 2. Students have demonstrated skills on investigating the course topics related materials by themselves and they have generated new content, based on course learnings. 3. Utilize the knowledge to explain the current similarities and differences between Finnish and Russian waste management operations. 4. Students possess the knowledge of current digitalization matters around basic waste management and they can demonstrate the innovative ways to utilize waste as raw material, both in industrial and in artistic context.
content: Familiarizing student to the Finnish and Russian waste management systems basics. Course will be giving the students a general insights of basics of daily waste management matters in Finland and Russia and course will also be discussion on current trends of digitalization, related to the topic. As a contrast to local Finnish and Russian matters, course also opens up current global views to the waste management, connects the content to United Nations sustainability development goals and reveals different open data bases and statistics information sources conveying the real rate different nations are able to recycle waste to raw materials, how much waste is utilized as heat and power in incineration context etc. Lastly, course reveals some up to date waste to business models in Russia and discusses on how creative people can see waste as source as art and design elements. The course ends with a project work, in which the students combine their new knowledge to material which can be later on used e.g. in high schools and lower levels to introduce waste management views to wider audience, seen from the current student generation point of view.
prerequisites: Engineering / business school bachelor level degree OR equivalent knowledge base
learningMaterial: Needed materials for the course, will be delivered through Moodle system and study material is pointed for the students, within the course lessons. Student can refer for the following three books, for additional material to support course studies and to deepen the general understanding on the topics, presented in course lectures. · Trevor M. Letcher & Daniel A. Vallero (2019): Waste: A Handbook for Management · Stuart Edwards (2014): My Rubbish Career: Municipal Waste Management · Atiq Zaman (2019): Zero-Waste: Reconsidering Waste Management for the Future (Routledge Studies in Waste Management and Policy)
evaluationCriteria: Passed/failed, continuous evaluation (no exam).
workload: Assessment items are compulsory: When assessment items are compulsory, the student must complete them all. This course is implemented as distance learning packet, course self study content is delivered through Moodle system. Lectures are given trough distance / remote teaching tools. Total workload is based on courses 3ECTS size, meaning that the estimated work load for passing the course is around 81 hours.

name: Basics of Power Plant Engineering
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course the students will be able to 1. explain the basic processes of thermal power plants (excl. nuclear energy) and the impact of various factors on process efficiency, 2. apply mass and energy balances at energy production processes, and 3. explain the operating principle and role of main power plant components 4. calculate the operating values of basic power plant processes 5. calculate the costs of energy production. Completion of the course supports the development of the following generic competences for working life: Know-how on own field; Working independently; Problem solving; Time management and prioritizing tasks; Analytical thinking skills
content: The operation of thermal power plants and power plant processes. Engineering design: calculation methods of power cycles and calculation of production costs. Condensing power plants, cogeneration (CHP) plants, gas turbine power plants, combined cycle power plants.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of engineering thermodynamics
learningMaterial: Lecture materials and related calculation examples in Moodle. Water vapour h,s chart.

name: Electronics project

name: Engineering Thermodynamics
learningOutcomes: After completing thecourse students are familiar with basic concepts in energy technology, such astemperature, state properties, systems and processes, control volume analysis,different forms of energy and fundamental laws of thermodynamics. Students areable to use different charts and tables to find thermodynamic properties ofdifferent substances. After completing the course students can formulate theequation for the conservation of energy for an open control volume. Ideal gas mixtures, heating, ventilation and air conditioning processes, refirgeration and heat pump systems, energy conversion processes: internal combustion engine, steam power plant, gas turbine process. Course includes Power-to-X themes. Expertise and skills: mathematics and natural sciences, practical application of theories, working independently, problem solving, and time management and prioritizing tasks. name: Introduction to Nuclear Power Engineering

Completing the course supports the development of the following general working life skills: mathematics and natural sciences, independent work, and problem solving.
content: Radiation and its occurrence. Health effects of radiation, principles of radiation protection. Utilization of nuclear power (fission and fusion). Basic structure of nuclear reactors. Fundamentals of pressurized and boiling water reactor designs. Fundamentals of nuclear safety. Fuel cycle and nuclear waste management. Accidents and their classification (INES scale). Utilization of nuclear energy in Finland and worldwide.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes.

name: Management and Leadership Skills in Mechanical Engineering
learningOutcomes: After having passed this course, focusing on engineering tasks, the students will be able to: - utilize basics of effective delegation and meeting management also in a networking environment - utilize methods provided by digitalized tools - employ effective communication techniques and apply both social and leadership skills to optimize end results and to manage possible conflicts in contexts of teamwork or projects - utilize the effective communication techniques through digital devices - set and achieve goals for the set work and projects and lead themselves - set and achieve goals via digital tools utilizing - identify opportunities to enhance cooperation among their colleagues - identify methods to utilize digital environments in reaching set objectives - manage day-to-day challenges of leading a team and manage time and prioritize work - use effective strategies for organizing projects and negotiating resources - apply problem-solving and decision-making skills to accomplish tasks - assess their flexibility and openness to new ideas to inspire other team members and to create and sustain a positive, productive atmosphere - create and implement changes as applicable to lead team work or projects when needed . create and implement the performance produced by digitalized tools to achieve set goals - understand the role of financial and business management in engineering projects - understand the basics and roles of financial and business management in projects.
content: This course introduces fundamentals of leadership and management as regards contexts of engineering projects. The students gain experience in project work, develop team work skills, apply self-management and implement work discipline. Through interactive activities, self- assessments, discussions, and practical team and project work, the students learn how to lead either product design tasks, production or larger scale projects with the focus on the field of mechanical engineering in particular. The skills introduced include communicating effectively, solving problems, making decisions, working in teams, building relationships, creating and implementing changes in an organization, and aligning one's goals with the organization's mission, goals, and objectives. Depending on the given task within the course module, the students are advised to recognize the special skills and competences needed for leading design tasks, production or larger scale projects.
prerequisites: B.Sc. degree in mechanical engineering or other equivalent field of engineering(Changed 20.5.2019/TP)
learningMaterial: Lecture notes
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, continuous and comprehensive evaluation of success in teamwork and project work, peer review of management and leadership skills and the evaluation of a leadership journal.
workload: Lectures and literature review 18 h, periods 1-2, orientation meetings 6 h, periods 2-4 and group discussions 10 h, periods 2-4. Depending on the given task within the course, participation in the board meetings of virtual companies 4 h, periods 1-4. Building of a networking environment for the teamwork and project management 10 h, period 1. Exercises and the utilization of a leadership journal to get practical experience in working as a project manager, production manager, design manager, team leader etc. 87-91 h, periods 1-4. Total workload 135 h.

name: Reliability Based Machine Element Design
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing this course, the student will be able to: - utilize different reliability based measures for machine element design as well as manufacturing - apply tools and techniques for risk analysis of a machine or mechanical system - compare materials and manufacturing processes for reliable machine elements - use principles, with which the designer can improve the product to reduce the failure probability - apply failure mode analysis, especially in context of wear and corrosion phenomena - choose an appropriate distribution to analyze reliability aspects of a component
content: The course will cover the following topics: - The importance of multidisciplinary optimization including reliabilioty based constraints in design is discussed - Tools and techniques for both qualitative and quantitative risk analysis of an assembly or a technical system are presented. - Aspects, how uncertainties associated with statistical distributions and any insufficient information may lead to large errors in probability calculations in engineering are clarified. - Analytical tools for analyzing failure modes of machine elements, machines and technical systems are taught. - Guidelines to choose an appropriate distribution to analyze reliability aspects and lifetime of a component are presented.
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Mech.Eng.) Degree or equivalent knowledge.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes and other learning materials to be provided during the course on Moodle Birolini, Alessandro. Reliability engineering. Vol. 5. Berlin: Springer, 2007.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, 4 group exercises (20%/each, in total 80%, instructions of exercises will be given together with lectures), final presentation (20%, mandatory attendance in campus for students in Lahti and Lappeenranta, in addition to giving presentation, each group is expected to listen to at least 3 presentations)
workload: Lectures 10h, presentation 1h, exercise in class 2h, groupwork 122 h, total workload 135 h. Lappeenranta students and Lahti students have different schedules. As for contact teaching degree programme, students are expected to present in classroom.

name: Welding Quality and Economy
learningOutcomes: The aim of the course is to guide the student to develop, manage, control and ensure the quality and sustainability in welding production as well as get knowledge and familiar with the welding work and its economy. After having completed and passed this course, the student: understands the meaning of sustainability and quality in welding production, knows how to implement quality assurance systems, knows quality levels and classifications in welding, is familiar with the concept of Welding Procedure Specification (WPS), its development, approval, and implementation, understands welding imperfections and various testing procedures (destructive and non-destructive) of weld joints, is familiar with most important welding quality standards, knows special welding process variations for enhancing productivity, has a knowledge regarding the production chain of welded structures, understands economics, costs, and productivity of welding production, understands welding networks and supply chains, has a general overview of production management systems and methods, is familiar with welding safety and health hazards.
content: The course comprises lectures, of which themes are: Concept of sustainability and quality Welding coordination and standards Welding procedure specification (WPS) and welding procedure test Welding defects and imperfections as well as weld classification system and levels Testing methods in welding production Repair welding Welding productivity improvement methods Economics and cost accounting of welding procedures and investments Welding work indicators Welding networks and supply chains Welding safety aspects in workshop production Case examples from practical welding industry work The course contains laboratory exercises, some practical case studies based on industrial tasks of a welding engineer and assignments related to productivity, economy, profitability and safety of welding work, such as: Designing the Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) and performing the welding procedure test according to standards. Identifying welding defects and imperfections from real weldments. Interpreting results of destructive and non-destructive welding tests. Coordination and reporting of the welding procedure test. Modifications and developments of welding processes. Cost calculations of welding operations. Different levels of welding production chains. Evaluating the safety risks of welding production and workplaces.
prerequisites: Basic understanding and knowledge of welding and welding processes.
learningMaterial: Lectures in Moodle. Welding: Principles and Applications, L. Jeffus, Cengage. The Welding Workplace, R. Boekholt, Woodhead Publishing. Standards related to welding quality and production. Videos of welding quality operations and processes in Moodle. Additional material (e.g., laboratory demos) in Moodle. Case materials from welding industry.
evaluationCriteria: Grading: 0-5. Exam 50 %, exercises, tasks and project works 50 %.
workload: The course is arranged in the form of lectures, practical laboratory exercises and project works. Lectures: 28 h. Laboratory exercises, tasks and analyses including manual welding in practice, macrographic inspections as well as destructive and non-destructive tests: 20 h. Preparation of WPS and execution of welding procedure test including independent study and report writing: 67 h. Exercises and tasks concerning welding investment calculations: 10 h. Preparation for exam: 10 h. Total workload: 135 h. The course is suitable for distance learning.

name: Code Camp for Bachelor’s Programs
learningOutcomes: The students learn to work with given software engineering related technologies, software development practices, solution development and technology debug knowledge etc. in teams and innovate solutions to given development challenges in predefined time window. At the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. Identify and conceptualize a viable technological solution or architectural / process design for a given challenge 2. Demonstrate team-working skills 3. Demonstrate the knowledge and skills of the selected technologies and methods in the given problem domain 4. Demonstrate software engineering skills. 5. Appreciate the need for lifelong learning
content: Students are presented a project / course challenge or theme in the beginning of each code camp and they develop solutions to the problem in the given time frame with the given technologies. After the presentation of the code camp challenge, the students innovate possible solutions and start learning or using the selected technologies. The main part of the code camp is spend developing the solution and in some cases learning to use the selected technologies in a collaborative manner before the working solutions are presented in the closing seminar. A code camp lasts typically a weekend or a week, and the technologies used in each code camp are decided case by case. The detailed implementation of each code camp is designed to support the degree programs goals, and the detailed course instructions are published in Moodle.

name: Democracy, Soft Power, News & AI
learningOutcomes: After completing this course, the students will be able to: understand how strategic narratives are constructed and deconstructed and how soft power works be aware of new forms of influence, soft power and disinformation, for example, around debates on clean air, water & energy and more broadly, around sustainability and green transition. recognise the role of news in sustaining democracy. distinguish new opportunities and challenges posed by AI and new forms of soft power to news and democracy. examine and understand a broad array of theoretical perspectives and approaches related to different forms of influence, and search for recent scientific knowledge and debates on these. independently and critically read and evaluate soft power literature.
content: This course focuses on how various emerging forms of influence, soft power and disinformation are challenging journalistic practices and democratic ideals. These themes are discussed in the context of issues related to for example to climate change, sustainability and green transition.
prerequisites: Bachelor's degree or alike in an appropriate field in the social sciences or communication sciences that gives eligibility to enrol into the master’s program.
learningMaterial: Literature will be announced in the beginning of the course.
evaluationCriteria: Numerical assessment on a scale of 0–5. Attending lectures and completing group work (50 %) and final literature review assignment (50 %). Please note that unless part of the given assignment instructions, using conversational AI-systems or equivalent in writing the course work, or any part of it, is forbidden and will result in failing the course.
workload: Attending lectures and workshops/seminars (20h), group work (20h), final literature review assignment (16 h), and independent study.

name: Exchange period in China
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: apply cultural-specific knowledge to think critically and comparatively about global and local issues, describe the role of customs and tradition in determining acceptable behaviour, attitudes, and perceptions, demonstrate personal growth and intercultural competency, develop career readiness and leadership skills in a global context, demonstrate increased language proficiency in the Chinese language
content: This course can be completed as part of an exchange period of at least 6 months at Hebei University of Technology in Tianjing, China. The exchange will be offered from approximately mid-June to mid-December in the student’s third year of studies. Students will attend cultural activities and participate in everyday life while reflecting on their experiences in a learning diary. Observations of life in China will be recorded related to the course learning objectives. These observations should pertain to all aspects of culture, but should include the student’s chosen academic field and intended career path when possible. Cultural items should be described in a manner that is consistent with how the items are viewed within the context of China, while also noting how other cultures may view the same item differently. A final presentation will document the student’s journey and experiences. Final presentations can be in the form of written summary, pictorial essay, video production, or combination of all three.
evaluationCriteria: Pass/Fail. Continuous assessment during monthly tutorials. Learning Diary (50%), Final presentation (50%).
workload: Monthly tutorials 18 h, weekly learning diary 30 h, participation in events in China 60 h, preparation of and participation in final presentation 27 h. Total workload 135 h.

name: Global Communications, Soft Power and Climate Change
learningOutcomes: The learning outcomes for the course are: (1) ability to describe and understand key concepts and approaches related to global communications and soft power in the context of climate change. (2) ability to compare and contrast how different theories on soft power and global communication can be applied to study and discuss climate change. (3) ability to analyse the impact of soft power and global communications in international climate-related issues. (4) ability to apply theories and concepts from previous studies related to global communications, soft power and strategic narratives to empirical cases related to climate change.
content: In this course, we explore how global communication and questions of soft power and geopolitics are related to climate change and other environmental issues. During the course, we discuss various empirical cases that illustrate different aspects of these phenomena and analyse how global communications and soft power shape the narratives with which we communicate about climate change related issues in a complex media environment.

name: Robotics
learningOutcomes: In this course, the students will obtain the knowledge and gain the ability in the area as follows: 1. Understanding composition of a generic robotic system. 2. Comprehension of robotic coordinate system and homogenous transformation. 3. Ability to construct DH (Denavit-Hartenberg) parameters of a robotic system. 4. Ability to compute forward kinematics of robotic system. 5. Ability to analyze and compute inverse kinematics of robotic system. 6. Ability to design a robotic system and verify the design in simulation. Through this course, you will learn the necessary knowledge of design and analysis of a generic robotic system, and you will also build up a solid knowledge ground for the further study of advanced topics in robotics, e.g., the trajectory planning, Jacobian analysis, statics, and dynamics analysis etc.
content: The course consists of lectures, simulation tutorials and an independent robotic system design project. There are five topics covered in the course lectures . 1. Robotics introduction. Under this topic, we will introduce what a robot is, morphology of robot, and the composition of a generic robotic system, where you learn the components of a robotic system. 2. Robot design. Under this topic, we will introduce the concepts of DOF (degrees of freedom) of a robot and the concept of robot workspace, and how to compute the DOF and workspace, which are the most important two facts to consider when you start to design a robotic system. A introduction to end-effector (gripper) will also be introduced at the end. 3. Robotic coordinate system. Under this topic, we will introduce the robot coordinate system. Homogenous transformation will be elaborated in detail, which are the base of the robotic kinematics computation. The construction of robot DH (Denavit-Hartenberg) parameters table will be demonstrated in great detail where the widely used 6DOF industrial robots will be taken as the study objects. 4. Robotic kinematics analysis. Under this topic, we will introduce how the forward kinematics of a serial robot is computed based on the DH convention. The analysis of inverse kinematics of a 6DOF serial robot will be elaborated, and the computation will be presented using Matlab Codes. The analysis and computation of parallel structure robot will be also introduced. 5. Introduction of advanced robotic topics. Under this topic, we will generally introduce the advanced robotics, including the trajectory planning, Jacobian analysis, the statics and dynamics. Regarding the simulation tutorials , we will demonstrate how to build and simulate a robotic multibody model in the Simscape Multibody, where you could build and verify your own robot design.
prerequisites: The course is designed for B.Sc. students, who have the background in mechanical or electrical engineering studies. The students should have the generic knowledge of mechatronic system design, understood the basics of mechanisms and machine theory. Regarding the mathematics, the students should have learnt the Linear Algebra and have the comprehensive understandings on vectors and linear transformation. The student should have the basic concepts and skills of programming, and we will use the Matlab for the computation and the MATLAB. Simulink for the robotic system simulation in the course.

name: Inverse Problems
searchTags: Written examination in the examination schedule
learningOutcomes: The student learns - how to recognize an inverse problem, - the main challenges related to them (instability, non-uniqueness) and - knows the main computational approaches to solve them.
content: Inverse problems appear in several fields, including medical imaging, image processing, mathematical finance, astronomy, geophysics, nondestructive material testing and sub-surface prospecting. Typical inverse problems arise from asking simple questions "backwards". For instance, the simple question might be "If we know precisely the structure of the inner organs of a patient, what kind of X-ray images would we get from her?" The same question backwards is "Given a set of X-ray images of a patient, what is the three-dimensional structure of her inner organs?" This is the inverse problem of Computerized Tomography, or CT imaging. Usually the inverse problem is more difficult than the simple question that it reverses. Successful solution of inverse problems requires specially designed algorithms that can tolerate errors in measured data.
prerequisites: Bachelor level studies in mathematics. Completion of the course BM20A7300 Functional analysis or a similar course is a recommended prerequisite.
learningMaterial: Lecture notes based on various materials. Recommended reading includes Kirsch: An Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of Inverse Problems, Springer 2011.
evaluationCriteria: Written examination with grading 0-5. Home exercises provide additional points towards the course grade.

name: Control and Design of Robot Systems
learningOutcomes: As robotics and computers become increasingly prevalent in industry and our lives, understanding programming and programming concepts is becoming very important for students' success. Robots are a fun, easy, and effective way to learn about computer programming as well. Programming a robot has tangible, observable effects. The course aims to give the student a deeper understanding of Robotics systems from the practical perspective. In this course, modeling, programming and simulation tools and methods are introduced for students. Via this course, the student will learn the basic theories and practices of robotics. The student is able to design robotic mechanisms for industrial applications; analyses and evaluate the performance of robot; design controller for robot. After successfully completing the course, students are able to: • Use experimental tools to verify simulation models and analyzes • Form the design of experiments, arrange an appropriate environment for the studied device or machine to get reliably measured results • Run planned tests and analyze the results • Solve and analyze Robotics problems using simulation tools such as MATLAB & SIMULINK • Use modern automation systems in order to implement controllers using SIMULINK and LabVIEW languages to program Robotic systems • Explain the basis for problem formulation, and coding/solving using Robotics packages • Solve simple control problems using one’s own codes, algorithms and designs • Start working on various topics in Robotics for advanced designs or analysis

name: Laser Based Manufacturing for Design
learningOutcomes: After having passed the course, the student will: - understand how laser beams and systems are used in materials processing - realize how these processes can be utilized to full in product development of a company - be able to compare and generalize the special features gained with creative use of different laser based processes and the impact and utilization of the special features of these processes on product design - understand what kind of properties can be gained with use of laser based processes and how does this effect on design flow of a product - understand how the real total cost analysis and sustainability studies can be carried out and how they compete with conventional manufacturing technologies - Realizes what kind of quality can be reached and how these technologies can be used for increasing energy efficiency and save material.
content: The possibilities and limitations of laser processing on the product design. The utilization of laser based processes into design routines and philosophies, together with mechanical properties in comparison with conventional manufacturing technologies. Practical case examples. Economic aspects of laser materials processing. The features of most common laser based processes i.e. various different versions and applications of e.g. laser marking, cutting, welding and surface treatment processes.

name: Manufacturing
learningOutcomes: After successfully completing the course, students are able to: • Know and apply the principles of different manufacturing methods such as machining (conventional and unconventional), casting, metal forming, welding and joining, and additive manufacturing. • list the most common manufacturing methods, equipment and equipment systems used to produce different engineering products. • compare the different manufacturing methods for the case of choosing the manufacturing process(es) for a certain product(s), considering sustainable manufacturing and product development (including power-to-x products). • compare communication between designing and manufacturing, and explain how to design with product specifications, which allow for efficient, trouble free and economical manufacturing and assembly. • recognize modern manufacturing technologies and their requirements for engineering applications.
content: This course will present the role of manufacturing in modern and sustainable society. The course will consider economical feasibility and potential consequences of manufacturing. Topics covered: Machining (conventional and unconventional) Mechanical joining and welding techniques Casting Metal forming Rapid prototyping and additive manufacturing. The course will include lectures and demonstration exercises in Jamie Hyneman Centre.

name: Productivity and Sustainability of Metal Cutting
learningOutcomes: After having completed this course module the student should: - be able to manufacture machined products in their own factory or order machined parts from subcontractors - understand how the price of a machined part is formed and be able to compare different production and procurement methods - understand the sources of waste in machining processes and the economical tradeoffs in reducing waste and increasing productivity - know how to use computer-aided machining systems and simulate the manufacturability of the parts - be able to describe and compare the most common metal cutting processes - be able to apply modern metal cutting theory in practice for the most common metal cutting processes - understand the importance of automation, such as process monitoring and adaptive control systems - know the most common safety risks in machine shops, the mitigation of the risks and the supervisor's responsibility - knows about the information safety aspects in modern machine shops - be able to read and write short scientific texts, search and critically evaluate scientific information
content: The course focuses on manufacturing and manufacturability of machined products, concentrating on the most common metal cutting methods. While the course delves deeper into the theory of the metal cutting methods, a strong emphasis is kept on the effect on productivity, the possibilities and limitations of machining, and sustainability issues. The applications of the metal cutting theories for a higher degree of automation are explored. In addition, both traditional occupational safety and information safety issues apparent in both traditional and modern automated machine shops, are examined.
learningMaterial: All the material is available in the Moodle
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, exam 100%, with optional extra points from exercises, seminar work presentation and excursion. Pass-fail, if not taking the exam but completing exercises and seminar.

name: Steel Structures 1

name: Foundation of Cybersecurity
learningOutcomes: The aim of this course is to give an in-depth understanding of cybersecurity to the students by covering relevant concepts, theories, tools, and practical methods. After completing the course, the students will be able to. 1. Analyze and evaluate the cybersecurity needs of an organization. 2. Develop skills in cybersecurity, networks, and their management. 3. Evaluate and implement new and future technologies into current system. 4. Gaining a holistic view of new and evolving security techniques and advanced tools to secure data & information for your organization. 5. Develop the necessary study skills and knowledge to pursue further study.
content: CHAPTER 1: Introduction to Cybersecurity: 1. Understand the relevant role of cybersecurity and why it is important 2. Describe how business stakeholders play a role in cybersecurity 3. Identify common security regulations and frameworks 4. Categorize assets, risks, threats, vulnerabilities, and exploits 5. Determine the phase of a cyber-attack CHAPTER 2: Network Security: 1. Basic and Advance concepts of Cryptography that includes Encryption/decryption 2. Attack classification (ciphertext-only, known plaintext, chosen plaintext, chosen ciphertext) 3. Secret key (symmetric), cryptography and publickey (asymmetric) cryptography, Key distribution 4. Transport layer security, Internet protocol security, Wireless security 5. Network monitoring, Intrusion detection system, Virtual private network, and firewall CHAPTER 3: Evolving Security Techniques: 1. IoT and its application Security 2. Artificial Intelligence for Security (Basic of Machine Learning, Deep Learning and Federated Learning) 3. Blockchain and Smart Contracts for Security CHAPTER 4: Governance, Risk, and Compliance 1. Explain the key functions of each of the Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) roles 2. Articulate the connection between GRC roles 3. Demonstrate the importance of cybersecurity GRC in accomplishing cybersecurity objectives and business goals 4. Understand audit and assessment goals 5. Learn how to facilitate and control audits 6. Develop management responses and remediation plans for audit
prerequisites: Python programming language
learningMaterial: Cryptography And Network Security: Principles and Practices 4th Edition by William Stallings Cybersecurity: The Beginner's Guide: A comprehensive guide to getting started in cybersecurity by Dr. Erdal Ozkaya

name: Creativity and Entrepreneurship in New Product Development from Silicon Valley's Perspectives
learningOutcomes: Learning outcomes: - To understand important elements of marketing strategy that is related to product management. - To develop an in-depth understanding of new product/service development and management. - To understand and utilise a process-oriented framework for making new product/service development decisions. - To enhance business communication skills through preparation and presentation of new concepts for products and services via prototyping as well as its marketing plan.
content: This course is designed to explore two critical business topics related to product management strategy in marketing: - the design and development of new ideas for product/service innovations - the management of new and existing products and services for sustainable business. First, topics in new product development include idea generation and screening, design, planning, and prototyping, and new product roll-out, as well as the development of marketing strategies and implementation plans for new products and services. Second, management of new and existing products involves in integration of new products into the product line, management of the marketing mix, quality of service, and customer development strategies. Throughout this project-based course, the importance of creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship will be emphasised as the sources of initiating and managing new products and innovation.

name: Reliability Based Machine Element Design
learningOutcomes: After having passed this course, the student will be able to: - utilize two reliability measures: safety index and probability of failure - apply tools and techniques for risk analysis of a machine or mechanical system - use principles, with which the designer can improve the geometries, shapes, sizes, material properties, and topology of a product to reduce the failure probability - utilize statistical information to support reliability design - apply failure mode analysis, especially in context of wear and corrosion phenomena - choose an appropriate distribution to analyze reliability aspects of a component
content: The importance of multidisciplinary optimization including reliability-based constraints in design is discussed. Two significant reliability measures, safety index and probability of failure, are compared and discussed. Tools and techniques for both qualitative and quantitative risk analysis of an assembly or any technical system are presented. Principles, with which the designer can modify the geometries, shapes, sizes, material properties, and topology of a product to reduce the failure probability are discussed. Possibilities to utilize statistical information to support reliability design are evaluated. Aspects, how uncertainties associated with statistical distributions and any insufficient information may lead to large errors in probability calculations in engineering, are clarified. Tools for analyzing failure modes of machine elements, machines and technical systems especially in context of wear and corrosion phenomena, are taught. Guidelines to choose an appropriate distribution to analyze reliability aspects and lifetime of a component are presented. Team and project works deal with practical industrial applications of reliability based engineering.
prerequisites: B.Sc. (Mech.Eng.) Degree or equivalent knowledge.
learningMaterial: Patrick O’Connor, Andre Kleyner, Practical Reliability Engineering, 5th Edition, 978-0-470-97982-2. Erdman, A.G., Mechanism Design. Norton, R.L., Design of Machinery. Thompson, G., Improving Maintainability and Reliability through Design. Lecture notes and exercise materials in the Moodle.
evaluationCriteria: 0-5, continuous and comprehensive evaluation of project work 70 %, seminar 30 %.

name: Lean Management
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: Relate the development process of Lean Management, the role in the social and economic system and the way to play a role. Master the basic theory of Lean Management and develop a clear sense of lean thinking. Master the basic technology and method of Lean Management, develop the ability of systematic planning, design, evaluation, improvement and innovation. Obtain the ability of curriculum objectives through practice, and be able to put forward, analyze and solve problems in combination with enterprise production system and its management characteristics. Have in-depth work in manufacturing enterprises and competent for comprehensive management. Have the ability to work in service industry, administrative agencies and other fields.
content: The course introduces students to the concept of lean management, which includes delivering value from a customer’s perspective, eliminating waste or other elements that do not add value to end products, and a commitment to continuous learning. Lean management is a concept adapted from the Toyota Production System whereby companies have a deep respect for people while continually improving work processes and purposes. The key concepts of lean management can be applied to a number of business sectors, such as manufacturing or software development.

name: Probabilistic Simulation
learningOutcomes: The course gives an introduction to the concepts of discrete simulation models and methods together with numerical examples. After the course, the student is able to create and use different simulation models to solve practical problems. Among the discrete-event based models, the student is able to simulate basic queuing, server, scheduling systems and implement stochastic dynamical simulations.
content: Basic concepts of discrete systems. Model-based design, basic simulation work-flow, running the simulations and interpreting the results. Random numbers, discrete event generation by random numbers. Statistical and empirical distributions for event generation. Basics of stochastic differential equations. Building numerical simulation examples with Matlab. Application examples: queuing systems, storage size optimization, stochastic dynamical systems and agent-based modelling.

name: Smart Materials and Nanotechnology
learningOutcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: understand structures, properties and some applications of the actuator and sensor materials, characterize properties of selected smart materials in laboratory exercises, know how selected smart materials are manufactured using 4D printing, understand how micro- and nanotechnologies can be utilized in adaptronics, design own smart material device and demonstrate its workability (not required for passing the course), and understand the importance of the smart materials technology for conserving material and energy resources.
content: The course introduces smart materials technology (adaptronics) that integrates actuator and sensor functions into materials and structures so that the adaptronic system can react to environmental stimuli. The goal is to create an intelligent and simple construction that replaces separate machine parts in a way similar to how semiconducting materials replaced separate electronic components. In the course, it is taught how adaptronics can be miniaturized into a micro- and nanoscales through the integration of separate functional components and how smart materials structures can be manufactured using 4D printing.
